title: Pointwise Convergence Rate of the Local Polynomial Estimator
informal: Consider the fixed-design regression model $Y_i = f(X_i) + \xi_i$, $i = 1,\dots,n$, with deterministic design points $X_1,\dots,X_n \in [0,1]$ and independent noise satisfying $\mathbb{E}[\xi_i] = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}[\xi_i^2] \le \sigma^2_{\max}$, in the setting of the bias–variance bound for the local polynomial estimator: (LP1) the local design matrix $\mathcal{B}_{nx}$ has smallest eigenvalue at least $\lambda_0 > 0$, uniformly over $x \in [0,1]$; (LP2) every interval $[a,b]$ contains at most $a_0\, n \max(b-a,\, 1/n)$ of the design points; (LP3) the kernel $K$ is supported in $[-1,1]$ with $|K| \le K_{\max}$; and $f$ lies in the Hölder class $\Sigma(\beta, L)$ on $[0,1]$ — it is $\ell$ times continuously differentiable with $|f^{(\ell)}(x) - f^{(\ell)}(x^\prime)| \le L\,|x - x^\prime|^{\beta-\ell}$, $\ell$ being the greatest integer strictly less than $\beta$. Choose the bandwidth $h = \alpha\, n^{-\frac{1}{2\beta+1}}$ for some $\alpha > 0$. Then, provided $h \ge 1/(2n)$ (true for all sufficiently large $n$), the LP($\ell$) estimator satisfies, at every $x_0 \in [0,1]$ and for every such $f$, the finite-sample bound $$\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\hat f_n(x_0) - f(x_0)\big)^2\Big]\ \le\ C\, n^{-\frac{2\beta}{2\beta+1}}, \qquad C = q_1^2\,\alpha^{2\beta} + \frac{q_2}{\alpha},$$ where $q_1 = C_* L/\ell!$, $q_2 = \sigma^2_{\max} C_*^{\,2}$ and $C_* = \max\{2K_{\max}/\lambda_0,\, 4K_{\max} a_0/\lambda_0\}$. In particular $\psi_n = n^{-\beta/(2\beta+1)}$ is a uniform rate of convergence over $\Sigma(\beta, L)$, in the sense that $\limsup_{n \to \infty}\, \sup_{f \in \Sigma(\beta,L)}\, \psi_n^{-2}\, \mathbb{E}\big[(\hat f_n(x_0) - f(x_0))^2\big] < \infty$.

title: Integrated Squared-Error Rate of the Local Polynomial Estimator
informal: Take the fixed-design regression model $Y_i = f(X_i) + \xi_i$ with deterministic design points in $[0,1]$, independent noise of mean zero and second moments at most $\sigma^2_{\max}$, and the three standing assumptions of the local polynomial analysis: (LP1) the local design matrix has smallest eigenvalue at least $\lambda_0 > 0$ uniformly over $x \in [0,1]$; (LP2) every interval $[a,b]$ contains at most $a_0\, n \max(b-a,\, 1/n)$ design points; and (LP3) the kernel is supported in $[-1,1]$ with $|K| \le K_{\max}$, here assumed in addition measurable. Let $f$ lie in the Hölder class $\Sigma(\beta, L)$ on $[0,1]$ — $\ell$ times continuously differentiable with $|f^{(\ell)}(x) - f^{(\ell)}(x^\prime)| \le L\,|x-x^\prime|^{\beta-\ell}$, $\ell$ the greatest integer strictly less than $\beta$, and take the bandwidth $h = \alpha\, n^{-\frac{1}{2\beta+1}}$ with $\alpha > 0$ and $h \ge 1/(2n)$. Then the LP($\ell$) estimator attains in integrated squared error the same rate as in the pointwise bound: $$\mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^1 \big(\hat f_n(t) - f(t)\big)^2\, dt\right]\ \le\ \Big(q_1^2\,\alpha^{2\beta} + \frac{q_2}{\alpha}\Big)\; n^{-\frac{2\beta}{2\beta+1}},$$ with the same explicit constants $q_1 = C_* L/\ell!$ and $q_2 = \sigma^2_{\max} C_*^{\,2}$, where $C_* = \max\{2K_{\max}/\lambda_0,\, 4K_{\max} a_0/\lambda_0\}$. In particular $\psi_n = n^{-\beta/(2\beta+1)}$ is a uniform rate of convergence over $\Sigma(\beta, L)$ for the $L^2([0,1])$ risk as well: $\limsup_{n \to \infty}\, \sup_{f \in \Sigma(\beta,L)}\, \psi_n^{-2}\, \mathbb{E}\,\|\hat f_n - f\|_2^2 < \infty$.
summary: With the rate-optimal bandwidth, the expected integrated squared error over [0,1] of the LP(ℓ) estimator obeys the same n^{−2β/(2β+1)} bound as the pointwise risk, with the same explicit constant.

title: Sup-Norm Rate of the Local Polynomial Estimator
informal: Let $f$ belong to the Hölder class $\Sigma(\beta, L)$ on $[0,1]$ with $\beta > 0$, and let $\hat f_n$ be the LP($\ell$) estimator, $\ell$ the greatest integer strictly less than $\beta$, with the sup-norm bandwidth $h = \alpha \left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\beta+1}}$, $\alpha > 0$. Assume the design points are deterministic and lie in $[0,1]$, with (LP1) the smallest eigenvalue of the local design matrix $\mathcal{B}_{nx}$ at least $\lambda_0 > 0$ uniformly over $x \in [0,1]$, and (LP2) every interval $[a,b]$ containing at most $a_0\, n \max(b-a,\, 1/n)$ of the design points; that the kernel is bounded and supported in $[-1,1]$ (LP3) and moreover Lipschitz, $|K(u) - K(u')| \le L_K\,|u - u'|$; and that the noise variables $\xi_i$ are i.i.d. Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\xi^2)$. Then there is a constant $C > 0$, depending only on $\beta, L, \alpha, K, \lambda_0, a_0$ and $\sigma_\xi^2$, such that for every $n \ge 2$ at which the bandwidth satisfies $1/(2n) \le h \le 1$, $$\mathbb{E}\Big[\, \big\|\hat f_n - f\big\|_\infty^2 \Big] \;\le\; C \left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{\frac{2\beta}{2\beta+1}}, \qquad \|g\|_\infty = \sup_{t \in [0,1]} |g(t)|.$$ Compared with the pointwise and $L^2$ rates, the supremum costs exactly a logarithmic factor — and this rate is optimal, in that no estimator attains a faster uniform rate over $\Sigma(\beta, L)$ in sup-norm loss.
summary: With Gaussian noise and bandwidth h = α(log n/n)^{1/(2β+1)}, the expected squared sup-norm error of the LP(ℓ) estimator is at most C·(log n/n)^{2β/(2β+1)} — the pointwise rate times a log factor.

title: Projection Estimator on the Trigonometric Basis
informal:
Consider the nonparametric regression model $Y_i = f(x_i) + \xi_i$, $i = 1, \dots, n$, observed at the regular design $x_i = i/n$, and let $\{\varphi_j\}_{j \ge 1}$ be the trigonometric basis of $L^2[0,1]$: $$\varphi_1(x) \equiv 1, \qquad \varphi_{2k}(x) = \sqrt{2}\,\cos(2\pi k x), \qquad \varphi_{2k+1}(x) = \sqrt{2}\,\sin(2\pi k x), \qquad k = 1, 2, \dots$$ From the observations $Y_1, \dots, Y_n$ one estimates the Fourier coefficients $\theta_j = \int_0^1 f \varphi_j$ of $f$ by the empirical averages $$\hat\theta_j \;=\; \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i\, \varphi_j(x_i).$$

For an integer order $N \ge 1$, the projection estimator (or orthogonal series estimator) of the regression function $f$ at a point $x$ is $$\hat f_{nN}(x) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{N} \hat\theta_j\, \varphi_j(x).$$ The order $N$ plays the same smoothing role as the bandwidth of a kernel estimator: it governs the balance between bias (small $N$, oversmoothing) and variance (large $N$, undersmoothing).
summary: The projection estimator f̂_nN = Σ_{j≤N} θ̂ⱼφⱼ with coefficient estimates θ̂ⱼ = n⁻¹ Σᵢ Yᵢφⱼ(i/n), on the trigonometric basis at the regular design i/n.

noncomputable def coeffEstimator {n : ℕ} (Y : Fin n → ℝ) (j : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  (n : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ i, Y i * trigBasis j (regularDesign n i)

noncomputable def projEstimator {n : ℕ} (Y : Fin n → ℝ) (N : ℕ) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 N, coeffEstimator Y j * trigBasis j x
formalizationNotes: `trigBasis` is 1-indexed exactly as in the classical display: `trigBasis 1` is the constant $1$, and for $j \ge 2$ the frequency is the natural-number quotient $j/2$, giving $\sqrt2\cos(2\pi kx)$ at $j = 2k$ and $\sqrt2\sin(2\pi kx)$ at $j = 2k+1$; index $0$ is inert (`trigBasis 0 = 0`), so all sums run over $j = 1, \dots, N$ (`Finset.Icc 1 N`). The regular design is encoded as `regularDesign n i = (i+1)/n` for `i : Fin n`, i.e. the design points $1/n, 2/n, \dots, 1$. In the surrounding risk analysis the coefficient sequence $\theta$ is the primitive object and the target is defined as `seriesFun θ`, the pointwise sum $\sum_j \theta_j \varphi_j$ — membership of $f$ in a smoothness class becomes a statement about its coefficient sequence, which keeps every risk theorem self-contained without invoking completeness of the trigonometric system.

title: Discrete Orthonormality of the Trigonometric Basis at the Regular Design
informal:
Let $\{\varphi_j\}_{j \ge 1}$ be the trigonometric basis of $L^2[0,1]$. Then the first $n-1$ basis functions are exactly orthonormal also in the discrete inner product generated by the regular design $x_s = s/n$: for all indices $1 \le j \le n-1$ and $1 \le k \le n-1$, $$\frac{1}{n} \sum_{s=1}^{n} \varphi_j(s/n)\, \varphi_k(s/n) \;=\; \delta_{jk},$$ where $\delta_{jk}$ is the Kronecker delta.

Equivalently, the empirical Gram matrix of $\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_{n-1}$ at the regular design is the identity — the discrete counterpart of the orthonormality relation $\int_0^1 \varphi_j \varphi_k = \delta_{jk}$. This is the reason the coefficient estimates $\hat\theta_j$ of the projection estimator behave exactly like Fourier coefficients: the stochastic part of their risk is exactly $\sigma_\xi^2/n$, with no cross-frequency contamination below index $n$.
summary: The first n−1 trigonometric basis functions are exactly orthonormal in the discrete inner product n⁻¹ Σₛ φⱼ(s/n)φₖ(s/n) at the regular design.
leanSignature:
theorem trigBasis_discrete_orthonormal {n j k : ℕ}
    (hj : 1 ≤ j) (hj' : j ≤ n - 1) (hk : 1 ≤ k) (hk' : k ≤ n - 1) :
    (n : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ i : Fin n, trigBasis j (regularDesign n i) * trigBasis k (regularDesign n i)
      = if j = k then 1 else 0
formalizationNotes: The statement is the book's identity with the Kronecker delta rendered as an if-then-else and the design sum over `i : Fin n` (design points $(i+1)/n = 1/n, \dots, 1$). The proof reduces each product $\varphi_j\varphi_k$ by product-to-sum identities to discrete cosine/sine sums at the integer frequencies $j/2 \pm k/2$, which — by exact roots-of-unity summation — vanish unless the frequency is a multiple of $n$; the range $1 \le j, k \le n-1$ keeps these frequencies inside $(-n, n)$, so only the zero frequency survives, precisely at equal same-parity indices, where the normalization $(\sqrt2)^2 \cdot \tfrac12 = 1$ gives the diagonal. The book proves one representative parity case and leaves the rest 'along similar lines'; the Lean proof covers all nine parity cases. The continuous companion `trigBasis_orthonormal` establishes the $L^2[0,1]$ orthonormality $\int_0^1 \varphi_j\varphi_k = \delta_{jk}$ for all $j, k \ge 1$.

hypotheses.note: 1 ≤ j ≤ n − 1: the frequency of φⱼ stays below the design size; beyond n − 1 exact orthonormality fails (aliasing).

hypotheses.label: index range for k
hypotheses.note: 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1, the same range for the second index.

title: Mean and Quadratic Risk of the Coefficient Estimates
informal:
Consider the regression model $Y_i = f(i/n) + \xi_i$, $i = 1, \dots, n$, at the regular design, where the target has the trigonometric expansion $f = \sum_{j \ge 1} \theta_j \varphi_j$ with absolutely summable coefficients $\sum_j |\theta_j| < \infty$, and the errors $\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n$ are independent with $\mathbb{E}[\xi_i] = 0$ and common second moment $\mathbb{E}[\xi_i^2] = \sigma_\xi^2 < \infty$. Then the coefficient estimates $\hat\theta_j = n^{-1} \sum_{i} Y_i \varphi_j(i/n)$ satisfy $\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_j] = \theta_j + \alpha_j$ for every $j$, and, for every index $1 \le j \le n-1$, the exact quadratic-risk identity $$\mathbb{E}\big[(\hat\theta_j - \theta_j)^2\big] \;=\; \frac{\sigma_\xi^2}{n} + \alpha_j^2, \qquad \alpha_j = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(i/n)\, \varphi_j(i/n) \;-\; \theta_j.$$

Here $\alpha_j$ is the residual of approximating the Fourier coefficient $\theta_j = \int_0^1 f \varphi_j$ by its Riemann sum over the design — the aliasing bias of the discretization. The entire stochastic contribution to the risk is exactly $\sigma_\xi^2/n$, a consequence of the exact discrete orthonormality of the first $n-1$ trigonometric basis functions at the regular design, $n^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{n} \varphi_j(s/n)\varphi_k(s/n) = \delta_{jk}$ for $1 \le j, k \le n-1$.
summary: Coefficient estimates satisfy E θ̂ⱼ = θⱼ + αⱼ and, for 1 ≤ j ≤ n−1, E(θ̂ⱼ − θⱼ)² = σ_ξ²/n + αⱼ² exactly, where αⱼ is the Riemann-sum (aliasing) residual.

title: Exact MISE Decomposition of the Projection Estimator
informal:
In the regression model $Y_i = f(i/n) + \xi_i$ at the regular design, with target $f = \sum_{j \ge 1} \theta_j \varphi_j$, $\sum_j |\theta_j| < \infty$, and independent errors of mean zero and common second moment $\sigma_\xi^2$, the mean integrated squared error of the projection estimator $\hat f_{nN} = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \hat\theta_j \varphi_j$ of any order $1 \le N \le n-1$ decomposes exactly: $$\mathbb{E}\,\big\|\hat f_{nN} - f\big\|_2^2 \;=\; \frac{\sigma_\xi^2 N}{n} \;+\; \sum_{j=1}^{N} \alpha_j^2 \;+\; \rho_N, \qquad \rho_N = \sum_{j=N+1}^{\infty} \theta_j^2,$$ where $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the $L^2$ norm on $[0,1]$ and $\alpha_j = n^{-1}\sum_i f(i/n)\varphi_j(i/n) - \theta_j$ is the residual of approximating the Fourier coefficient $\theta_j = \int_0^1 f\varphi_j$ by its Riemann sum over the design — the aliasing bias of the coefficient estimates.

The three terms are the stochastic (variance) term $\sigma_\xi^2 N/n$, the aliasing term $\sum_{j \le N} \alpha_j^2$, and the approximation term $\rho_N$ — the energy of the discarded coefficient tail. This exact identity is the starting point of the risk analysis of series estimators over Sobolev classes.

title: MISE Rate of the Projection Estimator over Sobolev Ellipsoids
informal:
Let $\beta \ge 1$ and $L > 0$, and consider the Sobolev class of targets $f = \sum_{j \ge 1} \theta_j \varphi_j$ whose coefficient sequence lies in the Sobolev ellipsoid $\Theta(\beta, Q) = \big\{\theta : \sum_{j \ge 1} a_j^2 \theta_j^2 \le Q\big\}$ of radius $Q = L^2/\pi^{2\beta}$, with the standard weights $a_j = j^{\beta}$ for even $j$ and $a_j = (j-1)^{\beta}$ for odd $j$. Observations follow the regression model $Y_i = f(i/n) + \xi_i$ at the regular design $i/n$, with independent errors of mean zero and common second moment $\sigma_\xi^2$. For a tuning constant $\alpha > 0$, choose the order $N = \big\lceil \alpha\, n^{1/(2\beta+1)} \big\rceil$.

Then there is a constant $C = C(\beta, L, \alpha, \sigma_\xi^2) > 0$ such that for every sample size with $n \ge 3$ and $N \le n-1$ (both hold for all $n$ large enough), the projection estimator $\hat f_{nN} = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \hat\theta_j \varphi_j$ satisfies $$\mathbb{E}\,\big\|\hat f_{nN} - f\big\|_2^2 \;\le\; C\, n^{-\frac{2\beta}{2\beta+1}}$$ uniformly over the class and over every error distribution satisfying these conditions. The projection estimator thus attains the rate $n^{-\beta/(2\beta+1)}$ in the $L^2[0,1]$ norm on the Sobolev class — the same rate as for pointwise estimation over Hölder classes.

title: Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces and the Reproducing Kernel
informal:
Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space of functions $f : X \to \mathbb{F}$ (scalars $\mathbb{F} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$) such that for every point $x \in X$ the evaluation functional $f \mapsto f(x)$ is a bounded linear functional on $\mathcal{H}$ — a reproducing kernel Hilbert space on $X$. By the Riesz representation theorem, each point $x$ then has a unique representer $k_x \in \mathcal{H}$, the kernel function of the point $x$, characterized by the reproducing identity $f(x) = \langle f, k_x\rangle$ for every $f \in \mathcal{H}$.

The reproducing kernel of $\mathcal{H}$ is the function of two variables $K(x, y) = k_y(x)$, so that $K(x,y) = \langle k_y, k_x\rangle$ is the Gram function of the kernel functions.
summary: The kernel function k_x representing evaluation at x, the reproducing kernel K(x,y) = k_y(x) = ⟨k_y, k_x⟩, and the reproducing identity f(x) = ⟨f, k_x⟩.

title: The Exact Norm of an Evaluation Functional
informal:
Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of scalar-valued functions on a set $X$ — a Hilbert space of functions on which every evaluation $f \mapsto f(x)$ is a bounded linear functional — with kernel function $k_x$ at each point and reproducing kernel $K(x,y) = k_y(x)$, as in the definition of the reproducing kernel. Then the evaluation functional $E_x(f) = f(x)$ at any point $x \in X$ attains its operator norm exactly at the kernel function: $$\lVert E_x \rVert \;=\; \lVert k_x \rVert \;=\; \sqrt{K(x,x)}.$$

Consequently $|f(x)| \le \sqrt{K(x,x)}\,\lVert f\rVert$ for every $f \in \mathcal{H}$, with the best possible constant, and convergence in the norm of $\mathcal{H}$ implies pointwise convergence at every point of $X$ — uniformly so on any set where the kernel diagonal $K(x,x)$ stays bounded.
summary: The evaluation functional E_x of an RKHS attains its norm: ‖E_x‖ = ‖k_x‖ = √K(x,x); hence norm convergence implies pointwise convergence.

title: Kernel Functions: Positive Semidefinite Functions of Two Variables
informal:
A function $K : X \times X \to \mathbb{F}$ on a set $X$ (scalars $\mathbb{F} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$) is a kernel function if it is Hermitian: $\overline{K(x,y)} = K(y,x)$ for all $x, y \in X$, and positive semidefinite: for every finite list of points $x_1, \dots, x_n \in X$ and scalars $a_1, \dots, a_n$, $$\operatorname{Re} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \bar a_i\, a_j\, K(x_i, x_j) \;\ge\; 0.$$ The points are not required to be distinct: merging the coefficients of repeated points shows this formulation agrees with the distinct-points one, and by Hermitian symmetry the quadratic form is in fact real.

Over the complex scalars the Hermitian condition is automatic from positivity of the quadratic form; over the reals it is not — a real function of two variables can have identically vanishing quadratic form without being symmetric — so symmetry is built into the definition. Kernel functions form a cone stable under natural operations: nonnegative combinations $p_1 K_1 + p_2 K_2$ and conjugations $(x,y) \mapsto \overline{g(x)}\,K(x,y)\,g(y)$ by any scalar function $g$ are again kernel functions.
summary: K : X × X → 𝔽 is a kernel function if it is Hermitian and every finite quadratic form Σ āᵢaⱼK(xᵢ,xⱼ) is nonnegative; the class is a cone closed under conjugation.

title: Reproducing Kernels Are Kernel Functions
informal:
Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space of scalar-valued functions on a set $X$ with bounded point evaluations — a reproducing kernel Hilbert space — and let $K(x,y) = k_y(x)$ be its reproducing kernel, $k_x$ denoting the element representing evaluation at $x$. Then $K$ is a kernel function in the sense of the definition: it is Hermitian and every finite quadratic form is nonnegative, by the identity $$\operatorname{Re}\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \bar a_i\, a_j\, K(x_i, x_j) \;=\; \Big\lVert \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\, k_{x_i} \Big\rVert^2 \;\ge\; 0.$$

More generally, the Gram function $(x,y) \mapsto \langle \varphi(y), \varphi(x)\rangle$ of an arbitrary map $\varphi$ from $X$ into an inner product space is a kernel function, by the same computation; the reproducing kernel is the special case of the embedding $\varphi : x \mapsto k_x$.

title: The Grammian Is Positive Definite iff the Family Is Linearly Independent
informal:
Let $h_1, \dots, h_n$ be a finite family of vectors in an inner product space over the real or complex scalars. Their Grammian is the $n \times n$ matrix of pairwise inner products $G_{ij} = \langle h_j, h_i\rangle$. The Grammian is always positive semidefinite — its quadratic form is $\sum_{i,j} \bar a_i a_j G_{ij} = \lVert \sum_i a_i h_i \rVert^2$ — and it is positive definite if and only if the family $h_1, \dots, h_n$ is linearly independent.

Applied to the kernel functions $k_{x_1}, \dots, k_{x_n}$ of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, the Grammian is the kernel matrix $\big[K(x_i, x_j)\big]_{i,j}$, so the criterion detects linear independence of kernel functions directly from kernel values.
summary: The matrix of pairwise inner products Gᵢⱼ = ⟨hⱼ,hᵢ⟩ of a finite family is positive semidefinite, and positive definite iff the family is linearly independent.

title: The Moore–Aronszajn Theorem: Every Kernel Function Generates an RKHS
informal:
Let $K : X \times X \to \mathbb{F}$ be a kernel function on a set $X$ — a Hermitian function all of whose finite quadratic forms $\sum_{ij} \bar a_i a_j K(x_i, x_j)$ are nonnegative, as in the definition of a kernel function — over the real or complex scalars. Then there exists a reproducing kernel Hilbert space whose reproducing kernel is exactly $K$: a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ of $\mathbb{F}$-valued functions on $X$ with bounded point evaluations, in which the representer $k_y$ of evaluation at $y$ satisfies $k_y(x) = K(x, y)$ for all $x, y \in X$.

Combined with the converse — the reproducing kernel of any such space is a kernel function — and with the fact that the kernel determines the space, this establishes the classical one-to-one correspondence between kernel functions on $X$ and reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces on $X$.
summary: Every Hermitian positive semidefinite K : X × X → 𝔽 is the reproducing kernel of some RKHS on X — Moore's half of the kernel–space correspondence.

title: The Kernel Determines the Space
informal:
Let $\mathcal{H}_1$ and $\mathcal{H}_2$ be two reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces of scalar-valued functions on the same set $X$ — Hilbert spaces of functions with bounded point evaluations — and suppose they have the same reproducing kernel: $K_1(x,y) = K_2(x,y)$ for all $x, y \in X$, where $K_i(x,y)$ is the value at $x$ of the representer of evaluation at $y$ in $\mathcal{H}_i$. Then the two spaces coincide: there is an isometric linear isomorphism $U : \mathcal{H}_1 \to \mathcal{H}_2$ commuting with point evaluation, $(Uf)(x) = f(x)$ for all $f \in \mathcal{H}_1$ and $x \in X$.

In particular $\mathcal{H}_1$ and $\mathcal{H}_2$ consist of exactly the same functions on $X$, with equal norms, and the identifying map is unique among evaluation-commuting maps. This is the uniqueness half of the correspondence whose existence half is the Moore–Aronszajn theorem.
summary: Two RKHSs on the same set with equal reproducing kernels are identified by a unique isometric isomorphism commuting with evaluation — same functions, same norms.

title: Pointwise Expansion of the Kernel Along an Orthonormal Basis
informal:
Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of scalar-valued functions on a set $X$ — a Hilbert space of functions with bounded point evaluations — with reproducing kernel $K$, and let $\{e_i\}_{i \in I}$ be an orthonormal basis of $\mathcal{H}$; the index set need not be countable. Then the kernel expands pointwise through the basis: for all $x, y \in X$, $$K(x, y) \;=\; \sum_{i \in I} e_i(x)\, \overline{e_i(y)},$$ the unordered sum converging in the net sense over finite partial sums.

On the diagonal this is the Parseval identity $K(x,x) = \sum_{i \in I} |e_i(x)|^2$; in particular the values of any orthonormal basis at a fixed point are square-summable, with sum exactly the kernel diagonal. The expansion is the standard route from an explicit orthonormal basis of a function space to a closed formula for its kernel.
summary: For an orthonormal basis {eᵢ} of an RKHS, K(x,y) = Σᵢ eᵢ(x)ēᵢ(y) pointwise; on the diagonal, K(x,x) = Σᵢ|eᵢ(x)|².

title: Parseval Frames and the Reconstruction Formula
informal:
A family of vectors $\{f_i\}_{i \in I}$ in a Hilbert space $\mathcal{E}$ is a Parseval frame if the Parseval identity $\lVert h\rVert^2 = \sum_{i \in I} |\langle h, f_i\rangle|^2$ holds for every $h \in \mathcal{E}$, with unordered convergence. Orthonormality — even linear independence — is not required: every orthonormal basis is a Parseval frame, and so is the orthogonal projection of an orthonormal basis of a larger Hilbert space onto a closed subspace.

Parseval frames reproduce vectors exactly as orthonormal bases do: a Parseval frame satisfies the reconstruction formula $h = \sum_{i \in I} \langle h, f_i\rangle\, f_i$ for every $h$, with unordered convergence in norm, and conversely any family satisfying the reconstruction formula for every vector is a Parseval frame.
summary: A family with ‖h‖² = Σᵢ|⟨h,fᵢ⟩|² for all h; equivalent to the reconstruction formula h = Σᵢ⟨h,fᵢ⟩fᵢ and to the analysis operator being an isometry into ℓ².
formalizationNotes: The definition is the unordered `HasSum` form of the identity. `HilbertBasis.isParsevalFrame` and `isParsevalFrame_orthogonalProjection` give the two example classes (the book's Proposition 2.7); the analysis-operator and reconstruction characterizations (Proposition 2.8) are `isParsevalFrame_iff_exists_isometry` and `hasSum_reconstruction` / `isParsevalFrame_of_hasSum_reconstruction`, proved through square-summability (`Memℓp`) of the coefficient family and the `lp`-norm dictionary, together with the polarized identity `IsParsevalFrame.hasSum_inner`; the Han–Larson dilation (Proposition 2.9) is `IsParsevalFrame.exists_dilation`, stated via the adjoint of the analysis operator on the canonical `ℓ²` basis. Frame vectors automatically have norm at most one (`IsParsevalFrame.norm_le_one`).

title: Papadakis' Theorem: Parseval Frames Are Exactly the Kernel Expansions
informal:
Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of scalar-valued functions on a set $X$ — a Hilbert space of functions with bounded point evaluations — with reproducing kernel $K$, and let $\{f_i\}_{i \in I}$ be a family of members of $\mathcal{H}$. Then $\{f_i\}$ is a Parseval frame for $\mathcal{H}$ — meaning $\lVert h\rVert^2 = \sum_{i \in I} |\langle h, f_i\rangle|^2$ for every $h \in \mathcal{H}$, as in the definition of a Parseval frame — if and only if the family expands the kernel pointwise: $$K(x, y) \;=\; \sum_{i \in I} f_i(x)\, \overline{f_i(y)} \qquad \text{for all } x, y \in X.$$

This generalizes the orthonormal-basis expansion of the kernel — frames need not be linearly independent — and is the practical tool for recognizing a reproducing kernel Hilbert space from a series representation of its kernel: any family of members through which the kernel expands pointwise already reconstructs every element of the space.
summary: A family {fᵢ} in an RKHS is a Parseval frame iff K(x,y) = Σᵢfᵢ(x)f̄ᵢ(y) pointwise — the criterion for recognizing an RKHS from a kernel series.

title: The Min Kernel Is a Kernel Function
informal:
On the half-line $[0, \infty)$, the function of two variables $K(x, y) = \min(x, y)$ is a kernel function: it is symmetric, and every finite quadratic form $\sum_{i,j} a_i a_j \min(x_i, x_j)$ with real coefficients is nonnegative (the definition of a kernel function).

Positivity is exhibited by a feature map into $L^2[0,\infty)$: since $$\int_0^\infty \mathbf{1}_{[0,x]}(t)\, \mathbf{1}_{[0,y]}(t)\, dt \;=\; \min(x, y),$$ the min kernel is the Gram function of the indicator embedding $x \mapsto \mathbf{1}_{[0,x]}$, and Gram functions are always positive semidefinite. The min kernel is the covariance function of Brownian motion; its reproducing kernel Hilbert space is the Cameron–Martin space of absolutely continuous paths $f$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $f(0) = 0$ and square-integrable derivative.
summary: K(x,y) = min(x,y) on [0,∞) is positive semidefinite: it is the Gram function of the indicator embedding x ↦ 𝟙_{[0,x]} in L²[0,∞) — the Brownian covariance.

title: The Sobolev Space H¹₀[0,1] and Its Green's-Function Kernel
informal:
Consider the Sobolev space $H_0^1[0,1]$ of absolutely continuous functions $f : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}$ with square-integrable derivative and boundary values $f(0) = f(1) = 0$, under the Dirichlet inner product $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^1 f'(t)\, g'(t)\, dt$. The formalization models each function by its derivative: the carrier is the subspace of mean-zero elements $g$ of $L^2[0,1]$ — the orthogonal complement of the constants — an element $g$ acting as the function $x \mapsto \int_0^x g(t)\, dt$; the mean-zero constraint is exactly the boundary condition $f(1) = 0$.

This space is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space on $[0,1]$, and its reproducing kernel is the Green's function of the operator $-d^2/dt^2$ with Dirichlet boundary conditions: $$K(x, y) \;=\; \min(x,y) - xy \;=\; \begin{cases} (1-y)\,x, & x \le y, \\ (1-x)\,y, & x > y. \end{cases}$$ In particular the norm of evaluation is $\lVert E_x\rVert^2 = K(x,x) = x(1-x)$, giving the sharp bound $|f(x)| \le \sqrt{x(1-x)}\,\lVert f\rVert$ for every member — an improvement on the naive Cauchy–Schwarz bound $\sqrt{x}\,\lVert f\rVert$. This space is the Cameron–Martin space of the Brownian bridge.
summary: H¹₀[0,1] with the Dirichlet inner product ∫f'g' is an RKHS whose kernel is the Dirichlet Green's function K(x,y) = min(x,y) − xy, with ‖E_x‖² = x(1−x).

title: The Mercer Integral Operator Is Self-Adjoint and Positive
informal:
Let $X$ be a compact metric space, $\mu$ a finite Borel measure on $X$, and $K$ a Mercer kernel: a jointly continuous kernel function on $X \times X$ — Hermitian, with all finite quadratic forms $\sum_{ij} \bar a_i a_j K(x_i, x_j)$ nonnegative, as in the definition of a kernel function. Then the associated integral operator on $L^2(X, \mu)$, $$T_K\, g(x) \;=\; \int_X K(x, y)\, g(y)\, d\mu(y),$$ is a positive operator: it is self-adjoint, $\langle T_K g, h\rangle = \langle g, T_K h\rangle$, and satisfies $\langle T_K g, g\rangle \ge 0$ for every $g \in L^2(X, \mu)$.

Conversely, if a jointly continuous Hermitian function $K$ has positive integral operator against a measure of full support, then $K$ is positive semidefinite, hence a Mercer kernel — so for full-support measures, positivity of the kernel and positivity of its integral operator are equivalent.
summary: For a continuous positive semidefinite kernel on a compact metric space, T_K g(x) = ∫K(x,y)g(y)dμ(y) is a self-adjoint positive operator on L²(X,μ); a full-support converse holds.

Positivity is proved by expanding $\langle h, T_K g\rangle$ against a Hilbert basis of the Moore RKHS of $K$ and passing to the limit along the uniformly convergent kernel expansion. In the converse, averaging the quadratic form over shrinking balls needs neither disjoint neighborhoods nor distinct points — the bilinear expansion works for overlapping balls — so the book's reduction to distinct points is not needed.

title: The Mercer Integral Operator Is Compact
informal:
Let $X$ be a compact metric space, $\mu$ a finite Borel measure on $X$, and $K$ a Mercer kernel — a jointly continuous, Hermitian, positive semidefinite function on $X \times X$. Then the integral operator $T_K\, g(x) = \int_X K(x,y)\, g(y)\, d\mu(y)$ is a compact operator on $L^2(X, \mu)$: it maps bounded sets to relatively compact sets.

Compactness is what makes the spectral analysis of $T_K$ available — a countable spectrum of eigenvalues accumulating only at zero, with finite-dimensional eigenspaces for nonzero eigenvalues — and, together with self-adjointness and positivity, it feeds the spectral theorem that produces the eigensystem of Mercer's theorem.
summary: The integral operator of a continuous positive semidefinite kernel on a compact metric space is a compact operator on L²(X,μ) — the gateway to its spectral theory.

title: Mercer's Theorem I: Existence of the Eigensystem
informal:
Let $X$ be a compact metric space, let $\mu$ be a finite Borel measure on $X$ of full support — every nonempty open set has positive measure — and let $K$ be a Mercer kernel on $X$: a jointly continuous, Hermitian, positive semidefinite function on $X \times X$. Then the integral operator $T_K\, g(x) = \int_X K(x,y)\, g(y)\, d\mu(y)$ on $L^2(X, \mu)$ admits a Mercer eigensystem: a countable index set, continuous eigenfunctions $e_n : X \to \mathbb{F}$, and strictly positive eigenvalues $\lambda_n > 0$, such that the $e_n$ are orthonormal in $L^2(X, \mu)$, the eigenfunction equation $(T_K\, e_n)(x) = \lambda_n\, e_n(x)$ holds at every point $x \in X$ — not merely almost everywhere — and $T_K$ diagonalizes through the system: for every $g \in L^2(X, \mu)$, $$T_K\, g \;=\; \sum_n \lambda_n\, \langle g, e_n\rangle\, e_n,$$ with unordered convergence in $L^2(X, \mu)$.

Only the strictly positive part of the spectrum is enumerated — the null space of $T_K$ contributes nothing to the expansion. The expansion of the kernel itself along the eigensystem, with uniform convergence, is the second half of Mercer's theorem.
summary: A Mercer kernel against a full-support finite Borel measure admits countably many continuous L²-orthonormal eigenfunctions with positive eigenvalues, diagonalizing T_K.

title: Mercer's Theorem II: Uniform Expansion of the Kernel
informal:
Let $X$ be a compact metric space, $\mu$ a finite Borel measure on $X$ of full support, $K$ a Mercer kernel — jointly continuous, Hermitian, positive semidefinite on $X \times X$ — and $\{(e_n, \lambda_n)\}$ a Mercer eigensystem for $K$ against $\mu$: countably many continuous, $L^2(X,\mu)$-orthonormal eigenfunctions of the integral operator $T_K\, g(x) = \int_X K(x,y)\, g(y)\, d\mu(y)$ with strictly positive eigenvalues, through which $T_K$ diagonalizes, as furnished by the existence half of Mercer's theorem. Then the kernel itself expands along the eigensystem: $$K(x, y) \;=\; \sum_n \lambda_n\, e_n(x)\, \overline{e_n(y)},$$ where the finite partial sums converge to $K$ uniformly on $X \times X$, and at each point the sum converges absolutely.

Two classical companions come with the expansion: the eigenvalues are summable, and the trace formula holds, $\sum_n \lambda_n = \int_X K(x,x)\, d\mu(x)$.
summary: K(x,y) = Σₙλₙeₙ(x)ēₙ(y) with uniform convergence on X × X, plus the trace formula Σₙλₙ = ∫K(x,x)dμ — the classical statement of Mercer's theorem.

title: Mercer's Theorem III: The Spectral Description of the RKHS
informal:
Let $X$ be a compact metric space, $\mu$ a full-support finite Borel measure on $X$, and $K$ a Mercer kernel — jointly continuous, Hermitian, positive semidefinite — with Mercer eigensystem $\{(e_n, \lambda_n)\}$: countably many continuous, $L^2(X,\mu)$-orthonormal eigenfunctions of the integral operator $T_K g(x) = \int_X K(x,y)\, g(y)\, d\mu(y)$ with strictly positive eigenvalues, through which $T_K$ diagonalizes. Let $\mathcal{H}$ be the reproducing kernel Hilbert space on $X$ whose reproducing kernel is $K$. Then a function $g : X \to \mathbb{F}$ belongs to $\mathcal{H}$ if and only if there are coefficients $a_n$ with $\sum_n |a_n|^2 / \lambda_n < \infty$ such that $$g(x) \;=\; \sum_n a_n\, e_n(x) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X.$$

In other words, $\mathcal{H} = \big\{\sum_n a_n e_n \,:\, \sum_n |a_n|^2/\lambda_n < \infty\big\}$: membership in the measure-independent space $\mathcal{H}$ is read off from the spectral data of the operator $T_K$.
summary: g ∈ 𝓗(K) iff g = Σₙaₙeₙ pointwise with Σₙ|aₙ|²/λₙ < ∞; the rescaled eigenfunctions {√λₙeₙ} are an orthonormal basis of 𝓗(K).

title: Feature Maps: Every Kernel Is a Gram Function
informal:
A feature map is a function $\varphi : X \to \mathcal{L}$ from a data domain $X$ into an auxiliary inner product space $\mathcal{L}$, the feature space; it induces on $X$ the Gram kernel $K(x, y) = \langle \varphi(y), \varphi(x)\rangle$, which is always a kernel function — Hermitian and positive semidefinite — since its quadratic forms are $\lVert \sum_i a_i \varphi(x_i)\rVert^2 \ge 0$.

Conversely, every kernel function $K$ on a set $Y$ arises from a feature map: there exist an inner product space $\mathcal{L}'$ and a map $\varphi : Y \to \mathcal{L}'$ with $K(x, y) = \langle \varphi(y), \varphi(x)\rangle$ for all $x, y$. Indeed, by the Moore–Aronszajn theorem $K$ is the reproducing kernel of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and the kernel-function embedding $x \mapsto k_x$ of that space is a feature map for $K$. This two-way correspondence is the kernel trick of statistical learning: optimizing linear predictors $x \mapsto \langle w, \varphi(x)\rangle$ over the feature space is optimizing over the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of $K$, and only inner products — kernel evaluations — ever need to be computed.
summary: Feature maps φ : X → 𝓛 induce kernels K(x,y) = ⟨φ(y),φ(x)⟩, and every kernel function arises this way via its RKHS embedding x ↦ k_x — the kernel trick.

title: The Representer Theorem
informal:
Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of scalar-valued functions on a set $X$, with kernel functions $k_x$ — the representers of evaluation, $f(x) = \langle f, k_x\rangle$, as in the definition of the reproducing kernel — and let $x_1, \dots, x_n \in X$ be data points. Consider the regularized empirical risk $$J(f) \;=\; W\big(\lVert f\rVert^2\big) \;+\; L\big(f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n)\big),$$ where the regularizer $W : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is strictly increasing and the loss $L$ depends on $f$ only through its values at the data points — no convexity or continuity of $L$ is assumed. If $f_0$ minimizes $J$ over all of $\mathcal{H}$, then $$f_0 \;\in\; \operatorname{span}\{k_{x_1}, \dots, k_{x_n}\}.$$

The infinite-dimensional optimization is thus intrinsically finite-dimensional: writing $f_0 = \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j k_{x_j}$ reduces it to a problem in the $n$ coefficients, in which only the kernel values $K(x_i, x_j)$ enter. If $W$ is merely nondecreasing, the conclusion weakens accordingly: the orthogonal projection of any minimizer onto the span of $k_{x_1}, \dots, k_{x_n}$ is again a minimizer, with the same data values. For the ridge form $J(f) = \lVert f\rVert^2 + L(f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n))$ with $L$ convex, a minimizer exists and is unique.
summary: Every minimizer of W(‖f‖²) + L(f(x₁),…,f(xₙ)) with W strictly increasing lies in span{k_{x₁},…,k_{xₙ}} — RKHS learning problems are finite-dimensional.

title: The Maximal Margin Classifier
informal:
Let $E$ be a real Hilbert space and consider labeled data $(x_i, \ell_i)$, $i = 1, \dots, n$, with $n \ge 1$, carrying binary labels $\ell_i \in \{+1, -1\}$ of which both values occur. An affine hyperplane $\{u : \langle u, v\rangle = c\}$ separates the data if every point lies strictly on the side prescribed by its label, and its margin on the data is the least distance from a data point to the hyperplane. Normalizing, call a vector $v$ feasible if for some offset $c$ every constraint clears the threshold one: $\ell_i \big(\langle x_i, v\rangle - c\big) \ge 1$ for all $i$; a feasible pair $(v, c)$ separates the data with margin at least $1/\lVert v\rVert$.

Suppose $w$ is feasible and of minimal norm among all feasible vectors — such a $w$ exists and is unique whenever the data is linearly separable, since the feasible set is closed, convex and nonempty. Then there is an offset $c$ such that all constraints hold at threshold one and the hyperplane $\{u : \langle u, w\rangle = c\}$ is a maximal margin hyperplane: it separates the data, and its margin, namely $1/\lVert w\rVert$, dominates the margin of every separating hyperplane. Moreover $w$ lies in the span of the data, so the optimization reduces to minimizing the Gram quadratic form $\sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j \langle x_j, x_i\rangle$ subject to the constraints — in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, after a feature-map embedding, only kernel values enter.
summary: For separable ±1-labeled data, the minimal-norm feasible vector w gives a hyperplane with margin 1/‖w‖ dominating all separating hyperplanes — the hard-margin SVM.

title: Bernstein–von Mises Theorem
informal:
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be an independent identically distributed sample from a family of probability distributions $P_\theta$ indexed by a parameter $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^k$, where every $P_\theta$ has a probability density $p_\theta$ with respect to one fixed $\sigma$-finite dominating measure $\mu$, and each density integrates to one. Assume that the family is differentiable in quadratic mean at the true parameter $\theta_0$, with score function $\dot\ell_{\theta_0}$, that the Fisher information matrix $I_{\theta_0}$ is nonsingular, and that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exist tests $\varphi_n$ of the data with $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}\varphi_n \to 0$ and $\sup_{\|\theta - \theta_0\| \ge \varepsilon} \mathbb{E}_{\theta}(1 - \varphi_n) \to 0$. Finally, let the prior distribution $\Pi$ satisfy absolute continuity on some ball around $\theta_0$, with a Lebesgue density that is continuous and strictly positive at $\theta_0$ (outside that ball the prior is unrestricted). Then the posterior distribution of the locally rescaled parameter $h = \sqrt{n}\,(\theta - \theta_0)$ merges in total variation with a random normal law:

$$\Bigl\| \Pi\bigl(\sqrt{n}(\theta - \theta_0) \in \cdot \mid X_1,\dots,X_n\bigr) - N\bigl(\Delta_{n,\theta_0},\, I_{\theta_0}^{-1}\bigr) \Bigr\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{in } P_{\theta_0}^{n}\text{-probability},$$

where the centring sequence is the efficient normalized score $\Delta_{n,\theta_0} = n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n} I_{\theta_0}^{-1}\dot\ell_{\theta_0}(X_i)$.
summary: Under quadratic-mean differentiability, a nonsingular Fisher information, consistent tests and a prior with a positive continuous density at the truth, the posterior law of the rescaled parameter is asymptotically normal in total variation, centred at an efficient estimator.

formalizationNotes: Faithful to Theorem 10.1 with three recorded conventions. title: Bernstein–von Mises in Mean
informal:
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be an independent identically distributed sample from a dominated family $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \mathbb{R}^k\}$ satisfying the conditions of the Bernstein–von Mises theorem: the family is differentiable in quadratic mean at the true parameter $\theta_0$, with score $\dot\ell_{\theta_0}$, the Fisher information matrix $I_{\theta_0}$ is nonsingular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are tests $\varphi_n$ with $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}\varphi_n \to 0$ and $\sup_{\|\theta - \theta_0\| \ge \varepsilon} \mathbb{E}_{\theta}(1 - \varphi_n) \to 0$, and the prior $\Pi$ is absolutely continuous on a ball around $\theta_0$, with a Lebesgue density that is continuous and strictly positive at $\theta_0$. Then the total-variation deviation of the posterior of the local parameter $h = \sqrt{n}(\theta - \theta_0)$ from its Gaussian approximation converges not merely in probability but also in mean:

$$\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}^{\,n} \Bigl\| \Pi\bigl(\sqrt{n}(\theta - \theta_0) \in \cdot \mid X_1,\dots,X_n\bigr) - N\bigl(\Delta_{n,\theta_0},\, I_{\theta_0}^{-1}\bigr) \Bigr\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \longrightarrow 0 ,$$

where $\Delta_{n,\theta_0} = n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n} I_{\theta_0}^{-1}\dot\ell_{\theta_0}(X_i)$ is the efficient normalized score.
summary: The expected total-variation distance between the posterior of the rescaled parameter and its Gaussian approximation tends to zero.

title: Posterior Normality Around an Efficient Estimator
informal:
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be an independent identically distributed sample from a dominated family $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \mathbb{R}^k\}$ satisfying the conditions of the Bernstein–von Mises theorem: the family is differentiable in quadratic mean at the true parameter $\theta_0$, with score $\dot\ell_{\theta_0}$, the Fisher information matrix $I_{\theta_0}$ is nonsingular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are tests $\varphi_n$ with $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}\varphi_n \to 0$ and $\sup_{\|\theta - \theta_0\| \ge \varepsilon} \mathbb{E}_{\theta}(1 - \varphi_n) \to 0$, and the prior $\Pi$ is absolutely continuous on a ball around $\theta_0$, with a Lebesgue density that is continuous and strictly positive at $\theta_0$. $$\Bigl\| \Pi\bigl(\theta \in \cdot \mid X_1,\dots,X_n\bigr) - N\bigl(\hat\theta_n,\, (n I_{\theta_0})^{-1}\bigr)\Bigr\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{in } P^n_{\theta_0}\text{-probability} .$$

title: Exponentially Powerful Tests for Shrinking Alternatives
informal:
Let the model be differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with nonsingular Fisher information $I_{\theta_0}$, and suppose for each fixed $\varepsilon>0$ there are tests that asymptotically separate $\theta_0$ from all alternatives at distance at least $\varepsilon$. Then for every sequence of radii $M_n \to \infty$ there exist tests $\varphi_n$ and a constant $c > 0$ such that

$$\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}\varphi_n \to 0, \qquad \mathbb{E}_{\theta}(1 - \varphi_n) \le e^{-c\,n\,(\|\theta - \theta_0\|^2 \wedge 1)} \quad \text{for all } \|\theta - \theta_0\| \ge M_n/\sqrt{n},$$

for all sufficiently large $n$.
summary: Consistent tests can be upgraded to tests whose type-II error decays exponentially in the sample size, uniformly over alternatives at distance at least of the order of the root-n scale.

title: Contiguity of the True Law and the Localized Prior Mixture
informal: Let the model be differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with nonsingular Fisher information $I_{\theta_0}$, and let the prior be absolutely continuous near $\theta_0$ with a density continuous and positive at $\theta_0$. For a fixed radius $u > 0$ let $P_{n,U}$ denote the law of the sample when the parameter is drawn from the prior conditioned to the shrinking ball $\{\|\theta - \theta_0\| < u/\sqrt{n}\}$, $$P_{n,U}(A) = \int P^n_\theta(A)\, d\Pi\bigl(\theta \mid \|\theta - \theta_0\| < u/\sqrt{n}\bigr) .$$ Then $P^n_{\theta_0}$ and $P_{n,U}$ are mutually contiguous: a sequence of events is asymptotically negligible under one of them if and only if it is asymptotically negligible under the other.
summary: The law of the sample under the true parameter and the mixture of sample laws over a shrinking prior ball are mutually contiguous, so null sets and convergence in probability may be transferred between them.

hypotheses.label: quadratic-mean differentiability
hypotheses.note: The square root of the density is differentiable in $L^2(\mu)$ at $\theta_0$, with derivative determined by the score $\dot\ell_{\theta_0}$ — a smoothness requirement weaker than pointwise differentiability.

hypotheses.label: nonsingular Fisher information
hypotheses.note: The Fisher information matrix $I_{\theta_0}$ is positive definite, so the limiting log-likelihood ratio is a nondegenerate normal variable.

hypotheses.label: locally positive prior density
hypotheses.note: The prior is absolutely continuous on a ball around $\theta_0$ with a density continuous and strictly positive at $\theta_0$, hence comparable with Lebesgue measure on small balls.

hypotheses.label: fixed mixing radius
hypotheses.note: The mixing radius $u > 0$ is fixed; the ball $\|\theta - \theta_0\| < u/\sqrt{n}$ shrinks at rate $n^{-1/2}$.

formalizationNotes: The per-alternative contiguity is obtained from an integral-comparison version of Le Cam's first lemma, which — unlike the classical common-support formulation — needs no assumption that the densities share a support, matching van der Vaart's setting. The mixture direction combines a two-sided prior-versus-Lebesgue comparison on small balls with an almost-everywhere subsequence extraction.

reference.formal: A. W. van der Vaart, *Asymptotic Statistics*, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics, Cambridge University Press, 1998.
reference.biblio: Contiguity was introduced by L. Le Cam (1960) and is developed in van der Vaart's Chapter 6; its use to exchange the true law with a Bayesian mixture over a shrinking neighbourhood is the opening move of the proof of Theorem 10.1 (Le Cam 1953). The formalization proves mutual contiguity of the two sequences of laws in the sense of the Contiguity development of this library.

title: Prior Condition of the Bernstein–von Mises Theorem
informal:
A prior distribution $\Pi$ on $\mathbb{R}^k$ has a local density at $\theta_0$ if there is a radius $r_0 > 0$ and a function $f \ge 0$ such that the restriction of $\Pi$ to the ball $\{\|\theta - \theta_0\| < r_0\}$ has Lebesgue density $f$, and $f$ is continuous at $\theta_0$ with $f(\theta_0) > 0$.

Outside the ball the prior is completely arbitrary: it may have atoms, may be singular with respect to Lebesgue measure, and may put most of its mass far away.
summary: The prior is absolutely continuous on some ball around the true parameter, with a Lebesgue density that is measurable, nonnegative, continuous at the true parameter and strictly positive there.
leanSignature:
structure HasLocalDensity (π : Measure (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k)))
    (θ₀ : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k)) (r₀ : ℝ) (f : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k) → ℝ) :
    Prop where
  /-- Constitutive (vdV §10.2): the neighborhood of absolute continuity is nonempty. -/
  rad_pos : 0 < r₀
  /-- Constitutive (vdV §10.2): `f` is a density — wlog nonnegative. -/
  nonneg : ∀ θ, 0 ≤ f θ
  /-- Constitutive (vdV §10.2): `f` is a density — wlog Borel measurable
  (Radon–Nikodym supplies a measurable version). -/
  measurable : Measurable f
  /-- Constitutive (vdV §10.2): on `B(θ₀, r₀)` the prior has Lebesgue density `f`. -/
  restrict_eq : π.restrict (Metric.ball θ₀ r₀)
    = (volume.restrict (Metric.ball θ₀ r₀)).withDensity fun θ => ENNReal.ofReal (f θ)
  /-- Constitutive (vdV §10.2): the density is continuous at `θ₀`. -/
  continuousAt : ContinuousAt f θ₀
  /-- Constitutive (vdV §10.2): the density is positive at `θ₀`. -/
  pos : 0 < f θ₀
formalizationNotes: Formalized as a structure whose fields are exactly the constitutive requirements: a positive radius, a nonnegative measurable density, the restriction identity, continuity at $\theta_0$, and positivity at $\theta_0$. Nonnegativity and measurability of the density are recorded as fields rather than derived, since a Radon–Nikodym derivative is only determined almost everywhere and the statement below uses a fixed version.

reference.formal: A. W. van der Vaart, *Asymptotic Statistics*, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics, Cambridge University Press, 1998.
reference.biblio: The condition goes back to the classical formulations of Bernstein and von Mises, which assumed a positive continuous prior density everywhere; the localized form — arbitrary prior away from the truth — is due to Le Cam (1953) and is the form stated by van der Vaart. Note that no moment or tail condition on the prior appears here; such a condition is needed only for the asymptotics of Bayes point estimators.

title: Asymptotics of Bayes Point Estimators
informal:
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be an independent identically distributed sample from a dominated family $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \mathbb{R}^k\}$ satisfying the conditions of the Bernstein–von Mises theorem: the family is differentiable in quadratic mean at the true parameter $\theta_0$, with score $\dot\ell_{\theta_0}$, the Fisher information matrix $I_{\theta_0}$ is nonsingular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are tests $\varphi_n$ with $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}\varphi_n \to 0$ and $\sup_{\|\theta - \theta_0\| \ge \varepsilon} \mathbb{E}_{\theta}(1 - \varphi_n) \to 0$, and the prior $\Pi$ is absolutely continuous on a ball around $\theta_0$ with a density continuous and strictly positive at $\theta_0$. Let $\ell$ be a loss function on $\mathbb{R}^k$ that is separated, in the sense that the values of $\ell$ on the ball of radius $M$ never exceed its values outside the ball of radius $2M$, with a strict gap for at least one $M$, and of polynomial growth, $\ell(h) \le 1 + \|h\|^p$. Assume the prior has a finite moment of order $p$. Let $T_n$ be a measurable estimator sequence that minimizes the posterior risk $t \mapsto \int \ell\bigl(\sqrt{n}(t - \theta)\bigr)\, d\Pi(\theta \mid X_1,\dots,X_n)$ up to a tolerance tending to zero, and let $u_0$ be the unique minimizer of the limiting criterion $g(u) = \int \ell(u - z)\, dN(0, I_{\theta_0}^{-1})(z)$. Then

$$\sqrt{n}\,(T_n - \theta_0) - \Delta_{n,\theta_0} \longrightarrow u_0 \quad \text{in } P^n_{\theta_0}\text{-probability},$$

with $\Delta_{n,\theta_0}$ the efficient normalized score.
summary: Minimizers of the posterior risk for a separated loss of polynomial growth are asymptotically equivalent to the efficient centring shifted by the minimizer of the limiting Gaussian criterion.

hypotheses.note: The square root of the density is differentiable in $L^2(\mu)$ at $\theta_0$, with derivative determined by the score $\dot\ell_{\theta_0}$ — a smoothness requirement weaker than pointwise differentiability.

hypotheses.label: separated loss
hypotheses.note: There is a scale $M$ with $\sup_{\|h\| \le M} \ell(h) < \inf_{\|h\| \ge 2M} \ell(h)$, and at every scale the values of the loss on $\{\|h\| \le M\}$ never exceed its values on $\{\|h\| \ge 2M\}$.

hypotheses.label: polynomial growth
hypotheses.note: The loss satisfies $\ell(h) \le 1 + \|h\|^p$ for the fixed exponent $p \ge 0$.

hypotheses.label: finite prior moment
hypotheses.note: The prior has finite $p$-th absolute moment, $\int \|\theta\|^p \, d\Pi(\theta) < \infty$, matching the growth exponent of the loss.

hypotheses.label: approximate risk minimizer
hypotheses.note: For each $n$ the estimator $T_n$ minimizes the posterior risk $t \mapsto \int \ell\bigl(\sqrt{n}(t - \theta)\bigr) \, d\Pi(\theta \mid X_1,\dots,X_n)$ up to an additive tolerance $\varepsilon_n \to 0$; an exact minimizer is the case $\varepsilon_n = 0$.

hypotheses.label: unique limit minimizer
hypotheses.note: The limiting criterion $g(u) = \int \ell(u - z) \, dN(0, I_{\theta_0}^{-1})(z)$ has a strict unique minimizer $u_0$.

formalizationNotes: Three deliberate deviations from the book's proof, all strengthenings or generalizations. (i) The argmax continuous-mapping route through weak convergence of processes is replaced by a recentred majorant approximation plus deterministic argmin consistency: after recentring by the efficient score, the limit criterion is deterministic, so no process convergence is needed. (ii) The estimator is only required to be an approximate minimizer, with tolerance tending to zero; the book's exact minimizer is the case of zero tolerance. (iii) The conclusion is strengthened to convergence in probability of the recentred sequence, from which the book's weak convergence follows by the central limit theorem for the score and Slutsky's lemma. Measurable selection of the estimator is a hypothesis, as it is in the book.

reference.formal: A. W. van der Vaart, *Asymptotic Statistics*, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics, Cambridge University Press, 1998.
reference.biblio: Asymptotics of Bayes point estimators for general losses go back to Ibragimov and Has'minskii (1981), who analyse the normalized posterior risk directly; the route through the total-variation Bernstein–von Mises theorem is Le Cam's (1986). The formalization states van der Vaart's Theorem 10.8 with the separation condition made pointwise and with the uniqueness proviso in its recentred deterministic form.

title: Limit Distribution of Bayes Point Estimators
informal:
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be an independent identically distributed sample from a dominated family $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \mathbb{R}^k\}$ satisfying the conditions of the Bernstein–von Mises theorem — differentiability in quadratic mean at the true parameter $\theta_0$ with score $\dot\ell_{\theta_0}$, a nonsingular Fisher information matrix $I_{\theta_0}$, tests $\varphi_n$ with $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}\varphi_n \to 0$ and $\sup_{\|\theta - \theta_0\| \ge \varepsilon} \mathbb{E}_{\theta}(1 - \varphi_n) \to 0$ for each $\varepsilon > 0$, and a prior $\Pi$ that is absolutely continuous near $\theta_0$ with a density continuous and strictly positive at $\theta_0$ — and let the loss $\ell$ on $\mathbb{R}^k$ be separated: its values on the ball of radius $M$ never exceed its values outside the ball of radius $2M$, with a strict gap for at least one $M$ and of polynomial growth, $\ell(h) \le 1 + \|h\|^p$, with a prior having finite moment of order $p$. If the estimators $T_n$ minimize the posterior risk $t \mapsto \int \ell\bigl(\sqrt{n}(t - \theta)\bigr)\, d\Pi(\theta \mid X_1,\dots,X_n)$ up to a tolerance tending to zero and the limiting criterion $g(u) = \int \ell(u - z)\, dN(0, I_{\theta_0}^{-1})(z)$ has a unique minimizer $u_0$, then the standardized Bayes estimators converge in distribution:

$$\sqrt{n}\,(T_n - \theta_0) \rightsquigarrow N\bigl(u_0,\, I_{\theta_0}^{-1}\bigr) \qquad \text{under } P^n_{\theta_0} .$$
summary: The standardized Bayes point estimators converge in distribution to a normal law with mean the minimizer of the limiting criterion and covariance the inverse Fisher information.

title: Bayes Estimators Are Asymptotically Efficient for Subconvex Losses
informal:
Keep the setting of the asymptotics of Bayes point estimators: an independent identically distributed sample from a dominated family satisfying the conditions of the Bernstein–von Mises theorem — differentiability in quadratic mean at the true parameter $\theta_0$ with score $\dot\ell_{\theta_0}$, a nonsingular Fisher information matrix $I_{\theta_0}$, tests $\varphi_n$ with $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}\varphi_n \to 0$ and $\sup_{\|\theta - \theta_0\| \ge \varepsilon} \mathbb{E}_{\theta}(1 - \varphi_n) \to 0$ for each $\varepsilon > 0$, and a prior $\Pi$ that is absolutely continuous near $\theta_0$ with a density continuous and strictly positive at $\theta_0$ — and estimators $T_n$ that minimize the posterior risk $t \mapsto \int \ell\bigl(\sqrt{n}(t - \theta)\bigr)\, d\Pi(\theta \mid X_1,\dots,X_n)$ up to a tolerance tending to zero. Let the loss be bowl-shaped: symmetric, with convex sublevel sets — the subconvex losses of decision theory, for example $\ell(h) = \|h\|^2$ or any nondecreasing function of $\|h\|$. Assume also that the loss is separated: there is a scale $M$ with $\sup_{\|h\| \le M} \ell(h) < \inf_{\|h\| \ge 2M} \ell(h)$ and of polynomial growth, $\ell(h) \le 1 + \|h\|^p$, that the prior has the matching finite moment, $\int \|\theta\|^p \, d\Pi(\theta) < \infty$, and that the limiting criterion $g(u) = \int \ell(u - z)\, dN(0, I_{\theta_0}^{-1})(z)$ has a unique minimizer. Then that minimizer is the origin, and the Bayes point estimators are asymptotically efficient:

$$\sqrt{n}\,(T_n - \theta_0) \rightsquigarrow N\bigl(0,\, I_{\theta_0}^{-1}\bigr) \qquad \text{under } P^n_{\theta_0} .$$
summary: For a bowl-shaped (subconvex) loss the limiting criterion is minimized at the origin, so the standardized Bayes estimators converge to the efficient normal limit with no bias.

title: Uniform Tightness of Standardized Bayes Estimators
informal:
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be an independent identically distributed sample from a dominated family $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \mathbb{R}^k\}$ satisfying the conditions of the Bernstein–von Mises theorem — differentiability in quadratic mean at the true parameter $\theta_0$ with score $\dot\ell_{\theta_0}$, a nonsingular Fisher information matrix $I_{\theta_0}$, tests $\varphi_n$ with $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}\varphi_n \to 0$ and $\sup_{\|\theta - \theta_0\| \ge \varepsilon} \mathbb{E}_{\theta}(1 - \varphi_n) \to 0$ for each $\varepsilon > 0$, and a prior $\Pi$ that is absolutely continuous near $\theta_0$ with a density continuous and strictly positive at $\theta_0$ — so that the posterior of $\sqrt{n}(\theta - \theta_0)$ merges with $N(\Delta_{n,\theta_0}, I_{\theta_0}^{-1})$. Let the loss $\ell$ be separated, with a genuine gap between its values on a ball of radius $M$ and on the complement of the ball of radius $2M$, and of polynomial growth $\ell(h) \le 1 + \|h\|^p$, and let the prior have a finite moment of order $p$. If the estimators $T_n$ minimize the posterior risk $t \mapsto \int \ell\bigl(\sqrt{n}(t - \theta)\bigr)\, d\Pi(\theta \mid X_1,\dots,X_n)$ up to a tolerance tending to zero, then the standardized estimators are uniformly tight: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a radius $K$ with

$$P^n_{\theta_0}\bigl( \sqrt{n}\,\|T_n - \theta_0\| \ge K \bigr) \le \varepsilon \quad \text{for all sufficiently large } n .$$
summary: Separation and polynomial growth of the loss, with a matching prior moment, force the standardized Bayes point estimators into balls of fixed radius with probability tending to one.

hypotheses.note: There is a scale $M$ with $\sup_{\|h\| \le M} \ell(h) < \inf_{\|h\| \ge 2M} \ell(h)$, and at every scale the values of the loss on $\{\|h\| \le M\}$ never exceed its values on $\{\|h\| \ge 2M\}$.

hypotheses.label: polynomial growth
hypotheses.note: The loss satisfies $\ell(h) \le 1 + \|h\|^p$ for the fixed exponent $p \ge 0$.

hypotheses.label: finite prior moment
hypotheses.note: The prior has finite $p$-th absolute moment, $\int \|\theta\|^p \, d\Pi(\theta) < \infty$, matching the growth exponent of the loss.

hypotheses.label: approximate risk minimizer
hypotheses.note: For each $n$ the estimator $T_n$ minimizes the posterior risk $t \mapsto \int \ell\bigl(\sqrt{n}(t - \theta)\bigr) \, d\Pi(\theta \mid X_1,\dots,X_n)$ up to an additive tolerance $\varepsilon_n \to 0$; an exact minimizer is the case $\varepsilon_n = 0$.

formalizationNotes: This is Part 2 of van der Vaart's proof, isolated as a standalone statement. The additive gap is read off the strict part of the separation condition (an explicit separating level rather than a supremum/infimum pair, which avoids suprema over uncountable sets and rules out the degenerate zero-one loss on a continuum, for which tightness does not hold). The polynomial tail of the posterior is controlled through the localized prior mixture.

reference.formal: A. W. van der Vaart, *Asymptotic Statistics*, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics, Cambridge University Press, 1998.
reference.biblio: Tightness of the normalized Bayes estimators is the first substantive step in the Ibragimov–Has'minskii (1981) analysis as well; van der Vaart obtains it from the separation condition alone. The formalization proves the uniform tightness statement for approximate minimizers.

title: Doob's Posterior Consistency Theorem
informal:
Let the observations take values in a standard Borel space, let the parameter space be a Polish metric space, and let the model $\theta \mapsto P_\theta$ be identifiable: distinct parameters give distinct distributions. Let $\Pi$ be an arbitrary prior probability measure on the parameter space. Then for $\Pi$-almost every $\theta$, the posterior is strongly consistent at $\theta$: for almost every infinite sequence $X_1, X_2, \dots$ drawn independently from $P_\theta$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$,

$$\Pi\bigl( \|\vartheta - \theta\| < \varepsilon \;\big|\; X_1,\dots,X_n \bigr) \longrightarrow 1 \qquad \text{as } n \to \infty .$$
summary: For an identifiable model on a standard Borel sample space with a Polish parameter space, the posterior is strongly consistent at almost every parameter under any prior.
leanSignature:
theorem doob_consistency [MetricSpace Θ] [PolishSpace Θ] [BorelSpace Θ] [Nonempty Θ]
    [StandardBorelSpace 𝓧]
    (K : Kernel Θ 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel K]
    (hK_inj : Function.Injective fun θ => K θ)
    (π : Measure Θ) [IsProbabilityMeasure π] :
    ∀ᵐ θ ∂π, StronglyConsistentAt K π θ

hypotheses.label: identifiability
hypotheses.note: The map $\theta \mapsto P_\theta$ is injective: distinct parameters give distinct sampling distributions, so the parameter can in principle be recovered from the data.

hypotheses.label: arbitrary prior
hypotheses.note: $\Pi$ is any probability measure on the parameter space — no density, support or smoothness requirement — and the conclusion holds up to a $\Pi$-null set.

formalizationNotes: Consistency is stated in ball form (the posterior mass of every $\varepsilon$-ball around the true parameter tends to one, on one almost-sure event valid for all $\varepsilon$ simultaneously); this is equivalent to van der Vaart's weak convergence of the posterior to the Dirac measure at the truth, since the limit is a point mass. Van der Vaart's assumption of a Euclidean sample space is generalized to standard Borel, and his Lemmas 10.12 and 10.13 on accessible functions are replaced by an explicit measurable retraction recovering the parameter from the data sequence.

reference.formal: A. W. van der Vaart, *Asymptotic Statistics*, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics, Cambridge University Press, 1998.
reference.biblio: The theorem and its martingale proof are due to J. L. Doob (1949). The sharpness of the null-set caveat is the subject of P. Diaconis and D. Freedman (1986), who construct priors with large inconsistency sets; the complementary everywhere-consistency theory under testing and Kullback–Leibler support conditions is L. Schwartz's (1965). The formalization states the theorem for an identifiable Markov kernel model with a Polish parameter space and an arbitrary prior.

title: Posterior Probabilities Form a Convergent Martingale
citation: van der Vaart (1998), Thm 10.10, martingale step (p. 149)
shortRef: van der Vaart (1998), Thm 10.10, martingale step (p. 149)
informal:
Consider the joint experiment in which the parameter $\vartheta$ is drawn from the prior and, given $\vartheta$, the observations $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are independent and identically distributed from $P_\vartheta$. Suppose the parameter can be recovered from the infinite data sequence: there is a measurable map $g$ with $g(X_1, X_2, \dots) = \vartheta$ almost surely, which identifiability guarantees by the measurable-retraction theorem. Then for every measurable set $A$ of parameters, the sequence of posterior probabilities

$$M_n = \Pi\bigl( \vartheta \in A \mid X_1, \dots, X_n \bigr)$$

is a uniformly bounded martingale with respect to the filtration generated by the observations, and it converges almost surely to the indicator $\mathbf{1}_A(\vartheta)$.
summary: The posterior probability of a fixed parameter set is a bounded martingale in the observation filtration and converges almost surely to the indicator of that set evaluated at the random parameter.

      ∀ᵐ ω ∂(doobJoint K π), g ω.1 = ω.2)
    {A : Set Θ}

    ∀ᵐ ω ∂(doobJoint K π),
      Tendsto (fun n => (((iidKernel K n)†π) (doobData n ω) A).toReal) atTop
        (𝓝 (A.indicator (fun _ => (1 : ℝ)) ω.2))

hypotheses.note: There is a measurable map $g$ with $g(X_1, X_2, \dots) = \vartheta$ almost surely, so the parameter is determined by the infinite data sequence.

hypotheses.label: measurable parameter set
hypotheses.note: The parameter event $A$ whose posterior probability is tracked is measurable.

formalizationNotes: The martingale property is not asserted separately: the statement is proved by identifying the posterior kernel with the regular conditional distribution of the parameter given the first $n$ observations (both are conditional kernels of the same joint law) and then applying Lévy's upward convergence theorem for conditional expectations. The limit variable is measurable with respect to the sigma-algebra generated by the whole data sequence exactly because of the parameter-recovery hypothesis; the convergence is of real-valued quantities, the posterior masses being finite.

reference.formal: A. W. van der Vaart, *Asymptotic Statistics*, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics, Cambridge University Press, 1998.
reference.pointer: §10.4, proof of Theorem 10.10, pp. 149–150 (the martingale display (10.11))
reference.biblio: This is the display (10.11) in van der Vaart's proof and is Doob's (1949) original argument: posterior probabilities are martingales, and Lévy's upward theorem gives their limit. The formalization states almost-sure convergence of the posterior masses to the indicator of the event at the random parameter, on the joint parameter-and-data space.

title: The Parameter Is a Measurable Function of the Data Sequence
informal:
Let the sample space be standard Borel, let the parameter space be standard Borel and nonempty, and let the model be identifiable: distinct parameters give distinct sampling distributions. Let $\Pi$ be any prior probability measure. Then there exists a measurable map $g$ from infinite data sequences to parameters such that, in the joint experiment where $\vartheta \sim \Pi$ and the data are independent and identically distributed from $P_\vartheta$,

$$g(X_1, X_2, X_3, \dots) = \vartheta \qquad \text{almost surely}.$$
summary: Under identifiability the parameter can be reconstructed from the infinite data sequence by a measurable map, almost surely under the joint law.
leanSignature:
theorem exists_measurable_retraction [StandardBorelSpace Θ] [Nonempty Θ]
    [StandardBorelSpace 𝓧]
    (K : Kernel Θ 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel K]
    (hK_inj : Function.Injective fun θ => K θ)
    (π : Measure Θ) [IsProbabilityMeasure π] :
    ∃ g : (ℕ → 𝓧) → Θ, Measurable g ∧
      ∀ᵐ ω ∂(doobJoint K π), g ω.1 = ω.2

hypotheses.label: identifiability
hypotheses.note: The map $\theta \mapsto P_\theta$ is injective: distinct parameters give distinct sampling distributions.

hypotheses.label: arbitrary prior
hypotheses.note: $\Pi$ is any probability measure on the parameter space; the recovery identity is asserted almost surely under the resulting joint law.

formalizationNotes: This replaces van der Vaart's Lemmas 10.12 and 10.13 on accessible functions by an explicit construction, and generalizes his Euclidean sample space to an arbitrary standard Borel one. The empirical-limit map is made globally defined by using limit-superior expressions, so that it is measurable everywhere rather than only on the convergence set; off the range of the moment map a default parameter value is returned, which is why nonemptiness of the parameter space is assumed.

reference.formal: A. W. van der Vaart, *Asymptotic Statistics*, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics, Cambridge University Press, 1998.
reference.biblio: Doob (1949) phrased this step in terms of functions of the observations that are "accessible" from the data; the modern route via the strong law for empirical frequencies plus the Lusin–Souslin theorem is standard in the descriptive-set-theoretic treatment of statistical models. The formalization proves the existence of a measurable retraction satisfying the recovery identity almost surely.

title: Sequential Bayes: Today's Posterior Is Tomorrow's Prior
informal:
Let $\vartheta$ carry a prior $\Pi$, and let two observations $X$ and $Y$ be conditionally independent given $\vartheta$, with $X$ distributed according to a density $p_1(\cdot \mid \vartheta)$ with respect to a fixed dominating measure and $Y$ according to a density $p_2(\cdot \mid \vartheta)$ with respect to another fixed dominating measure. Then, for almost every pair $(x, y)$ under the prior predictive distribution,

$$\Pi\bigl( \,\cdot \mid X = x,\, Y = y \bigr) \; = \; \bigl(\Pi_x\bigr)_y, \qquad \text{where } \Pi_x = \Pi(\,\cdot \mid X = x)$$

and $(\Pi_x)_y$ denotes the posterior obtained by updating the prior $\Pi_x$ on the observation $Y = y$.
summary: Updating on one observation and then on a second gives the same posterior as updating once on the pair.

    {ν₁ : Measure 𝓧} [SigmaFinite ν₁] {ν₂ : Measure 𝓨} [SigmaFinite ν₂]
    {p₁ : Θ → 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞} {p₂ : Θ → 𝓨 → ℝ≥0∞}
    (hp₁ : Measurable (Function.uncurry p₁)) (hp₂ : Measurable (Function.uncurry p₂))
    (hκ₁ : ∀ θ, κ₁ θ = ν₁.withDensity (p₁ θ)) (hκ₂ : ∀ θ, κ₂ θ = ν₂.withDensity (p₂ θ)) :
    ∀ᵐ q ∂((κ₁ ×ₖ κ₂) ∘ₘ π),

hypotheses.note: The conditional law of the first observation has density $p_1(\cdot \mid \vartheta)$ with respect to a fixed $\sigma$-finite measure, jointly measurable in parameter and observation.

hypotheses.label: second coordinate dominated
hypotheses.note: The conditional law of the second observation has density $p_2(\cdot \mid \vartheta)$ with respect to its own fixed $\sigma$-finite measure, jointly measurable in parameter and observation.

formalizationNotes: The identity is an equality of measures for prior-predictive-almost-every observation pair — the sharpest form available, since posterior kernels are only determined almost everywhere. The intermediate update uses the generalized (unnormalized-density) posterior, so no positivity hypothesis on the first-stage predictive density is needed: degenerate values are absorbed by the extended-nonnegative conventions. The pair experiment is shown to be dominated by the product of the two dominating measures with the product density.

reference.biblio: Sequential coherence — today's posterior is tomorrow's prior — is the operational heart of Bayesian learning, already used by Laplace and made axiomatic by B. de Finetti (1937) and D. V. Lindley. The formalization proves the identity for a dominated pair experiment on standard Borel parameter spaces, with equality holding predictive-almost-everywhere.

title: Bayes' Theorem for a Finite Partition
informal:
Let $H_1, \dots, H_m$ be finitely many hypotheses that are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, and let $d$ be an observed event. Then for each one of the hypotheses $H_j$ in the list,

$$\mathbb{P}(H_j \mid d) \;=\; \frac{\mathbb{P}(d \mid H_j)\,\mathbb{P}(H_j)}{\sum_{i} \mathbb{P}(d \mid H_i)\,\mathbb{P}(H_i)} .$$
summary: The posterior probability of one hypothesis in a finite partition equals its likelihood times its prior divided by the total probability of the data.

    (hHc : ⋃ i ∈ s, H i = Set.univ)
    (μ : Measure Ω) [IsFiniteMeasure μ]
    {d : Set Ω} (hd : MeasurableSet d) {j : ι} (hj : j ∈ s) :
    μ[H j | d] = μ[d | H j] * μ (H j) / ∑ i ∈ s, μ[d | H i] * μ (H i)

hypotheses.note: The hypotheses $H_1,\dots,H_m$ are pairwise disjoint events.

hypotheses.label: exhaustive
hypotheses.note: The hypotheses cover the whole sample space, $\bigcup_j H_j = \Omega$.

hypotheses.label: hypothesis in the partition
hypotheses.note: The hypothesis $H_j$ whose posterior probability is computed is one of the listed parts.

formalizationNotes: Stated for a finite measure with values in the extended nonnegative reals, where the conventions make degenerate cases automatic: parts of prior probability zero contribute zero to both sides, and if the data event has probability zero both sides are zero. Consequently no positivity hypothesis on the data event or on the individual hypotheses is required, unlike the usual textbook statement. Conditional probability is Mathlib's conditioned measure.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: Bayes' theorem first appeared, for the binomial case, in the essay of T. Bayes read to the Royal Society and published posthumously by R. Price in 1763; P. S. Laplace rediscovered it in full generality in 1774, apparently unaware of Bayes's work, and the finite-partition computation formalized here is exactly Laplace's usage. The formalization is the measure-theoretic statement for an arbitrary finite measurable partition, free of positivity side conditions.

title: Berry–Esseen bound for the characteristic function of a standardized i.i.d. sum
informal: Let $X_0, X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be real random variables on a probability space that are jointly independent and identically distributed, and write $\mu$ for their common law. Assume $\mu$ is centred, i.e. $\mathbb{E}X_0 = 0$, that it has second moment $v = \mathbb{E}X_0^2$, and that its third absolute moment $\rho = \mathbb{E}|X_0|^3$ is finite. Let $S_n = n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} X_k$ and let $\varphi_{S_n}$ be its characteristic function. Then for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, writing $w = t/\sqrt{n}$, $$\bigl|\varphi_{S_n}(t) - e^{-n v w^{2}/2}\bigr| \;\le\; n\left(\frac{\rho\,|w|^{3}}{6} + \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{v w^{2}}{2}\right)^{\!2}\right).$$ In the standardized case $v = 1$ the right-hand side is $\dfrac{\rho\,|t|^{3}}{6\sqrt{n}} + \dfrac{t^{4}}{8n}$, so the characteristic function of the normalized sum approaches $e^{-t^{2}/2}$ at the Berry–Esseen rate $n^{-1/2}$, with the classical Lyapunov constant $\rho/6$.
summary: The characteristic function of a standardized sum of i.i.d. centred variables with finite third moment is within an explicit $O(n^{-1/2})$ distance of the Gaussian characteristic function.

        + (v * ((√n)⁻¹ * t) ^ 2 / 2) ^ 2 / 2)

hypotheses.note: The variables are jointly (not merely pairwise) independent.

hypotheses.label: identically distributed
hypotheses.note: Every variable has the same law as the first one.

hypotheses.label: centred law
hypotheses.note: The common law has mean zero, so no centring correction appears.

hypotheses.label: second moment $v$
hypotheses.note: The common second moment is named $v$; the Gaussian comparison uses variance $v$ per summand.

hypotheses.label: finite third moment

Converting it into a bound on cumulative distribution functions requires Esseen's smoothing inequality, which is built separately in the companion file EsseenSmoothing.lean. The constant is the elementary Lyapunov constant $\rho/6$ rather than the optimal Berry–Esseen constant ($\approx 0.4748$), and the statement is proved unconditionally (axiom-clean) from a telescoping product estimate plus a third-order Taylor bound for the complex exponential.

reference.biblio: The theorem is due independently to A. C. Berry (1941) and C.-G. Esseen (1942), who showed that a finite third absolute moment forces the Kolmogorov distance between the law of a standardized i.i.d. sum and the standard normal law to be $O(\rho/(\sigma^{3}\sqrt n))$. The route formalized here is the textbook one of Feller (1971, §XVI.3 and §XVI.5): a third-order Taylor expansion of the characteristic function, a telescoping product bound, and finally Esseen's smoothing inequality. title: Damped one-term Edgeworth expansion of a characteristic function power
informal: Let $\mu$ be a probability law on $\mathbb{R}$ with characteristic function $\varphi$. Assume $\mu$ is centred, has second moment $v$ and third moment $m_3$, and has a finite fourth moment $\beta_4 = \mathbb{E}X^4$; write $\rho = \mathbb{E}|X|^3$. title: Lindeberg–Feller central limit theorem for triangular arrays
informal: For each $n$ let $X_{n,1}, \ldots, X_{n,m_n}$ be a finite row of real random variables on a common probability space. Assume the entries of each row are jointly independent, are square-integrable, and are centred, that the row variances satisfy $\sum_i \operatorname{Var}(X_{n,i}) \to 1$, and that the Lindeberg condition $$\sum_i \mathbb{E}\bigl[X_{n,i}^{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{|X_{n,i}| > \varepsilon\}\bigr] \;\longrightarrow\; 0 \qquad \text{for every } \varepsilon > 0$$ holds. Then the row sums converge in distribution to the standard normal law, $$\sum_{i} X_{n,i} \;\rightsquigarrow\; N(0,1).$$ The rows are otherwise unrelated: the row lengths $m_n$ are arbitrary and need not increase, and there is no requirement that the $n$-th row extend the $(n-1)$-st.
