reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The comparison and uniqueness step for two-sided tests is part of the Neyman–Pearson (1936) analysis, resting on the sign-change properties of families with monotone likelihood ratio later systematized by Karlin and Rubin (1956). The formalized proof is the Lehmann comparison in its equality form: the difference of the two tests changes sign at most once along the statistic, and a difference with a single sign change that integrates to zero against two members with a strictly monotone likelihood ratio must vanish almost everywhere.

formalizationNotes: Uniqueness is stated as almost-everywhere equality with respect to the dominating measure; since the densities are strictly positive this coincides with almost-sure equality under every member of the family. The strict form of the monotone likelihood ratio is transcribed explicitly and division-free, matching the non-strict definition used elsewhere. Its sibling statement — that shifting the rejection interval to the right raises the power above $\theta_1$ and lowers it below — carries the extra assumption that the two tests are not almost-everywhere equal; the assumption is required because two almost-everywhere equal tests have identical power functions, and then no strict inequality is available.

title: Uniformly most accurate one-sided confidence bound
informal: Let $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \mathbb{R}\}$ have densities with respect to a $\sigma$-finite measure and monotone likelihood ratio in a measurable statistic $T$. Write $F_\theta(t) = \mathbb{P}_\theta\{T \le t\}$ and assume $F_\theta(t)$ is continuous in $t$ for each fixed $\theta$ (continuity in $\theta$ for each fixed $t$ is assumed as well) and distinct parameter values give distinct distributions. Fix a level $0 < \alpha < 1$ and assume the defining equation is solvable at every level of the statistic, i.e. for each $t$ there is a $\theta$ with $F_\theta(t) = 1 - \alpha$. Then there is a measurable lower bound $\underline{\theta}(x)$ such that the family of half-lines $[\underline{\theta}(x), \infty)$ is a uniformly most accurate family of confidence sets at level $1 - \alpha$: it covers each value $\theta_0$ other than the true one with the smallest possible probability, uniformly over the parameters $\theta > \theta_0$. Moreover $\underline{\theta}(x)$ is characterized as the unique solution of $$ F_\theta\bigl(T(x)\bigr) \;=\; 1 - \alpha . $$

hypotheses.label: continuity in the statistic

hypotheses.label: identifiable family

hypotheses.label: solvable equation
hypotheses.note: The equation F_θ(t) = 1 − α has a solution θ at every level t of the statistic, so the lower bound is a real number at every observation.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: Confidence sets, their coverage requirement and the accuracy criterion are due to Neyman (1937); optimal one-sided bounds for families with monotone likelihood ratio follow from the optimality theory of Karlin and Rubin (1956). The formalization obtains the bound by inverting the uniformly most powerful one-sided tests of each simple null and transferring their optimality along the test/confidence duality; because a competitor confidence family only controls its coverage at a single parameter value, the separating-multiplier step is redone against the *simple* null rather than reused from the composite one-sided theorem.

formalizationNotes: Following the printed statement we additionally assume that the defining equation $F_\theta(t) = 1 - \alpha$ is solvable at every level $t$ of the statistic. The hypothesis is needed because nothing in the printed version keeps the parameter range from being bounded: for the normal location family reparametrized by the arctangent the inverted confidence set is empty at large observations, which no real-valued lower bound can express. The added hypothesis is exactly the equation displayed in the conclusion, so it introduces no new notion, and it holds automatically for genuine location families. Separate continuity in each variable is assumed, following the printed version, but only continuity in the statistic is consumed; the parameter set is the whole real line rather than a general subset.

title: Boundary Optimality Implies UMP Unbiasedness
informal: Consider testing a null set $\Theta_0$ against an alternative set $\Theta_1$ at a level $\alpha$ with $0 \le \alpha \le 1$, and suppose every randomized test has a power function that is continuous in the parameter. Write $\omega_B = \overline{\Theta_0} \cap \overline{\Theta_1}$ for the common boundary of the two sets, that is, the parameter points that are points or limit points of both. Let $\varphi_0$ be a randomized test. If $\varphi_0$ has level $\alpha$ on the null set, so that $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi_0] \le \alpha$ for every $\theta \in \Theta_0$, if $\varphi_0$ is similar of size $\alpha$ on the boundary, that is $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi_0] = \alpha$ for every $\theta \in \omega_B$, and if $\varphi_0$ is at least as powerful on $\Theta_1$ as every randomized test that is similar of size $\alpha$ on $\omega_B$, then $\varphi_0$ is uniformly most powerful unbiased at level $\alpha$: it is unbiased of level $\alpha$, and $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\psi] \le \mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi_0]$ for every $\theta \in \Theta_1$ and every unbiased level-$\alpha$ test $\psi$. The mechanism has two halves. Continuity of the power function propagates the inequality $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\psi] \le \alpha$ from $\Theta_0$ to its closure and the inequality $\alpha \le \mathbb{E}_\theta[\psi]$ from $\Theta_1$ to its closure, so every unbiased level-$\alpha$ test is similar on $\omega_B$ and the boundary-similar class contains the unbiased class. Conversely, the constant test $\varphi \equiv \alpha$ is itself boundary-similar, and comparing $\varphi_0$ with it shows that $\varphi_0$ is unbiased.
summary: If every power function is continuous, a level-α test that is optimal among the tests similar on the common boundary of the null and alternative sets is uniformly most powerful unbiased.

hypotheses.label: continuous power

hypotheses.label: level α

title: Continuity of the Power Function of an Exponential Family
informal: Let $\{P_\eta\}$ be an exponential family on a finite-dimensional real inner product space of natural parameters, with natural statistic $T$, reference measure $ u$, and members given by the tilted densities proportional to $e^{\langle \eta, T(x) angle}$; let $\mathcal{N}$ denote the natural parameter set, the set of $\eta$ for which $e^{\langle \eta, T(x) angle}$ is $ u$-integrable. If $\varphi$ is a randomized test, that is, a measurable function of the observation with values in $[0,1]$, then the power function $$ \eta \;\longmapsto\; \mathbb{E}_\eta[\varphi] \;=\; rac{\int \varphi(x)\, e^{\langle \eta, T(x) angle}\, d u(x)}{\int e^{\langle \eta, T(x) angle}\, d u(x)} $$ is continuous at every point of the interior of $\mathcal{N}$.
summary: The power function of any randomized test against a finite-dimensional exponential family is continuous on the interior of the natural parameter set.

title: Similar Tests Have Neyman Structure under Bounded Completeness
informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a family of probability measures on the sample space, let $\omega$ be a set of boundary parameters, and let $T$ be a measurable statistic. Let $Q$ be a Markov kernel on the range of $T$, playing the role of the conditional distribution of the observation given $T = t$, and assume $T$ is sufficient for the boundary family, in the disintegration form that for every $\theta \in \omega$ the joint law of the pair $(T(X), X)$ under $P_\theta$ is the law of $T$ under $P_\theta$ composed with $Q$. Assume further that the family of laws of $T$ indexed by $\omega$ is boundedly complete: any bounded measurable function of $t$ whose mean vanishes under every one of those laws is almost everywhere zero. Then every randomized test $\varphi$ that is similar of size $\alpha$ on $\omega$, that is $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi] = \alpha$ for every $\theta \in \omega$ has *Neyman structure* with respect to $T$: for every $\theta \in \omega$ and almost every $t$ under the law of $T$, $$ \int \varphi \, dQ_t \;=\; \alpha . $$ Disintegrating the similarity equation along $T$ turns it into the statement that the bounded measurable function $t \mapsto \int \varphi \, dQ_t - \alpha$ has zero mean under every boundary law, and bounded completeness forces that function to vanish.
summary: If the family of laws of a sufficient statistic is boundedly complete, every similar test of size α has conditional size α given that statistic.

title: Neyman Structure for All Similar Tests Implies Bounded Completeness
informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a family of probability measures on the sample space, let $\omega$ be a set of boundary parameters, let $T$ be a measurable statistic, and let $Q$ be a Markov kernel on the range of $T$, playing the role of the conditional distribution of the observation given $T = t$. Then the family of laws of $T$ indexed by $\omega$ is boundedly complete: a bounded measurable function of $t$ whose mean vanishes under the law of $T$ for every $\theta \in \omega$ is almost everywhere zero. This is the converse of the statement that bounded completeness of the sufficient statistic forces every similar test to have Neyman structure.

title: Conditioning Eliminates the Nuisance Parameters
informal: Let the observation have a multiparameter exponential family distribution whose sufficient statistic splits into a real coordinate $U$ carrying the parameter of interest $\theta$ and a coordinate $T$, in a finite-dimensional inner product space, carrying the nuisance parameters $\vartheta$. Assume $U$ is measurable and $T$ is measurable, and assume the joint law of the pair $(U, T)$ is canonical on the parameter set $\Omega$, that is, for every $(\theta,\vartheta) \in \Omega$ it has density $$ C(\theta,\vartheta)\, \exp\bigl(\theta u + \langle \vartheta, t \rangle\bigr) $$ with respect to one fixed parameter-free measure $\nu$ on the range of the pair. Then there are a family of base measures $\nu_t$ on the line, depending only on $t$, and normalizing constants $C_t(\theta)$, depending only on $t$ and $\theta$ — in particular not on the nuisance parameters — such that for every parameter of $\Omega$ and almost every $t$ under the law of $T$, the conditional distribution of $U$ given $T = t$ has density $$ C_t(\theta)\, e^{\theta u} $$ with respect to $\nu_t$. Conditionally on $T = t$ the model is therefore a one-parameter exponential family in $\theta$ with natural statistic $u$, and the nuisance parameters have disappeared. Every test built on this conditional family has a nuisance-free conditional size, so the one-parameter optimality theory applies surface by surface.
summary: In a canonical multiparameter exponential family, the conditional law of the interest statistic given the nuisance statistic is a one-parameter exponential family whose base measure and normalizer do not involve the nuisance parameters.

No positivity or $\sigma$-finiteness is imposed on the base measures in the statement: those are consequences of the canonical form and belong in the proof.

title: UMP Unbiased Test of a Point Null in a One-Parameter Exponential Family
informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a one-parameter exponential family with natural statistic $T$ and densities $dP_\theta = C(\theta)\, e^{\theta T(x)}\, d\nu(x)$, and let $\Xi$ be a set of parameter values inside the interior of the natural parameter set, with the model agreeing with the canonical family at every $\theta \in \Xi$ and $\Xi$ open. Fix $\theta_0 \in \Xi$ and a level $0 < \alpha < 1$. Let $\varphi$ be a randomized test with critical values $C_1 \le C_2$ such that $\varphi$ rejects whenever $T < C_1$ or $T > C_2$, $\varphi$ accepts whenever $C_1 < T < C_2$, and $\varphi$ takes the constant randomization values $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ on $\{T = C_1\}$ and $\{T = C_2\}$. Suppose the constants satisfy both side conditions: the size condition $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[\varphi] = \alpha$, and the derivative condition $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[T\varphi] = \alpha\, \mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[T]$. Then $\varphi$ is uniformly most powerful unbiased at level $\alpha$ for testing $H : \theta = \theta_0$ against $K : \theta \neq \theta_0$, $\theta \in \Xi$. The second condition is not decoration. Unbiasedness forces the power function to have a minimum at $\theta_0$, and differentiating the power of an exponential family under the integral sign turns the vanishing of the derivative at $\theta_0$ into exactly $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[T\varphi] - \mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[T]\,\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[\varphi] = 0$, which combines with the size equation to give the displayed form. Neither equation may be dropped.
summary: For a point null in a one-parameter exponential family, the test rejecting outside an interval in the natural statistic is UMP unbiased once its constants satisfy the size and the derivative conditions.

title: UMP Unbiased Test of an Interval Null in a One-Parameter Exponential Family
informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a one-parameter exponential family with natural statistic $T$ and densities $dP_\theta = C(\theta)\, e^{\theta T(x)}\, d\nu(x)$, and let $\Xi$ be a set of parameter values inside the interior of the natural parameter set, with the model agreeing with the canonical family at every $\theta \in \Xi$ and $\Xi$ open. Fix $\theta_1 < \theta_2$ in $\Xi$ and a level $0 < \alpha < 1$. Let $\varphi$ be a randomized test with critical values $C_1 \le C_2$ such that $\varphi$ rejects whenever $T < C_1$ or $T > C_2$, $\varphi$ accepts whenever $C_1 < T < C_2$, and $\varphi$ takes the constant randomization values $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ at the two critical values. If $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_1}[\varphi] = \alpha$ and $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_2}[\varphi] = \alpha$, then $\varphi$ is uniformly most powerful unbiased at level $\alpha$ for testing $$ H : \theta_1 \le \theta \le \theta_2 \qquad\text{against}\qquad K : \theta < \theta_1 \ \text{ or }\ \theta > \theta_2 , \qquad \theta \in \Xi. $$ Here the boundary of the testing problem consists of the two endpoints, and unbiasedness together with continuity of the power function forces similarity there; so the two size equations replace the size-plus-derivative pair of the point-null problem. That the test also has level $\alpha$ at interior points of the null interval is a consequence, not an assumption: it follows from the variation-diminishing property of the exponential kernel, since the difference $\varphi - \alpha$ and a suitable combination $a e^{\theta_1 t} + b e^{\theta_2 t} - e^{\vartheta t}$ change sign at exactly the same two points.

title: UMP Unbiased One-Sided Test for a Multiparameter Exponential Family
informal: Let the observation have a multiparameter exponential family distribution whose sufficient statistic is a pair $(U, T)$, with $U$ real carrying the parameter of interest $\theta$ and $T$ carrying the nuisance parameters $\vartheta$ in a finite-dimensional space, and assume the joint law of $(U, T)$ is canonical on the parameter set $\Omega$, with density $C(\theta,\vartheta)\exp(\theta u + \langle \vartheta, t\rangle)$ against a fixed measure. Assume $(U, T)$ is sufficient in the operative sense that every randomized test of the observation is matched, in power at every parameter of $\Omega$, by a randomized test of the pair alone. Assume $\Omega$ is convex and $\Omega$ is not contained in any proper affine subspace, and that $\Omega$ reaches strictly below and strictly above the null value $\theta_0$. Let $C_0$ and $\gamma_0$ be measurable functions of $t$ with $\gamma_0(t) \in [0,1]$ for every $t$, and let $\varphi$ be the conditional one-sided test that, on the surface $T = t$, rejects when $U > C_0(t)$, randomizes with probability $\gamma_0(t)$ when $U = C_0(t)$, and accepts otherwise. If at every parameter of $\Omega$ whose interest coordinate equals $\theta_0$ the conditional size given $T = t$ is $\alpha$ for almost every $t$, then $\varphi$ is uniformly most powerful unbiased at level $\alpha$ for testing $$ H : \theta \le \theta_0 \qquad\text{against}\qquad K : \theta > \theta_0 $$ within $\Omega$, for any level $0 < \alpha < 1$.

formalizationNotes: **Two hypotheses are added relative to the transcribed statement, for independent reasons, and both are visible in the signature.** First, the transcription did not carry the book's standing convention that the observation *is* the sufficient statistic: the canonical hypothesis constrains only the law of the pair $(U, T)$, while uniform most powerful unbiasedness quantifies over all randomized tests of the sample space, so with a constant pair the remaining hypotheses say nothing about the model and the optimality conclusion is out of reach; the file records that configuration formally. The added sufficiency-reduction hypothesis restores the convention and is vacuously true in the book's own setting, where the sample space is the range of the pair. Second, the book's 'not contained in a linear space of dimension less than $k+1$' is read as an *affine* flat: the weaker linear-span condition does not suffice, since a convex set with full linear span can have a single-point boundary surface, leaving the completeness step without a full-dimensional slice. Two further instance hypotheses — Borel measurable structure and finite dimensionality of the nuisance space — are what make the canonical exponent measurable and the boundary slice full-dimensional. The conditional size conditions are imposed almost everywhere rather than everywhere, which is the weaker hypothesis and all the averaging identity consumes.

title: Family-Preserving Transformations Form a Group
informal: Call a bimeasurable bijection $g$ of the sample space *family-preserving* for a model $\{P_\theta\}$ when the law of $g(X)$ is again a member of the family: there is an induced map $\bar g$ of the parameter space *onto* itself with $$ P_\theta\{ g(X) \in A \} \;=\; P_{\bar g \theta}\{ X \in A \} $$ for every measurable set $A$. If the model is identifiable, that is, distinct parameters index distinct distributions, then the family-preserving transformations form a subgroup of the group of all permutations of the sample space: they contain the identity, are closed under composition, and are closed under inversion. The induced maps compose accordingly, $\overline{g' g} = \bar g' \, \bar g$ and $\overline{g^{-1}} = \bar g^{\,-1}$. Consequently any class of transformations leaving a testing problem invariant may be enlarged to a group of such transformations without loss, which is what makes the invariance reduction a group-theoretic device.
summary: For an identifiable model the bimeasurable bijections that preserve the family form a subgroup of the permutation group of the sample space.

hypotheses.label: identifiability

formalizationNotes: Preservation is defined set-theoretically: the induced parameter map is packaged existentially together with the surjectivity demanded of it (the 'onto' half of parameter preservation), rather than being bundled as a bijection. Injectivity of the induced map is deliberately **not** part of the definition — it is a consequence of identifiability, proved separately — which keeps the definition honest about what preservation alone delivers. This is why the subgroup construction carries the identifiability hypothesis explicitly: without it, closure under inversion is not available.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: Invariance as a systematic reduction principle for testing problems is due to Hunt and Stein (1946) and Stein (1956), developed in Lehmann's lecture tradition of the 1950s; the orbit and maximal-invariant calculus is treated systematically by Hall, Wijsman and Ghosh (1965). The book's Lemma 6.1.1 records that the family-preserving transformations form a group; the Lean version constructs the subgroup explicitly and isolates identifiability as the hypothesis that closure under inversion requires.

title: Invariant Tests Are the Measurable Functions of a Maximal Invariant
informal: Let a group $G$ act on the sample space, and let $M$ be a maximal invariant for the action: it is constant along each orbit, and it takes equal values only at points of a common orbit. Points on a common orbit are indistinguishable by an invariant test, so at the level of sets an invariant test is automatically a function of $M$; upgrading that factor to a *measurable* function requires a structural assumption. Suppose a complementary measurable coordinate $Y$ is given for which $x \mapsto (M(x), Y(x))$ is a measurable embedding — one-to-one onto a measurable subset of the product, with measurable inverse, and suppose this coordinate map is onto the whole product. Then for a real function $\varphi$ on the sample space: $$ \varphi \ \text{is measurable and invariant} \iff \varphi = h \circ M \ \text{for some measurable } h. $$ The standard instance is the sample space $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\}$ with $G$ the scalings, $M(x) = x/\|x\|$ and $Y(x) = \|x\|$.
summary: Under a measurable coordinate assumption, a test is measurable and invariant exactly when it is a measurable function of a maximal invariant.

hypotheses.note: The statistic is invariant along orbits and separates distinct orbits.

hypotheses.label: measurable coordinate system
hypotheses.note: The pair of the maximal invariant and a complementary coordinate is a measurable embedding.

hypotheses.label: complete coordinates
hypotheses.note: That coordinate map is onto the whole product, so a measurable section of the maximal invariant exists.

formalizationNotes: **Surjectivity of the coordinate map is a documented amendment.** The frozen statement asked only for a measurable embedding, which is not enough: the factor's superlevel set is then the projection of a measurable subset of a product, which is analytic rather than measurable on a general measurable space, and no measurable uniformization is available in the pinned Mathlib. What the classical setup actually provides is a *complete* coordinate system — the pair is a bijection onto the full product, as in the scaling example — and surjectivity, with nonemptiness of the complementary coordinate space, makes the inverse image of a fixed second coordinate a measurable section of the maximal invariant, after which the projection issue disappears. The purely set-level factorization, which needs no structural assumption at all, is available separately in the same file.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The characterization of invariant functions as the functions of a maximal invariant is the backbone of the invariance program of Hunt and Stein (1946) and Stein (1956); the measurability subtleties attached to 'a test depending only on the maximal invariant' go back to Lehmann and Stein (1949), and the relationship between invariance and sufficiency is treated by Hall, Wijsman and Ghosh (1965). The book's Theorem 6.2.1 states the equivalence; the Lean statement makes the structural assumption behind the measurable factorization explicit and strengthens it to a complete coordinate system, which is what the classical examples supply.

title: Stepwise Maximal Invariants
informal: Let a group $G$ act on the sample space and let $D$ and $E$ be subgroups with $D$ and $E$ together generating $G$. Let $s$ be a maximal invariant for the subgroup $D$, and suppose the action of $E$ descends along $s$: equal values of $s$ are carried to equal values of $s$ by every element of $E$, so that each $e \in E$ induces a transformation $e^{*}$ of the range of $s$ by $e^{*}(s(x)) = s(ex)$. If $t$ is invariant under the induced group, that is $t(s(ex)) = t(s(x))$ for every $e \in E$ and every $x$, and $t$ separates the orbits of the induced group, that is $t(s(x_1)) = t(s(x_2))$ implies $s(x_2) = s(e x_1)$ for some $e \in E$, then $t \circ s$ is a maximal invariant for the whole group $G$. A maximal invariant may therefore be computed in stages: reduce first by one subgroup, then by the action the second subgroup induces on the reduced data.
summary: A maximal invariant for a group generated by two subgroups can be computed in two stages, first for one subgroup and then for the induced action of the other.

hypotheses.label: generating subgroups
hypotheses.note: The two subgroups together generate the whole group.

hypotheses.label: first-stage maximal invariant
hypotheses.note: The first statistic is a maximal invariant for the first subgroup.

hypotheses.label: compatibility
hypotheses.note: The second subgroup's action descends along the first statistic, so the induced transformations are well defined.

hypotheses.label: invariance of the second stage
hypotheses.note: The second statistic is invariant under the induced group.

hypotheses.label: orbit separation
hypotheses.note: The second statistic separates the orbits of the induced group.

formalizationNotes: The induced group acting on the range of the first statistic is not built as an abstract group object; its maximal-invariance requirement is transcribed pointwise through the first statistic. This is faithful: the compatibility hypothesis makes the assignment $e \mapsto e^{*}$ multiplicative on the range, so the induced transformations already form a group there and the two readings agree. The invariance half of the conclusion is obtained by observing that the set of group elements leaving the composite unchanged is a subgroup containing both generators.

The book states it as Theorem 6.2.2; the Lean statement transcribes the induced group's maximal-invariance condition pointwise through the first-stage statistic rather than constructing the induced group as an object.

title: UMP Invariant Test under a Finite Group with Transitive Induced Action
informal: Let a finite group $G$ act on the sample space with an induced action on the parameter space, and suppose the model intertwines the two actions, so that the law of $gX$ under $P_\theta$ is $P_{g\theta}$. Suppose the model is dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$ with measurable nonnegative densities $p_\theta$ and that $\mu$ is itself invariant under the group. Assume the null class $\Theta_0$ and the alternative class $\Theta_1$ are stable under the induced action, that the induced action is transitive on $\Theta_0$, and that the induced action is transitive on $\Theta_1$. Fix representatives $\theta_0 \in \Theta_0$ and $\theta_1 \in \Theta_1$ and write $$ \bar p_\theta(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} p_\theta(g x) $$ for the orbit average of a density. Let $\varphi$ be an invariant randomized test that rejects wherever $\bar p_{\theta_1} > k\, \bar p_{\theta_0}$ and accepts wherever $\bar p_{\theta_1} < k\, \bar p_{\theta_0}$. If $\varphi$ has size exactly $\alpha$ at the null representative, then $\varphi$ is uniformly most powerful among invariant level-$\alpha$ tests.
summary: When a finite group acts transitively on the null and on the alternative classes, the Neyman–Pearson test for the orbit-averaged densities is UMP invariant.

hypotheses.label: transitive on the alternative

hypotheses.note: The family has measurable nonnegative densities against the dominating measure.

formalizationNotes: The book writes the rejection region through the *parameter-side* average of the translated densities; the Lean statement uses the *sample-side* orbit average, and a companion lemma in the same file shows the two agree almost everywhere once the dominating measure is invariant, so nothing is lost. Invariance of the dominating measure is **not** removable: with the two-element group acting on the line by reflection, every member symmetric but the dominating measure asymmetric, the sample-side ratio is not the likelihood ratio and the test is invariant but not optimal. Stability of the two classes under the induced action is stated separately from transitivity, since transitivity relates two points of a class while stability says the class is not left. Invariance of the candidate is a hypothesis rather than a conclusion because the Neyman–Pearson prescription leaves the test free on the boundary set where the ratio equals the threshold.

The book's Theorem 6.3.1 states the finite-group case; the Lean version states it on the sample side, adds the invariance of the dominating measure (which the book's setting supplies implicitly and which the argument requires), and derives the existence of such a test as a corollary.

title: Almost Invariant Tests Are Equivalent to Invariant Ones
informal: A function is almost invariant with respect to a measure $\mu$ when, for each group element separately, it is unchanged along the action outside a $\mu$-null set, the exceptional set being allowed to depend on the group element. This is strictly weaker than invariance in general, and it is the class that appears naturally when invariance is compared with unbiasedness or reached through a sufficiency reduction. Let a group $G$ act jointly measurably on the sample space — the pair map $(g, x) \mapsto g x$ being measurable on the product — and let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure on the sample space. Suppose the group carries a $\sigma$-finite measure $\nu$ which is not the zero measure and whose null sets are stable under right translation, so that $\nu(B) = 0$ implies $\nu(Bg) = 0$ for every group element $g$. Then every measurable function $\varphi$ that is almost invariant with respect to $\mu$ agrees $\mu$-almost everywhere with a measurable function that is genuinely invariant. The right-translation condition holds in particular for a right-invariant measure, whose existence is guaranteed for a large class of groups by Haar theory, but the weaker null-set form is what the argument needs and is often easier to check directly.
summary: If the group carries a nonzero σ-finite measure whose null sets survive right translation, every measurable almost invariant function agrees almost everywhere with a genuinely invariant one.

hypotheses.label: nonzero group measure
hypotheses.note: The auxiliary measure on the group is not the zero measure, so it can be normalized.

hypotheses.label: quasi-invariance
hypotheses.note: Null sets of the group measure are preserved by right translation.

hypotheses.label: measurable function
hypotheses.note: The function under consideration is measurable.

hypotheses.label: almost invariance
hypotheses.note: For each group element the function is unchanged off a null set.

formalizationNotes: Non-degeneracy of the group measure is stated explicitly; the averaging step normalizes it to a probability measure, which is impossible for the zero measure, and the source leaves this implicit. The normalization is carried out inside the proof: a $\sigma$-finite measure carries an everywhere-positive integrable density, hence is equivalent to a finite one, and only null sets enter the hypotheses. Because the function need not be integrable, the averaging is performed in the bounded chart $\arctan$ and read back through $\tan$; the invariant representative is the *essential value* of the orbit function, which is genuinely invariant — not merely invariant almost everywhere — because right translation preserves both the property of being essentially constant along an orbit and the value of that constant. Quasi-invariance is therefore enough: no invariant mean or amenability device is needed. The conclusion is almost everywhere for the measure to which almost invariance refers; the reading 'null for the whole family' is recovered by taking that measure equivalent to the family.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The equivalence of almost invariance and invariance under a group carrying a measure with right-translation-invariant null sets belongs to the circle of ideas of Hunt and Stein (1946) and Stein (1956), and is used throughout Lehmann's development of invariance to compare invariance with unbiasedness. Counterexamples delimiting the structural hypotheses are due to Berk and Bickel (1968). The Lean statement is the book's Theorem 6.5.1 with the non-degeneracy of the group measure made explicit and with the invariant representative constructed by essential-value averaging in a bounded chart.

title: Invariant Power Function versus Almost Invariant Test
informal: Restricting attention to invariant tests departs from comparing tests purely by their power functions, so it is natural to ask what invariance means at the level of power functions. One implication is immediate: an almost invariant test has a power function invariant under the induced parameter action. The converse fails in general, but holds once the problem has been reduced to a statistic whose family of laws is boundedly complete. Let $T$ be a statistic, let the group act on its range and on the parameter space, and suppose the family of laws of $T$ is boundedly complete: a bounded measurable function with zero mean under every one of those laws vanishes almost everywhere, the reduced problem is invariant, that is, the law of $T$ under the parameter $g\theta$ is the image under $g$ of its law under $\theta$, and the group acts on the range of $T$ by measurable maps. Then for a randomized test $\psi$ of the statistic: $$ \mathbb{E}_{g\theta}[\psi] = \mathbb{E}_\theta[\psi] \ \text{ for all } g, \theta \iff \psi \ \text{is almost invariant under every law of } T. $$
summary: For a boundedly complete family of laws of a statistic, a test of that statistic has invariant power function exactly when it is almost invariant.

hypotheses.note: The family of laws of the statistic is boundedly complete.

hypotheses.label: invariant reduced model
hypotheses.note: The reduced model intertwines the actions on the statistic space and the parameter space.

hypotheses.label: measurable action
hypotheses.note: The group acts on the range of the statistic by measurable maps.

hypotheses.label: randomized test
hypotheses.note: The test of the statistic is measurable with values in the unit interval.

formalizationNotes: Sufficiency is *not* assumed here: the source's lemma needs only bounded completeness of the family of laws of the statistic. Almost invariance is taken with respect to every member of that family, matching the source's exceptional-set convention. The measurability of the group action on the range of the statistic is a **documented amendment**: a bare action does not supply it, and with a non-measurable action the translated test is not a test at all. The forward direction is exactly where bounded completeness is consumed; the converse is a change of variables.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The interplay of sufficiency and invariance was settled in the invariance program of Hunt and Stein (1946) and Stein (1956), with the definitive treatment of when the two reductions commute due to Hall, Wijsman and Ghosh (1965). The Lean statement is the book's Lemma 6.5.1 with the measurability of the induced action added as an explicit hypothesis.

title: Unbiasedness and Invariance Coincide when the Unbiased Test Is Unique
informal: Unbiasedness and invariance are logically independent optimality restrictions: each succeeds on problems where the other does not. Where both deliver a uniformly most powerful member, however, the two answers agree, and this is not accidental. Consider an invariant testing problem: the model intertwines the actions on the sample space and the parameter space, the null class is preserved by the induced action, and the alternative class is preserved by it. Let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure equivalent to the family, and let the level satisfy $0 \le \alpha \le 1$. If $\varphi^{*}$ is uniformly most powerful unbiased at level $\alpha$ and the UMP unbiased test is unique up to sets of measure zero, then any test $\varphi$ that is uniformly most powerful among almost invariant level-$\alpha$ tests satisfies $\varphi = \varphi^{*}$ almost everywhere — and the UMP almost invariant test is itself unique up to null sets.
summary: In an invariant problem with an essentially unique UMP unbiased test, that test and the UMP almost invariant test agree almost everywhere.

title: Convex Acceptance Regions Are Admissible in an Exponential Family
informal: Optimality within a restricted class does not by itself make a test admissible: a uniformly most powerful invariant test can be beaten uniformly by a test that is not invariant. For exponential families the classical route to admissibility is convexity of the acceptance region. Work on the natural-statistic scale of an exponential family in $s$ real natural parameters, and let $\varphi_0$ be the nonrandomized test that rejects exactly outside a set $A_0$. Assume the null class lies inside the natural parameter set and the alternative class lies inside it as well, both nonempty and disjoint; assume $A_0$ is closed and $A_0$ is convex; and assume the ray condition: whenever an open half-space $\{t : \langle a, t\rangle > c\}$ misses $A_0$, the alternative class contains a point $\theta^{*}$ and scalars $\lambda_n \to \infty$ with $\theta^{*} + \lambda_n a$ in the alternative class for every $n$. Then $\varphi_0$ is d-admissible: any randomized test whose power is at least that of $\varphi_0$ everywhere on the alternatives and at most that of $\varphi_0$ everywhere on the null has the same power function as $\varphi_0$ throughout.
summary: In an exponential family, a nonrandomized test whose acceptance region is closed and convex is d-admissible against any alternative class satisfying the ray condition.

title: A Unique Bayes Test Is Admissible
informal: A general decision-theoretic route to admissibility is to exhibit a procedure as the unique Bayes solution of some prior problem. For testing, the prior problem is a pair of priors — one carried by the null class, one by the alternative class — under $0$–$1$ loss. Let the model be dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, with densities $f_\theta(x)$ that are nonnegative and jointly measurable in the parameter and the observation, and suppose the support $\{x : f_\theta(x) > 0\}$ does not depend on $\theta$. Let $\Lambda_0$ and $\Lambda_1$ be prior probability measures on the parameter space with $\Lambda_0$ carried by the null class and $\Lambda_1$ carried by the alternative class, and form the mixture densities $$ h_i(x) \;=\; \int f_\theta(x)\, d\Lambda_i(\theta), \qquad i = 0, 1 . $$ Consider the nonrandomized Bayes test that rejects exactly where $h_1 \ge k\,h_0$. If the Bayes boundary $\{x : h_1(x) = k\,h_0(x)\}$ is $\mu$-null, then this test is d-admissible for testing the null class against the alternative class: any randomized test at least as powerful on the alternatives and no more powerful on the null has the same power function. The test is a Neyman–Pearson test for the simple problem $h_0$ versus $h_1$; a null boundary makes that test unique, and uniqueness upgrades directly to admissibility of the original test.
summary: The nonrandomized Bayes test for a pair of priors under 0–1 loss is d-admissible whenever its boundary set is null.

title: The Sign-Change Identity for Tests of Symmetry
informal: Tests of the hypothesis that a distribution is symmetric about the origin are usually built from the ranks of the absolute observations together with the signs, and are calibrated under the assumption that the observations are an independent sample from continuous distributions symmetric about the origin. That assumption is often the doubtful part of the model — the observations may be gathered under different experimental conditions and need be neither identically distributed nor independent. Let $\varphi$ be a randomized test of $N$ real observations, and suppose $\varphi$ has mean $\alpha$ under every product of continuous distributions symmetric about the origin — that is, whenever the coordinates are independent with atomless marginals each unchanged by sign reversal. Let $Q$ be a joint law of the $N$ observations which is unchanged by all $2^N$ coordinatewise sign changes and which assigns probability zero to every Lebesgue-null set. Then $\varphi$ has mean $\alpha$ under $Q$ as well. So the calibration survives the loss of both independence and identical distribution. In the paired-comparison design the sign-change invariance is guaranteed by construction, since the treatment is assigned at random within each pair; the stated significance level is therefore exactly right regardless of how the pairs differ from one another.
summary: A test calibrated on independent continuous symmetric samples keeps its level under every absolutely continuous joint law invariant under coordinatewise sign changes.

hypotheses.note: The test is measurable with values in the unit interval.

hypotheses.label: calibration
hypotheses.note: The test has mean α under every independent sample from continuous distributions symmetric about the origin.

hypotheses.label: sign-change invariance
hypotheses.note: The joint law is unchanged by every one of the coordinatewise sign changes.

hypotheses.label: absolute continuity
hypotheses.note: The joint law charges no Lebesgue-null set.

formalizationNotes: **Two hypotheses of the printed identity are adjusted.** The calibration hypothesis pins the sign-average to $\alpha$ only off a set that is null for every *non-atomic* law, and a sign-change invariant law may sit entirely on that set: with one observation, level $0$, the test the indicator of the origin and the joint law a Dirac mass at the origin, every printed hypothesis holds while the two integrals differ. The file records that configuration formally, together with a second one carrying no zeros and no ties. Absolute continuity of the joint law is therefore **required**, and it is exactly what rules atomic configurations of this kind out. Separately, the calibration class is widened from the independent identically distributed products to the merely independent ones. This second change is not forced: keeping the narrower class would require a completeness statement for order statistics from non-atomic laws, whose standard proof is an inclusion–exclusion over $N^N$ terms, whereas with independent marginals the same conclusion is one application of the product structure. Once the class is widened, the permutation-symmetry hypothesis of the printed statement is no longer needed and is dropped, so the identity holds for every randomized test.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: Randomization within matched pairs as the source of exact significance levels for sign and signed-rank procedures goes back to Fisher (1935), and the one-sample signed-rank statistic to Wilcoxon (1945). The observation that a symmetric rank test retains its level under any sign-change-invariant joint law, dispensing with both independence and identical distribution, belongs to the non-parametric program of Lehmann and Stein (1949). The Lean statement is the book's Lemma 6.10.1 with two documented amendments — a forced absolute-continuity assumption on the joint law, and a calibration class of independent but not necessarily identically distributed samples — both adjustments, and the situations that motivate them, documented in the same file.

title: Uniformly Most Accurate Equivariant Confidence Sets
informal: The duality between tests and confidence sets — the parameter $\theta$ lies in $S(x)$ exactly when $x$ lies in the acceptance region $A(\theta)$ — carries the invariance reduction across to interval estimation. A group acting on the data induces an action on the parameter space and hence on *sets* of parameters, and a confidence family is equivariant when transforming the data transforms the confidence statement in the matching way, so that the statement does not depend on the coordinate system. Let $A(\theta)$ be a family of acceptance regions with dual confidence family $S(x) = \{\theta : x \in A(\theta)\}$. Suppose the confidence family is equivariant, that is, applying the induced parameter action to $S(x)$ produces $S(gx)$, it has confidence level $1 - \alpha$, every acceptance region is measurable, and for each parameter value $\theta$ the nonrandomized test rejecting off $A(\theta)$ is uniformly most powerful at level $\alpha$ for testing $\theta' = \theta$ among the tests invariant under the transformations that fix $\theta$. Then the confidence family is uniformly most accurate equivariant at level $1 - \alpha$: among all equivariant families at that level, it minimizes the probability of covering each parameter value other than the true one.
summary: If each acceptance region is the UMP invariant test of its own parameter value, the dual equivariant confidence family is uniformly most accurate among equivariant families.

hypotheses.note: The family covers the true parameter with probability at least the stated level.

hypotheses.label: measurable acceptance regions
hypotheses.note: Each acceptance region is measurable, so that it can be read as a test.

hypotheses.label: UMP invariant acceptance regions
hypotheses.note: Each acceptance region is the UMP level-α test of its own parameter value among tests invariant under its stabilizer.

formalizationNotes: The source's group of transformations leaving the hypothesis $\theta' = \theta$ invariant is replaced here by the **stabilizer** of $\theta$, which is the largest such group, so the statement specializes to every group the source allows. The competitors are quantified over families with **measurable slices**, matching the sibling definition of uniform accuracy: without it the optimality transfer is not even expressible, since the argument inverts a competitor into a test that must be a critical function, and the coverage of a family with non-measurable slices is not a probability statement in the first place. Uniform accuracy is stated as the source defines it, by minimizing the probability of covering each value other than the true one. The dictionary between equivariant confidence families and equivariant acceptance regions is proved separately in the same file, in both directions; stabilizer-invariance of the acceptance regions alone is *not* enough to recover equivariance of the confidence family.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The duality between families of tests and confidence sets is due to Neyman (1937). The book's Lemma 6.11.1 states both halves; the Lean version proves the dictionary in both directions and the optimality transfer, using the stabilizer in place of an arbitrary group fixing the parameter.

title: Consistency of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test
informal: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be real-valued observations, let $F_0$ be a fully specified null distribution function, and let $\hat F_n$ be the empirical distribution function of the first $n$ observations. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic is $$ T_n \;=\; \sup_{t \in \mathbb{R}} \sqrt{n}\,\bigl|\hat F_n(t) - F_0(t)\bigr| \;=\; \sqrt{n}\, d_K(\hat F_n, F_0), $$ where $d_K$ denotes the sup (Kolmogorov) distance between distribution functions, and the test rejects when $T_n$ exceeds the calibrated critical value $s_\alpha = \sqrt{16 \log(4/\alpha)}$. Assume that the nominal level is a nondegenerate probability, $0 < \alpha < 1$, that the observations are independent and identically distributed with common sampling law $P$ whose distribution function is $F$, that $F_0$ is the distribution function of the null law, and that the alternative genuinely differs from the null, in the sense that $d_K(F, F_0) = \sup_t |F(t) - F_0(t)| > 0$. Then the power of the test tends to one, $$ \mathbb{P}\{T_n > s_\alpha\} \;\longrightarrow\; 1 \qquad (n \to \infty). $$
summary: Against any fixed alternative at positive Kolmogorov distance from the null, the power of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test tends to one.

hypotheses.label: independent observations

hypotheses.label: positive Kolmogorov distance
hypotheses.note: The alternative is separated from the null in the sup distance; this is what makes the separation $\sqrt n\, d_K(F,F_0)$ diverge.

formalizationNotes: Documented calibration deviation: the critical value is not the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the null law of $T_n$ but the constant $s_\alpha=\sqrt{16\log(4/\alpha)}$ obtained by solving $4e^{-s^2/16}=\alpha$, the envelope of the repository's uniform Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz deviation brick. Three consequences, all recorded in the source file: the critical value does not depend on $n$, so the companion level statement (`ks_dkw_level`) is nonasymptotic and no appeal to the Kolmogorov limit law $\mathbb P\{T_n>d\}\to 2\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^{k+1}e^{-2k^2d^2}$ is made; no continuity assumption on $F_0$ is needed anywhere; and the constants are conservative (the sharp tail is $2e^{-2d^2}$, the brick delivers $4e^{-d^2/16}$), so the calibrated test is conservative rather than exact. The theorem is derived as the constant selection of the triangular-array statement `ks_uniform_power`, the diverging separation being $\varepsilon_n=\sqrt n\,d_K(F,F_0)$. Measurability of the uncountable supremum defining $T_n$ is derived once, from right continuity of the distribution functions, rather than assumed.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The statistic and its limiting distribution are due to Kolmogorov (1933), with the further distribution theory developed by Smirnov (1948); the elementary consistency argument transcribed here goes back to Massey (1950). The book calibrates the test by the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the null law of $T_n$ and proves consistency from the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem together with convergence of the quantiles; the formalization instead calibrates through the uniform deviation inequality of Dvoretzky, Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956), whose sharp constant is due to Massart (1990), so that the critical value is an explicit constant and the level statement is nonasymptotic. What is formalized is therefore the same theorem for a slightly conservative critical value: the power against any fixed $F$ with $d_K(F,F_0)>0$ tends to one, with no continuity assumption on $F_0$.

title: Uniform power of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test over shrinking alternatives
informal: Consider a triangular array of experiments: at stage $n$ the sample $X_{n,1},\dots,X_{n,n}$ is drawn from a law with distribution function $F_n$, and $\hat F_n$ denotes the empirical distribution function of that sample. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test of a fixed, fully specified null distribution function $F_0$ rejects when $$ T_n \;=\; \sup_{t \in \mathbb{R}} \sqrt n\,\bigl|\hat F_n(t) - F_0(t)\bigr| \;=\; \sqrt n\, d_K(\hat F_n, F_0) $$ exceeds the critical value $s_\alpha = \sqrt{16 \log(4/\alpha)}$, where $d_K$ is the sup (Kolmogorov) distance between distribution functions; this is the same calibration under which the test is consistent against every fixed alternative. Assume the nominal level is a nondegenerate probability, $0 < \alpha < 1$, that at every stage the observations are independent and identically distributed, that the stage-$n$ alternative is separated from the null by $\sqrt{n}\, d_K(F_n, F_0) \ge \varepsilon_n$, and that the separation diverges, $\varepsilon_n \to \infty$. Then the power tends to one, $$ \mathbb{P}\{T_n > s_\alpha\} \;\longrightarrow\; 1 . $$ Equivalently: the power of the test converges to one uniformly over the classes of alternatives $\{F : \sqrt n\, d_K(F, F_0) \ge \varepsilon_n\}$. Behind it lies the nonasymptotic bound $\mathbb{P}\{T_n > s_\alpha\} \ge 1 - 4\exp\bigl(-(\varepsilon - s_\alpha)^2/16\bigr)$ valid whenever $\sqrt n\, d_K(F,F_0) \ge \varepsilon > s_\alpha$.
summary: The power of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test tends to one uniformly over alternatives separated from the null by more than $\varepsilon_n/\sqrt n$ whenever $\varepsilon_n \to \infty$.

title: The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test has no power at $o(n^{-1/2})$
informal: Consider a triangular array of experiments in which the stage-$n$ sample $X_{n,1},\dots,X_{n,n}$ is drawn from a law with distribution function $F_n$, and let $\hat F_n$ be its empirical distribution function. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test of a fixed, fully specified null distribution function $F_0$ rejects when $$ T_n \;=\; \sqrt n\, d_K(\hat F_n, F_0) \;=\; \sup_{t \in \mathbb{R}} \sqrt n\,\bigl|\hat F_n(t) - F_0(t)\bigr| $$ exceeds the critical value $s_\alpha = \sqrt{16 \log(4/\alpha)}$, where $d_K$ is the sup (Kolmogorov) distance; against a fixed alternative at positive Kolmogorov distance this test has power tending to one. Assume the nominal level is a nondegenerate probability, $0 < \alpha < 1$, that at every stage the observations are independent and identically distributed, and that the alternatives approach the null faster than $n^{-1/2}$, that is $\sqrt n\, d_K(F_n, F_0) \to 0$. Then $$ \limsup_{n \to \infty} \; \mathbb{P}\{T_n > s_\alpha\} \;\le\; \alpha : $$ the test cannot distinguish sequences of alternatives at Kolmogorov distance $o(n^{-1/2})$ from the null, so $n^{-1/2}$ is the exact resolution of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. More generally, if $\sqrt n\, d_K(F_n,F_0) \to \delta$ with $\delta < s_\alpha$, then the limiting power is at most $4\exp\bigl(-(s_\alpha-\delta)^2/16\bigr)$.
summary: Against alternatives approaching the null faster than $n^{-1/2}$ in Kolmogorov distance, the limiting power of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test is at most the nominal level.

title: Pearson's chi-squared statistic: the null limiting distribution
informal: In $n$ independent trials, each resulting in one of $k+1$ outcomes, let $Y_j$ denote the number of trials falling in cell $j$ and let $$ Q_n \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k+1} \frac{(Y_j - n\pi_j)^2}{n\pi_j} $$ be Pearson's chi-squared statistic for the simple null hypothesis that cell $j$ has probability $\pi_j$. Assume there is at least one degree of freedom, $k \ge 1$, that the null cell probabilities are strictly positive, i.e. an interior point of the simplex and sum to one, that at every stage the trials are independent and identically distributed, and that the null hypothesis holds, so that a single trial falls in cell $j$ with probability $\pi_j$. Then $Q_n$ converges in distribution to the chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom, $$ Q_n \;\Longrightarrow\; \chi^2_k . $$ The degrees of freedom are one fewer than the number of cells because the counts satisfy the linear constraint $\sum_j Y_j = n$, so only $k$ of the centred and scaled cell frequencies are free.
summary: Under a simple multinomial null, Pearson's chi-squared statistic converges in distribution to the chi-squared law with one degree of freedom fewer than the number of cells.

hypotheses.note: At each sample size the trials are jointly independent with a common law.

hypotheses.label: simple null hypothesis
hypotheses.note: The cell probabilities of the sampling law are exactly $\pi_1,\dots,\pi_{k+1}$.

formalizationNotes: The statistic is defined directly on categorical observations taking values in a $(k+1)$-element set rather than on a multinomial random vector: the cell counts are then genuine functions of the sample, the multinomial law is a consequence of independence rather than an assumption, and independence enters exactly as in the other sampling models of the area. Cell probabilities are recorded through the law of a single observation, which keeps the null and the local alternatives in one format. Degenerate cells ($\pi_j=0$) or an empty sample make the corresponding summand a division by zero, i.e. the junk value $0$; every statement carries the interior-point hypothesis. The proof is the multivariate central limit theorem for the vector of the first $k$ centred cell frequencies followed by the continuous mapping theorem for the quadratic form with the inverse covariance matrix; the algebraic identity that this quadratic form equals $Q_n$ (which reintroduces the $(k+1)$-st cell through a Sherman–Morrison inverse) is the only combinatorial step.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The statistic and the chi-squared approximation to its null distribution are due to Pearson (1900). The book's Theorem 16.3.1 is stated for the simple null hypothesis and proved by the multivariate central limit theorem; the formalization follows that route verbatim, with the degrees of freedom $k$ arising from the linear constraint on the cell counts, and adds the interior-point requirement $\pi_j>0$ explicitly, since without it the limiting covariance matrix is singular and the statistic itself divides by zero.

title: Pearson's statistic under local alternatives: the noncentral chi-squared limit
informal: In $n$ independent trials, each resulting in one of $k+1$ outcomes, let $Y_j$ be the number of trials falling in cell $j$ and let $$ Q_n \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k+1} \frac{(Y_j - n\pi_j)^2}{n\pi_j} $$ be Pearson's chi-squared statistic for the simple null hypothesis that cell $j$ has probability $\pi_j$, whose null limiting law is the chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom. Now let the true cell probabilities move towards the null at the parametric rate, $$ p^{(n)}_j \;=\; \pi_j + \frac{h_j}{\sqrt n}, \qquad j = 1, \dots, k+1 . $$ Assume the null cell probabilities are strictly positive and sum to one, that the local shifts sum to zero, so that the perturbed vector is again a probability vector, that at every stage the trials are independent and identically distributed, and that at stage $n$ a single trial falls in cell $j$ with probability $\pi_j + h_j/\sqrt n$. Then $$ Q_n \;\Longrightarrow\; \chi^2_k(\lambda), \qquad \lambda \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k+1} \frac{h_j^2}{\pi_j}, $$ the noncentral chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter $\lambda$. The noncentrality is the squared length of the local shift measured in the multinomial information metric.
summary: Along local alternatives $\pi_j + h_j n^{-1/2}$, Pearson's statistic converges in distribution to a noncentral chi-squared law with noncentrality $\sum_j h_j^2/\pi_j$.

title: Pearson's chi-squared test is asymptotically maximin
informal: In $n$ independent trials, each falling in one of $k+1$ cells, let $Y_j$ be the cell counts and let $$ Q_n \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k+1} \frac{(Y_j - n\pi_j)^2}{n\pi_j} $$ be Pearson's chi-squared statistic for the simple null $p = \pi$. Consider the shrinking families of alternatives $p = \pi + h/\sqrt n$ whose standardized distance $$ \lambda(h) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k+1} \frac{h_j^2}{\pi_j} $$ from the null is at least $b^2$, whose shifts are centred ($\sum_j h_j = 0$), and which keep $\pi + h/\sqrt n$ a probability vector. Assume the family has positive radius, $b > 0$, that the critical value $c$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom, that the null cell probabilities are strictly positive, that under every local parameter the trials are independent and identically distributed, and that under the local parameter $h$ a single trial falls in cell $j$ with probability $\pi_j + h_j/\sqrt n$. Then the minimum power of Pearson's test, which rejects when $Q_n > c$, converges over that family to $$ \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\chi^2_k(b^2) > c\bigr\}, $$ and no sequence of tests based on the sample whose power at the null tends to $\alpha$ can exceed that value in the limit. Pearson's chi-squared test is therefore asymptotically maximin against these local alternatives; the worst case is asymptotically attained on the inner boundary $\lambda(h) = b^2$, the noncentral chi-squared tail being increasing in the noncentrality parameter.
summary: Over the local multinomial alternatives at standardized distance at least $b$ from the null, Pearson's test attains the maximal limiting minimum power among all sample-based tests of asymptotic level $\alpha$.

title: Chi-squared power decreases in the number of degrees of freedom
informal: Let $$ M(k,h) \;=\; \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\chi^2_k(h^2) > c_k\bigr\} $$ be the limiting power of the chi-squared test with $k$ degrees of freedom against a local alternative at standardized distance $|h|$ from the null, where $c_k$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the central chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom, for every $k \ge 1$ — so that $M(k,0) = \alpha$ — and the nominal level is a nondegenerate probability, $0 < \alpha < 1$. Then $M(\cdot, h)$ is nonincreasing in the number of degrees of freedom, and strictly decreasing when $h \ne 0$: $$ 1 \le k_1 \le k_2 \;\Longrightarrow\; M(k_2, h) \le M(k_1, h), $$ with strict inequality when $k_1 < k_2$ and $h \ne 0$. Spending degrees of freedom on directions in which the alternative does not move costs power; this is the quantitative reason why the number of cells of a chi-squared test cannot be increased for free.
summary: For a fixed noncentrality, the power of the level-$\alpha$ chi-squared test is nonincreasing in the degrees of freedom, and strictly decreasing whenever the noncentrality is positive.

title: Asymptotic maximin upper bound for multisided local alternatives
informal: Let $\{Q_{n,h}\}$ be a triangular array of local experiments indexed by a local parameter $h \in \mathbb{R}^k$ — in the applications, the law of a sample of size $n$ under $\theta_0 + h n^{-1/2}$ — standardized so that the information matrix is the identity, and let $\varphi_n$ be any sequence of randomized tests. Assume the sphere of alternatives has positive radius $b$, that the critical value $c$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom, that the tests are asymptotically of level $\alpha$, i.e. their power at the null tends to $\alpha$, that the centring statistics $Z_n$ converge in distribution to the standard Gaussian law $N(0, I_k)$ under the null experiment, that the log-likelihood ratio of $Q_{n,h}$ against $Q_{n,0}$ admits the quadratic expansion $\langle h, Z_n\rangle - \tfrac12\|h\|^2$ uniformly over the sphere $\|h\| = b$, with remainder dominated by an envelope that is negligible in probability under the null, and that the families of alternatives eventually contain that sphere. Then $$ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\; \inf_{h \in S_n} \; \mathbb{E}_{Q_{n,h}}[\varphi_n] \;\le\; \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\chi^2_k(b^2) > c\bigr\}. $$ The bound is proved by the least-favourable mixture route: the minimum power over the alternatives is at most the power against the uniform mixture over the sphere, the Neyman–Pearson lemma bounds the latter by the power of the likelihood-ratio test, and the sphere-averaged limiting likelihood ratio is a monotone function of $\|x\|$, so that the limiting Neyman–Pearson test *is* the chi-squared test.
summary: In an asymptotically normal array of local experiments, no test sequence of asymptotic level $\alpha$ can exceed the noncentral chi-squared value in minimum power over a sphere of local alternatives.

title: Neyman's smooth test is asymptotically maximin
informal: To test a fully specified null law $P_0$ on an arbitrary sample space, embed it in the $k$-parameter exponential family of densities $$ p_\theta(x) \;=\; C_k(\theta)\exp\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\theta_j\,\psi_j(x)\Bigr) $$ relative to $P_0$, and test $\theta = 0$ with Neyman's smooth statistic $$ S_n \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k} Z_{n,j}^2, \qquad Z_{n,j} \;=\; n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_j(X_i), $$ rejecting when $S_n > c$. Assume the shell of alternatives has positive inner radius $b$ and a finite outer radius $B > b$, that the critical value $c$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom, that the score functions $\psi_1,\dots,\psi_k$ are orthonormal in $L^2(P_0)$ and orthogonal to the constants, i.e. have mean zero under $P_0$, that the null value $\theta = 0$ is an interior point of the natural parameter set, and that under the local parameter $h$ the observations are an independent sample from $p_{h n^{-1/2}}$. Then the minimum power of the smooth test over the local alternatives $\theta = h n^{-1/2}$ with $b \le \|h\| \le B$ converges to $$ \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\chi^2_k(b^2) > c\bigr\}, $$ and no sequence of sample-based tests of asymptotic level $\alpha$ does better in the limit. The worst case is asymptotically attained on the inner boundary $\|h\| = b$.
summary: Over the local alternatives $b \le \|h\| \le B$ of the embedding exponential family, Neyman's smooth test attains the maximal limiting minimum power among all sample-based tests of asymptotic level $\alpha$.

hypotheses.label: local experiments
hypotheses.note: The local experiment indexed by $h$ is the i.i.d. law of the embedding family at $\theta = h n^{-1/2}$.

formalizationNotes: Adjusted hypothesis: in the optimality half the competitors are required to be measurable functions of the sample, a restriction that appears inside the second conjunct of the conclusion. It is needed because the local experiment is abstract data and may encode $\|h\|$ in a coordinate the observations do not see, which a competitor reading that coordinate can exploit; the source file records such a local experiment. The upper-bound half is the instance of `asymptotic_maximin_upper_bound` with information matrix the identity — orthonormality of the scores is exactly what makes the Fisher information of the embedding family at the null equal to the identity, so the local shell is the Euclidean shell and the maximin value is the same noncentral chi-squared number that appears for Pearson's test. The upper bound remains true, a fortiori, with the outer radius removed; the attainment half genuinely needs $B<\infty$, its lower half being a compactness argument on the shell. The companion `smoothStat_weakConverges_chiSquared` gives the null limit $S_n\Rightarrow\chi^2_k$, which is what makes the test asymptotically of level $\alpha$. The chi-squared test of the multinomial problem is the special case in which the sample space is finite and the scores are the whitened cell indicators.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The smooth test, the embedding family and the asymptotic maximin property against the alternatives it generates are due to Neyman (1937); the statistic it specializes is Rao's (1948) score statistic, and the reduction of the local optimality question to a Gaussian shift experiment follows Le Cam (1960). The special case in which the statistic reduces to Pearson's (1900) is the multinomial one. The book states the theorem for the shell $b\le\|h\|\le B$; the formalization proves both halves for exactly that shell and records the sample-measurability restriction on competitors that the optimality half requires.

title: Neyman's smooth test with a growing number of score directions
informal: Neyman's smooth test of a fully specified null law $P_0$ is based on the statistic $$ S_{n,k} \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k} Z_{n,j}^2, \qquad Z_{n,j} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_j(X_i), $$ built from a system $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots$ of score functions on the sample space. For a fixed number $k$ of score directions the test is asymptotically maximin against the local alternatives those $k$ directions generate, but it is consistent only against alternatives that move one of the first $k$ scores. Letting $k$ grow with the sample size removes that restriction, at the price of a different limit theory: since $\chi^2_k \approx N(k, 2k)$ for large $k$, the chi-squared approximation is replaced by a normal one. Assume the score functions are orthonormal in $L^2(P_0)$ and orthogonal to the constants, that their third absolute moments are finite and uniformly bounded, $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}|\psi_j(X)|^3 \le B$ for every $j$, and that the number of directions diverges, $k_n \to \infty$, but slowly enough that $k_n^3/n \to 0$. Then, under the null hypothesis that the observations are an independent sample from $P_0$, $$ \frac{S_{n,k_n} - k_n}{(2k_n)^{1/2}} \;\Longrightarrow\; N(0,1), $$ so that the test rejecting when that ratio exceeds the standard normal upper-$\alpha$ quantile is asymptotically of level $\alpha$.
summary: If the number of score directions grows with $k_n^3/n \to 0$, the standardized smooth statistic is asymptotically standard normal under the null.

formalizationNotes: The proof consumes a multivariate Berry–Esseen bound over Euclidean balls with a *dimension-free* constant, stated in this file as `bentkus_berry_esseen_ball` and discharged by `berryEsseen_ball_elementary` in the area's `ForMathlib` layer. Honest deviation: Bentkus (2003) states the sharp rate $C\beta/\sqrt n$ by Fourier analysis over convex bodies; what is proved in the library is the strongest bound the elementary “smooth the indicator and swap” route delivers, $C(\beta/\sqrt n)^{1/4}$ with $\beta=\int\|y\|^3\,d\nu$, which still suffices here — with $\beta \le Bk^{3/2}$ the error is $O((Bk_n^{3/2}/\sqrt n)^{1/4})$, and that tends to zero under exactly the source's condition $k_n^3/n\to0$. The absence of a dimensional factor in the constant is what makes the growth condition as weak as $k_n^3/n\to0$; the convex-set bound, whose constant carries a factor $k^{1/4}$, would force the strictly stronger $k_n^{7/2}/n\to0$. The reduction runs through distribution functions and is closed by a Helly–Bray/Levy inversion built from the pi-system criterion for weak convergence.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The smooth test and its score system are due to Neyman (1937); the multivariate Berry–Esseen bound over convex sets and, with a dimension-free constant, over Euclidean balls is due to Bentkus (2003), whose one-dimensional ancestors are Berry (1941) and Esseen (1942). Normal limits for chi-squared-type statistics with growing dimension go back, in the goodness-of-fit setting, to the analyses of the number of cells by Mann and Wald (1942). The book quotes the ball bound without proof; the formalization proves the limit theorem outright, from a version of the ball bound with an honest but weaker rate that still suffices under the printed growth condition.

title: Limit law of an efficient estimator under local alternatives
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent observations from a model $\{P_\theta\}$ that is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with score $\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}$, given by densities with respect to a dominating measure, and whose Fisher information matrix $I(\theta_0)$ is nonsingular. Let $\hat\theta_n$ be an asymptotically linear (efficient) estimator sequence at $\theta_0$, i.e. one satisfying $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0) = I^{-1}(\theta_0) Z_n + o_P(1)$ under $P^n_{\theta_0}$, where $$ Z_n \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i \le n} \tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(X_i) $$ is the normalized score. The expansion is assumed *only at $\theta_0$*. Then for every local alternative sequence $\theta_n = \theta_0 + h_n/\sqrt n$ with $h_n \to h$, under $P^n_{\theta_n}$, $$ \sqrt{n}\,(\hat\theta_n - \theta_n) \;\rightsquigarrow\; N\bigl(0, I^{-1}(\theta_0)\bigr), $$ the same law as under $\theta_0$; equivalently $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0) \rightsquigarrow N(h, I^{-1}(\theta_0))$. This weak robustness of the limiting law under perturbations of size $n^{-1/2}$ is what makes such estimator sequences the backbone of asymptotic testing theory.
summary: An asymptotically linear estimator sequence, recentred at a local alternative, has the same Gaussian limit law there as it has at the null.

formalizationNotes: The parameter set is the whole Euclidean space, which is open, so the source's “open subset of $\mathbb R^k$” needs no separate hypothesis. Because each sample size lives on its own sample space, the $o_P(1)$ of the linearization is spelled out as: for every $\varepsilon>0$ the probability that the remainder has norm at least $\varepsilon$ tends to zero. The proof route is contiguity of the local experiments plus Le Cam's third lemma applied to the pair (linearized estimator, log-likelihood ratio), followed by the Cramér–Wold device; the fixed-direction case is proved for the full sequence, with no subsequence extraction, because asymptotic linearity identifies the joint limit outright, and the moving direction $h_n$ is replaced by its limit through an $n$-fold Hellinger estimate obtained by tensorising the per-sample residual. The file is free of unproved content. The delta-method consequence $\sqrt n(g(\hat\theta_n)-g(\theta_n))\rightsquigarrow N(0,\dot g(\theta_0)I^{-1}(\theta_0)\dot g(\theta_0)^\top)$ is the companion `weak_limit_g_estimator_under_local_alternatives`.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: Contiguity, local asymptotic normality and the third lemma are due to Le Cam (1960), with the quadratic-mean differentiability hypothesis introduced in Le Cam (1970); the systematic use of contiguity to transfer limit laws to local alternatives, and the notion of a regular estimator sequence, are due to Hájek (1962). The book assumes the linear expansion of the estimator at $\theta_0$ only and deduces the limit along every local alternative; the formalization does the same, assuming neither a construction of the estimator nor any expansion away from $\theta_0$.

title: The normalized score vector under local alternatives
informal: Let the model be differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with score $\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}$, given by densities with respect to a dominating measure, and with nonsingular Fisher information matrix $I(\theta_0)$. Under $P^n_{\theta_0}$ the normalized score $$ Z_n \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i\le n}\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(X_i) $$ is asymptotically $N(0, I(\theta_0))$. Then along a local alternative sequence $\theta_n = \theta_0 + h_n/\sqrt n$ with $h_n \to h$, the limit is the *same Gaussian, shifted by* $I(\theta_0)h$: $$ Z_n \;\rightsquigarrow\; N\bigl(I(\theta_0)h,\; I(\theta_0)\bigr) \qquad \text{under } P^n_{\theta_n}. $$ The alternative moves the mean of the limiting law while leaving the covariance unchanged, which is exactly what makes the local power of the score test computable.
summary: Along local alternatives the normalized score vector converges to the same Gaussian law as under the null, shifted in mean by the information matrix applied to the local direction.

title: The Rao score statistic is asymptotically chi-squared
informal: Test the simple null $\theta = \theta_0$ in an i.i.d. model with $k$-dimensional parameter, using the Rao score statistic $$ R_n \;=\; Z_n^{\top}\, I^{-1}(\theta_0)\, Z_n, \qquad Z_n \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i\le n}\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(X_i), $$ a quadratic form in the normalized score that uses no estimator of the parameter at all. Assume the model is a family of densities with respect to a dominating measure, that it is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with score $\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}$, and that the Fisher information matrix $I(\theta_0)$ is positive definite. Then, under $P^n_{\theta_0}$, $$ R_n \;\rightsquigarrow\; \chi^2_k . $$ Consequently the score test rejecting when $R_n$ exceeds the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\chi^2_k$ is asymptotically of level $\alpha$.
summary: Under the simple null, the Rao score statistic converges in distribution to the chi-squared law with as many degrees of freedom as parameters.

title: Asymptotic equivalence of the Wald, score and likelihood ratio statistics
informal: Three statistics test the same simple null $\theta = \theta_0$ in an i.i.d. model with $k$-dimensional parameter: the Wald statistic $W_n = n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)^{\top} I(\theta_0)(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)$, the Rao score statistic $R_n = Z_n^{\top} I^{-1}(\theta_0) Z_n$, and the likelihood ratio statistic $2\log \Lambda_n = 2[\ell_n(\hat\theta_n) - \ell_n(\theta_0)]$. Here $I(\theta_0)$ is the Fisher information at the null value, $$ Z_n \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i \le n} \tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(X_i) $$ is the normalized score, $\ell_n(\theta) = \sum_{i\le n}\log p_\theta(X_i)$ is the log-likelihood of the sample, and $\hat\theta_n$ is an estimator sequence for $\theta$. Assume the model is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with score $\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}$, that the Fisher information $I(\theta_0)$ is positive definite, that $\hat\theta_n$ is asymptotically linear at $\theta_0$, i.e. $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0) = I^{-1}(\theta_0)Z_n + o_P(1)$, and, for the likelihood ratio half, that there is an envelope function $M$ with finite mean under $P_{\theta_0}$ satisfying the two-point second-order bound $\bigl|\log(p_\theta(x)/p_{\theta_0}(x)) - \log(p_{\theta'}(x)/p_{\theta_0}(x)) - \langle\theta-\theta', \tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(x)\rangle\bigr| \le M(x)(\|\theta-\theta_0\| + \|\theta'-\theta_0\|)\|\theta-\theta'\|$ for all $\theta, \theta'$ in a neighbourhood of $\theta_0$ and all sample points $x$. Then, under $P^n_{\theta_0}$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $$ \mathbb{P}\{|W_n - R_n| \ge \varepsilon\} \to 0 \quad\text{and}\quad \mathbb{P}\{|2\log\Lambda_n - R_n| \ge \varepsilon\} \to 0 . $$ The three tests therefore reject the same data sets with probability tending to one, and each statistic converges in distribution to $\chi^2_k$.
summary: Under the simple null, the Wald and likelihood ratio statistics each differ from the Rao score statistic by a quantity tending to zero in probability.
