formalizationNotes: Adjusted hypothesis: the book's second-order remainder condition is *one-point*, controlling the Taylor remainder of $\theta\mapsto\log p_\theta(x)$ only at the base point $\theta_0$. That condition does not by itself deliver the uniform local expansion the likelihood-ratio half needs — the situation it leaves open is analysed at `sup_LAN_remainder_tendsto`, where a data-dependent direction inside the local ball keeps the remainder bounded away from zero — so the two-point form displayed above is used; setting $\theta'=\theta_0$ returns the printed condition verbatim, and the two-point form follows from an integrable bound on the second derivative of $\theta\mapsto\log p_\theta(x)$, which is how applications verify it. Hypotheses are assigned per statistic rather than globally: the envelope is imposed only on the likelihood-ratio half, the Wald half needing only quadratic mean differentiability, the score limit and the assumed expansion. The Wald statistic is normalized by $I(\theta_0)$ rather than $I(\hat\theta_n)$, the source noting the two are interchangeable. Likelihood ratios are read through the density ratio, so points where both densities vanish contribute zero.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The three statistics are due to Wald (1943), Rao (1948) and Wilks (1938). The modern proof, which replaces classical third-derivative conditions by quadratic-mean differentiability and contiguity, is due to Le Cam (1960, 1970). The book states the whole trinity under one set of standing assumptions; the formalization splits them, imposing the second-order envelope only where it is consumed, and strengthens the printed one-point envelope to its two-point form, which is the minimal repair that makes the uniform expansion at a random direction true.

title: Wilks' theorem for an affine composite null
informal: Let the null hypothesis restrict $\theta$ to an affine subspace $a + \operatorname{range} B$ of the $k$-dimensional parameter space — equivalently, $A(\theta - a) = 0$ for a matrix $A$ of full rank $p$ — where the chart $B$ is injective and the codimension is the difference of dimensions, $m + p = k$ with $p \ge 1$. Write $\ell_n(\theta) = \sum_{i \le n}\log p_\theta(X_i)$ for the log-likelihood of an independent sample. Let $\hat\theta_n$ be an asymptotically linear (efficient) estimator sequence in the full model and $\hat\beta_n$ an asymptotically linear estimator sequence in the restricted model $\beta \mapsto P_{a + B\beta}$, and form $$ 2\log\Lambda_n \;=\; 2\bigl[\ell_n(\hat\theta_n) - \ell_n(a + B\hat\beta_n)\bigr]. $$ Assume the model is differentiable in quadratic mean at a null point $\theta_0 = a + B\beta_0$ with score $\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}$ and positive definite Fisher information, that there is a function $M$ with finite mean under $P_{\theta_0}$ satisfying the two-point second-order bound $\bigl|\log(p_\theta(x)/p_{\theta_0}(x)) - \log(p_{\theta'}(x)/p_{\theta_0}(x)) - \langle\theta-\theta', \tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(x)\rangle\bigr| \le M(x)(\|\theta-\theta_0\| + \|\theta'-\theta_0\|)\|\theta-\theta'\|$ for all $\theta, \theta'$ in a neighbourhood of $\theta_0$ and all sample points $x$ — the condition that makes the quadratic expansion of the log-likelihood ratio uniform over bounded local directions — and that the densities have a common support: every parameter value gives positive density at every sample point where $\theta_0$ does. Then, under $P^n_{\theta_0}$, $$ 2\log\Lambda_n \;\rightsquigarrow\; \chi^2_p : $$ the degrees of freedom count the restrictions, i.e. the dimension of the full parameter space minus that of the null.
summary: For a null restricting the parameter to an affine subspace of codimension $p$, the likelihood ratio statistic converges in distribution to the chi-squared law with $p$ degrees of freedom.

hypotheses.label: common support

hypotheses.note: The increment of the log-likelihood-ratio remainder between two parameter values is bounded by $M(x)$ times the product of $\|\theta-\theta'\|$ with $\|\theta-\theta_0\|+\|\theta'-\theta_0\|$, for all $\theta,\theta'$ near $\theta_0$ and all sample points.

formalizationNotes: The composite null is presented as an affine subspace given by a chart rather than by constraint equations, which lets the restricted model be an honest parametric family in the chart, so that “efficient estimator assuming the null” is the *same* predicate applied to the restricted model rather than an unverified formula for its influence function; differentiability in quadratic mean, the score and the information matrix all transport along the chart, the restricted score being the adjoint image of the full one. The smooth constraint version (null $\{\theta : g(\theta)=0\}$ with a continuously differentiable $g$ of full-rank Jacobian) is not stated separately: at $\theta_0$ it is this statement in the chart supplied by the implicit function theorem, with the same $p$ degrees of freedom. Two adjustments are recorded on the declaration: the common-support hypothesis, without which the splitting of the affine likelihood ratio does not hold at the points where a density vanishes and the ratio takes its junk value, and the two-point envelope condition. Joint measurability of the densities in parameter and sample point is required for the statistic to be a measurable function of the sample.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The chi-squared limit of the likelihood ratio statistic for a composite null is Wilks' (1938) theorem; the companion Wald (1943) formulation tests the same restrictions through the estimator. The modern proof under quadratic-mean differentiability and contiguity is due to Le Cam (1960, 1970). The book states the result for a null given either by linear restrictions or by smooth constraints; the formalization proves the affine case in a chart of the null subspace — which is the same statement — and identifies the affine likelihood ratio with the difference of two simple-null score statistics, whence the $p$ degrees of freedom.

title: Uniform local asymptotic normality over bounded directions
informal: The quadratic expansion of the log-likelihood ratio $$ \log L_{n,h} \;=\; \langle h, Z_n\rangle - \tfrac12\langle h, I(\theta_0)h\rangle + o_P(1), \qquad L_{n,h} = \frac{L_n(\theta_0 + h/\sqrt n)}{L_n(\theta_0)}, $$ holds under quadratic mean differentiability for each *fixed* direction $h$; here $L_n(\theta) = \prod_{i \le n} p_\theta(X_i)$ is the likelihood of an independent sample, $I(\theta_0)$ is the Fisher information at $\theta_0$ and $Z_n = n^{-1/2}\sum_{i \le n}\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(X_i)$ is the normalized score. Arguments that substitute a *random* direction — most importantly $\hat h_n = \sqrt n(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0)$ in the analysis of the likelihood ratio statistic — need the remainder to be small uniformly over $\|h\| \le c$. Assume the model is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with score $\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}$, that there is an envelope $M$ with finite mean under $P_{\theta_0}$ satisfying the two-point second-order bound $\bigl|\log(p_\theta(x)/p_{\theta_0}(x)) - \log(p_{\theta'}(x)/p_{\theta_0}(x)) - \langle\theta-\theta', \tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(x)\rangle\bigr| \le M(x)(\|\theta-\theta_0\|+\|\theta'-\theta_0\|)\|\theta-\theta'\|$ for all $\theta, \theta'$ in a neighbourhood of $\theta_0$ and all sample points $x$, and fix a radius $c > 0$. Then, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, the probability under $P^n_{\theta_0}$ that *some* direction with $\|h\| \le c$ has remainder at least $\varepsilon$ tends to zero; equivalently $$ \epsilon_{n,c} \;=\; \sup_{\|h\|\le c}\Bigl|\log L_{n,h} - \bigl[\langle h, Z_n\rangle - \tfrac12\langle h, I(\theta_0)h\rangle\bigr]\Bigr| \;\xrightarrow{\;P\;}\; 0 . $$
summary: Under quadratic mean differentiability and a two-point second-order envelope condition, the remainder of the quadratic log-likelihood expansion is small uniformly over every bounded set of local directions.

hypotheses.note: Differentiability in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with the stated score; it gives the expansion for each fixed direction.

hypotheses.label: integrable envelope
hypotheses.note: The envelope has finite mean under the single-observation law at $\theta_0$.

hypotheses.label: two-point second-order envelope
hypotheses.note: The increment of the log-likelihood-ratio remainder between two parameter values is bounded by $M(x)$ times the product of $\|\theta-\theta'\|$ with $\|\theta-\theta_0\|+\|\theta'-\theta_0\|$, for all $\theta,\theta'$ near $\theta_0$ and all sample points.

hypotheses.label: radius of directions
hypotheses.note: Uniformity is claimed over the closed ball of radius $c$ in the local parameter.

formalizationNotes: Documented adjustment of the envelope condition. The source's condition is one-point, $|\log p_\theta(x)-\log p_{\theta_0}(x)-\langle\theta-\theta_0,\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(x)\rangle|\le M(x)\|\theta-\theta_0\|^2$, and it does not by itself give the uniform statement; the source file records the configuration it leaves open, a model on $[0,1]$ whose densities carry a perturbation $\exp(|\theta-\theta_0|^2(2\cdot\mathbf{1}_{A_{|\theta-\theta_0|}}-1))$ indexed by finite sets $A_s$ chosen so that for each $n$ some direction with $\|h\|\le c$ picks out the observed sample. Every fixed direction then has vanishing remainder almost surely, as it must, while at a data-dependent direction the remainder is at least $2c^2 n/(n+1)$, so the probability in the conclusion tends to one. The two-point form used here is the weakest strengthening that covers this: taking $\theta'=\theta_0$ returns the printed condition verbatim, it follows from an integrable bound on the second derivative of the log-density, and it is exactly what makes the remainder class stochastically equicontinuous. The supremum over an uncountable ball is avoided at statement level: instead of asserting that a possibly non-measurable supremum converges in probability, the statement bounds the (outer) measure of the event that some admissible direction has remainder at least $\varepsilon$, which is equivalent when quantified over all $\varepsilon>0$ and needs no measurable-selection argument. The proof is a net argument: the two-point envelope makes the remainder Lipschitz in $h$ with a random constant that is bounded in probability, and a finite net of the compact ball reduces uniformity to finitely many fixed-direction statements.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The quadratic expansion of the log-likelihood ratio and the local asymptotic normality framework are due to Le Cam (1960), with the quadratic-mean differentiability hypothesis introduced in Le Cam (1970). Uniform-in-direction control of the remainder is the technical device by which the classical likelihood ratio theory of Wilks (1938) is recovered without third-derivative conditions. The book states the expansion for fixed directions and uses it at a random one; the formalization isolates the uniform version, shows that the printed hypotheses do not imply it, and proves it under the two-point strengthening.

title: The Randomization Hypothesis
informal: Let $\mathbf{G}$ be a finite group of transformations acting on the sample space $\mathcal{X}$, and let $P$ be a candidate null distribution of the data $X$. The randomization hypothesis holds for $P$ when the law of the data is unchanged by every element of the group: for each $g \in \mathbf{G}$ the transformed observation $gX$ has the same distribution as $X$, that is, the image of $P$ under the map $x \mapsto gx$ is again $P$. Only the null law is required to be invariant; nothing at all is assumed about the distribution of the data under an alternative. Two standard instances are the group of the $2^n$ sign changes $x \mapsto (\pm x_1, \ldots, \pm x_n)$, for which the hypothesis says that the observations are symmetric about $0$, and the group of the $N!$ permutations of the coordinates of a pooled sample, for which it says that the pooled observations are exchangeable.
summary: The null distribution of the data is invariant under every element of a finite group of transformations of the sample space.
leanSignature:
def RandomizationHypothesis (P : Measure 𝓧) : Prop :=
  ∀ g : G, P.map (g • ·) = P
formalizationNotes: Stated for an arbitrary finite group acting on an arbitrary measurable space; invariance is expressed as equality of the pushforward measure with the original one. Measurability of the individual transformations is deliberately not built into the definition — it is carried as an explicit hypothesis wherever it is needed, because the group action is user-supplied data rather than something the setup forces.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: Randomization tests originate with R. A. Fisher (1935) and E. J. G. Pitman (1937); the group-theoretic formulation used here, in which a finite group of transformations leaves the null law invariant, is due to E. L. Lehmann and C. Stein (1949). The reference text isolates the invariance requirement as the defining condition of the whole construction, and the formalization follows it literally: invariance of $P$ under each element of the group, with no requirement whatsoever on the alternative.

title: The Randomization Test
informal: Fix a finite group $\mathbf{G}$ of transformations of the sample space, write $M = |\mathbf{G}|$, and let $T$ be an arbitrary real-valued test statistic. Given an observed data point $x$, order the $M$ values $T(gx)$, $g \in \mathbf{G}$, taken by the statistic over the orbit of $x$ as $$ T^{(1)}(x) \le T^{(2)}(x) \le \cdots \le T^{(M)}(x) , $$ and put $k = M - \lfloor M\alpha \rfloor$, so that $T^{(k)}(x)$ is the critical orbit order statistic. Write $M^{+}(x)$ for the number of group elements with $T(gx) > T^{(k)}(x)$ and $M^{0}(x)$ for the number with $T(gx) = T^{(k)}(x)$, and set $$ a(x) \;=\; \frac{M\alpha - M^{+}(x)}{M^{0}(x)} . $$ The randomization test is the critical function $\varphi$ that rejects when $T(x) > T^{(k)}(x)$, rejects with probability $a(x)$ when $T(x) = T^{(k)}(x)$, and accepts when $T(x) < T^{(k)}(x)$. The boundary weight is chosen so that $M^{+}(x) + a(x)\,M^{0}(x) = M\alpha$ exactly, which is what lets the construction calibrate without any integrality assumption on $M\alpha$.
summary: The level-$\alpha$ randomization test, which compares the observed statistic with the order statistics of its values over the orbit and randomizes on the boundary.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def randTest (T : 𝓧 → ℝ) (α : ℝ) (x : 𝓧) : ℝ :=
  if randCritValue G T α x < T x then 1
  else if T x = randCritValue G T α x then randGamma G T α x
  else 0
formalizationNotes: All constructions are total. Out-of-range orbit order statistics return $0$, and the boundary weight's denominator $M^{0}(x)$ is at least $1$ whenever the observed statistic equals the critical value (the identity element of the group always contributes), so the $0/0$ corner is unreachable in every statement that uses the test. That the resulting value always lies in $[0,1]$ — i.e. that this really is a critical function — is proved from the orbit identity rather than assumed.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The construction is Fisher's (1935) randomization test in the group-theoretic form of E. L. Lehmann and C. Stein (1949), with the boundary randomization that makes the level exact for arbitrary $M\alpha$. M. Dwass (1957) showed that a random subset of the group may be used in place of the whole group. The formalization transcribes the reference text's definition, including the ordering of the orbit values and the critical index $k = M - \lfloor M\alpha\rfloor$; it is defined for an arbitrary statistic, with no distributional input.

title: Exact Finite-Sample Level of the Randomization Test
informal: Let $\mathbf{G}$ be a finite group of transformations of the sample space, $M = |\mathbf{G}|$, and let $\varphi$ be the randomization test at nominal level $\alpha$ built from a real-valued statistic $T$: with $T^{(1)}(x) \le \cdots \le T^{(M)}(x)$ the ordered values of $T$ over the orbit $\{gx : g \in \mathbf{G}\}$ and $k = M - \lfloor M\alpha\rfloor$, it rejects when $T(x) > T^{(k)}(x)$, accepts when $T(x) < T^{(k)}(x)$, and rejects with the boundary probability that makes $\sum_{g \in \mathbf{G}}\varphi(gx) = M\alpha$ when $T(x) = T^{(k)}(x)$. Assume that the statistic $T$ is measurable, that each transformation $x \mapsto gx$ is measurable, and that the null law $P$ is invariant under every element of the group. If the nominal level satisfies $\alpha > 0$ and $\alpha < 1$, then the test has size exactly $\alpha$, $$ \mathbb{E}_P[\varphi(X)] \;=\; \alpha , $$ at every finite sample size.
summary: Under the randomization hypothesis the randomization test built from any statistic has size exactly $\alpha$ at every finite sample size.

theorem randTest_exact_level (P : Measure 𝓧) [IsProbabilityMeasure P] (T : 𝓧 → ℝ)
    (hT : Measurable T)
    (hsmul : ∀ g : G, Measurable (fun x : 𝓧 => g • x))
    (hrand : RandomizationHypothesis G P)
    {α : ℝ}
    (hα₀ : 0 < α) (hα₁ : α < 1) :
    powerAgainst P (randTest G T α) = α

title: Super-Uniformity of the Randomization $p$-Value
informal: With $\mathbf{G}$ a finite group of transformations, $M = |\mathbf{G}|$ and $T$ a real-valued statistic, the randomization $p$-value at a data point $x$ is the proportion of the orbit on which the statistic is at least as large as the observed value, $$ \hat p(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{M}\,\#\{\, g \in \mathbf{G} : T(x) \le T(gx) \,\} . $$ Assume that the statistic is measurable, that each transformation of the sample space is measurable, and that the null law is invariant under every element of the group. Then the $p$-value is super-uniform under the null law, $$ \mathbb{P}\{\hat p(X) \le u\} \;\le\; u \qquad \text{for all } 0 \le u \le 1 , $$ so that the nonrandomized test rejecting when $\hat p(X) \le \alpha$ has level $\alpha$ at every finite sample size, with no boundary randomization.
summary: Under the randomization hypothesis the randomization $p$-value is stochastically at least uniform, so rejecting when it is at most $\alpha$ gives a level-$\alpha$ test.

title: The Conditional Law Given the Orbit is the Randomization Distribution
informal: The orbits $\mathbf{G}x = \{gx : g \in \mathbf{G}\}$ of a finite transformation group partition the sample space; write $\mathcal{G}$ for the $\sigma$-field of sets that are unions of orbits, and $M = |\mathbf{G}|$. Assume that the statistic $T$ is measurable, that each transformation of the sample space is measurable, and that the null law is invariant under every element of the group. Then, for every threshold $t$, $$ \mathbb{P}\{\, T(X) \le t \mid \mathcal{G} \,\} \;=\; \frac{1}{M}\sum_{g \in \mathbf{G}} \mathbf{1}\{T(gX) \le t\} \qquad \text{almost surely,} $$ that is, the conditional distribution function of the statistic given the orbit of the data is exactly the randomization distribution.
summary: Under the randomization hypothesis the conditional distribution of the statistic given the orbit of the data is the uniform distribution on the orbit values, i.e. the randomization distribution.

hypotheses.label: measurable group action
hypotheses.note: Each of the finitely many transformations of the sample space is a measurable map.

hypotheses.label: randomization hypothesis
hypotheses.note: The null law is invariant under every element of the finite group.

formalizationNotes: The orbit $\sigma$-field is realized as the $\sigma$-algebra of measurable sets invariant under every group element. For a finite group this coincides with the $\sigma$-field generated by the orbit partition — a measurable set is a union of orbits precisely when each group element maps it onto itself — and working with the invariant sets directly avoids constructing the generated $\sigma$-field and makes measurability of the orbit average immediate. The general statement is proved for bounded measurable integrands; the displayed distribution-function form is its specialization to indicators of half-lines. Boundedness rather than integrability is the honest hypothesis, since it is what the indicator application supplies.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The conditional-uniformity description of randomization tests is due to E. L. Lehmann and C. Stein (1949), building on R. A. Fisher (1935) and E. J. G. Pitman (1937). The reference text derives it as the structural reason the construction is exact: the conditional law given the orbit does not depend on which invariant null distribution generated the data. The formalization proves the conditional-expectation identity against the $\sigma$-algebra of invariant sets and then specializes to indicators of half-lines to identify the right-hand side with the randomization distribution.

title: Asymptotic Behaviour of the Randomization Distribution
informal: Consider a triangular array: for each sample size $n$ a law $P_n$ on a sample space $\mathcal{X}_n$, a finite group $\mathbf{G}_n$ acting on it, and a real-valued statistic $T_n$. Write $$ \hat R_n(t) \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathbf{G}_n|}\sum_{g \in \mathbf{G}_n} \mathbf{1}\{T_n(gX^n) \le t\} $$ for the randomization distribution, and let $G_n, G_n'$ be independent and uniformly distributed on $\mathbf{G}_n$, independent of the data $X^n$. Assume that each statistic is measurable, that each group element acts measurably, and that the pair $\bigl(T_n(G_nX^n), T_n(G_n'X^n)\bigr)$ converges in distribution to a pair of independent random variables with common distribution $R$. Then, at every continuity point $t$ of the limiting distribution function, $$ \hat R_n(t) \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathbb{P}\;}\; R(t) . $$ Nothing here assumes the randomization hypothesis: the result describes the behaviour of the randomization distribution even when the null invariance fails, which is exactly what is needed to decide whether a randomization test remains asymptotically level $\alpha$. Under the same joint condition the $(1-\alpha)$-quantile of the randomization distribution — the data-dependent critical value — converges in probability to the corresponding quantile of the limit law, provided the latter is continuous and strictly increasing there.
summary: If the statistic recomputed at two independent uniform group elements is asymptotically independent with a common limit law, the randomization distribution converges in probability to that limit law.

Because such an array has no single fixed probability space, convergence in probability is expressed in its explicit epsilon form rather than through the fixed-space notion. A converse is proved in the same file: pointwise convergence in probability of the randomization distribution to a limiting distribution function forces the joint asymptotic-independence condition.

title: Asymptotic Normality of the Sign-Change Randomization Distribution
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent observations on the line with common law $P$, and take as randomization group the group of the $2^n$ sign changes $(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n)\cdot(x_1,\dots,x_n) = (\varepsilon_1x_1, \dots, \varepsilon_nx_n)$ with $\varepsilon_i \in \{\pm 1\}$; the associated randomization distribution of a statistic $T_n$ is $$ \hat R_n(t) \;=\; \frac{1}{2^n}\sum_{\varepsilon \in \{\pm1\}^n} \mathbf{1}\{T_n(\varepsilon X) \le t\} . $$ Let $\tilde P$ denote the symmetrization of $P$, the law of $X$ multiplied by an independent random sign, whose distribution function is $\tilde F(t) = \tfrac12\bigl[F(t) + 1 - F(-t)\bigr]$ at continuity points of $F$. Assume that the influence function $\psi$ is odd, that it is measurable, that it is square-integrable under the symmetrized law, that its second moment under the symmetrized law equals $\tau^2$, that each statistic $T_n$ is measurable, and that the statistic is asymptotically linear under the symmetrized law, meaning that $T_n - n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi(X_i)$ tends to $0$ in probability when the data are drawn from $\tilde P$. Then, under the original law $P$, $$ \hat R_n(t) \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathbb{P}\;}\; \Phi(t/\tau) \qquad \text{for every } t , $$ with $\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function; correspondingly the data-dependent critical value converges in probability to $\tau\,z_{1-\alpha}$. Symmetry of $P$ is not required: the randomization distribution still stabilizes, but at the scale of the symmetrized model rather than at the true sampling scale. When $P$ is symmetric about $0$ the randomization hypothesis holds, $\tilde P = P$, and the test is in addition exact at every finite sample size.

title: Two-Sample Permutation Central Limit Theorem
informal: Let $Y_1, \dots, Y_m$ be independent with law $P_Y$ and $Z_1, \dots, Z_n$ independent with law $P_Z$, independent of the first sample, and pool them into a vector of length $N = m + n$ on which the group of all $N!$ coordinate permutations acts. The statistic is the scaled difference of sample means $$ T_{m,n} \;=\; \sqrt{m}\,\bigl(\bar Y_m - \bar Z_n\bigr) . $$ Assume that both sample sizes tend to infinity, that the ratio $m/n$ converges to a limit $\lambda$ which is strictly positive, that both populations have finite second moments, that they share a common mean $\mu$, that both population variances are strictly positive, and write $\tau^2 = \lambda\,\sigma^2(P_Y) + \sigma^2(P_Z)$ for the permutation scale. Let $\pi$ and $\pi'$ be independent uniform random permutations of the pooled sample. Then $$ \bigl(T_{m,n}(\pi X),\; T_{m,n}(\pi' X)\bigr) \;\xrightarrow{\;d\;}\; N(0,\tau^2)\otimes N(0,\tau^2) , $$ the two coordinates being independent in the limit.
summary: The scaled difference of two sample means, evaluated at two independent uniform random permutations of the pooled data, converges jointly to a pair of independent centred normal variables with permutation variance $\lambda\sigma_Y^2 + \sigma_Z^2$.

formalizationNotes: The permutation action used is Mathlib's arrow action, which sends a data vector to its composition with the inverse permutation rather than with the permutation itself. The two conventions differ by inversion, a bijection of the group, so every group-averaged object — the randomization distribution, the test, the $p$-value, the randomized pair law — is literally unchanged; only the labelling of individual summands moves. title: A Slutsky Theorem for Randomization Distributions
informal: Let $T_n$, $A_n$ and $B_n$ be statistics defined on a triangular array with finite groups $\mathbf{G}_n$ acting on the sample spaces, and write $$ \hat R_n^{AT+B}(t) \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathbf{G}_n|}\sum_{g \in \mathbf{G}_n} \mathbf{1}\bigl\{A_n(gX^n)\,T_n(gX^n) + B_n(gX^n) \le t\bigr\} $$ for the randomization distribution of the affinely transformed statistic. Assume that the base statistic evaluated at two independent uniform group elements converges jointly in law to a pair of independent variables with common law $R$, that the random scaling converges in probability to a constant $a$ when evaluated at randomized data, and that the random shift converges in probability to a constant $b$ at randomized data. Then, at every continuity point $t$ of the law of $aT + b$, $$ \hat R_n^{AT+B}(t) \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathbb{P}\;}\; \mathbb{P}\{aT + b \le t\} . $$ The convergence required of the scaling and shift is at the randomized data $G_nX^n$, with $G_n$ uniform on the group and independent of the data — not at $X^n$ itself; equivalently, the group average of the failure probabilities tends to zero. No invariance of the scaling or shift under the group is assumed, which matters because in the studentized application the scale is a sample variance that is genuinely not invariant.
summary: If a base statistic satisfies the joint asymptotic-independence condition and a random scaling and shift stabilize at constants under a random group element, the randomization distribution of the affine combination converges to the law of the transformed limit.

title: Asymptotic Validity of the Studentized Two-Sample Permutation Test
informal: Pool two independent samples $Y_1, \dots, Y_m \sim P_Y$ and $Z_1, \dots, Z_n \sim P_Z$, and studentize the scaled difference of sample means by $$ \tilde T_{m,n} \;=\; \frac{\sqrt{m}\,(\bar Y_m - \bar Z_n)}{D_{m,n}} , \qquad D_{m,n}^2 \;=\; S_Y^2 + \frac{m}{n}\,S_Z^2 , $$ with $S_Y^2 = m^{-1}\sum_i (Y_i - \bar Y_m)^2$ and $S_Z^2 = n^{-1}\sum_j (Z_j - \bar Z_n)^2$. Let $\varphi_{m,n}$ be the level-$\alpha$ randomization test built from $\tilde T_{m,n}$ and the group of all $(m+n)!$ permutations of the pooled sample: it compares the observed value of the statistic with the order statistics of its values over the permutation orbit, rejecting above the critical order statistic and randomizing on ties. Assume that both sample sizes tend to infinity, that the ratio $m/n$ converges to a strictly positive limit $\lambda$, that both populations are square-integrable, that they have equal means, that both population variances are strictly positive, and that the nominal level lies strictly between $0$ and $1$. Then $$ \mathbb{E}_{P_Y^m \times P_Z^n}\bigl[\varphi_{m,n}\bigr] \;\longrightarrow\; \alpha . $$ No equal-variance assumption and no balance condition on the sample sizes appears anywhere — that absence is the content of the theorem. Both the permutation distribution of $\tilde T_{m,n}$ and its unconditional law converge to the standard normal, so the two match. Moreover, dividing numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{m}$ turns $\tilde T_{m,n}$ into the two-sample $t$-statistic with unpooled (Welch) standardization, $(\bar Y_m - \bar Z_n)/\sqrt{S_Y^2/m + S_Z^2/n}$, so the statement applies verbatim to that statistic. Finally, when the two populations coincide the randomization hypothesis holds and the test is in addition exact at every finite sample size, so studentization costs nothing.
summary: The permutation test based on the studentized difference of sample means has rejection probability tending to the nominal level for testing equality of means, with no equal-variance and no balanced-sample-size assumption.

The reference text develops the quadratic-form building block, the joint convergence under two independent sign assignments, and the independent chi-squared pair limit as three lemmas; the formalization proves all three, deriving the chi-squared identification from the fact that the quadratic form of a nondegenerate centred Gaussian in its own inverse covariance is chi-squared.

title: General Bootstrap Consistency, Uniform Form
informal: Let $J_n(Q)$ denote the sampling distribution function of a root under $n$ observations from a law $Q$, let $\hat P_n$ be an estimate of the unknown law computed from the sample, and let $\mathcal{C}_P$ be a class of sequences of laws. Assume that the constant sequence at the data-generating law $P$ belongs to the class, that along every sequence in the class the sampling distribution functions converge pointwise to one and the same limit $J$, that this common limit is continuous, that every sampling distribution is a genuine distribution function, and that the estimated sequence $n \mapsto \hat P_n$ belongs to the class for almost every sample path. Then, almost surely, $$ \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \bigl| J_n(P)(x) - J_n(\hat P_n)(x) \bigr| \;\longrightarrow\; 0 . $$ That is, substituting the estimated law for the unknown one inside the sampling distribution is asymptotically harmless, uniformly in the argument. The only stochastic ingredient is the membership of the random sequence of estimated laws in the class; the upgrade from pointwise to uniform convergence is Pólya's theorem, and it is exactly here that continuity of the limit is used.
summary: If the sampling distributions converge to a common continuous limit along every sequence of a class of laws, and the estimated sequence of laws lies in that class almost surely, then the bootstrap sampling distribution is uniformly close to the true one, almost surely.

reference.biblio: The bootstrap is due to B. Efron (1979); its first consistency theory to P. J. Bickel and D. A. Freedman (1981) and K. Singh (1981). The reference text states the criterion with a metric on laws; the formalization keeps the class of sequences abstract, supplied as data together with its defining convergence property, and derives the uniform conclusion by Pólya's argument applied first along each fixed sequence of the class and then transported to the random sequence on the almost-sure event.

title: Asymptotic Coverage of the Bootstrap Confidence Set
informal: Let $J_n(Q)$ denote the sampling distribution function of a root $R_n$ under $n$ observations from a law $Q$, let $\hat P_n$ be an estimate of the unknown law computed from the sample, and let $\mathcal{C}_P$ be a class of sequences of laws along which those sampling distribution functions converge to one common limit — the setting of the uniform bootstrap consistency criterion. The bootstrap confidence set for the parameter of interest consists of those parameter values whose root does not exceed the estimated $1-\alpha$ quantile of the bootstrap sampling distribution; the true parameter is covered exactly when $$ R_n \;\le\; J_n(\hat P_n)^{-1}(1-\alpha) , $$ where $R_n$ is the root evaluated at the true parameter and $J_n(\hat P_n)^{-1}$ is the generalized inverse of the bootstrap sampling distribution function. Assume that the constant sequence at the true law belongs to the class, that the sampling distribution functions converge to a common limit along the class, that the estimated sequence of laws belongs to the class almost surely, that the nominal level lies strictly between $0$ and $1$, that the limit law is strictly increasing at its $1-\alpha$ quantile, and that at the data-generating law the sampling distribution field really is the distribution function of the root. Then the coverage probability converges to the nominal level, $$ \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\, R_n \le J_n(\hat P_n)^{-1}(1-\alpha) \,\bigr\} \;\longrightarrow\; 1 - \alpha . $$
summary: The bootstrap confidence set built from the estimated $1-\alpha$ quantile of the root covers the true parameter with probability tending to the nominal level.

title: Consistency of the Nonparametric Bootstrap for a Mean
informal: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be independent and identically distributed real observations with common law $Q$, and let $\hat Q_n$ be the empirical measure of the first $n$ of them. Write $$ J_n(F)(x) \;=\; \mathbb{P}_{F^{\,n}}\bigl\{\, \sqrt{n}\,(\bar X_n - \mathbb{E}_F X) \le x \,\bigr\} $$ for the sampling distribution function of the centred and scaled sample mean under $n$ independent draws from $F$. Assume that the sampling law is square-integrable and that its variance is strictly positive. Then, almost surely, $$ \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \bigl| J_n(Q)(x) - J_n(\hat Q_n)(x) \bigr| \;\longrightarrow\; 0 . $$
summary: For an independent identically distributed sample from a square-integrable law with nonzero variance, the bootstrap sampling distribution of the centred and scaled sample mean is uniformly close to the true one, almost surely.

title: Consistency of the Studentized (Bootstrap-$t$) Approximation
informal: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be real observations and let $\hat Q_n$ be the empirical measure of the first $n$ of them, as in the nonparametric bootstrap for a mean. Replace the centred root by the studentized one and write $$ K_n(F)(x) \;=\; \mathbb{P}_{F^{\,n}}\Bigl\{\, \frac{\sqrt{n}\,(\bar X_n - \mathbb{E}_F X)}{\hat\sigma_n} \le x \,\Bigr\} , $$ with $\hat\sigma_n$ the plug-in sample standard deviation, for the sampling distribution function of the studentized sample mean under $n$ independent draws from $F$. Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be independent, identically distributed with common law $Q$, let $Q$ be square-integrable and let its variance be strictly positive. Then, almost surely, $$ \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \bigl| K_n(Q)(x) - K_n(\hat Q_n)(x) \bigr| \;\longrightarrow\; 0 . $$ The common limit is now the standard normal distribution function, free of the unknown scale, which is what makes the studentized (bootstrap-$t$) construction the natural one for confidence intervals for a mean.
summary: The bootstrap sampling distribution of the studentized sample mean, computed at the empirical measure, is uniformly close to the true one, almost surely.

title: Bootstrap Consistency for Smooth Functions of Means
informal: Let each coordinate of the parameter be an expectation $\theta_j = \mathbb{E}_P[h_j(X)]$, estimated by the corresponding sample mean, and let $f$ be a smooth map of the parameter vector. The estimator is $f(\hat\theta_n)$ and the error is $f(\hat\theta_n) - f(\theta)$; the bootstrap replaces it by the resampled error $f(\hat\theta_n^{*}) - f(\hat\theta_n)$, where the resample consists of $n$ independent draws from the empirical measure of the observed sample. Assume that the observations are independent and identically distributed with law $P$, that the coordinate functions are square-integrable, that $f$ is differentiable at the parameter with differential $Df$, that the differential is continuous at the parameter, that the limiting covariance $D\,\Sigma_h\,D^{\top}$ of the error is not identically zero, and that the norm used on the image space is subadditive, absolutely homogeneous and positive definite. Then, almost surely, $$ \sup_{s \in \mathbb{R}} \Bigl| \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\|f(\hat\theta_n) - f(\theta)\| \le s\bigr\} - \mathbb{P}^{*}\bigl\{\|f(\hat\theta_n^{*}) - f(\hat\theta_n)\| \le s\bigr\} \Bigr| \;\longrightarrow\; 0 . $$ Taking the maximum norm on the image space, this is the statement behind simultaneous confidence rectangles for the coordinates of $f(\theta)$. The underlying limit is the delta method: the centred and scaled image converges weakly to the centred multivariate normal law with covariance $D\,\Sigma_h\,D^{\top}$, where $\Sigma_h$ is the covariance matrix of the vector of coordinate functions.

title: Asymptotic Level of a Bootstrap Test
informal: Let the data be generated by a null law $P$, let $T_n$ be a test statistic with sampling distribution function $G_n(\cdot, Q)$ under $n$ observations from $Q$, and let $\hat Q_n$ be an estimate of the generating law that satisfies the constraints of the null hypothesis. The bootstrap test rejects when $T_n$ exceeds the estimated critical value $G_n(\cdot, \hat Q_n)^{-1}(1-\alpha)$. Assume that the constant sequence at the data-generating law belongs to the null class, that along every sequence of the null class the distribution functions of the statistic converge to one common continuous limit, that the null-restricted estimator lies in the null class in probability, that the nominal level lies strictly between $0$ and $1$, that the limit law is strictly increasing at its $1-\alpha$ quantile, and that at the data-generating law the field really is the distribution function of the statistic. Then $$ \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\, G_n(\cdot, \hat Q_n)^{-1}(1-\alpha) < T_n \,\bigr\} \;\longrightarrow\; \alpha . $$ The essential point is which law is resampled: resampling from the unrestricted empirical measure estimates the distribution of the statistic under the law that actually generated the data, whether or not it satisfies the null, and the resulting test has asymptotic rejection probability $\alpha$ even against alternatives, hence no power. Estimating under the null constraints makes the critical value behave, under an alternative, like the critical value at some null law, against which a divergent statistic rejects with probability tending to one — the accompanying consistency claim, proved separately in the same file.
summary: A test whose critical value is the estimated $1-\alpha$ quantile of the statistic under a null-restricted resampling law has rejection probability tending to the nominal level.

title: Local Power of the Parametric Bootstrap Test
informal: In a parametric model indexed by $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^k$, consider testing $g(\theta) \le 0$ with the statistic $\sqrt{n}\,g(\hat\theta_n)$, calibrated by the estimated $1-\alpha$ quantile of the parametric bootstrap sampling distribution at the estimated parameter. Assume that the nominal level lies strictly between $0$ and $1$, that the tested parameter lies on the boundary of the null hypothesis, that $g$ is differentiable at $\theta$ with gradient $\nabla g(\theta)$, that the limiting standard deviation $\sigma$ of the root is strictly positive, that under the contiguous alternatives the rescaled statistic is asymptotically normal, centred at the directional derivative, and that under those alternatives the estimated critical value converges in probability to the critical value of the limit law. Then, along the local alternatives $\theta + n^{-1/2}h$, $$ \mathbb{P}_{\theta + n^{-1/2}h}\bigl\{\, \text{reject} \,\bigr\} \;\longrightarrow\; 1 - \Phi\Bigl( z_{1-\alpha} - \frac{\langle \nabla g(\theta), h\rangle}{\sigma} \Bigr) . $$ So the bootstrap test attains the same limiting local power as the test that would be used if the limiting normal law were known.
summary: Against contiguous alternatives at distance $n^{-1/2}$ from the boundary of the null hypothesis, the bootstrap test's rejection probability converges to the limiting power of the corresponding normal-theory test.

title: One-Term Edgeworth Expansion for the Centred Mean
informal: Let $F$ be a law on the line with mean $\mu$, variance $\sigma^2$ and skewness $\gamma$, and let $$ J_n(t) \;=\; \mathbb{P}_{F^{\,n}}\bigl\{\, \sqrt{n}\,(\bar X_n - \mu) \le t \,\bigr\} $$ be the sampling distribution function of the centred and scaled sample mean. Assume that $F$ has a finite fourth moment, that its variance is strictly positive, and that $F$ satisfies Cramér's condition, i.e. the modulus of its characteristic function is eventually bounded by a constant strictly below $1$ at infinity. Then there is a constant $C$, depending only on $F$, such that for every sample size $n \ge 1$ and every $t$, $$ \Bigl| J_n(t) - \Bigl[\Phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{t}{\sigma}\bigr) - \tfrac{\gamma}{6}\,\phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{t}{\sigma}\bigr)\Bigl(\tfrac{t^2}{\sigma^2} - 1\Bigr) n^{-1/2} \Bigr] \Bigr| \;\le\; \frac{C}{n} , $$ where $\Phi$ and $\phi$ are the standard normal distribution function and density. Consistency says the bootstrap approximation is asymptotically correct; it says nothing about how fast, and the comparison of competing confidence intervals for a mean is decided at exactly this next order.
summary: Under a finite fourth moment and Cramér's condition, the sampling distribution function of the centred and scaled sample mean equals the normal approximation plus an explicit skewness term of order $n^{-1/2}$, with remainder uniformly $O(1/n)$.

title: Cornish–Fisher Inversion of an Edgeworth Expansion
informal: Let $S_n$ be a family of distribution functions and $\gamma$ a real constant. Assume that a positive constant $C_0$ is given, that each $S_n$ is a distribution function, and that the family admits the one-term Edgeworth expansion $$ \Bigl| S_n(t) - \Bigl[\Phi(t) + \tfrac{\gamma}{6}\,\phi(t)\,(2t^2 + 1)\,n^{-1/2}\Bigr] \Bigr| \;\le\; \frac{C_0}{n} \qquad \text{for all } t \text{ and all } n \ge 1 . $$ Then, for any margin $\varepsilon \in (0, 1/2)$, there is a constant $C$ such that for every $n \ge 1$ and every level $\alpha \in [\varepsilon, 1-\varepsilon]$ the quantiles satisfy $$ \Bigl| S_n^{-1}(1-\alpha) - \Bigl[ z_{1-\alpha} - \tfrac{\gamma}{6}\,\bigl(2 z_{1-\alpha}^2 + 1\bigr) n^{-1/2} \Bigr] \Bigr| \;\le\; \frac{C}{n} , $$ where $z_{1-\alpha}$ is the standard normal quantile.
summary: A uniform $O(1/n)$ Edgeworth expansion of a family of distribution functions inverts to a uniform $O(1/n)$ expansion of their quantiles, over levels bounded away from $0$ and $1$.

u}(x)=\exp igl(\langle\eta,T(x)angle-A(\eta) igr),\qquad A(\eta)=\log\int_{\mathcal{X}} e^{\langle\eta,T(x)angle}\,d

u$-integrable, that is, the largest set of parameters for which the normalizing constant is finite and the member $P_\eta$ is defined. The familiar general presentation $p_	heta(x)=\exp igl(\sum_{i=1}^{s}\eta_i(	heta)T_i(x)-B(	heta) igr)h(x)$ relative to a dominating measure $\mu$ is recovered by absorbing the carrier $h$ into the reference measure, $d

formalizationNotes: The family is packaged as the pair (reference measure, measurable natural statistic), with the carrier already absorbed; members are realized as exponential tilts of the reference measure. This fixes a junk convention: for $\eta$ outside the natural parameter space the member is the zero measure rather than being undefined, which removes membership side conditions from downstream statements. No finiteness or $\sigma$-finiteness assumption on the reference measure is built into the definition; individual theorems add it where their proofs need it.

reference.biblio: Exponential families were isolated independently by Fisher (1934), Darmois (1935), Koopman (1936) and Pitman (1936) as the families admitting a sufficient statistic of fixed dimension. The formalization takes the canonical form as primitive — the data of a reference measure and a measurable natural statistic — and recovers the general form as the special case in which a carrier has been absorbed into the reference measure.

title: The natural parameter space is convex
informal: The natural parameter space of an exponential family is a convex subset of the parameter space: if $e^{\langle\eta_0,T(\cdot)\rangle}$ and $e^{\langle\eta_1,T(\cdot)\rangle}$ are both integrable with respect to the reference measure and $\alpha,\beta\ge 0$ satisfy $\alpha+\beta=1$, then $e^{\langle\alpha\eta_0+\beta\eta_1,T(\cdot)\rangle}$ is integrable as well.
summary: The set of natural parameters at which an exponential family is defined is a convex set.

formalizationNotes: Holds for an arbitrary reference measure — no finiteness, $\sigma$-finiteness or nondegeneracy assumption is used. The statement is about the parameter set only; convexity of the log-partition function itself is a separate fact and is not part of this declaration.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Convexity of the natural parameter space is stated by Lehmann and Casella immediately after the canonical form (5.2) and is one of the standard structural facts about exponential families; the convex-analytic development around it is due to Barndorff-Nielsen (1978) and Brown (1986). The formalization proves it for an arbitrary reference measure, with no finiteness or nondegeneracy assumption, by the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality rather than by Hölder's inequality in its usual form.

title: Differentiation under the integral sign for exponential integrals
informal: Let $T$ be the natural statistic of an exponential family with reference measure $ u$, let $f$ be a measurable weight function on the sample space, and consider the weighted exponential integral $$I(\eta)=\int f(x)\,e^{\langle\eta,T(x) angle}\,d u(x),$$ defined on the set of parameters at which $|f(x)|e^{\langle\eta,T(x) angle}$ is $ u$-integrable. At every parameter $\eta$ interior to that set the function $I$ is differentiable, and its derivative is obtained by differentiating under the integral sign: the gradient is $$ abla I(\eta)=\int f(x)\,e^{\langle\eta,T(x) angle}\,T(x)\,d u(x),$$ so that the derivative in the direction $u$ equals $\int f(x)\,\langle u,T(x) angle\,e^{\langle\eta,T(x) angle}\,d u(x)$. Taking $f\equiv 1$ this is the differentiability of the normalizing constant of the family, from which $ abla A(\eta)=\mathbb{E}_\eta[T]$ follows.
summary: On the interior of its domain of absolute convergence, a weighted exponential integral is differentiable in the natural parameter and may be differentiated under the integral sign.

hypotheses.note: The weight $f$ is a measurable real-valued function on the sample space.

hypotheses.label: interior parameter
hypotheses.note: The parameter $\eta$ lies in the interior of the set on which $|f(x)|e^{\langle\eta,T(x)\rangle}$ is $\nu$-integrable.

This is a Lean-side requirement, not a restriction of the book: it is what makes the local dominating envelope (built from the finitely many sign vectors of an orthonormal basis) available, and every intended instantiation is a Euclidean parameter space. The derivative is presented as the Riesz vector of the differential — the honest 'integral of the differentiated integrand' — rather than as an abstract linear map. Continuity on the same interior is recorded separately as `continuousOn_integral_exp_inner`, and the derivatives of all orders along a fixed direction as `iteratedDeriv_integral_exp_inner`.

The formalization proves the differentiability statement for an arbitrary measurable weight $f$ rather than only for $f\equiv 1$, which is what the moment identities need, and represents the differential by the vector of the integral of the differentiated integrand.

title: Analyticity of exponential integrals in the natural parameter
informal: For a measurable weight function $f$ on the sample space, the weighted exponential integral $\eta\mapsto\int f(x)\,e^{\langle\eta,T(x)\rangle}\,d\nu(x)$ is real-analytic on the interior of the set of parameters at which $|f(x)|e^{\langle\eta,T(x)\rangle}$ is integrable: near every such point it is the sum of a convergent power series. In particular it has derivatives of all orders there, and each of them may be computed by repeated differentiation under the integral sign, the $n$-th derivative in the direction $u$ being $\int f(x)\,\langle u,T(x)\rangle^{\,n}\,e^{\langle\eta,T(x)\rangle}\,d\nu(x)$. With $f\equiv 1$ this is the classical statement that the normalizing constant of an exponential family — and hence the log-partition function — is infinitely differentiable, indeed analytic, on the interior of the natural parameter space.
summary: A weighted exponential integral is real-analytic in the natural parameter on the interior of its domain of absolute convergence.

title: Moment generating function of the natural statistic
informal: Let $X$ follow the member $P_\eta$ of a canonical exponential family with natural statistic $T$, log-partition function $A$ and a reference measure that is not the zero measure. The formalization states the identity in the multivariate canonical form, valid whenever both the base point and the shifted point are natural parameters.

title: Mean of the natural statistic as the derivative of the log-partition function
informal: For a one-parameter canonical exponential family on the line — the natural statistic $T$ being real valued — and a natural parameter $\eta$ interior to the natural parameter space, the expectation of the natural statistic under $P_\eta$ is the derivative of the log-partition function: $$\mathbb{E}_\eta\bigl[T(X)\bigr]=A'(\eta).$$ This is what one obtains by differentiating the normalization identity $\int e^{\eta T(x)-A(\eta)}\,d\nu(x)=1$ under the integral sign.
summary: At an interior natural parameter the mean of the natural statistic equals the first derivative of the log-partition function.

hypotheses.label: interior natural parameter
hypotheses.note: The parameter lies in the interior of the natural parameter space, where the log-partition function is differentiable.

formalizationNotes: The companion declaration `variance_stat_P`, in the same file, gives the second moment identity: at an interior natural parameter the variance of the natural statistic equals the second derivative of the log-partition function. Neither statement needs a nondegeneracy hypothesis on the reference measure — both sides vanish for the zero measure.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: That the successive derivatives of the log-partition function are the cumulants of the natural statistic — the mean being the first derivative and the variance the second — is part of Theorem 5.10 of Lehmann and Casella and goes back to Fisher (1934); see Barndorff-Nielsen (1978) and Brown (1986) for the convex-analytic treatment. The formalization gives the one-dimensional statement; the multivariate gradient and Hessian identities are obtained by combining the generating-function identity with the differentiation-under-the-integral results.

title: The natural statistic is itself exponentially distributed
informal:
If $X$ follows the member $P_\eta$ of a canonical exponential family with natural statistic $T$ and reference measure $
u$, then $T(X)$ again follows an exponential family — the one carried by the statistic's own scale, whose reference measure is the image $
u\circ T^{-1}$ of $
u$ under $T$ and whose natural statistic is the identity: $$ rac{dP^{T}_\eta}{d(
u\circ T^{-1})}(t)=\exp igl(\langle\eta,tangle-A(\eta) igr).$$ The two families share the same natural parameter space and the same log-partition function $A$. Consequently all inference about $\eta$ may be carried out on the scale of the statistic, which is the reduction under which completeness of $T$ is proved.
summary: The law of the natural statistic under an exponential family member is again an exponential family member, with the identity as natural statistic and the same log-partition function.

formalizationNotes: The statement is unconditional — it holds for every $\eta$, not only for natural parameters: off the natural parameter space both sides are the zero measure, since the two families are shown to have the same natural parameter space. Consumers therefore never carry a membership side condition through the push-forward. Combined with the $n$-fold product family (whose natural statistic is $\sum_i T(X_i)$) this gives the classical corollary that a sum of independent natural statistics is again exponentially distributed.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Theorem 5.17 of Lehmann and Casella records that the natural statistic of an exponential family is itself exponentially distributed with the same natural parameter; together with the closure of the class under independent sampling this is part of the classical theory of Fisher (1934), Darmois (1935), Koopman (1936) and Pitman (1936), see also Barndorff-Nielsen (1978, Ch. 8). The formalization proves it as the commutation of exponential tilting with the push-forward along $T$, the tilting density factoring through the statistic.

title: Stein's identity for a one-parameter exponential family on the line
informal: Let $X$ have the one-parameter density $\exp\bigl(\eta\,T(x)-A(\eta)\bigr)h(x)$ with respect to Lebesgue measure on the whole line, the carrier $h$ being a nonnegative weight of the reference measure, and let $\eta$ be a natural parameter. Let $g$ be a differentiable function with $\mathbb{E}_\eta|g'(X)|<\infty$, and assume the boundary term $g(x)\,e^{\eta T(x)}\,h(x)$ tends to zero both as $x\to+\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty$. Then $$\mathbb{E}_\eta\Bigl[\Bigl(\frac{h'(X)}{h(X)}+\eta\,T'(X)\Bigr)g(X)\Bigr]=-\,\mathbb{E}_\eta\bigl[g'(X)\bigr].$$ The bracketed factor is the derivative of the log-density with respect to the sample argument — the score in the sample argument — so the identity states that this score is orthogonal to differentiation. For the normal family with mean $\eta$ and unit variance, where $h(x)=e^{-x^{2}/2}$ and $T(x)=x$, it reduces to Stein's identity $\mathbb{E}\bigl[(X-\eta)g(X)\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[g'(X)\bigr]$.
summary: Integration by parts on the line turns the expectation of the sample score times a test function into minus the expectation of the test function's derivative.

hypotheses.note: The reference measure is Lebesgue measure on the line weighted by the nonnegative carrier $h$.

hypotheses.label: natural parameter
hypotheses.note: The parameter lies in the natural parameter space, so that the member is a probability measure.

hypotheses.label: integrable derivative
hypotheses.note: The derivative of the test function has a finite expectation under the member, $\mathbb{E}_\eta|g'(X)|<\infty$.

hypotheses.label: boundary term at $+\infty$
hypotheses.note: The product $g(x)\,e^{\eta T(x)}\,h(x)$ tends to $0$ as $x\to+\infty$.

hypotheses.label: boundary term at $-\infty$
hypotheses.note: The product $g(x)\,e^{\eta T(x)}\,h(x)$ tends to $0$ as $x\to-\infty$.

formalizationNotes: Three further hypotheses accompany the classical ones: differentiability of the carrier and of the natural statistic (needed for $h'/h$ and $T'$ to exist) and integrability of the left-hand integrand, which the classical statement leaves implicit but without which the left-hand expectation would silently be read as zero. The boundary condition is stated with the factor $g$ included, which is what integration by parts actually needs and is weaker (hence safer) than the classical form asking only for decay of $e^{\eta T}h$. On the set where the carrier vanishes the ratio $h'/h$ takes the value zero by the division convention; that set is null under the member, so the statement is unaffected. The variant with support a bounded interval is not formalized.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.

title: The natural statistic of a full-rank exponential family is minimal sufficient
informal: Consider a canonical exponential family $\{P_\eta:\eta\in\Xi\}$ with natural statistic $T$, where the parameter set $\Xi$ is contained in the natural parameter space and the reference measure is not the zero measure. If $\Xi$ contains $s+1$ parameter points lying in no proper affine subspace of the parameter space — which is the case, in particular, when the family has full rank, since a parameter set with nonempty interior in an $s$-dimensional space always contains such a configuration — then $T$ is minimal sufficient: it is sufficient, and every sufficient statistic determines it almost surely.
summary: In a canonical exponential family whose parameter set contains an affinely spanning configuration, the natural statistic is minimal sufficient.

hypotheses.note: The parameter set lies inside the natural parameter space, so that every member is a genuine probability measure of the family.

hypotheses.label: nonzero reference measure
hypotheses.note: Nondegeneracy of the reference measure, so that the members are probability measures rather than the zero measure.

hypotheses.label: affinely spanning parameters
hypotheses.note: The parameter set contains $s+1$ points lying in no proper affine subspace, so that their differences from a baseline point span the natural parameter space.

formalizationNotes: Affine independence of the natural statistic — the other half of the classical full-rank condition — is what makes the parametrization identifiable and is not needed here; the companion `fullRank_exists_affineSpan` supplies the span hypothesis from full rank. $\sigma$-finiteness of the reference measure is a Lean-side instance needed to pass from the density factorization to parameter-free conditional determinations; every dominated model supplies it. The classical 'common support' proviso does not appear as a hypothesis because the exponential density is strictly positive, so all members are mutually equivalent.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Minimal sufficiency and the likelihood-ratio construction behind this corollary are due to Lehmann and Scheffé (1950), with the general theory developed by Dynkin (1951) and Bahadur (1954); that exponential structure characterizes families with low-dimensional sufficient statistics goes back to Fisher (1934) and Koopman (1936). The formalization separates the two halves of the classical full-rank condition: the affine-span condition is what the minimality proof consumes and is therefore the hypothesis of the theorem, while a companion result derives it from a parameter set with nonempty interior in a finite-dimensional parameter space.

title: Sufficient statistic
informal: A statistic $T$ is sufficient for a family $\{P_\theta\}$ when the conditional distribution of the data given $T$ can be chosen free of the parameter: for every measurable event $A$ of the sample space there is a measurable function $t\mapsto\kappa_A(t)\in[0,1]$, not depending on $\theta$, which is a version of $P_\theta(A\mid T=t)$ for every $\theta$, that is, $$\int_{\{T\in B\}}\kappa_A\bigl(T(x)\bigr)\,dP_\theta(x)=P_\theta\bigl(A\cap\{T\in B\}\bigr)$$ for every measurable set $B$ of values of the statistic and every parameter $\theta$. Informally: once the value of $T$ has been reported, the residual randomness in the data carries no further information about $\theta$, so nothing is lost by discarding the data and keeping only $T$.
summary: A statistic is sufficient when every event admits a version of its conditional probability given the statistic that does not depend on the parameter.

The stronger regular-conditional carrier `HasSufficientKernel`, defined in the same file, asks for a single parameter-free Markov kernel disintegrating the joint law of the statistic and the data; on a standard Borel sample space the two agree.

reference.biblio: Sufficiency was introduced by Fisher (1922); its measure-theoretic treatment for dominated families, and the equivalence of the conditional-distribution definition with the analytic factorization criteria, is due to Halmos and Savage (1949), with the decision-theoretic reading — a sufficient statistic is one admitting a parameter-free reconstruction mechanism — due to Bahadur (1954). The formalization records three carriers of the notion: this per-event definition, a regular-conditional (Markov kernel) form, and the Fisher–Neyman factorization of densities, together with the theorems relating them.

title: Fisher–Neyman factorization: a factorized density makes the statistic sufficient
informal: Suppose the model is dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, with densities $p_\theta=dP_\theta/d\mu$, and let $T$ be a measurable statistic. If the densities split into a factor that sees the data only through $T$ and a factor that does not see the parameter at all, $$p_\theta(x)=g_\theta\bigl(T(x)\bigr)\,h(x)\qquad\text{for $\mu$-almost every }x,\ \text{for every }\theta,$$ then $T$ is sufficient for the family.
summary: If the densities of a dominated family factor as a function of the statistic times a parameter-free function, the statistic is sufficient.

hypotheses.label: dominated model
hypotheses.note: Each member is the given density with respect to one $\sigma$-finite dominating measure $\mu$.

hypotheses.label: measurable statistic
hypotheses.note: The statistic is measurable into its value space.

hypotheses.label: Fisher–Neyman factorization
hypotheses.note: The densities factor almost everywhere as a function of the statistic times a parameter-free carrier.

formalizationNotes: Densities are extended-nonnegative-real valued, so no positivity or finiteness side conditions appear; measurability of the densities and of the two factors is what the change-of-variables steps consume. The proof runs through an equivalent countable mixture of members (the Halmos–Savage device), so this direction consumes the existence of such a mixture for a dominated family.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The factorization criterion is due to Neyman (1935), following Fisher's (1922) introduction of sufficiency; its measure-theoretic form for arbitrary dominated families — which is what is formalized here — is due to Halmos and Savage (1949) and appears as Corollary 2.6.1 of Lehmann and Romano (2022). The formalization states the criterion relative to an arbitrary $\sigma$-finite dominating measure and fixed densities, with the factorization holding almost everywhere rather than pointwise.

title: Fisher–Neyman factorization: a sufficient statistic factorizes the densities
informal: Suppose the model is dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, with densities $p_\theta=dP_\theta/d\mu$ and that the measurable statistic $T$ is sufficient, in the sense that every measurable event of the sample space admits a version of its conditional probability given $T$ that does not depend on the parameter. Then the densities admit a factorization: there are measurable functions $g_\theta$ on the value space of the statistic and a measurable function $h$ on the sample space, the latter not depending on the parameter, such that $$p_\theta(x)=g_\theta\bigl(T(x)\bigr)\,h(x)\qquad\text{for $\mu$-almost every }x,\ \text{for every }\theta.$$ Combined with the converse implication — that a density factorizing through $T$ makes $T$ sufficient — this is the Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem: for a dominated family, sufficiency of $T$ is exactly the factorization of the densities through $T$.
summary: A sufficient statistic for a dominated family produces a Fisher–Neyman factorization of the densities.

hypotheses.note: The members are the given densities against a $\sigma$-finite dominating measure.

hypotheses.label: sufficiency
hypotheses.note: Sufficiency in the per-event sense: each event has a parameter-free version of its conditional probability given the statistic.

reference.biblio: This is the converse half of the criterion of Neyman (1935) in the general dominated form of Halmos and Savage (1949); see Corollary 2.6.1 of Lehmann and Romano (2022). title: Halmos–Savage criterion for sufficiency
informal: Let $\{P_ heta\}$ be a family of probability measures and let $ u=\sum_i c_i P_{ heta_i}$ be a finite countable mixture of members of the family which dominates every member. Such a $ u$ is *equivalent* to the family — the reverse implication, that a set null under every member is $ u$-null, is automatic because $ u$ is built from members — and for a dominated family such a mixture always exists. Then a measurable statistic $T$ is sufficient if and only if every member has a density with respect to $ u$ that is a function of $T$ alone: for every $ heta$ there is a measurable $g_ heta$ with $$ rac{dP_ heta}{d u}(x)=g_ heta igl(T(x) igr)\qquad u ext{-almost everywhere.}$$
summary: Relative to an equivalent countable mixture of members, sufficiency of a statistic is exactly the statement that all densities against the mixture factor through the statistic.

title: Existence of a parameter-free regular conditional distribution
informal: On a standard Borel sample space, let $T$ be a measurable statistic which is sufficient in the per-event sense — each event admits a version of its conditional probability given $T$ that is free of the parameter. Then there is a *single* parameter-free Markov kernel $Q$, from the value space of the statistic to the sample space, which is a regular conditional distribution of the data given $T$ simultaneously under every member: for every $\theta$ the joint law of $\bigl(T(X),X\bigr)$ under $P_\theta$ is the law of $T(X)$ followed by $Q$. In particular the data may be regenerated from the reported value of the statistic by a random mechanism that does not involve the parameter, and $Q$ puts all of its mass on the fibre $\{x: T(x)=t\}$ for almost every $t$.
summary: A sufficient statistic on a standard Borel sample space admits a single parameter-free Markov kernel that disintegrates the joint law of the statistic and the data under every member.

title: The likelihood-ratio vector is minimal sufficient
informal: Let $P_0,\dots,P_k$ be a finite family of probability measures dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, with densities $p_0,\dots,p_k$ that are almost everywhere strictly positive, so that the members share a common support and almost everywhere finite. Then the vector of likelihood ratios against the baseline member, $$T(x)=\Bigl(\frac{p_1(x)}{p_0(x)},\dots,\frac{p_k(x)}{p_0(x)}\Bigr),$$ is minimal sufficient: it is sufficient, and it reduces the data as far as any sufficient statistic can, in the sense that for every sufficient statistic $U$ there is a measurable map $H$ with $T=H\circ U$ almost surely under every member.

title: Sufficiency costs nothing: risk-equal estimators based on a sufficient statistic
informal: Let $T$ be sufficient for the model in the regular-conditional sense, let $L(\theta,d)$ be a loss function that is measurable in the decision argument, and let $\delta$ be any measurable estimator of the data. Consequently the class of risk functions attainable by arbitrary procedures coincides with the class attainable by procedures depending on the data only through a sufficient statistic.

hypotheses.note: The statistic admits a parameter-free Markov kernel disintegrating the joint law of the statistic and the data under every member.

hypotheses.label: measurable loss
hypotheses.note: For each parameter the map $d\mapsto L(\theta,d)$ is measurable; no integrability of the loss is assumed.

hypotheses.label: measurable estimator
hypotheses.note: The estimator being matched is a measurable map from the sample space to the decision space.

formalizationNotes: Risks are extended-nonnegative-real lower integrals, so the identity is an honest equality even when both sides are infinite and no integrability hypothesis is needed anywhere. No convexity of the loss is used: this is the risk-*equality* statement, not the Rao–Blackwell improvement statement. The version for randomized estimators being matched is `exists_riskRand_eq_of_sufficient`; the fibre property of the reconstruction kernel is not used.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The reading of sufficiency as 'no information is lost', made precise by regenerating the data from the statistic with an auxiliary random mechanism, goes back to Fisher (1922). The decision-theoretic form proved here — the attainable risk functions are the same whether or not procedures are restricted to depend on a sufficient statistic — is due to Bahadur (1954), building on Blackwell (1947). The formalization states it for arbitrary losses and gives both the randomized and the nonrandomized version.

title: Complete family of distributions; complete and ancillary statistics
informal: A family of probability measures $\{Q_\theta\}$ is complete when the only integrable functions whose expectation vanishes identically in the parameter are those that vanish almost surely: if $f$ is measurable and integrable under every $Q_\theta$ and $\int f\,dQ_\theta=0$ for every $\theta$, then $f=0$ almost everywhere under every $Q_\theta$. A statistic $T$ is complete for a model when the family of its laws is complete; equivalently, an unbiased estimator of zero based on $T$ must be zero, which is what makes an unbiased estimator based on a complete sufficient statistic unique. Restricting the test to uniformly bounded $f$ gives the weaker notion of bounded completeness, and a statistic whose distribution is the same under every parameter value is called ancillary (first-order ancillary when only its mean is parameter-free).
summary: A family is complete when no nonzero integrable function has expectation zero under every member.
formalizationNotes: The full (unbounded) variant quantifies over measurable functions that are integrable under every member, and concludes almost-everywhere vanishing under every member — the classical 'almost everywhere with respect to the family' conclusion. Completeness and bounded completeness are kept as independent predicates; the implication from the former to the latter is proved separately for families of probability measures, where bounded implies integrable.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Completeness, and its use for unbiased estimation and for similar tests, is due to Lehmann and Scheffé (1950, 1955). Ancillarity goes back to Fisher, and the theorem linking the two notions — a complete sufficient statistic is independent of every ancillary statistic — to Basu (1955). The formalization states completeness family-first, so that the same predicate applies to laws of statistics, to exponential families on the natural-statistic scale, and to the bounded variant used in the theory of similar tests.

title: Basu's theorem
informal: Let $T$ be a sufficient statistic in the parameter-free regular-conditional sense which is moreover boundedly complete, and let $V$ be ancillary, that is, a statistic whose distribution is the same under every parameter value. Then $T$ and $V$ are independent under every member of the family.
summary: A boundedly complete sufficient statistic is independent of every ancillary statistic under every member of the family.

theorem indepFun_of_boundedlyComplete_sufficient {P : Θ → Measure 𝓧} {T : 𝓧 → S} {V : 𝓧 → S'}
    [∀ θ, IsProbabilityMeasure (P θ)]
    (hT : Measurable T)

    (hcomp : IsBoundedlyCompleteStat P T)
    (hanc : IsAncillary P V) :

hypotheses.label: sufficiency (kernel form)
hypotheses.note: The joint law of the statistic and the data disintegrates, under every member, through one Markov kernel that does not depend on the parameter.

hypotheses.label: bounded completeness
hypotheses.note: Every bounded measurable function of the statistic whose expectation vanishes at every parameter is zero almost surely.

hypotheses.label: ancillarity
hypotheses.note: The law of the second statistic is the same under every parameter value.

formalizationNotes: Sufficiency is taken in the kernel (joint-law) form: that is what delivers a single parameter-free determination of the conditional probabilities simultaneously for all events, together with the fibre property that turns the identity $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\eta_A(T)]=P_\theta(V\in A)$ into a plain disintegration computation. The two statistics may take values in different measurable spaces, with no structure required beyond measurability.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The independence theorem proved here is due to Basu (1955); the completeness notion it rests on is due to Lehmann and Scheffé (1950, 1955). It appears as Theorem 6.21 of Lehmann and Casella. The formalization assumes only bounded completeness — all the proof consumes — which makes the statement strictly more applicable than the version with full completeness; a separate bridge derives bounded completeness from completeness for families of probability measures.

title: The natural statistic of a full-rank exponential family is complete
informal: Consider a canonical exponential family with an $s$-dimensional natural parameter and natural statistic $T$, and a parameter set $\Xi$ that is contained in the natural parameter space and whose interior is nonempty — the rank condition of the classical statement. Then the family of laws of $T$ is complete: if $f$ is integrable with $\mathbb{E}_\eta\bigl[f(T)\bigr]=0$ for every $\eta\in\Xi$, then $f=0$ almost surely under every member. Indeed, on the scale of the statistic the hypothesis reads $$\int f(t)\,e^{\langle\eta,t\rangle}\,d\nu_T(t)=0\qquad\text{for all }\eta\in\Xi,$$ so the two finite measures obtained by weighting $\nu_T$ with the positive and the negative part of $f$ have the same Laplace transform on a set with nonempty interior; uniqueness of Laplace transforms on an open set forces them to coincide, that is, $f=0$ almost everywhere.
summary: If the parameter set of a canonical exponential family has nonempty interior, the family of laws of the natural statistic is complete.
