hypotheses.label: reference scale-equivariant estimator
hypotheses.note: A fixed scale-equivariant estimator of degree $r$ with finite risk.

hypotheses.label: nowhere vanishing
hypotheses.note: The reference estimator vanishes nowhere, so that division by it is defined at every sample point.

hypotheses.label: maximal invariant defined a.s.
hypotheses.note: The set where the last coordinate vanishes is null, so the ratios are well defined almost surely.

hypotheses.label: fibrewise minimality
hypotheses.note: In almost every fibre no constant divisor beats $w^*(z)$ in conditional expected loss.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Equivariant estimation of a scale parameter is due to Pitman (1939), with the general group formulation of Hunt and Stein (1946, unpublished) reported by Girshick and Savage (1951); the entropy (Stein) loss used in the accompanying explicit corollaries was introduced by James and Stein (1961). The formalization shares a single conditional-risk engine with the location theory, so the scale construction differs from the location one only in the template family.

formalizationNotes: Three honest deviations. (i) As in the location case, fibrewise minimality is assumed almost everywhere rather than in every fibre, and measurability of the minimizer is a genuine requirement with no classical counterpart. (ii) The minimality hypothesis quantifies over all real divisors $w$, including $w = 0$ and negative values. The full range is needed because the equivariant class contains opposite-signed competitors and, through the convention that division by zero returns zero, the identically zero estimator; a hypothesis restricted to positive or merely nonzero $w$ would therefore not dominate every equivariant competitor. (iii) The null-set hypothesis is used only for the minimality half; equivariance of the constructed estimator holds without restriction.

title: Least Squares as an Orthogonal Projection
informal: In the linear model the observation $Y$ has mean vector $\xi$ constrained to a linear subspace $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. The least-squares estimator of $\xi$ is the orthogonal projection of the observation onto that subspace, $$\hat\xi(y) \;=\; P_W\,y \;=\; \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\zeta \in W} \|y - \zeta\|^2 ,$$ and the associated residual sum of squares is $S^2 = \|y - \hat\xi(y)\|^2$.
summary: The least-squares estimator of the mean vector of a linear model is the orthogonal projection of the observation onto the mean subspace.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def lse (W : Submodule ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)))
    [W.HasOrthogonalProjection] (y : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)) :
    EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) :=
  W.starProjection y

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.pointer: Chapter 3, §3.4 (canonical and subspace forms of the normal linear model)
reference.biblio: Least squares and the optimality of its linear functionals are due to Gauss (1821/1823) and Markov (1912); the coordinate-free treatment used here, in which the estimator is literally the orthogonal projection onto the mean subspace, follows Kruskal (1965) and Scheffé (1959). The formalization takes the projection as the definition and derives the classical normal equations as identities of inner products.

formalizationNotes: The observation space is Euclidean space so that projection geometry and measure theory coexist; the product normal law lives naturally on the coordinate space and is transported to the Euclidean space along a measurable linear isometry. Finite-dimensional subspaces automatically carry the orthogonal-projection instance, so the definition is total and needs no side condition.

title: UMVU Estimation of Linear Functionals in the Canonical Model
informal: In the canonical normal linear model the observations $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$, with $n = s+m$, are independent and normal with a common unknown variance $\sigma^2$: the first $s$ have free means $\eta_1,\dots,\eta_s$ and the remaining $m$ have mean zero. If there is at least one residual coordinate, that is $s < n$, then for known coefficients $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_s$ the statistic $$\sum_{i=1}^{s} \lambda_i\,Y_i$$ is the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator of $\sum_{i=1}^{s} \lambda_i\,\eta_i$. In particular each $Y_i$ is UMVU for $\eta_i$.
summary: In the canonical normal linear model every linear combination of the signal coordinates is the UMVU estimator of the corresponding linear combination of the means.
leanSignature:
theorem isUMVU_linear_combination
    (hm : 0 < m)
    (lam : Fin s → ℝ) :
    IsUMVU (canonicalModel (s := s) (m := m)) (fun p => ∑ i, lam i * p.1 i)
      (fun y => ∑ i, lam i * canonicalHead y i)

hypotheses.label: at least one residual coordinate
hypotheses.note: The number of free means is smaller than the number of observations, $s<n$, so at least one coordinate has mean zero and the variance is estimable.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The canonical reduction of the normal linear model by an orthogonal transformation goes back to Gauss (1821/1823) and Markov (1912), with the modern treatment in Scheffé (1959) and Rao (1973); the minimum-variance property rests on the completeness theory of Lehmann and Scheffé (1950). The formalization proves completeness and sufficiency of the canonical statistic and derives the optimality of each linear combination from them.

formalizationNotes: The observation dimension is written as $s + m$ rather than through an inequality $s \le n$, so “the first $s$” and “the last $m$” coordinates carry no arithmetic side conditions and the standing assumption $s < n$ becomes positivity of $m$. The variance is restricted to be strictly positive, the degenerate member being outside the classical statements. Completeness goes through the full-rank exponential-family theorem with natural statistic the signal block together with the residual sum of squares.

title: Optimality of the Least-Squares Functional
informal: Let the observation be normal with mean vector $\xi$ ranging over a subspace $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and unknown common variance $\sigma^2 > 0$, and let $\hat\xi(y) = P_W y$ be the least-squares estimator. If the mean subspace is proper, $\dim W < n$, then for a known coefficient vector $\gamma$ lying in the mean subspace the statistic $$y \;\longmapsto\; \langle \gamma,\ \hat\xi(y)\rangle$$ is the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator of $\xi \mapsto \langle\gamma,\xi\rangle$. Since $\langle\gamma,\xi\rangle = \langle P_W\gamma,\xi\rangle$ for $\xi \in W$, restricting the coefficient vector to the subspace is no restriction: a general one is replaced by its projection without changing either the estimand or the estimator.
summary: With the mean vector confined to a subspace and the variance unknown, the least-squares functional is the UMVU estimator of the corresponding linear functional of the mean.

hypotheses.note: The dimension of the mean subspace is strictly less than the number of observations, so the variance is estimable.

hypotheses.label: coefficient vector in the subspace

reference.biblio: Least squares and the optimality of its linear functionals are due to Gauss (1821/1823) and Markov (1912); the coordinate-free formulation follows Kruskal (1965), Scheffé (1959) and Rao (1973), while the minimum-variance property in the normal model rests on Lehmann and Scheffé (1950). title: Optimality of the Residual Variance Estimator
informal: Let the observation be normal with mean vector confined to a subspace $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and unknown common variance $\sigma^2 > 0$. The result is obtained by transporting the canonical-model statement — the residual sum of squares divided by the number of residual coordinates — along the adapted-basis rotation, using that the rotation carries the residual sum of squares to itself.

title: Least Squares Is Minimum Risk Equivariant

Then the least-squares functional $$y \;\longmapsto\; \langle \gamma,\ P_W\,y\rangle$$ is minimum risk equivariant: its (constant) risk is smallest among all measurable equivariant estimators.

reference.biblio: Equivariant estimation of location parameters is due to Pitman (1939); its use in the linear model follows Scheffé (1959) and Rao (1973), with the coordinate-free viewpoint of Kruskal (1965). The formalization proves the canonical-coordinates version first — using that the reflection of the signal block is a symmetry of the base law that negates the estimator and is itself a translation — and transports it by the adapted-basis isometry.

formalizationNotes: Equivariance is expressed by explicit functional equations rather than through the general group-and-action framework: the acting groups here are concrete and the induced action on decisions is a shift, so routing through the general machinery would force an instance-heavy encoding for no gain. Because the risk of an equivariant estimator is constant in the parameter, minimality is stated at the single base parameter $\xi = 0$, and the loss enters the risk through its nonnegative part so that no integrability hypothesis is needed.

title: MRE Estimation of the Variance in the Linear Model
informal: In the canonical normal linear model — the observations $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ independent and normal with a common unknown variance $\sigma^2$, the first $s$ having free means $\eta_1,\dots,\eta_s$ and the remaining $m = n-s$ having mean zero, so that the residual sum of squares is $S^2=\sum_{i=s+1}^{n} Y_i^2$ — consider the group generated by the translations of the signal block together with the scale changes $y \mapsto c\,y$ for $c > 0$, under which $\sigma^2 \mapsto c^2\sigma^2$, and the standardized squared-error loss $$L(\sigma^2, d) \;=\; \frac{(d - \sigma^2)^2}{\sigma^4}.$$ If there is at least one residual coordinate, then the minimum risk equivariant estimator of $\sigma^2$ is $$\frac{S^2}{n - s + 2},$$ where $S^2$ is the residual sum of squares. The denominator is larger than the $n-s$ of the unbiased estimator: the optimal multiplier is the ratio $\mathbb{E}[V]/\mathbb{E}[V^2]$ of chi-square moments with $n-s$ degrees of freedom, and $\mathbb{E}[V] = m$, $\mathbb{E}[V^2] = m(m+2)$.
summary: Under the location-scale group and standardized squared error, the minimum risk equivariant estimator of the variance is the residual sum of squares divided by the residual degrees of freedom plus two.

    (hm : 0 < m) :

hypotheses.label: at least one residual coordinate
hypotheses.note: The number of residual coordinates satisfies $m=n-s\ge 1$.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Equivariant estimation of a scale parameter is due to Pitman (1939); its use in the linear model follows Scheffé (1959) and Rao (1973). The distribution of the residual sum of squares goes back to Helmert (1876). The formalization computes the chi-square moments from a Gamma-moment brick, so the classical constant $1/(n-s+2)$ is derived rather than assumed.

formalizationNotes: The optimal multiplier is only pinned down once the acting group contains the scale changes; under translations alone the risk still depends on the variance. The general power case, in which the minimum risk equivariant estimator of $(\sigma^2)^r$ is the chi-square moment ratio times $(S^2)^r$, is proved first and this is its case $r = 1$, with the moment ratio evaluated explicitly.

title: The Gauss–Markov Theorem
informal: Drop both normality and independence and retain only the first two moments: the mean vector lies in the subspace $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, and the coordinates of the observation are uncorrelated with common variance $\sigma^2$ and square-integrable. Let $\gamma$ be a known coefficient vector, and let $y \mapsto \langle c, y\rangle$ be a competing linear estimator which is unbiased throughout the mean subspace, that is $\langle c,\zeta\rangle = \langle \gamma,\zeta\rangle$ for every $\zeta \in W$. Then $$\operatorname{Var}\big(\langle \gamma,\ P_W\,Y\rangle\big) \;\le\; \operatorname{Var}\big(\langle c,\ Y\rangle\big).$$ The least-squares functional therefore has the smallest variance among all linear estimators unbiased on the mean subspace. Geometrically, unbiasedness forces $P_W c = P_W\gamma$, so $\|c\|^2 = \|P_W\gamma\|^2 + \|c - P_W c\|^2$, and both variances are $\sigma^2$ times the respective squared norms.
summary: Among linear estimators unbiased throughout the mean subspace, the least-squares functional has the smallest variance, assuming only uncorrelated coordinates with a common variance.

theorem gauss_markov {W : Submodule ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))}
    [W.HasOrthogonalProjection] {σ2 : ℝ} {γ c : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)}
    {P : Measure (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))} [IsProbabilityMeasure P]
    (hcov : ∀ i j, covariance (fun y => y i) (fun y => y j) P = if i = j then σ2 else 0)
    (hL2 : ∀ i, MemLp (fun y => y i) 2 P)
    (hc : ∀ ζ ∈ W, ⟪c, ζ⟫_ℝ = ⟪γ, ζ⟫_ℝ) :
    variance (fun y => ⟪γ, lse W y⟫_ℝ) P ≤ variance (fun y => ⟪c, y⟫_ℝ) P

hypotheses.note: The second-moment assumption: coordinate covariances vanish off the diagonal and equal $\sigma^2$ on it.

hypotheses.label: square-integrable coordinates
hypotheses.note: Every coordinate of the observation has a finite second moment.

hypotheses.label: unbiased on the subspace
hypotheses.note: The competitor has the right expectation for every admissible mean vector.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.

title: Uniqueness of the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator
informal: Assume the observation is nondegenerate, $\sigma^2 > 0$, its coordinates are uncorrelated with common variance $\sigma^2$ and square-integrable, and let $y \mapsto \langle c, y\rangle$ be a linear estimator that is unbiased throughout the mean subspace and whose variance is no larger than that of the least-squares functional $y \mapsto \langle\gamma, P_W y\rangle$, where $P_W$ is the orthogonal projection onto the mean subspace $W$. Then its coefficient vector is forced: $$c \;=\; P_W\,\gamma,$$ so the estimator is the least-squares functional $y \mapsto \langle\gamma, P_W y\rangle$. The best linear unbiased estimator of $\langle\gamma,\xi\rangle$ is therefore unique. Nondegeneracy is needed: with $\sigma^2 = 0$ every coefficient vector ties.
summary: A linear estimator unbiased on the mean subspace and of minimal variance must be the least-squares functional.

title: Optimality of the Regression Coefficient Estimator
informal: In the regression form of the normal linear model the observation $Y$ has independent normal coordinates with a common unknown variance $\sigma^2$ and mean vector $\xi = \theta A$, for a known $s \times n$ design matrix $A$ and an unknown coefficient vector $\theta$, and the least-squares estimator of the coefficient vector is $$\hat\theta(y) \;=\; y\,A^{\mathsf T}\,(A A^{\mathsf T})^{-1}.$$ If the design has full row rank $s$ and there are more observations than coefficients, $s < n$, then for known coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_s$ the statistic $\sum_i c_i\,\hat\theta_i(y)$ is the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator of $\sum_i c_i\,\theta_i$. Moreover the covariance matrix of the least-squares coefficients is $\sigma^2 (A A^{\mathsf T})^{-1}$.
summary: For a design of full row rank, every linear function of the least-squares coefficients is UMVU for the corresponding linear function of the regression coefficients.

hypotheses.label: more observations than coefficients

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The regression form of the linear model and the covariance formula $\sigma^2 (A A^{\mathsf T})^{-1}$ are classical, going back to Gauss (1821/1823) and Markov (1912); see Scheffé (1959), Kruskal (1965) and Rao (1973). Under the printed hypothesis alone a symmetric two-point design law is admissible, and for such a law the design information is constant, so a best linear unbiased estimator does exist.

title: Event-Time Laws and the Survival Function
informal:
An event-time law is a probability distribution $\mu$ on the real line that assigns no mass to negative times — the law of a nonnegative random time $T$. Its survival function is $S(t) = P(T > t)$, the mass of the open upper tail $(t, \infty)$, and its left limit is $S(t^-) = P(T \ge t)$, defined directly as the mass of the closed upper tail $[t, \infty)$ rather than as a topological limit; a companion lemma certifies that this defined quantity agrees with the left limit of $S$ in the usual sense, so no regularity bookkeeping enters the definition.

A sub-event-time law relaxes the total mass to at most one; the deficit $1 - \mu(\mathbb{R})$ is the mass of subjects who never experience the event (the cure fraction). The survival function is nonincreasing, satisfies $S(t) \le S(t^-)$ with gap $S(t^-) - S(t) = P(T = t)$, equals one at every negative time, tends to zero at infinity, and in real-valued form is one minus the distribution function.
summary: An event-time law is a probability distribution on [0, ∞); its survival function S(t) = P(T > t), with the left limit S(t−) = P(T ≥ t) taken as a measure value by definition.
leanSignature:
def IsEventTimeLaw (μ : Measure ℝ) : Prop :=
  IsProbabilityMeasure μ ∧ μ (Iio 0) = 0

noncomputable def survival (μ : Measure ℝ) (t : ℝ) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  μ (Ioi t)

noncomputable def survivalLeft (μ : Measure ℝ) (t : ℝ) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  μ (Ici t)

hypotheses.note: A probability distribution on the real line assigning no mass to the negative half-line.

The real-valued `survivalReal` connects to Mathlib's CDF via `survivalReal_eq_one_sub_cdf`, from which right-continuity of the survival function is inherited from the Stieltjes-function API. title: The Cumulative-Hazard Measure
informal:
Let $\mu$ be the distribution of a random time $T$, with distribution function $F(t) = P(T \le t)$ and at-risk mass $S(t^-) = P(T \ge t)$. The cumulative-hazard measure of $\mu$ is the law $\mu$ reweighted by the reciprocal of the at-risk mass, $$\Lambda(dt) \;=\; \frac{F(dt)}{S(t^-)}, \qquad \Lambda(A) \;=\; \int_A \frac{\mu(dt)}{P(T \ge t)}.$$ The definition is distribution-agnostic: continuous, discrete, and mixed laws are covered by one formula, with no density, no differentiability, and no atomlessness assumed. On the region where $S(t^-) = 0$ the integrand is conventionally infinite, but that region is null for $\mu$ itself, so it never carries hazard mass.

The hazard jump at $t$ is $\Delta\Lambda(t) = \Lambda\{t\}$, the atom of the cumulative-hazard measure; it equals $P(T = t)/P(T \ge t)$ wherever $P(T \ge t) > 0$, and satisfies $\Delta\Lambda(t) \le 1$ without any hypothesis. Up to any time $t$ with $S(t^-) > 0$ the accumulated hazard $\Lambda(-\infty, t]$ is at most $S(t^-)^{-1}$, hence finite.
summary: The distribution-agnostic cumulative-hazard measure Λ(dt) = F(dt)/S(t−), with hazard jump ΔΛ(t) = Λ{t} = P(T = t)/P(T ≥ t) at atoms and ΔΛ ≤ 1 unconditionally.

  μ.withDensity fun t => (μ (Ici t))⁻¹

  cumHazard μ {t}

hypotheses.note: Λ(dt) = F(dt)/S(t−): the law reweighted by the reciprocal at-risk mass S(t−) = μ[t, ∞); the region where S(t−) = 0 is null for μ, so the formula is safe.

title: Right Censoring and the Random-Censorship Model
informal:
Let $T$ be an event time and $C$ a censoring time. Under right censoring the pair $(T, C)$ is not observed; one sees only the observed time and the event indicator $(\tilde T, \Delta) = (\min(T, C),\ \mathbf{1}\{T \le C\})$, with ties $T = C$ counted as events. The random-censorship model takes $T$ and $C$ independent, with arbitrary distributions: the observed-data law is the image of the product distribution of $(T, C)$ under this coarsening map, so independence is built into the construction rather than assumed as a side condition.

From any observed-data law one reads off the marginal distribution of the observed time $\tilde T$. Under the random-censorship model it factorizes: $$P(\tilde T > t) \;=\; S_T(t)\, S_C(t), \qquad P(\tilde T \ge t) \;=\; S_T(t^-)\, S_C(t^-),$$ where $S_T$ and $S_C$ are the survival functions of the event and censoring times.
summary: The random-censorship model: (T, C) independent, observed as (T ∧ C, 1{T ≤ C}); the observed-data law is the product law pushed through the coarsening map, and the observed survival factorizes.

noncomputable def censoredLaw (μT μC : Measure ℝ) : Measure (ℝ × Bool) :=
  (μT.prod μC).map censorObserve

noncomputable def observedTimeLaw (P : Measure (ℝ × Bool)) : Measure ℝ :=
  P.map Prod.fst

hypotheses.note: The pair (T, C) is observed as (T ∧ C, 1{T ≤ C}); ties T = C count as events.

hypotheses.label: independent censoring
hypotheses.note: The joint law of (T, C) is the product measure: censoring is independent of the event time by construction.

Independent censoring is structural — `censoredLaw` is by definition the image of the product measure — so no independence hypothesis appears in downstream theorems. title: The Uncensored Sub-Distribution Formula
informal:
Let the event time $T$ and the censoring time $C$ be independent, with $T$ following an arbitrary probability distribution $F_T$ on the real line and $C$ following an arbitrary probability distribution, with survival function $S_C$; one observes $\tilde T = \min(T, C)$ and $\Delta = \mathbf{1}\{T \le C\}$. Consider the sub-distribution of uncensored observations, $A \mapsto P(\tilde T \in A,\ \Delta = 1)$. It admits the exact representation $$P(\tilde T \in dt,\ \Delta = 1) \;=\; S_C(t^-)\, F_T(dt),$$ the event-time law weighted by the probability $S_C(t^-) = P(C \ge t)$ that censoring has not yet struck.

The identity holds for arbitrary distributions — atoms are permitted on both sides, and ties $T = C$, counted as events, are handled exactly by the left limit $S_C(t^-)$. This formula is the engine behind the identifiability of the event-time hazard from censored data.
summary: Under independent censoring, the sub-distribution of uncensored observations is exactly P(T̃ ∈ dt, Δ = 1) = S_C(t−) dF_T(t), for arbitrary (possibly atomic) laws.

    [IsProbabilityMeasure μC] :
    uncensoredSubLaw (censoredLaw μT μC) = μT.withDensity fun t => μC (Ici t)

hypotheses.note: P(T̃ ∈ ·, Δ = 1): the observed-time law restricted to uncensored observations; its total mass is P(Δ = 1) ≤ 1.

hypotheses.label: event-time distribution
hypotheses.note: The event time T has an arbitrary probability distribution on ℝ; no continuity is assumed.

hypotheses.label: censoring distribution
hypotheses.note: The censoring time C has an arbitrary probability distribution on ℝ, independent of T under the random-censorship model.

The proof is a product-measure computation — the event $\{\Delta = 1\}$ pulls back to $\{(t,c) : t \le c\}$, whose Fubini sections are exactly the closed tails $[t, \infty)$ of the censoring law. No continuity or atomlessness is assumed anywhere; the tie convention (ties are events) is what makes the left limit $S_C(t^-)$, rather than $S_C(t)$, the correct weight.

title: Crude Equals Net Hazard under Independent Censoring
informal: Under the random-censorship model — an event time $T$ with arbitrary probability distribution, censored by an independent time $C$ with arbitrary probability distribution — one observes only $\tilde T = \min(T, C)$ and $\Delta = \mathbf{1}\{T \le C\}$. The crude cumulative hazard of the observed data is the measure with increments $P(\tilde T \in dt,\ \Delta = 1)\big/P(\tilde T \ge t)$ — uncensored event increments over the observable at-risk probability, a quantity computable from the censored observations alone. The theorem: the crude hazard coincides with the net cumulative hazard $\Lambda_T$ of the unobservable event time, on the region where censoring survives: $$\tilde\Lambda(dt) \;=\; \Lambda_T(dt) \qquad \text{on } \{t : S_C(t^-) > 0\}.$$
summary: Under independent censoring the crude hazard of the observed data equals the net hazard of the event time on {t : S_C(t−) > 0} — the identifiability theorem licensing Nelson–Aalen and Kaplan–Meier estimation from censored data.

hypotheses.label: event-time distribution

formalizationNotes: The conclusion is an equality of measures, with the net hazard restricted to $\{t : \mu_C[t,\infty) > 0\}$. On the complement the crude side vanishes by the extended-real convention $0 \cdot \infty = 0$ — that region is exactly what the restriction removes, so nothing is asserted where the censored data carry no information. The proof merges the sub-distribution formula $P(\tilde T \in dt, \Delta = 1) = S_C(t^-)\,dF_T(t)$ with the at-risk factorization $P(\tilde T \ge t) = S_T(t^-) S_C(t^-)$ and cancels $S_C(t^-)$ in the density. Independence cannot be dropped: without it the joint law is not identifiable from the observed data (Tsiatis's nonidentifiability theorem, recorded as a non-theorem in the module documentation).

Tsiatis's nonidentifiability theorem, *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA* **72** (1975), 20–22.

title: The Kaplan–Meier and Nelson–Aalen Estimators
informal:
Let $(\tilde T_1, \Delta_1), \dots, (\tilde T_n, \Delta_n)$ be right-censored observations — an observed time and an event indicator per subject, with $\Delta_i = 1$ marking an event and $\Delta_i = 0$ a censored observation. At each time $s$ write $Y(s) = \#\{i : \tilde T_i \ge s\}$ for the number at risk and $\Delta N(s) = \#\{i : \tilde T_i = s,\ \Delta_i = 1\}$ for the number of observed events; the observed event times form a finite set. The hazard increment at $s$ is $\Delta N(s)/Y(s)$.

The Nelson–Aalen estimator of the cumulative hazard is the sum of the hazard increments over the observed event times up to $t$, $$\hat\Lambda(t) \;=\; \sum_{s \le t} \frac{\Delta N(s)}{Y(s)},$$ and the Kaplan–Meier product-limit estimator of the survival function is the product of one minus the hazard increments, $$\hat S(t) \;=\; \prod_{s \le t} \Bigl(1 - \frac{\Delta N(s)}{Y(s)}\Bigr).$$ The Kaplan–Meier estimator is nonincreasing in $t$, takes values in $[0, 1]$, and is piecewise constant between event times.
summary: The Nelson–Aalen estimator Λ̂(t) = Σ_{s≤t} ΔN(s)/Y(s) and the Kaplan–Meier product-limit estimator Ŝ(t) = ∏_{s≤t} (1 − ΔN(s)/Y(s)) on right-censored data.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def atRisk (d : Fin n → ℝ × Bool) (t : ℝ) : ℕ :=
  (univ.filter fun i => t ≤ (d i).1).card

noncomputable def eventCount (d : Fin n → ℝ × Bool) (t : ℝ) : ℕ :=
  (univ.filter fun i => (d i).1 = t ∧ (d i).2 = true).card

noncomputable def naJump (d : Fin n → ℝ × Bool) (s : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (eventCount d s : ℝ) / (atRisk d s : ℝ)

noncomputable def nelsonAalen (d : Fin n → ℝ × Bool) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ s ∈ (eventTimes d).filter (· ≤ t), naJump d s

noncomputable def kaplanMeier (d : Fin n → ℝ × Bool) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∏ s ∈ (eventTimes d).filter (· ≤ t), (1 - naJump d s)

title: The Product-Limit Relation Between Kaplan–Meier and Nelson–Aalen
informal: For right-censored data, write $Y(s)$ for the number of subjects with observed time at least $s$ and $\Delta N(s)$ for the number of uncensored events at $s$. The Kaplan–Meier and Nelson–Aalen estimators stand in the product-limit relation $$\hat S(t) \;=\; \prod_{s \le t} \bigl(1 - \Delta\hat\Lambda(s)\bigr),$$ the product over observed event times of one minus the jumps of the estimated cumulative hazard. In this formalization the Kaplan–Meier estimator is defined as the product of one-minus-increments, so the relation is structural; the mathematical content is the identification of the increment as the genuine jump of the Nelson–Aalen estimator: at every observed event time $s$, $$\hat\Lambda(s) \;=\; \sum_{u < s} \frac{\Delta N(u)}{Y(u)} \;+\; \frac{\Delta N(s)}{Y(s)},$$ the strict-past partial sum plus the increment — that is, $\Delta\hat\Lambda(s) = \hat\Lambda(s) - \hat\Lambda(s^-) = \Delta N(s)/Y(s)$.
summary: The Nelson–Aalen increment ΔN(s)/Y(s) is the genuine jump of the Nelson–Aalen estimator at each event time, which is the content of the classical relation KM = ∏(1 − ΔNA).

hypotheses.label: observed event time
hypotheses.note: s is one of the finitely many times at which an uncensored event occurs in the sample.

formalizationNotes: Because `kaplanMeier` is defined as $\prod_{s \le t}(1 - \Delta N(s)/Y(s))$, the display $\hat S = \prod(1 - \Delta\hat\Lambda)$ holds by construction once the increment is known to be the jump of $\hat\Lambda$ — which is what this proposition proves, by splitting the truncated set of event times at its top point. The hypothesis that $s$ is an observed event time is statement scoping: off the event times the increment is zero and the estimator does not move.

reference.formal: P. K. Andersen, Ø. Borgan, R. D. Gill, and N. Keiding, *Statistical Models Based on Counting Processes*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag, New York, 1993.
reference.biblio: The product-limit idea is E. L. Kaplan and P. Meier's, "Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations," *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **53** (1958), 457–481; the hazard-increment reading and the jump relation are W. Nelson's, *Journal of Quality Technology* **1** (1969), 27–52, and O. O. Aalen's, *Annals of Statistics* **6** (1978), 701–726.

title: The Kaplan–Meier Estimate as a Sub-Probability Law
informal:
Let $\hat S$ be the Kaplan–Meier estimator computed from $n$ right-censored observations with nonnegative observed times. Since $\hat S$ is nonincreasing and right-continuous, starts at one, and decreases towards the terminal value $\hat S(\infty)$ — the full product of one-minus-increments over all observed event times, the function $1 - \hat S$ is a distribution function, and its Stieltjes measure turns the Kaplan–Meier estimate into a bona fide law on the real line. The theorem: this law is a sub-event-time law — it assigns no mass to negative times and has total mass $1 - \hat S(\infty) \le 1$.

The mass deficit $\hat S(\infty)$ is the classical defect of the product-limit estimate.
summary: The Kaplan–Meier estimate, read as the Stieltjes measure of 1 − Ŝ, is a sub-event-time law of total mass 1 − Ŝ(∞); the defect Ŝ(∞) is positive when the largest observation is censored.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def kmLimit (d : Fin n → ℝ × Bool) : ℝ :=
  ∏ s ∈ eventTimes d, (1 - naJump d s)

noncomputable def kaplanMeierMeasure (d : Fin n → ℝ × Bool) : Measure ℝ :=
  (kaplanMeierSF d).measure

theorem isSubEventTimeLaw_kaplanMeierMeasure (d : Fin n → ℝ × Bool)
    (hd : ∀ i, 0 ≤ (d i).1) :
    IsSubEventTimeLaw (kaplanMeierMeasure d)

hypotheses.label: terminal value
hypotheses.note: Ŝ(∞), the full product over all event times; positive when the largest observation is censored — the defect (cure) mass of the Kaplan–Meier law.

hypotheses.label: Stieltjes law
hypotheses.note: The measure of the monotone right-continuous distribution function 1 − Ŝ(t).

hypotheses.label: nonnegative observation times
hypotheses.note: Every observed time is nonnegative, so the estimate is supported on [0, ∞).

formalizationNotes: The Stieltjes packaging is `kaplanMeierSF`: $t \mapsto 1 - \hat S(t)$ is monotone by `antitone_kaplanMeier` and right-continuous because $\hat S$ is locally constant to the right of every point — no filter bookkeeping is needed. The total mass is computed from the limits of the Stieltjes function at $\pm\infty$: it equals $1 - \hat S(\infty)$ with $\hat S(\infty)$ the full product `kmLimit`. The nonnegativity hypothesis on the observed times places the law on $[0, \infty)$; without it the estimate is still a sub-probability law, just not an event-time one. The defect-versus-largest-observation dichotomy is stated here in its untied-case reading; with ties at the maximum, censored subjects tied with the last event keep the final factor away from zero.

reference.formal: E. L. Kaplan and P. Meier, "Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations," *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, vol. 53, no. 282, pp. 457–481, 1958.
reference.biblio: The measure-theoretic packaging of the product-limit estimate as a (possibly defective) distribution follows the counting-process treatment of P. K. Andersen, Ø. Borgan, R. D. Gill, and N. Keiding, *Statistical Models Based on Counting Processes*, Springer, 1993, §IV.3.

title: Kaplan–Meier Without Censoring: the Empirical Survival Function
informal: Suppose every observation in the sample is an event — no subject is censored — and the sample is nonempty. Then the Kaplan–Meier product-limit estimator collapses, at every time $t$, to the empirical survival function: $$\hat S(t) \;=\; \frac{\#\{i : \tilde T_i > t\}}{n}.$$ With no censoring the risk set at each event time consists of the events there together with all strictly later observations, so the product of one-minus-hazard-increments telescopes exactly: consecutive factors cancel, and the running product equals the fraction of the sample surviving past $t$.
summary: With no censoring the Kaplan–Meier estimator equals the empirical survival function #{i : T̃ᵢ > t}/n exactly, by a telescoping cancellation of the product factors.

theorem kaplanMeier_of_no_censoring {d : Fin n → ℝ × Bool}
    (hall : ∀ i, (d i).2 = true)
    (hn : n ≠ 0) (t : ℝ) :
    kaplanMeier d t = ((univ.filter fun i => t < (d i).1).card : ℝ) / n

hypotheses.note: Every observation is an event: all indicators Δᵢ equal one.

hypotheses.label: nonempty sample
hypotheses.note: At least one observation; with n = 0 the two sides read different division conventions.

formalizationNotes: The proof is a strong induction over down-closed sets of event times, peeling the largest: without censoring, $Y(s_{k+1}) = Y(s_k) - \Delta N(s_k)$ holds exactly because no subject leaves the risk set between events, and the product telescopes to a counting fraction. The nonemptiness hypothesis is Lean-side: for $n = 0$ the right side reads against the $0/0 = 0$ convention while the empty product is one, so the identity genuinely needs a nonempty sample.

reference.formal: E. L. Kaplan and P. Meier, "Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations," *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, vol. 53, no. 282, pp. 457–481, 1958.

title: Self-Consistency of the Kaplan–Meier Estimator
informal:
Compute the Kaplan–Meier estimator $\hat S$ from a right-censored sample and read it as a law — the Stieltjes measure of $1 - \hat S$. At an observed event time $s$ where the left limit $\hat S(s^-) = \prod_{u < s} (1 - \Delta N(u)/Y(u))$ is positive, and provided the estimate carries no defect — the terminal value $\hat S(\infty)$ vanishes, as happens when the largest observation is an event, the hazard jump of the Kaplan–Meier law reproduces the Nelson–Aalen increment: $$\Delta\Lambda_{\hat S}(s) \;=\; \frac{\Delta N(s)}{Y(s)}.$$ The estimator thus solves the sample version of the hazard identity that defines the population relation between a law and its cumulative hazard.

The no-defect hypothesis is genuinely needed for the identity in this form. For a defective estimate the hazard denominator is the tail mass $\hat S(s^-) - \hat S(\infty)$ rather than $\hat S(s^-)$, which changes the jump: a two-observation dataset — one event at time $1$, one observation censored at time $2$ — has increment $\Delta N(1)/Y(1) = 1/2$ but hazard jump $1$ at $s = 1$, since all of the defective law's mass sits at the single atom.
summary: For a non-defective Kaplan–Meier estimate the hazard jump of the Kaplan–Meier law at each event time equals the Nelson–Aalen increment ΔN(s)/Y(s); a defective two-point dataset shows the no-defect hypothesis is required.

theorem cumHazardJump_kaplanMeierMeasure {d : Fin n → ℝ × Bool} {s : ℝ}
    (hs : s ∈ eventTimes d)
    (hpos : 0 < ∏ u ∈ (eventTimes d).filter (· < s), (1 - naJump d u))
    (hdefect : kmLimit d = 0) :
    cumHazardJump (kaplanMeierMeasure d) s = ENNReal.ofReal (naJump d s)

title: The Continuous Bridge: Cumulative Hazard Equals Minus Log-Survival
informal: Let $T$ have an event-time law: a probability distribution on the real line with no mass at negative times, which is continuous (atomless), and let $t$ be a time with positive survival, $S(t) = P(T > t) > 0$. Then the cumulative hazard accumulated on $(0, t]$ is minus the logarithm of survival: $$\Lambda(0, t] \;=\; -\log S(t), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad S(t) \;=\; e^{-\Lambda(0,\, t]},$$ and the accumulated hazard $\Lambda(0, t]$ is finite.
summary: For an atomless event-time law, on the region of positive survival, Λ(0, t] = −log S(t) — equivalently S(t) = exp(−Λ(0, t]) — with the accumulated hazard finite.

    (cumHazard μ (Ioc 0 t)).toReal = -Real.log (survivalReal μ t)

title: The Discrete Product Formula for the Survival Function
informal: Let $T$ have an event-time law $\mu$: a probability distribution on the real line with no mass at negative times, and fix a time $t$ such that all the mass of $\mu$ up to $t$ sits on a given finite set $E$ — the restriction of the law to $(-\infty, t]$ is purely atomic, with atoms among $E$. Then the survival function is the product of one-minus-hazard-jumps over the atoms up to $t$: $$S(t) \;=\; \prod_{s \in E,\ s \le t} \bigl(1 - \Delta\Lambda(s)\bigr),$$ where $\Delta\Lambda(s) = P(T = s)/P(T \ge s)$ is the hazard jump at $s$.
summary: For an event-time law whose mass below t sits on a finite set, S(t) = ∏_{s ≤ t} (1 − ΔΛ(s)) — the population identity mirrored by the Kaplan–Meier estimator.

    survivalReal μ t = ∏ s ∈ E.filter (· ≤ t), (1 - (cumHazardJump μ s).toReal)

title: The Cox Proportional-Hazards Model
informal:
Let $\{P_z\}$ be a family of event-time distributions indexed by a covariate vector $z \in \mathbb{R}^p$. The family satisfies the proportional-hazards structure with regression coefficient $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and baseline $\Lambda_0$ when for every covariate $z$ the cumulative-hazard measure of $P_z$ is the baseline scaled by the relative risk $e^{\beta^\top z}$: $$\Lambda_{P_z}(dt) \;=\; e^{\beta^\top z}\, \Lambda_0(dt).$$ The baseline $\Lambda_0$ is an arbitrary measure and the structure is an identity of measures — no hazard density is assumed. Letting the baseline range over a finite-dimensional class recovers parametric survival regression; letting it range over all measures gives Cox's semiparametric model, with parameter $(\beta, \Lambda_0)$ split into the target $\beta$ and the infinite-dimensional nuisance $\Lambda_0$.

For a continuous baseline the canonical survival curve of the model is the exponential-of-integrated-hazard formula $$S(t \mid z) \;=\; \exp\bigl(-e^{\beta^\top z}\, \Lambda_0(0, t]\bigr);$$ that this construction realizes the structure exactly is a separate theorem.
summary: Cox's model as a predicate on covariate-indexed families of event-time laws: the cumulative-hazard measure at covariate z is e^{β·z} Λ₀, with the baseline an arbitrary measure.

formalizationNotes: The proportionality predicate is stated on cumulative-hazard measures, so it is fully distribution-agnostic; the scaling coefficient $e^{\beta^\top z}$ is finite and strictly positive, so no degenerate-scaling corner arises. Baseline conventions — mass on the positive axis, local finiteness, atomlessness for the canonical construction — enter as hypotheses of the construction and realization theorems, not as parts of the structure. A companion structure `CoxModel` bundles the model's constitutive index data: an admissible baseline class (finite-dimensional for parametric survival, all measures for the semiparametric model) and a covariate design region.

Gill, and N. title: Realization of the Cox Model by the Canonical Cox Law
informal:
Fix $\beta, z \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and a baseline hazard measure $\Lambda_0$ that is carried by the positive half-line, locally finite — $\Lambda_0(0, t]$ is finite for every $t$, atomless, and of infinite total mass, $\Lambda_0(0, t] \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty$. The canonical Cox law at covariate $z$ is the distribution on $[0, \infty)$ whose survival function is $S(t \mid z) = \exp(-e^{\beta^\top z}\Lambda_0(0, t])$. The theorem: this law is a genuine atomless event-time distribution, and its cumulative-hazard measure is exactly the proportional-hazards prescription $$\Lambda(dt) \;=\; e^{\beta^\top z}\, \Lambda_0(dt).$$ The Cox model is therefore nonvacuous: every pair $(\beta, \Lambda_0)$ of coefficient and admissible baseline is realized by an explicit covariate-indexed family of laws.

The divergence of the total baseline hazard says the constructed law has no cure mass. We state the realization under this hypothesis because the identity requires it in this form: with a finite total baseline hazard the constructed law is defective, the hazard denominator carries the cure mass, and the resulting cumulative hazard exceeds $e^{\beta^\top z}\Lambda_0$ — a uniform baseline on $(0, 1]$ witnesses the discrepancy.

title: Identifiability of the Cox Parameters
informal:
Let $\{P_z\}$ be one covariate-indexed family of event-time distributions carrying the proportional-hazards structure for two parameter pairs on a common covariate design $Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p$: $\Lambda_{P_z} = e^{\beta^\top z}\Lambda_0$ for all $z \in Z$, and $\Lambda_{P_z} = e^{\beta'^\top z}\Lambda_0'$ for all $z \in Z$. Assume the design is rich: it contains a base covariate $z_0$ such that the differences $z - z_0$ over $z \in Z$ span all of $\mathbb{R}^p$; assume the baseline $\Lambda_0$ is not the zero measure and both baselines are $\sigma$-finite. Then the parameters coincide: $$\beta = \beta' \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Lambda_0 = \Lambda_0'.$$

The Cox parametrization is thus identified from the family of laws alone, by pure measure algebra with no estimation theory. Cross-multiplying the two representations at $z$ and at the base point turns proportionality into the scalar identity $e^{(\beta - \beta')^\top (z - z_0)} = 1$ on the design, and a linear functional vanishing on a spanning set of differences vanishes identically. Covariate variation is exactly what resolves the scale ambiguity between an intercept in $\beta$ and a rescaled baseline.
summary: Two proportional-hazards representations of one covariate-indexed family, over a design with a base point whose differences span ℝᵖ and a nonzero σ-finite baseline, have equal coefficients and equal baselines.

title: The Cox Partial Likelihood
informal:
Let $(\tilde T_i, \Delta_i, z_i)$, $i = 1, \dots, n$, be right-censored observations with covariates — an observed time, an event indicator, and a covariate vector in $\mathbb{R}^p$ per subject. The risk set at time $t$ is $R(t) = \{j : \tilde T_j \ge t\}$, the subjects still under observation at $t$. The Cox partial likelihood of a coefficient $\beta$ is the product over observed events of the failing subject's relative risk over the total relative risk of its risk set: $$L(\beta) \;=\; \prod_{i \,:\, \Delta_i = 1} \frac{e^{\beta^\top z_i}}{\sum_{j \in R(\tilde T_i)} e^{\beta^\top z_j}},$$ and the partial log-likelihood is $$\ell(\beta) \;=\; \sum_{i \,:\, \Delta_i = 1} \Bigl(\beta^\top z_i - \log \sum_{j \in R(\tilde T_i)} e^{\beta^\top z_j}\Bigr).$$ The unknown baseline hazard cancels from each ratio, so the factors depend on $\beta$ alone — this is what makes estimation of $\beta$ possible without estimating the baseline.

Each event subject belongs to its own risk set, so every denominator is positive, $L(\beta) > 0$, and $\log L(\beta) = \ell(\beta)$ exactly.

title: Concavity of the Cox Partial Log-Likelihood
informal:
For any right-censored sample with covariates — observed times, event indicators, and covariate vectors in $\mathbb{R}^p$ — the Cox partial log-likelihood $$\ell(\beta) \;=\; \sum_{i \,:\, \Delta_i = 1} \Bigl(\beta^\top z_i \;-\; \log \sum_{j \in R(\tilde T_i)} e^{\beta^\top z_j}\Bigr)$$ is a concave function of $\beta$ on all of $\mathbb{R}^p$. Each summand is a linear function of $\beta$ minus a log-sum-exp term $\beta \mapsto \log \sum_j e^{\beta^\top z_j}$, and log-sum-exp is convex — by Hölder's inequality in its weighted arithmetic–geometric-mean form — so a sum of linear-minus-convex terms is concave.

No hypotheses are needed: concavity holds for every dataset, every censoring pattern, and every dimension.

title: Cumulative Incidence and the Cause-Specific Hazard
informal:
In a competing-risks observation each subject contributes an observed time $\tilde T$ and a mark $\kappa$ recording either the failure cause $j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$ or censoring; let $P$ be a finite observed-data law on such marked observations. The identity is exact in measure form, with no continuity assumed.

title: The Statistical Model Calculus
informal:
A statistical model is a family $P = (P_\theta)_{\theta \in \Theta}$ of probability distributions on a sample space, indexed by a parameter $\theta$ ranging over an arbitrary set $\Theta$: a finite-dimensional $\Theta$ gives a parametric model, a class of functions or measures a nonparametric one, and a product $\Theta = \Psi \times H$ a semiparametric one — all instantiations of the same notion. Structured models are assembled from simpler ones by a small calculus of operations.

The pushforward model is the family of laws of a statistic $T$: $\theta \mapsto P_\theta \circ T^{-1}$. Observation passes the data through a parameter-free stochastic channel: when the full datum is $x$, the observed datum is a draw from $\kappa(\cdot \mid x)$, giving the observed-data model $\theta \mapsto \int \kappa(\cdot \mid x)\,P_\theta(dx)$ — the common form of censoring readouts, missingness masks, and randomized coarsening. Mixing marginalizes a latent variable through a parameter-dependent family of channels, $\theta \mapsto \int K_\theta(\cdot \mid x)\,P_\theta(dx)$, as in mixed-effects, frailty, latent-class, and mixture models. Replication forms the model of an independent sample of size $n$, $\theta \mapsto P_\theta^{\otimes n}$. Reparameterization and restriction to a submodel need no new definitions: they are composition of $P$ with a map into $\Theta$.
summary: The compositional calculus of statistical models on a bare family θ ↦ P_θ: pushforward by a statistic, observation through a parameter-free Markov kernel, latent-variable mixing, and n-fold i.i.d. replication.

title: Target Identifiability and I.I.D. Replication
informal:
Let $P = (P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a statistical model on a sample space and let $\psi$ be a target functional assigning to each parameter the quantity $\psi(\theta)$ to be inferred. Call $\psi$ identified by the model if the law of the data determines the target: $P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2}$ implies $\psi(\theta_1) = \psi(\theta_2)$ — equivalently, $\psi$ factors as a function of the distribution of the data. Identifiability of the parametrization itself — distinct parameters give distinct laws — is the special case of the identity target.

Suppose each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure and $n \ge 1$. Then $\psi$ is identified by the model of $n$ independent, identically distributed observations, $\theta \mapsto P_\theta^{\otimes n}$, if and only if it is identified by a single observation: replication neither creates nor destroys identification. The same equivalence holds for the model of an infinite i.i.d. sequence.
summary: A target functional is identified from n ≥ 1 i.i.d. observations iff it is identified from one — i.i.d. replication is lossless for identification.
formalizationNotes: `IdentifiesTarget P ψ` is `Function.FactorsThrough ψ P` (defined in `Identifiability/Defs.lean`); model identifiability (`Identifiable P`, injectivity of $\theta \mapsto P_\theta$, reused from the PointEstimation area) is definitionally target identifiability of the identity. The backward direction is an instance of the general transfer principle that post-processing the laws can only make identification harder (`identifiesTarget_of_comp`); the forward direction recovers the single-observation marginal from a coordinate evaluation of the product model, which is where $n \neq 0$ is spent — for $n = 0$ every parameter yields the same one-point law, so the hypothesis is genuinely needed. Companions in the same file: `identifiable_iid_iff`, the infinite-sequence version `identifiable_iidSeq_iff`, pullback along reparameterizations, restriction to semiparametric nuisance sections, and the coarsening destroy-directions (`identifiesTarget_of_observe`, `identifiesTarget_of_pushforward`); `lawFunctional` realizes an identified target as an actual functional of the law via `Function.extend`.

title: Sufficiency Preserves Identifiability
informal:
Let $P = (P_\theta)_{\theta \in \Theta}$ be a family of probability measures on a sample space $\mathcal X$ and let $T : \mathcal X \to S$ be a measurable statistic. Assume $T$ is sufficient in the regular-conditional sense: there is a single Markov kernel $Q$ from $S$ to $\mathcal X$, not depending on $\theta$, such that under every $P_\theta$ the joint law of $(T(X), X)$ is the law of $T(X)$ composed with $Q$ — that is, $Q(\cdot \mid s)$ serves as the conditional distribution of the full data given $T(X) = s$, simultaneously for all $\theta$.

Then the reduced model $\theta \mapsto \operatorname{law}(T(X))$ is identifiable if and only if the full model is: reducing the data to a sufficient statistic loses no identification power. One direction holds for an arbitrary statistic — anything identified from coarsened data was identified from the full data. The converse is the reconstruction property of sufficiency: $P_\theta = \int Q(\cdot \mid s)\, d\operatorname{law}(T(X))(s)$, so equal laws of the statistic force equal full-data laws. The same equivalence holds for identifiability of any target functional.
summary: For a statistic with a θ-free sufficient kernel, the model of the statistic is identifiable iff the full model is: sufficiency is exactly lossless coarsening.

title: The Covariance Matrix under Affine Transformation
informal:
For a random vector $X$ with distribution $\mu$, a probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d}$, write $m = \mathbb E[X]$ for its mean vector and $\Sigma_{ij} = \operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j)$ for its covariance matrix. Let $A$ be a $k \times d$ matrix and $b \in \mathbb R^k$ a shift vector, and assume $X$ is square-integrable, $\mathbb E\lVert X\rVert^2$ finite. Then the law of the affine image $AX + b$ has covariance matrix $$\operatorname{Cov}(AX + b) \;=\; A\,\Sigma\,A^{\mathsf T}.$$

Companion facts proved alongside: $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite (the quadratic form $u^{\mathsf T}\Sigma u$ is the variance of $\langle u, X\rangle$); the mean transforms as $\mathbb E[AX + b] = Am + b$; the multivariate Gaussian $N(m, \Sigma)$ has mean $m$ and covariance $\Sigma$; and for independent vectors the cross terms vanish, $\operatorname{Cov}(AX + BY) = A\,\operatorname{Cov}(X)\,A^{\mathsf T} + B\,\operatorname{Cov}(Y)\,B^{\mathsf T}$, with a finite-product version for sums over independent coordinates.
summary: The covariance matrix of a law on Euclidean space and the affine transformation law Cov(AX + b) = A Σ Aᵀ, with symmetry, positive semidefiniteness, Gaussian evaluations, and independent-sum additivity as companions.

title: Gaussian Conditioning as Exact Disintegration
informal:
Let $(X_1, X_2)$ be jointly Gaussian on $\mathbb R^{d_1} \times \mathbb R^{d_2}$ with mean blocks $(m_1, m_2)$ and block covariance $$\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_{11} & \Sigma_{12} \\ \Sigma_{21} & \Sigma_{22} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Sigma_{21} = \Sigma_{12}^{\mathsf T}, $$ assumed positive semidefinite; assume the conditioning block $\Sigma_{11}$ is positive definite. Then the conditional law of $X_2$ given $X_1 = x$ is Gaussian with the regression mean and the Schur-complement covariance: $$X_2 \mid X_1 = x \;\sim\; N\big(m_2 + \Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}(x - m_1),\; \Sigma_{22} - \Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}\Sigma_{12}\big),$$ the conditional covariance not depending on $x$.

The statement is in exact disintegration form: composing the first marginal $N(m_1, \Sigma_{11})$ with the Gaussian kernel $x \mapsto N\big(m_2 + \Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}(x - m_1),\, \Sigma_{22} - \Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}\Sigma_{12}\big)$ reproduces the joint block Gaussian exactly. The regression matrix $\Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}$ and the Schur complement are the two defined objects displayed with the theorem; that the Schur complement is again positive semidefinite is proved alongside, so the kernel's values are genuine Gaussian laws.
summary: The block-Gaussian conditional law: N(m₁, Σ₁₁) composed with the kernel x ↦ N(m₂ + Σ₂₁Σ₁₁⁻¹(x − m₁), Σ₂₂ − Σ₂₁Σ₁₁⁻¹Σ₁₂) equals the joint block Gaussian — Gaussian conditioning as an exact disintegration.

title: Uniqueness of the Gaussian Conditional Kernel
informal:
On a product of standard Borel spaces every probability measure disintegrates through an essentially unique regular conditional kernel — a measurable family of conditional distributions of the second coordinate given the first. For a jointly Gaussian vector $(X_1, X_2)$ with mean blocks $(m_1, m_2)$, positive-semidefinite block covariance $\Sigma$ with blocks $\Sigma_{11}, \Sigma_{12}, \Sigma_{21} = \Sigma_{12}^{\mathsf T}, \Sigma_{22}$, and positive-definite conditioning block $\Sigma_{11}$, this abstract conditional kernel agrees, for almost every $x$ under the marginal $N(m_1, \Sigma_{11})$, with the explicit Gaussian kernel $$x \;\mapsto\; N\big(m_2 + \Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}(x - m_1),\; \Sigma_{22} - \Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}\Sigma_{12}\big).$$

In other words, the closed-form conditional Gaussian of the Gaussian conditioning theorem is not merely one valid disintegration of the joint law: by almost-everywhere uniqueness of disintegrations it is a version of the regular conditional distribution of $X_2$ given $X_1$.
summary: The abstract disintegration kernel of a joint block Gaussian agrees almost everywhere with the explicit Gaussian conditional kernel — the closed form is the regular conditional distribution.

title: The Linear Mixed Model
informal:
The linear mixed model for one cluster of $n$ observations is $$Y \;=\; X\beta + Zb + \varepsilon,$$ where $X$ (of size $n \times p$) and $Z$ (of size $n \times q$) are the fixed-effects and random-effects design matrices, $\beta \in \mathbb R^p$ is the fixed-effects vector, and the two stochastic ingredients are independent: the random effect $b$, drawn from a law $G$ on $\mathbb R^q$, and the noise $\varepsilon$, drawn from a law $R$ on $\mathbb R^n$. The observation law of the model is the distribution of $X\beta + Zb + \varepsilon$ — the image of the product law $G \otimes R$ under the affine map $(b, \varepsilon) \mapsto X\beta + Zb + \varepsilon$.

Both latent laws are arbitrary: Gaussianity is not part of the definition. The classical Gaussian mixed model, $b \sim N(0, G)$ and $\varepsilon \sim N(0, R)$, is one instantiation, and the marginal-moment identities of the model hold with no Gaussianity at all. A companion definition forms $M$ independent clusters, each with its own design and its own latent draw.
summary: The latent-variable form of the linear mixed model Y = Xβ + Zb + ε with arbitrary independent laws for the random effects b and the noise ε — Gaussianity is one instantiation, not part of the definition.

title: Marginal Moments and the Gaussian Marginal of the Mixed Model
informal:
Consider the linear mixed model $Y = X\beta + Zb + \varepsilon$ for one cluster, with random effect $b \sim G$ and noise $\varepsilon \sim R$ independent.

Without any Gaussianity: if both latent laws are centered and integrable, then $\mathbb E\,Y = X\beta$; and if both have finite second moments, then $$\operatorname{Cov}(Y) \;=\; Z\,\operatorname{Cov}(b)\,Z^{\mathsf T} + \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)$$ — the variance-components decomposition, valid for arbitrary latent laws.

In the Gaussian case: if $b \sim N(0, G)$ and $\varepsilon \sim N(0, R)$ with $G$ and $R$ positive semidefinite, the marginal law of the response is exactly Gaussian, $$Y \;\sim\; N\big(X\beta,\; Z G Z^{\mathsf T} + R\big).$$
summary: Marginal moments of the linear mixed model with no Gaussianity — E Y = Xβ and Cov Y = Z Cov(b) Zᵀ + Cov(ε) — and the exact Gaussian marginal Y ~ N(Xβ, ZGZᵀ + R) in the Gaussian case.

title: BLUP as Gaussian Conditioning
informal:
In the Gaussian linear mixed model $Y = X\beta + Zb + \varepsilon$ with $b \sim N(0, G)$ and $\varepsilon \sim N(0, R)$ independent, the pair $(Y, b)$ is jointly Gaussian with $\operatorname{Cov}(Y) = V := Z G Z^{\mathsf T} + R$, $\operatorname{Cov}(Y, b) = Z G$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(b) = G$. For symmetric $G$, the Gaussian regression matrix at these blocks is Henderson's weight matrix: $(ZG)^{\mathsf T} V^{-1} = G Z^{\mathsf T} V^{-1}$.

Assume $G$ and $R$ are positive semidefinite and $V$ is positive definite. Then the joint law of $(Y, b)$ disintegrates exactly through the Gaussian conditional kernel of the Gaussian conditioning theorem: the marginal law of $Y$ composed with the kernel $$y \;\mapsto\; N\big(G Z^{\mathsf T} V^{-1}(y - X\beta),\; G - G Z^{\mathsf T} V^{-1} Z G\big)$$ equals the joint law of $(Y, b)$.
summary: In the Gaussian mixed model the joint law of (Y, b) disintegrates through the Gaussian conditional kernel with mean GZᵀV⁻¹(y − Xβ): the BLUP is the Gaussian conditional expectation E[b | Y].

title: Optimality of the BLUP without Gaussianity
informal:
In the linear mixed model $Y = X\beta + Zb + \varepsilon$, let the random effect $b$ and the noise $\varepsilon$ be independent with centered laws having finite second moments — no Gaussianity is assumed. Write $G = \operatorname{Cov}(b)$, $R = \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)$, and $V = Z G Z^{\mathsf T} + R$, and assume $V$ is positive definite. Predict the random effects linearly from the centered response, $\hat b = A\,(Y - X\beta)$, and measure quality by the mean-squared prediction risk $\rho(A) = \mathbb E\,\lVert b - A(Y - X\beta)\rVert^2$.

Then for every weight matrix $A$, $$\rho\big(G Z^{\mathsf T} V^{-1}\big) \;\le\; \rho(A);$$ indeed the risk decomposes exactly as $\rho(A) = \rho(A^*) + \operatorname{tr}\big((A - A^*)\,V\,(A - A^*)^{\mathsf T}\big)$ with $A^* = G Z^{\mathsf T} V^{-1}$. The best linear predictor of the random effects is thus the same weight matrix that arises as the Gaussian conditional mean in the conditioning form of BLUP — but its optimality holds for arbitrary latent laws.
summary: For arbitrary centered second-moment latent laws, the Henderson weight A* = GZᵀV⁻¹ minimizes the mean-squared prediction risk among all linear predictors of the random effects, with an exact excess-risk decomposition.

title: Henderson's Mixed-Model Equations
informal:
In the linear mixed model $Y = X\beta + Zb + \varepsilon$ with variance components $G = \operatorname{Cov}(b)$ and $R = \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)$ both positive definite, write $V = Z G Z^{\mathsf T} + R$ for the marginal covariance. For any candidate pair $(\hat\beta, \hat b)$ and any data vector $y$, the pair solves Henderson's mixed-model equations $$\begin{pmatrix} X^{\mathsf T} R^{-1} X & X^{\mathsf T} R^{-1} Z \\ Z^{\mathsf T} R^{-1} X & Z^{\mathsf T} R^{-1} Z + G^{-1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \hat\beta \\ \hat b \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} X^{\mathsf T} R^{-1} y \\ Z^{\mathsf T} R^{-1} y \end{pmatrix}$$ if and only if $\hat b = G Z^{\mathsf T} V^{-1} (y - X \hat\beta)$ — the BLUP weight applied to the residual at $\hat\beta$ — and $\hat\beta$ solves the generalized-least-squares normal equations $X^{\mathsf T} V^{-1} X \hat\beta = X^{\mathsf T} V^{-1} y$.

The bridge between the two forms is the push-through identity $$G Z^{\mathsf T} \big(Z G Z^{\mathsf T} + R\big)^{-1} \;=\; \big(Z^{\mathsf T} R^{-1} Z + G^{-1}\big)^{-1} Z^{\mathsf T} R^{-1},$$ which converts the covariance form of the BLUP weight into its precision form. The practical point of the equations is that they involve only $R^{-1}$ and $G^{-1}$ — often diagonal or block-diagonal — and never the $n \times n$ inverse of $V$ itself.
summary: Henderson's block system in R⁻¹ and G⁻¹ is solved by (β̂, b̂) iff b̂ is the BLUP at β̂ and β̂ solves the GLS normal equations in V = ZGZᵀ + R; the push-through identity bridges the covariance and precision forms of the BLUP weight.

title: Unbiasedness of the Generalized Estimating Equations
informal:
A longitudinal subject record consists of $m$ visits: visit times $t_j$, per-visit covariates $x_j$, and responses $y_j$. A generalized-estimating-equations specification consists of three modeling choices — a marginal mean function $\mu(\beta; t, x)$, a user-supplied Jacobian $D$ (the $m \times q$ matrix of derivatives $\partial \mu_j / \partial \beta_k$), and a working covariance matrix $V$ for the responses — the latter two functions of the visit data only. The estimating function of one record is $$U(\beta) \;=\; D^{\mathsf T} V^{-1} \big(y - \mu(\beta)\big).$$

Assume the marginal mean model holds at $\beta_0$: conditionally on the visit times and covariates, each response has mean $\mathbb E[\,y_j \mid t, x\,] = \mu(\beta_0; t_j, x_j)$ — nothing else about the law of the record is restricted, in particular no dependence structure across visits. Under square-integrability of the responses and fitted values, square-integrability of the weight entries, and their measurability as functions of the visit data, every coordinate of the estimating function is centered at the truth: $$\mathbb E\,\big[U(\beta_0)\big] \;=\; 0,$$ whatever working covariance was chosen. The mechanism: each coordinate of $U$ is a sum of products of a covariate-measurable weight with a conditionally centered residual. This unbiasedness — robustness to misspecification of the working covariance — is the property that drives consistency of GEE under correctness of the mean model alone.
summary: Under the marginal mean model alone, the GEE estimating function U(β₀) = DᵀV⁻¹(y − μ(β₀)) has mean zero coordinate by coordinate — whatever the working covariance.

title: The Exact Sandwich Covariance of the GEE Estimator
informal:
Consider $N$ independent subjects, each contributing $m$ visits, in the fixed-design (conditional-on-covariates) GEE setting: subject $i$ has a fixed Jacobian $D_i$ (of size $m \times q$), a symmetric working covariance $V_i$, and a response vector $y_i$ whose law $Q_i$ has true covariance $\Sigma_i$ and finite second moments. Define the bread $B = \sum_i D_i^{\mathsf T} V_i^{-1} D_i$, the meat $M = \sum_i D_i^{\mathsf T} V_i^{-1} \Sigma_i V_i^{-1} D_i$, and the linear GEE estimator $\hat\beta(y) = B^{-1} \sum_i D_i^{\mathsf T} V_i^{-1} y_i$.

Then, exactly at finite $N$, $$\operatorname{Cov}\big(\hat\beta\big) \;=\; B^{-1}\, M\, B^{-1}.$$ Companion identities in the same file: the linearization $\hat\beta(y) = \beta_0 + B^{-1}\,U(\beta_0)(y)$ around the centered total estimating function $U(\beta_0)(y) = \sum_i D_i^{\mathsf T} V_i^{-1}(y_i - D_i\beta_0)$; unbiasedness $\mathbb E\,\hat\beta = \beta_0$ when the marginal means are correct, $\mathbb E\,y_i = D_i \beta_0$, and the bread is invertible; and the meat as the exact covariance of the total estimating function.
summary: The finite-sample form of the Liang–Zeger robust covariance: the linear GEE estimator has exact covariance B⁻¹ M B⁻¹ with bread B = Σ DᵢᵀVᵢ⁻¹Dᵢ and meat M = Σ DᵢᵀVᵢ⁻¹ΣᵢVᵢ⁻¹Dᵢ.

title: Godambe Optimality of the True Covariance
informal:
In the fixed-design GEE setting of the exact sandwich — $N$ independent subjects with Jacobians $D_i$, symmetric working covariances $V_i$, and positive-definite true response covariances $\Sigma_i$ — the estimator built with working covariances $V$ has exact covariance $S(V) = B^{-1} M B^{-1}$, with bread $B = \sum_i D_i^{\mathsf T} V_i^{-1} D_i$ and meat $M = \sum_i D_i^{\mathsf T} V_i^{-1} \Sigma_i V_i^{-1} D_i$. Let $K = \sum_i D_i^{\mathsf T} \Sigma_i^{-1} D_i$ be the Godambe information — the bread evaluated at the true covariances.

Assuming the designs are identified — $K$ positive definite and $B$ invertible — the sandwich dominates the inverse Godambe information in the Loewner (positive-semidefinite) order: $$S(V) - K^{-1} \;\succeq\; 0 \quad \text{for every working covariance,}$$ and with $V = \Sigma$ the sandwich collapses to $K^{-1}$ exactly. The true covariance is therefore the optimal working covariance: no other choice produces a smaller estimator covariance. The statement is a pure matrix theorem; that $S(V)$ and $K^{-1}$ are the covariances of the two competing estimators is the content of the sandwich entry.
summary: The exact GEE sandwich dominates the inverse Godambe information K⁻¹ = (Σ DᵢᵀΣᵢ⁻¹Dᵢ)⁻¹ in the Loewner order for every working covariance, with equality at the truth — no working covariance beats the true one.

title: Missingness Mechanisms: MCAR, MAR, and the Propensity
informal:
The single-outcome missing-data model has an always-observed covariate $x$, a possibly missing real outcome $y$, and a response indicator $r$. The full data $(x, y, r)$ are generated by composing the outcome law $Q$, the joint distribution of $(x, y)$, with the missingness mechanism $\rho$ — a Markov kernel giving the conditional distribution of the indicator given the full datum $(x, y)$. The observed datum is $(x, r, r\,y)$: the outcome is revealed exactly when $r = 1$ and masked to $0$ otherwise.

Two mechanism classes are defined. Missing completely at random (MCAR): the mechanism is a constant kernel, ignoring the data entirely. Missing at random (MAR, in this monotone single-outcome pattern): the mechanism factors through the always-observed covariate, so that $\mathbb P(r = 1 \mid x, y) = \pi(x)$ depends on $x$ alone. The function $\pi$ is the propensity (response probability), and uniform positivity, or overlap, requires $\pi(x) \ge \delta$ for all $x$. These definitions feed the Horvitz–Thompson identity and Rubin's ignorability factorization.
summary: The missing-data model for a single outcome: full-data law composed with a missingness kernel, the MCAR and MAR mechanism classes, the propensity π(x) = P(R = 1 | x), and the uniform-positivity (overlap) condition.

title: The Horvitz–Thompson Inverse-Probability-Weighting Identity
informal:
Let $(x, y)$ have joint law $Q$, with the outcome $y$ observed only when the response indicator $r$ equals $1$, under a missing-at-random mechanism: a Markov kernel on the covariate gives the response probability $\pi(x) = \mathbb P(r = 1 \mid x, y)$, depending on $x$ alone. Assume uniform positivity: $\pi(x) \ge \delta$ for all $x$, with $\delta$ positive, and that the outcome is integrable.

Then the inverse-propensity-weighted observed outcome recovers the full-data mean exactly: $$\mathbb E_{\mathrm{obs}}\!\left[\frac{r\,y}{\pi(x)}\right] \;=\; \mathbb E_Q[\,y\,],$$ the expectation on the left taken under the observed-data law of $(x, r, r\,y)$. Complete cases with small response probability are up-weighted by exactly the factor that undoes the selection, so the mean of $y$ — though $y$ is never seen on the incomplete cases — is identified from the observed data under missingness at random plus overlap.
summary: Under a MAR mechanism with uniform positivity, E[R·Y/π(X)] computed under the observed-data law equals the full-data mean E[Y] — the Horvitz–Thompson inverse-probability-weighting identity.

title: Rubin's Ignorability: the Observed-Data Likelihood Factorizes
informal:
In the single-outcome missing-data model — always-observed covariate $x$, outcome $y$ revealed exactly when the response indicator is $1$ — let the mechanism be missing at random: a Markov kernel on the covariate gives the response probability $\pi(x)$. The observed-data law of $(x, r, r\,y)$ then splits by the value of the indicator: restricted to the complete cases $\{r = 1\}$ it is the outcome law $Q$ reweighted by the density $\pi(x)$, transported to the observed record; restricted to the incomplete cases $\{r = 0\}$ it is the covariate marginal reweighted by $1 - \pi(x)$; and the two slices sum back to the observed law.

Consequently, when the outcome law is dominated — $Q$ has a measurable density $f$ with respect to a σ-finite reference measure $\nu$ — the complete-case slice has density $$f(x, y)\,\pi(x)$$ with respect to $\nu$: the likelihood factor of the outcome model and the factor of the missingness mechanism multiply. When outcome law and mechanism are governed by separate (distinct) parameters, the mechanism factor is constant in the outcome parameter, so it drops out of likelihood inference about the outcome law — the missingness mechanism is ignorable.
summary: Under MAR the observed-data law splits into a π-reweighted complete-case slice and a (1−π)-reweighted incomplete slice; with a dominated outcome law the complete-case density is f(x,y)·π(x) — the factorization behind Rubin's ignorability.

title: Attenuation of the Regression Slope under Measurement Error
informal: Let the true covariate $X$, the measurement error $U$, and the response noise $\varepsilon$ be pairwise independent real random variables with finite second moments. One observes the error-contaminated covariate $W = X + U$ and the response $Y = \alpha + \beta X + \varepsilon$. The population least-squares slope of $Y$ on $W$ is $\operatorname{cov}(Y, W)/\operatorname{Var}(W)$. Then, with the observed covariate nondegenerate, $\operatorname{Var} X + \operatorname{Var} U \neq 0$, $$\frac{\operatorname{cov}(Y, W)}{\operatorname{Var} W} \;=\; \beta\,\frac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_U^2},$$ where $\sigma_X^2 = \operatorname{Var} X$ and $\sigma_U^2 = \operatorname{Var} U$: the naive slope is the true slope multiplied by the reliability ratio, strictly smaller in magnitude whenever $\sigma_U^2$ is positive — regression dilution.
summary: The classical errors-in-variables identity: with W = X + U and Y = α + βX + ε pairwise independent, the population slope of Y on W equals β·σ_X²/(σ_X² + σ_U²) — the true slope attenuated by the reliability ratio.

title: The Linear Factor Model
informal:
A factor model accounts for the joint variation of $p$ observed variables by a smaller number $q$ of unobserved ones. Writing $x \in \mathbb{R}^p$ for the observed vector and $y \in \mathbb{R}^q$ for the vector of latent factors, the linear factor model asserts $$x \;=\; \mu + \Lambda y + e,$$ where $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^p$ is a mean vector, $\Lambda$ is the $p \times q$ matrix of factor loadings, its entry $\lambda_{ij}$ recording how strongly observed variable $i$ responds to factor $j$, and $e \in \mathbb{R}^p$ collects the specific factors — the part of each observed variable that no factor explains — drawn independently of $y$.

Neither latent ingredient is required to be Gaussian: the factor $y$ follows an arbitrary distribution on $\mathbb{R}^q$ and the specific factor $e$ an arbitrary distribution on $\mathbb{R}^p$. Given the factor, the observation is the specific-factor distribution translated by $\mu + \Lambda y$, and the law of the observed vector is that conditional law averaged over the distribution of the factor. It is a probability distribution whenever the two ingredients are.

Two covariance matrices travel with the model as parameters in their own right: $\Phi$, the covariance matrix of the factors, and $\Psi$, the covariance matrix of the specific factors. They are carried separately from the two distributions, and that the distributions really have these moments is a condition stated separately rather than built in. Two named normalizations single out the classical model: the factors are standardized when $\Phi = I$, so they are uncorrelated with unit variance, and the specific covariance is diagonal when the specific factors are uncorrelated across coordinates — the assumption that forces the factors to carry all of the observed dependence.
summary: The latent-variable form x = μ + Λy + e of the linear factor model, with the factor law and the specific-factor law both arbitrary: the observed law is the specific-factor law translated by μ + Λy and mixed over the factor.

title: The Mean of the Observed Vector
informal:
In the linear factor model $x = \mu + \Lambda y + e$ the distribution of the factor $y$, the distribution of the specific factor $e$ and the covariance parameters $(\Phi, \Psi)$ are separate inputs, so nothing yet ties the parameters to the two distributions. Say that the distributions realize the parameters when both are centred and carry the declared covariances: $$\mathbb{E}[y] = 0, \quad \operatorname{Cov}(y) = \Phi, \qquad \mathbb{E}[e] = 0, \quad \operatorname{Cov}(e) = \Psi.$$ Without this the observed law ignores $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ altogether.

Suppose the factor law and the specific-factor law are probability distributions and both have finite first moments. Then the observed vector has mean $$\mathbb{E}[x] \;=\; \mu.$$ Centring the factors is exactly what makes the loading matrix contribute nothing to the mean, so $\mu$ is the mean of the data and not merely a location parameter of the model. title: The Factor-Analytic Covariance Decomposition
informal:
Consider the linear factor model $x = \mu + \Lambda y + e$ with $p$ observed variables and $q$ factors, and suppose the factor and the specific factor are centred with covariance matrices $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ and that both have finite second moments. Then the covariance matrix of the observed vector splits into a common part and a specific part: $$\Sigma \;=\; \operatorname{Cov}(x) \;=\; \Lambda \Phi \Lambda^{\mathsf T} + \Psi.$$ The first term is the variation the $q$ factors explain, the second the variation specific to each coordinate. When $\Psi$ is diagonal — the factor-analytic assumption — the specific factors contribute only to the diagonal, so every observed covariance between two distinct variables comes from the common term alone.

For standardized factors, $\Phi = I$, this is the classical identity $$\Sigma \;=\; \Lambda\Lambda^{\mathsf T} + \Psi,$$ so that the covariance matrix of $p$ observed variables is a matrix of rank at most $q$ plus the specific covariance — a diagonal matrix, in the factor-analytic model. That shape is the entire content of a $q$-factor model. When $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are genuine covariance matrices, both $\Lambda\Phi\Lambda^{\mathsf T}$ and $\Sigma$ are positive semidefinite, so the decomposition never leaves the cone of covariance matrices.
summary: The covariance matrix of the observed vector of a linear factor model is Σ = ΛΦΛᵀ + Ψ, the common part explained by the factors plus the specific part; at Φ = I this is the classical Σ = ΛΛᵀ + Ψ.

title: The Common Part Has Rank at Most the Number of Factors
informal:
In a factor model with $p$ observed variables and $q$ factors the observed covariance matrix decomposes as $\Sigma = \Lambda\Phi\Lambda^{\mathsf T} + \Psi$, where $\Lambda$ is $p \times q$ and $\Phi$ is the covariance matrix of the factors. The common part obeys $$\operatorname{rank}\big(\Lambda\Phi\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\big) \;\le\; q,$$ and more sharply it never exceeds the rank of the loading matrix. Whenever $\Phi$ is a genuine covariance matrix the common part is itself positive semidefinite, so it is a covariance matrix of rank at most $q$.

This is the structural restriction a $q$-factor model imposes. For $q < p$ it is a real constraint: an arbitrary covariance matrix of $p$ variables need not be a rank-$q$ matrix plus a diagonal one, and a covariance matrix that is not of that shape cannot have been generated by $q$ common factors. It is also the reason a $q$-factor model has fewer free parameters than an unrestricted covariance matrix, which is how the fit of a factor model is judged.
summary: The common part ΛΦΛᵀ of a q-factor covariance has rank at most q — a genuine restriction on Σ whenever q < p, and the structural content of factor analysis.

title: Communality and Specific Variance
informal:
Read the covariance decomposition $\Sigma = \Lambda\Phi\Lambda^{\mathsf T} + \Psi$ of a factor model one observed variable at a time. The communality of variable $i$ is the sum of its squared loadings, $h_i^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{q} \lambda_{ij}^2$, and its specific variance is the $i$-th diagonal entry $\psi_i$ of $\Psi$. For standardized factors, $\Phi = I$, the variance of the $i$-th observed variable splits as $$\operatorname{Var}(x_i) \;=\; h_i^2 + \psi_i,$$ the part explained by the common factors plus the part specific to that variable. For a general factor covariance the same identity holds with $h_i^2$ replaced by the $i$-th diagonal entry of $\Lambda\Phi\Lambda^{\mathsf T}$, and then needs no hypothesis at all.

Communalities are nonnegative, being sums of squares, and when $\Psi$ is a genuine covariance matrix a communality never exceeds the variance it decomposes, so the specific variance $\psi_i = \operatorname{Var}(x_i) - h_i^2$ is nonnegative as well. In the scaling in which factor analyses are usually reported each observed variable is standardized to unit variance, so that $\Sigma$ is a correlation matrix; then $h_i^2 \le 1$ and the communality is the fraction of the variable's variance attributable to the common factors, the remaining $1 - h_i^2$ being its own. Determining the communalities from the off-diagonal correlations alone — the classical communality problem — is exactly the question of splitting $\Sigma$ into a low-rank part and a diagonal part.
summary: The coordinatewise reading of Σ = ΛΦΛᵀ + Ψ: for standardized factors Var(xᵢ) = hᵢ² + ψᵢ with communality hᵢ² = Σⱼ λᵢⱼ², and hᵢ² ≤ 1 when the observed variable is standardized.

title: The Normal Factor Model and Its Marginal Law
informal:
Instantiate the linear factor model $x = \mu + \Lambda y + e$ with Gaussian latent ingredients: $y \sim N_q(0, \Phi)$ and $e \sim N_p(0, \Psi)$, independent. Assume $\Phi$ is a genuine covariance matrix and so is $\Psi$. Then the conditional law of the observation given the factor is the measurement model $$x \mid y \;\sim\; N_p\big(\mu + \Lambda y,\; \Psi\big),$$ and the observed vector is Gaussian again, with the structured covariance: $$x \;\sim\; N_p\big(\mu,\; \Lambda\Phi\Lambda^{\mathsf T} + \Psi\big).$$

Integrating the factors out therefore does not leave the normal family; it only replaces an unrestricted covariance matrix by one of the factor-analytic form. Consequently the observed data see the parameters only through the pair $(\mu, \Sigma)$, which is what makes the whole inferential story — likelihood, identifiability, factor scores — a story about $\Sigma = \Lambda\Phi\Lambda^{\mathsf T} + \Psi$. Read as a map from parameter quadruples with genuine covariance parameters to laws, the normal factor model sends $(\mu, \Lambda, \Phi, \Psi)$ to $N_p(\mu, \Sigma)$; its mean vector is $\mu$ and its covariance matrix $\Sigma$, so the Gaussian instantiation automatically satisfies the moment conditions that the general model states as hypotheses.
