title: Rademacher Complexity
informal: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a set of vectors and let $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ be independent signs, each equal to $+1$ or $-1$ with probability $\tfrac12$. The Rademacher complexity of $A$ is $$R(A)\;=\;\frac1n\,\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\Bigl[\,\sup_{a\in A}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_i a_i\Bigr].$$
summary: The Rademacher complexity of a set of vectors is the expected supremum of its correlation with a uniformly random sign vector, normalized by the dimension.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def radComplexity (A : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) : ℝ :=
  (n : ℝ)⁻¹ * signAvg n (fun ε => sSup ((fun a => ∑ i, ε i * a i) '' A))
formalizationNotes: The sign expectation is a finite average over the $2^n$ Boolean patterns, not an integral, so the definition needs no measure theory; the bridge to the product measure of independent signs is a separate lemma. The supremum is the supremum of the image set rather than an indexed supremum over the set, which avoids the junk floor at $0$ that the latter carries in Lean; the degenerate values are $R(\varnothing) = 0$, $R = 0$ for an image unbounded above, and $R = 0$ at $n = 0$, so theorems carry nonemptiness and (usually) finiteness hypotheses.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: Rademacher averages as a complexity measure for learning were introduced by V. Koltchinskii, “Rademacher penalties and structural risk minimization,” *IEEE Transactions on Information Theory* **47** (2001), 1902–1914, and by P. L. Bartlett and S. Mendelson, “Rademacher and Gaussian complexities: risk bounds and structural results,” *Journal of Machine Learning Research* **3** (2002), 463–482; the underlying symmetrization technique is classical in empirical process theory, see M. Ledoux and M. Talagrand, *Probability in Banach Spaces*, Springer, 1991.

title: Empirical Rademacher Complexity
informal: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of real-valued functions on the example domain, indexed by a set $K$, and let $S=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ be a sample. Evaluating the family on the sample produces the set of vectors $$\mathcal{F}\circ S\;=\;\bigl\{\,(f(z_1),\dots,f(z_n))\;:\;f\in\mathcal{F}\,\bigr\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n},$$ and the empirical Rademacher complexity of $\mathcal{F}$ on $S$ is the Rademacher complexity of that set, $$R(\mathcal{F}\circ S)\;=\;\frac1n\,\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\Bigl[\,\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_i f(z_i)\Bigr].$$
summary: The empirical Rademacher complexity of a function family on a sample is the Rademacher complexity of the set of its evaluation vectors on that sample.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def empRad (F : ι → Z → ℝ) (K : Set ι) (s : Sample Z n) : ℝ :=
  radComplexity (evalFamily F K s)
formalizationNotes: The family is given as a function on an index type together with a subset of indices, rather than as a set of functions, so that a hypothesis class and its loss family can be indexed by the same set. The evaluation set is the image of the index set, so the same degenerate conventions as for the Rademacher complexity apply.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: Data-dependent complexity measures of this form, and their use as penalties in structural risk minimization, are due to V. Koltchinskii, “Rademacher penalties and structural risk minimization,” *IEEE Transactions on Information Theory* **47** (2001), 1902–1914, and P. L. Bartlett and S. Mendelson, “Rademacher and Gaussian complexities: risk bounds and structural results,” *Journal of Machine Learning Research* **3** (2002), 463–482.

title: Symmetrization
informal: Let $\mathcal{F}=\{F_k\}_{k\in K}$ be a family of real-valued functions on the example domain, measurable in the example, with $K$ nonempty and countable, and suppose the family is uniformly bounded, $|F_k(z)|\le c$ for all $k\in K$ and all $z$. Then for every distribution $D$ and every sample size $n\ge1$, $$\mathbb{E}_{S\sim D^{n}}\Bigl[\,\sup_{k\in K}\bigl(L_D(F_k)-L_S(F_k)\bigr)\Bigr]\;\le\;2\,\mathbb{E}_{S\sim D^{n}}\bigl[R(\mathcal{F}\circ S)\bigr].$$
summary: The expected supremum of the gap between true and empirical risk over a bounded family is at most twice the expected Rademacher complexity of the family on the sample.
leanSignature:
theorem integral_sup_risk_sub_empRisk_le_two_mul_integral_empRad
    (F : ι → Z → ℝ) (K : Set ι) {c : ℝ}
    (hKc : K.Countable)
    (hK : K.Nonempty)
    (hmeas : ∀ k, Measurable (F k))
    (hbdd : ∀ k ∈ K, ∀ z, |F k z| ≤ c)
    (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    ∫ s, sSup ((fun k => risk D F k - empRisk F s k) '' K)
        ∂(sampleLaw D n) ≤
      2 * ∫ s, empRad F K s ∂(sampleLaw D n)
formalizationNotes: This is the one-sided form, without absolute values, which is what the constants of the high-probability Rademacher bounds require; the project's general symmetrization lemma proves the absolute-value form, so this version is proved afresh by the book's argument. Countability of the index set and the uniform bound are standing conventions for suprema in this development: they make the supremum measurable and integrable without a separability discussion. Suprema are taken over the image set, so no indexed-supremum junk value can intervene.

title: Massart's Lemma
informal: Let $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_N\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a finite nonempty set of vectors with mean $\bar a=\tfrac1N\sum_{j}a_j$. Then $$R(A)\;\le\;\max_{a\in A}\lVert a-\bar a\rVert_2\;\frac{\sqrt{2\log N}}{n},$$ where $R(A)$ is the Rademacher complexity of $A$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm.
summary: The Rademacher complexity of a finite set of vectors is at most its radius about the mean times the square root of twice the log-cardinality, divided by the dimension.
leanSignature:
theorem massart (A : Finset (Fin n → ℝ))
    (hne : A.Nonempty) :
    radComplexity (↑A : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) ≤
      (A.sup' hne fun a =>
          Real.sqrt (∑ i, (a i - (A.card : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ b ∈ A, b i) ^ 2)) *
        Real.sqrt (2 * Real.log A.card) / n
formalizationNotes: The Euclidean norm is written out as the square root of a sum of squares, because the ambient norm on the space of coordinate functions is the supremum norm. The class is a finite set so that the maximum is attained and the supremum in the Rademacher complexity is genuine. The centred variant, in which the mean is replaced by an arbitrary centre and the maximum by a radius bound, is proved alongside and is the form used downstream.

hypotheses.label: nonempty finite set
hypotheses.note: The set of vectors is finite and nonempty.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: The bound is due to P. Massart, “Some applications of concentration inequalities to statistics,” *Annales de la Faculté des Sciences de Toulouse* **9** (2000), 245–303; the underlying sub-Gaussian maximal inequality is classical, see W. Hoeffding, “Probability inequalities for sums of bounded random variables,” *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **58** (1963), 13–30.

title: Contraction Lemma for Rademacher Complexity
informal: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be finite and nonempty and let $\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_n:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be $\rho$-Lipschitz, so that $|\varphi_i(x)-\varphi_i(y)|\le\rho|x-y|$ for all $x,y$, with $\rho\ge0$. Write $\varphi\circ A=\{(\varphi_1(a_1),\dots,\varphi_n(a_n)):a\in A\}$. Then $$R(\varphi\circ A)\;\le\;\rho\,R(A).$$
summary: Composing each coordinate with a rho-Lipschitz map multiplies the Rademacher complexity of a finite set by at most rho.
leanSignature:
theorem radComplexity_contraction (A : Finset (Fin n → ℝ))
    (φ : Fin n → ℝ → ℝ) {ρ : ℝ}
    (hne : A.Nonempty)
    (hρ : 0 ≤ ρ)
    (hφ : ∀ i a b, |φ i a - φ i b| ≤ ρ * |a - b|) :
    radComplexity
        (↑(A.image fun a => fun i => φ i (a i)) : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) ≤
      ρ * radComplexity (↑A : Set (Fin n → ℝ))
formalizationNotes: This is the contraction of a Lipschitz composition inside a supremum, distinct from the coefficient contraction principle for norms of sign-weighted sums that appears elsewhere in the project. The maps may differ from coordinate to coordinate, as in the book. The class is a finite set so that suprema are attained, which the coordinate-by-coordinate pairing argument needs. The book's displayed inequality contains a typographical slip in one subscript; the statement here follows the corrected reading.

title: Rademacher Generalization Bound
informal: Let $\mathcal{F}=\{F_k\}_{k\in K}$ be a family of loss functions on the example domain, indexed by a countable nonempty set and measurable in the example, with $|F_k(z)|\le c$ for all $k\in K$ and all $z$. Let $n\ge1$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$. Then with probability at least $1-\delta$ over a sample $S$ of size $n$ drawn independently from $D$, simultaneously for every $k\in K$, $$L_D(F_k)-L_S(F_k)\;\le\;2\,\mathbb{E}_{S'\sim D^{n}}\bigl[R(\mathcal{F}\circ S')\bigr]\;+\;c\,\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(2/\delta)}{n}}.$$
summary: With high probability, every member of a uniformly bounded family has true risk exceeding its empirical risk by at most twice the expected Rademacher complexity plus a square-root deviation term.
leanSignature:
theorem rademacher_generalization_expected {δ : ℝ}
    (hKc : K.Countable)
    (hK : K.Nonempty)
    (hmeas : ∀ k, Measurable (F k))
    (hbdd : ∀ k ∈ K, ∀ z, |F k z| ≤ c)
    (hn : 1 ≤ n)
    (hδ : 0 < δ) (hδ1 : δ < 1) :
    ENNReal.ofReal (1 - δ) ≤
      sampleLaw D n {s | ∀ k ∈ K,
        risk D F k - empRisk F s k ≤
          2 * (∫ s', empRad F K s' ∂(sampleLaw D n)) +
            c * Real.sqrt (2 * Real.log (2 / δ) / n)}
formalizationNotes: The bounded-differences inequality is taken from the project's McDiarmid development, which is where the standard Borel and nonemptiness instances on the example space come from; they are formalization conventions with no counterpart in the book. The index set is countable and the family uniformly bounded, so that the supremum over the class is measurable and integrable. The degenerate case $c = 0$, in which every loss vanishes and both sides are $0$, is treated separately because the tail calibration divides by $c^2$.

informal: Let $\mathcal{F}=\{F_k\}_{k\in K}$ be a family of loss functions indexed by a countable nonempty set, measurable in the example and bounded by $c$ in absolute value. title: Excess Risk of Empirical Risk Minimization via Rademacher Complexity
informal: Let $\mathcal{F}=\{F_k\}_{k\in K}$ be a family of loss functions indexed by a countable nonempty set, measurable in the example and bounded by $c$ in absolute value. Let $A$ be a rule that returns an index in $K$ minimizing the empirical risk over the family at each sample, and let $k^\star$ be any fixed competitor in $K$. For $n\ge1$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over a sample $S$ of size $n$ from $D$, $$L_D\bigl(F_{A(S)}\bigr)-L_D\bigl(F_{k^\star}\bigr)\;\le\;2\,R(\mathcal{F}\circ S)\;+\;5c\,\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(8/\delta)}{n}}.$$

leanSignature:
theorem rademacher_erm_excess {A : Sample Z n → ι} {kStar : ι} {δ : ℝ}
    (hKc : K.Countable)
    (hK : K.Nonempty)
    (hmeas : ∀ k, Measurable (F k))
    (hbdd : ∀ k ∈ K, ∀ z, |F k z| ≤ c)
    (hA : ∀ s, A s ∈ K ∧ ∀ k ∈ K, empRisk F s (A s) ≤ empRisk F s k)
    (hkStar : kStar ∈ K)
    (hn : 1 ≤ n)
    (hδ : 0 < δ) (hδ1 : δ < 1) :

title: Polynomial Growth of the Loss Patterns of a VC Class
informal: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a class of binary classifiers on $\mathcal{X}$, identified with the class of sets $\{x:h(x)=1\}$, and suppose its VC dimension is at most $d$ — no set of more than $d$ instances is shattered, i.e. has every one of its labellings realized by a member of the class (see VC dimension). Fix a labelled sample $S=\bigl((x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_n,y_n)\bigr)$ and consider the set of loss patterns $$\bigl\{\,(\mathbf 1[h(x_1)\ne y_1],\dots,\mathbf 1[h(x_n)\ne y_n])\;:\;h\in\mathcal{H}\,\bigr\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}.$$ If $d\ge1$ and $n>d+1$, the number of distinct loss patterns is at most $$\Bigl(\frac{en}{d}\Bigr)^{d},$$ and in general at most $\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom{n}{j}$.

title: On-Average-Replace-One Stability
informal: Let $A$ be a learning rule and $\ell$ a loss. Given a sample $S=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$, an index $i$ and a fresh example $z'$, write $S^{(i)}$ for the sample obtained from $S$ by replacing its $i$-th example by $z'$. The rule is on-average-replace-one stable with rate $\epsilon(n)$ when, for every distribution $D$ on the example domain, $$\mathbb{E}_{S\sim D^{n},\,z'\sim D}\;\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl[\ell\bigl(A(S^{(i)}),z_i\bigr)-\ell\bigl(A(S),z_i\bigr)\Bigr]\;\le\;\epsilon(n).$$
summary: A rule is on-average-replace-one stable with a given rate when the expected increase in loss caused by replacing one training example is bounded by that rate.

  ∀ (D : Measure Z), IsProbabilityMeasure D →
    ∀ m : ℕ, stabilityGap D ℓ (A m) ≤ rate m
formalizationNotes: Stability is defined on average, which is the book's only formal notion; the pointwise bound that the Lipschitz analysis of regularized loss minimization actually establishes is strictly stronger and is relaxed to this notion where it is used. The joint law of the sample and the fresh example is the product of the sample law with the distribution, and the average over indices is an explicit sum rather than an expectation over a uniform index variable. The rate is a function of the sample size, with one hypothesis class for each size.

title: Change of Measure (Donsker–Varadhan)
informal: Let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on a countable index set with $Q$ absolutely continuous with respect to $P$ and finite Kullback–Leibler divergence $\mathrm{KL}(Q\Vert P)$, and let $f$ be a functional on the index set with $Q$-integrable value and $P$-integrable exponential. hypotheses.note: The sample size is at least two, so the denominator 2(n − 1) is positive.

hypotheses.note: The confidence parameter δ lies strictly between 0 and 1.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: PAC-Bayesian bounds originate with D. A. McAllester, “Some PAC-Bayesian theorems,” *Machine Learning* **37** (1999), 355–363; the change-of-measure step rests on the variational formula of M. D. Donsker and S. R. S. Varadhan, “Asymptotic evaluation of certain Markov process expectations for large time, I,” *Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics* **28** (1975), 1–47, and the moment bound on W. Hoeffding, “Probability inequalities for sums of bounded random variables,” *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **58** (1963), 13–30.

title: Weak Stationarity
informal: A real, two-sided discrete-time process $\{X_t\}_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ on a probability space is weakly stationary (also second-order, or covariance, stationary) when every coordinate is square-integrable, $E X_t^2<\infty$, the mean function is constant in time, $E X_s = E X_t$ for all $s,t$, and the lag-$k$ covariance does not depend on where it is anchored: $\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+k},X_t)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_k,X_0)$ for all $t,k\in\mathbb Z$.
summary: A process is weakly stationary when it has square-integrable coordinates, a constant mean, and a covariance depending only on the lag.
leanSignature:
structure IsStationary (X : ℤ → Ω → ℝ) (μ : Measure Ω) : Prop where
  memLp : ∀ t, MemLp (X t) 2 μ
  integral_eq : ∀ s t, ∫ ω, X s ω ∂μ = ∫ ω, X t ω ∂μ
  cov_shift : ∀ t k : ℤ, cov[X (t + k), X t; μ] = cov[X k, X 0; μ]
formalizationNotes: The index set is all of the integers, which is what the two-sided backshift operator of the source's Section 1.3.4 requires. Measurability of the coordinate maps is deliberately not a field: integrals and covariances are junk-total in Lean, and measurability is supplied as an explicit hypothesis by the theorems that need it. The covariance is Mathlib's `ProbabilityTheory.covariance`, so the second-moment field is what makes the third field's covariances well defined.

hypotheses.label: finite second moments
hypotheses.note: Every coordinate $X_t$ lies in $L^2$, so all covariances below are finite.

hypotheses.label: constant mean
hypotheses.note: The mean $E X_t$ is the same at every time $t$.

hypotheses.label: shift-invariant covariance
hypotheses.note: $\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+k},X_t)$ equals $\operatorname{Cov}(X_k,X_0)$ for every anchor $t$ and lag $k$.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.
reference.biblio: Weak stationarity and the correlation theory of stationary sequences are due to A. Ya. Khinchin, "Korrelationstheorie der stationären stochastischen Prozesse," *Mathematische Annalen* **109**, 1934, pp. 604–615; the systematic theory of stationary time series was developed by H. Wold, *A Study in the Analysis of Stationary Time Series*, Almqvist & Wiksell, Uppsala, 1938.

title: Strict Stationarity
informal: A process $\{X_t\}_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary when all of its finite-dimensional distributions are invariant under time shifts: for every finite tuple of times $t_1,\dots,t_n$ and every $k\in\mathbb Z$, the random vectors $(X_{t_1+k},\dots,X_{t_n+k})$ and $(X_{t_1},\dots,X_{t_n})$ have the same law.
summary: A process is strictly stationary when every finite-dimensional distribution is invariant under a shift of the time index.
formalizationNotes: The condition is stated over arbitrary finite time tuples rather than over the source's consecutive windows $(X_1,\dots,X_n)\overset{d}{=}(X_{1+k},\dots,X_{n+k})$. The two forms are equivalent, and the equivalence is proved separately (`isStrictlyStationary_iff_window`); the general-tuple form is what the shift arguments in the mixing theory consume directly. Equality of laws is stated as equality of pushforward measures on the product space, which is junk-tolerant: when the tuple map fails to be measurable both sides are the zero measure.

hypotheses.label: shift-invariant laws
hypotheses.note: For every finite tuple of times and every shift, the joint law of the shifted tuple equals that of the original.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.
reference.biblio: Strict stationarity in the modern measure-theoretic form goes back to A. N. Kolmogorov, *Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung*, Springer, Berlin, 1933, and to H. Wold, *A Study in the Analysis of Stationary Time Series*, Almqvist & Wiksell, Uppsala, 1938.

title: Autocovariance Function
informal: The autocovariance function of a process $\{X_t\}$ at lag $k\in\mathbb Z$ is $\gamma(k)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_k,X_0)$. For a weakly stationary process this is the covariance $\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+k},X_t)$ at every anchor $t$, and the autocorrelation function is the normalisation $\rho(k)=\gamma(k)/\gamma(0)$.
summary: The autocovariance at lag k is the covariance of the process with itself k steps apart, anchored at time zero.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def acvf (X : ℤ → Ω → ℝ) (μ : Measure Ω) (k : ℤ) : ℝ :=
  cov[X k, X 0; μ]
formalizationNotes: The definition is anchored at time $0$ so that it is a total function of the lag; that it is anchor-free is a theorem under weak stationarity (`IsStationary.cov_eq_acvf`), and for a non-stationary process the value is an anchored convention rather than the book's object. The companion autocorrelation `acf` divides by $\gamma(0)$ and therefore returns $0$ when $\gamma(0)=0$, by Lean's division convention; every autocorrelation theorem in the area carries an explicit positivity hypothesis on $\gamma(0)$.

hypotheses.label: lag-$k$ covariance
hypotheses.note: The value at lag $k$ is the covariance of $X_k$ with $X_0$.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.
reference.biblio: The autocovariance and autocorrelation vocabulary is standard since G. U. Yule, "On a method of investigating periodicities in disturbed series, with special reference to Wolfer's sunspot numbers," *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A* **226**, 1927, pp. 267–298, and H. Wold, *A Study in the Analysis of Stationary Time Series*, Almqvist & Wiksell, Uppsala, 1938.

title: Strict Stationarity with a Second Moment Implies Weak Stationarity
informal: Let $\{X_t\}_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be strictly stationary, i.e. all of its finite-dimensional distributions are invariant under time shifts, with measurable coordinates and a square-integrable marginal, $E X_0^2<\infty$. Then $\{X_t\}$ is weakly stationary: every $X_t$ is square-integrable, the mean is constant, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+k},X_t)$ depends only on the lag $k$. The converse fails.
summary: Shift-invariance of all finite-dimensional laws plus one finite second moment gives constant mean and lag-only covariance.
leanSignature:
theorem IsStrictlyStationary.isStationary [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (h : IsStrictlyStationary X μ)
    (hmeas : ∀ t, Measurable (X t))
    (hL2 : MemLp (X 0) 2 μ) :
    IsStationary X μ
formalizationNotes: The second-moment hypothesis is imposed at the single time $0$ and propagates to every time by identical distribution. The proof transports the mean and the lag-$k$ covariance along the equality of pair laws $(X_{t+k},X_t)\overset{d}{=}(X_k,X_0)$, which is the two-coordinate instance of strict stationarity; the covariance is a functional of the pair law once both coordinates are square-integrable. Measurability of the coordinates is a Lean-only hypothesis, implicit in the source.

hypotheses.label: strict stationarity
hypotheses.note: All finite-dimensional distributions of the process are invariant under time shifts.

hypotheses.label: measurable coordinates
hypotheses.note: Each $X_t$ is a measurable function on the sample space.

hypotheses.label: finite second moment
hypotheses.note: $X_0$ is square-integrable, $E X_0^2<\infty$.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.
reference.biblio: The strict-versus-weak dichotomy, and the observation that second-moment theory sees only the weak structure, are classical: A. Ya. Khinchin, "Korrelationstheorie der stationären stochastischen Prozesse," *Mathematische Annalen* **109**, 1934, pp. 604–615, and J. L. Doob, *Stochastic Processes*, John Wiley & Sons, New York, 1953, Chapter X.

title: Characterization of Autocovariance Functions
informal: A real sequence $\gamma:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$ is the autocovariance function of some weakly stationary process if and only if it is even, $\gamma(-k)=\gamma(k)$, and positive semidefinite, meaning that $$\sum_{i,j} a_i a_j\,\gamma(t_i-t_j)\ \ge\ 0$$ for every finite set of times $t_1,\dots,t_n$ and every real vector $a$.
summary: Even positive semidefinite sequences are exactly the autocovariance functions of weakly stationary processes.
leanSignature:
theorem isPosSemidefSeq_and_even_iff_acvf (γ : ℤ → ℝ) :
    ((∀ k, γ (-k) = γ k) ∧ IsPosSemidefSeq γ) ↔
      ∃ (Ω' : Type) (_ : MeasurableSpace Ω') (μ' : Measure Ω') (X' : ℤ → Ω' → ℝ),
        IsProbabilityMeasure μ' ∧ (∀ t, Measurable (X' t)) ∧ IsStationary X' μ' ∧
          acvf X' μ' = γ
formalizationNotes: The sufficiency half quantifies existentially over the probability space, matching the source's "of some stationary time series". It is proved by a random-phase construction over the spectral measure supplied by the Herglotz theorem, rather than by a Gaussian Kolmogorov-extension argument, so no extension theorem over the integers is needed. Positive semidefiniteness is the source's displayed condition (2.17), packaged as the predicate `IsPosSemidefSeq`.

hypotheses.leanToken: (∀ k, γ (-k) = γ k) ∧ IsPosSemidefSeq γ
hypotheses.label: even and positive semidefinite
hypotheses.note: $\gamma(-k)=\gamma(k)$ for all $k$, and every finite quadratic form $\sum_{i,j}a_ia_j\gamma(t_i-t_j)$ is nonnegative.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.
reference.biblio: The characterization of covariance functions by nonnegative definiteness is due to A. Ya. Khinchin, "Korrelationstheorie der stationären stochastischen Prozesse," *Mathematische Annalen* **109**, 1934, pp. 604–615; the construction of a process with a prescribed covariance is standard Kolmogorov-extension reasoning, A. N. Kolmogorov, *Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung*, Springer, Berlin, 1933.

title: Stationarity and Autocovariance of a Linear Process
informal: Let $\{\varepsilon_t\}$ be white noise with mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2$, let $\{\psi_j\}_{j\ge0}$ be absolutely summable, $\sum_j|\psi_j|<\infty$, and suppose $X_t=\sum_{j\ge0}\psi_j\varepsilon_{t-j}$ in the sense that the partial sums converge to $X_t$ in $L^2$ at every time $t$, with measurable coordinates. Then $\{X_t\}$ is weakly stationary with autocovariance $$\gamma(k)\ =\ \sigma^2\sum_{j\ge0}\psi_j\,\psi_{j+|k|}.$$
summary: A one-sided moving average of white noise with absolutely summable weights is weakly stationary, with autocovariance given by the convolution of the weights.
leanSignature:
theorem IsLinearProcessOf.isStationary [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {ψ : ℕ → ℝ} {σ2 : ℝ}
    {X ε : ℤ → Ω → ℝ} (hX : IsLinearProcessOf ψ X ε μ)
    (hψ : Summable fun j => |ψ j|) (hε : IsWhiteNoise ε σ2 μ)
    (hmeas : ∀ t, Measurable (X t)) :
    IsStationary X μ ∧
      ∀ k : ℤ, acvf X μ k = σ2 * ∑' j : ℕ, ψ j * ψ (j + k.natAbs)
formalizationNotes: The convergence mode of the defining series is made explicit as an $L^2$ limit of the one-sided partial sums, which is the mode the source works with but leaves implicit. Innovations are only assumed to be white noise — uncorrelated with common variance — not independent. The autocovariance formula interchanges covariance with the $L^2$ limits by continuity of the inner product and collapses the resulting double series by uncorrelatedness.

hypotheses.label: moving-average representation
hypotheses.note: The one-sided partial sums $\sum_{j<N}\psi_j\varepsilon_{t-j}$ converge to $X_t$ in $L^2$ at every time.

hypotheses.label: absolutely summable weights
hypotheses.note: $\sum_{j\ge0}|\psi_j|<\infty$.

hypotheses.label: white-noise innovations
hypotheses.note: The $\varepsilon_t$ have mean $0$, common variance $\sigma^2$, and are pairwise uncorrelated.

hypotheses.label: measurable coordinates
hypotheses.note: Each $X_t$ is a measurable function on the sample space.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.
reference.biblio: Infinite moving averages originate with E. Slutsky, "The summation of random causes as the source of cyclic processes," *Econometrica* **5**(2), 1937, pp. 105–146, and with H. Wold, *A Study in the Analysis of Stationary Time Series*, Almqvist & Wiksell, Uppsala, 1938.

title: Herglotz's Theorem
informal: Let $\gamma:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$ be even, $\gamma(-k)=\gamma(k)$, and positive semidefinite, so that $\sum_{i,j}a_ia_j\gamma(t_i-t_j)\ge0$ for all finite time sets and real coefficients. Then there is a finite measure $F$ on the circle $\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$, invariant under $\lambda\mapsto-\lambda$, whose Fourier coefficients are $\gamma$: $$\gamma(k)\ =\ \int e^{ik\lambda}\,dF(\lambda),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.$$
summary: Every even positive semidefinite sequence on the integers is the Fourier-coefficient sequence of a symmetric finite measure on the circle.
leanSignature:
theorem exists_measure_of_isPosSemidefSeq (γ : ℤ → ℝ)
    (heven : ∀ k, γ (-k) = γ k)
    (hpsd : IsPosSemidefSeq γ) :
    ∃ F : Measure (AddCircle (2 * π)), IsFiniteMeasure F ∧ NegInvariant F ∧
      ∀ k : ℤ, measureFourierCoeff F k = (γ k : ℂ)
formalizationNotes: The source states the result for the normalised autocorrelation, so that $F$ is a probability distribution; we state the unnormalised form of total mass $\gamma(0)$, from which the normalised version is a scalar rescaling. The book's "symmetric distribution on $[-\pi,\pi]$" is negation-invariance on the circle, and symmetry of the constructed measure is part of the conclusion here rather than left to the reader. The proof is the self-contained Fejér route: the Fejér densities built from $\gamma$ are nonnegative and define measures with trigonometric moments $(1-|j|/n)\gamma(j)$ and total mass $\gamma(0)$; normalising and extracting a weakly convergent subsequence by compactness of the space of probability measures on the circle passes the moments to the limit. The degenerate case $\gamma(0)=0$ forces $\gamma\equiv0$ and is handled by taking the zero measure.

hypotheses.label: even sequence
hypotheses.note: $\gamma(-k)=\gamma(k)$ for every integer $k$.

hypotheses.label: positive semidefinite sequence
hypotheses.note: Every finite quadratic form $\sum_{i,j}a_ia_j\gamma(t_i-t_j)$ is nonnegative.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.
reference.biblio: The moment theorem behind this statement is G. Herglotz, "Über Potenzreihen mit positivem, reellem Teil im Einheitskreis," *Berichte über die Verhandlungen der Königlich-Sächsischen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Leipzig* **63**, 1911, pp. 501–511; the real-line analogue is S. Bochner, *Vorlesungen über Fouriersche Integrale*, Akademische Verlagsgesellschaft, Leipzig, 1932. The time-series formulation followed here is that of P. J. Brockwell and R. A. Davis, *Time Series: Theory and Methods*, 2nd ed., Springer, New York, 1991, pp. 118–119.

title: Existence of the Spectral Measure
informal: Every weakly stationary process $\{X_t\}$ admits a spectral measure: a finite measure $F$ on the circle $\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$, invariant under $\lambda\mapsto-\lambda$, whose Fourier coefficients recover the autocovariances, $$\gamma(k)\ =\ \int e^{ik\lambda}\,dF(\lambda),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.$$ Its total mass is $\gamma(0)=\operatorname{Var}(X_0)$, and it is unique.
summary: Every weakly stationary process has a symmetric finite measure on the circle whose Fourier coefficients are its autocovariances.
formalizationNotes: The predicate `IsSpectralMeasure` bundles finiteness, negation-invariance and the coefficient identity, so the statement is the Wiener–Khintchine correspondence in process form: it combines the Herglotz theorem with the evenness and positive semidefiniteness of the autocovariance function. Uniqueness is not claimed in the source; it is supplied separately here (`IsSpectralMeasure.unique`) so that the phrase "the spectral measure" is meaningful, and it follows from the fact that a finite measure on the circle is determined by its Fourier coefficients. The book's conventions on $[-\pi,\pi]$ with endpoint identification are the circle picture, and the mass identity $F(\text{circle})=\gamma(0)$ is the coefficient at lag $0$.

hypotheses.label: weak stationarity
hypotheses.note: The process has square-integrable coordinates, a constant mean, and a covariance depending only on the lag.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.
reference.biblio: The correspondence between stationary processes and spectral measures is the Wiener–Khintchine theorem: N. Wiener, "Generalized harmonic analysis," *Acta Mathematica* **55**, 1930, pp. 117–258, and A. Ya. Khinchin, "Korrelationstheorie der stationären stochastischen Prozesse," *Mathematische Annalen* **109**, 1934, pp. 604–615; see also H. Wold, *A Study in the Analysis of Stationary Time Series*, Almqvist & Wiksell, Uppsala, 1938.

title: Spectral Density
informal: The spectral density of a process with autocovariance function $\gamma$ is the series $$g(\lambda)\ =\ \frac1{2\pi}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\gamma(k)\,\cos(k\lambda),\qquad \lambda\in\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z,$$ the real part of $\frac1{2\pi}\sum_k\gamma(k)e^{ik\lambda}$. When the autocovariances are absolutely summable the series converges uniformly, $g$ is continuous and nonnegative, and $g$ is the density of the spectral measure with respect to the rotation-invariant measure of total mass $2\pi$ on the circle.
summary: The spectral density is the Fourier series of the autocovariance function, normalised by 2 pi.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def spectralDensityOf (X : ℤ → Ω → ℝ) (μ : Measure Ω)
    (l : AddCircle (2 * π)) : ℝ :=
  (2 * π)⁻¹ * ∑' k : ℤ, acvf X μ k * (fourier k l).re
formalizationNotes: The $1/2\pi$ sits in the density and never in the forward transform, which is the source's unnormalised convention. Because $\gamma$ is even the series is real, so the definition takes the real part of the exponential series rather than a cosine series, which keeps the Fourier API of Mathlib available. The definition is total: when the autocovariances are not summable the unconditional sum returns the junk value $0$, and every theorem about $g$ carries an explicit summability hypothesis.

hypotheses.leanToken: (2 * π)⁻¹ * ∑' k : ℤ, acvf X μ k * (fourier k l).re
hypotheses.label: Fourier series of the autocovariance
hypotheses.note: $g(\lambda)=\frac1{2\pi}\sum_k\gamma(k)\cos(k\lambda)$, the real part of the autocovariance's Fourier series.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.
reference.biblio: The $\ell^1$ inversion pair between autocovariances and a continuous spectral density goes back to N. Wiener, "Generalized harmonic analysis," *Acta Mathematica* **55**, 1930, pp. 117–258; the time-series statement followed here is P. J. Brockwell and R. A. Davis, *Time Series: Theory and Methods*, 2nd ed., Springer, New York, 1991, Corollary 4.3.2.

title: The Spectral Measure Has a Continuous Density under Summable Autocovariances
informal: Let $\{X_t\}$ be weakly stationary with absolutely summable autocovariances, $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\gamma(k)|<\infty$. Then the function $$g(\lambda)=\frac1{2\pi}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\gamma(k)\cos(k\lambda)$$ is continuous and nonnegative, and the measure with density $g$ against the rotation-invariant measure of total mass $2\pi$ on the circle is the spectral measure of $\{X_t\}$; equivalently $\gamma(k)=\int e^{ik\lambda}g(\lambda)\,d\lambda$ for every lag $k$.
summary: Absolutely summable autocovariances make the spectral measure absolutely continuous with the continuous nonnegative density given by their Fourier series.
leanSignature:
theorem isSpectralMeasure_withDensity [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {X : ℤ → Ω → ℝ}
    (hstat : IsStationary X μ) (hsum : HasSummableACVF X μ) :
    IsSpectralMeasure X μ
      ((ENNReal.ofReal (2 * π) •
          (AddCircle.haarAddCircle : Measure (AddCircle (2 * π)))).withDensity
        fun l => ENNReal.ofReal (spectralDensityOf X μ l))
formalizationNotes: Uniform convergence of the series from the Weierstrass test gives continuity and justifies term-by-term integration. Pointwise nonnegativity of the density is not read off the shape of the series but obtained from the nonnegativity of the Fejér means, which is the source's in-text argument. The identification with the spectral measure uses orthonormality of the Fourier characters against Mathlib's probability Haar measure on the circle, with the mass-$2\pi$ rescaling converting the book's integral over $[-\pi,\pi]$.

hypotheses.label: weak stationarity
hypotheses.note: The process has square-integrable coordinates, a constant mean, and a covariance depending only on the lag.

hypotheses.label: summable autocovariances
hypotheses.note: $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\gamma(k)|<\infty$.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.
reference.biblio: The inversion pair is due to N. Wiener, "Generalized harmonic analysis," *Acta Mathematica* **55**, 1930, pp. 117–258; the form of the statement follows P. J. Brockwell and R. A. Davis, *Time Series: Theory and Methods*, 2nd ed., Springer, New York, 1991, Corollary 4.3.2.

title: Spectral Density of a Linearly Filtered Process
informal: Let $\{Y_t\}$ be weakly stationary with absolutely summable autocovariances, let $\{\varphi_k\}_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ be an absolutely summable filter, $\sum_k|\varphi_k|<\infty$, and let $\{X_t\}$ be the filtered process $X_t=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\varphi_k Y_{t-k}$, the symmetric partial sums converging in $L^2$ at every time, with measurable coordinates on both sides. Then the spectral densities satisfy $$g_X(\lambda)\ =\ |\Gamma(\lambda)|^2\,g_Y(\lambda),\qquad \Gamma(\lambda)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\varphi_k e^{-ik\lambda},$$ where $\Gamma$ is the transfer function of the filter.
summary: Filtering multiplies the spectral density by the squared modulus of the filter's transfer function.
leanSignature:
theorem IsFilteredBy.spectralDensityOf_eq [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {X Y : ℤ → Ω → ℝ}
    {φ : ℤ → ℝ} (h : IsFilteredBy X Y φ μ)
    (hφ : Summable fun k => |φ k|) (hY : IsStationary Y μ)
    (hYsum : HasSummableACVF Y μ)
    (hmeasY : ∀ t, Measurable (Y t)) (hmeasX : ∀ t, Measurable (X t))
    (l : AddCircle (2 * π)) :
    spectralDensityOf X μ l = ‖transferFun φ l‖ ^ 2 * spectralDensityOf Y μ l
formalizationNotes: Two things the source assumes are derived here instead: that the output process is again weakly stationary, and that its autocovariances are again absolutely summable. Both come out of the companion statement `IsFilteredBy.isStationary`, which also proves the double-convolution formula $\gamma_X(k)=\sum_{j,l}\varphi_j\varphi_l\gamma_Y(k+j-l)$ that the book glosses. The convergence mode of the two-sided filter is made explicit as an $L^2$ limit of the symmetric partial sums $\sum_{|k|\le N}$; existence of such an output for any summable filter and stationary input is proved separately. The density identity is obtained by rearranging the triple series on the series side of the spectral density.

hypotheses.label: filter representation
hypotheses.note: The symmetric partial sums $\sum_{|k|\le N}\varphi_kY_{t-k}$ converge to $X_t$ in $L^2$ at every time.

hypotheses.label: absolutely summable filter
hypotheses.note: $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\varphi_k|<\infty$, so the transfer function is a continuous function on the circle.

hypotheses.label: stationary input
hypotheses.note: The input process is weakly stationary.

hypotheses.label: summable input autocovariances
hypotheses.note: $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\gamma_Y(k)|<\infty$, so the input has a continuous spectral density.

hypotheses.label: measurable coordinates
hypotheses.note: Each $Y_t$ and each $X_t$ is a measurable function on the sample space.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.
reference.biblio: Linear filtering of stationary processes is classical Wiener–Kolmogorov theory, N. Wiener, "Generalized harmonic analysis," *Acta Mathematica* **55**, 1930, pp. 117–258; the statement followed here is P. J. Brockwell and R. A. Davis, *Time Series: Theory and Methods*, 2nd ed., Springer, New York, 1991, Theorem 4.4.1.

title: Spectral Density of an ARMA Process
informal: Let $\{X_t\}$ satisfy the ARMA$(p,q)$ equation $b(B)X_t=a(B)\varepsilon_t$ with white noise of variance $\sigma^2$, where $b(z)=1-b_1z-\dots-b_pz^p$ and $a(z)=1+a_1z+\dots+a_qz^q$. Assume the process is weakly stationary, it is the causal moving-average solution built from the transfer coefficients of $a/b$, $b(z)\neq0$ for $|z|\le1$, and the coordinates are measurable. Then $$g(\lambda)\ =\ \frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{|a(e^{-i\lambda})|^2}{|b(e^{-i\lambda})|^2}.$$
summary: A stationary causal ARMA process has the rational spectral density given by the squared moduli of its moving-average and autoregressive polynomials on the unit circle.
leanSignature:
theorem IsARMA.spectralDensityOf_eq [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {p q : ℕ}
    {b : Fin p → ℝ} {a : Fin q → ℝ} {σ2 : ℝ} {X ε : ℤ → Ω → ℝ}
    (h : IsARMA b a σ2 X ε μ)
    (hstat : IsStationary X μ)
    (hcausal : IsLinearProcessOf (armaPsi b a) X ε μ)
    (hroot : NoRootClosedDisc b)
    (hmeas : ∀ t, Measurable (X t))
    (l : AddCircle (2 * π)) :
    spectralDensityOf X μ l =

title: Partial Autocorrelation as the Last Autoregressive Coefficient
informal: For a weakly stationary process and a lag $k\ge1$, suppose the covariance matrix of the window $(X_2,\dots,X_k)$ is invertible and the residual of $X_1$ regressed on that window has positive variance. informal: For two sub-$\sigma$-algebras $\mathcal F_1$ and $\mathcal F_2$, the strong-mixing coefficient is $$\alpha(\mathcal F_1,\mathcal F_2)=\sup_{A\in\mathcal F_1,\,B\in\mathcal F_2}\left|P(A\cap B)-P(A)P(B)\right|.$$

The two $\sigma$-algebra arguments are arbitrary measurable-space structures on the sample space rather than sub-$\sigma$-algebras by construction, so the ordering hypotheses appear only on the lemmas that need them. The process-level coefficient anchors the past at time $0$, which is the source's convention for strictly stationary processes; that the anchor is immaterial under strict stationarity is proved separately and is what every blocking argument in this area uses. The $\beta$-coefficient is defined through the finite-partition formula rather than the book's conditional-probability form, the two being equivalent on standard Borel spaces.

title: Volkonskii–Rozanov Decoupling Inequality
informal: Let $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_k$ be complex random variables with $k\ge1$, each $\xi_l$ measurable for a $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal F_l$ contained in the ambient one, with $|\xi_l|\le1$ almost everywhere. Suppose the strong mixing coefficient between the accumulated past $\mathcal F_1\vee\dots\vee\mathcal F_l$ and the next block $\mathcal F_{l+1}$ is at most $a$ for every $l$. Then $$\Bigl|\,E\prod_{l=1}^{k}\xi_l-\prod_{l=1}^{k}E\xi_l\,\Bigr|\ \le\ 16\,(k-1)\,a .$$
summary: Unit-bounded blocks separated by small mixing gaps factorise up to sixteen times the number of gaps times the gap coefficient.

Without it the statement is refutable, and a machine-checked witness is recorded in the source file: with no blocks at all every hypothesis is vacuous, the empty products make the left-hand side exactly $0$, and the right-hand side reads $-16a$, which is negative for every positive $a$. title: Maximal Correlation Is Controlled by the Uniform Mixing Coefficient
informal: For any two sub-$\sigma$-algebras $\mathcal F_1,\mathcal F_2$ of a probability space, the maximal correlation coefficient $\rho=\sup|\operatorname{Corr}(f,g)|$ over square-integrable $f$ measurable for $\mathcal F_1$ and $g$ measurable for $\mathcal F_2$, and the uniform mixing coefficient $\varphi=\sup|P(B)-P(B\mid A)|$, satisfy $$\rho\ \le\ 2\sqrt{\varphi}.$$

formalizationNotes: The source records this as a display without proof; it is proved here. The declaration's name still carries the suffix under which it was first commissioned as a literature citation; the statement is proved and depends on no additional axioms.

title: Central Limit Theorem for Bounded Strongly Mixing Sequences
informal: Let $\{X_t\}$ be strictly stationary with measurable coordinates, uniformly bounded, $|X_t|\le C$ almost everywhere, and of mean zero. title: Birkhoff's Pointwise Ergodic Theorem
informal: Let $f$ be a measure-preserving and measurable self-map of a probability space, and let $g$ be integrable. summary: Time averages along a measure-preserving map converge almost everywhere to the conditional expectation on the invariant sigma-algebra.

The proof is Garsia's: the maximal ergodic theorem — the integral of an integrable observable over the set where some Birkhoff sum is positive is nonnegative — is proved first and then used to squeeze the upper and lower limits of the averages. The invariant $\sigma$-algebra is defined as the measurable sets that are exactly, not almost, invariant. The ergodic corollary, where the limit is the space mean, is stated separately.

title: Harris' Ergodic Theorem
informal: Let $P$ be a Markov transition kernel on a measurable state space. Suppose there is a nonnegative measurable function $V$ with a Lyapunov drift, $\int V\,dP(x,\cdot)\le\gamma V(x)+K$ for all $x$, with $0<\gamma<1$ and $K\ge0$, and a minorization on the sublevel set $\{V\le R\}$: $P(x,A)\ge\alpha\,\nu(A)$ there, for some probability measure $\nu$ and some $\alpha\in(0,1]$, with the level high enough that $R>2K/(1-\gamma)$. Then $P$ has a unique invariant probability measure $\pi$, and it is geometrically ergodic: there are $\rho<1$ and a starting-state-dependent constant with $$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{TV}\ \le\ C(x)\,\rho^{\,n}\qquad\text{for every }x.$$
summary: A Lyapunov drift together with a minorization on a high enough sublevel set gives a unique invariant law approached at a geometric rate from every state.
formalizationNotes: The formalization takes the Hairer–Mattingly route, which avoids the irreducibility and petite-set apparatus entirely, and departs from it at three points. There is no coupling construction: the contraction estimate falls out of the minimality of the Jordan decomposition of the difference of the two laws, which subtracts the minorization mass from both halves at once. There is no completeness argument: the invariant law is built explicitly by telescoping the one-step Jordan parts of the chain from a fixed starting state, both resulting series converging geometrically, with their tails as the explicit total-variation error. And uniqueness does not go through the contraction at all, but splits the difference of two invariant laws by a Hahn set and makes the minorizing measure vanish. Two definitions in this development were repaired after machine-checked counterexamples, both of which are retained in the source as commented witnesses: the weighted total-variation distance had been built from the singular part rather than from the Jordan decomposition, so it ignored absolutely continuous overlap and the contraction was false against it; and the drift condition had been stated with the Bochner integral, which Lean sets to zero on non-integrable functions, so it constrained nothing at states where $V$ is not integrable against the kernel, and both existence and uniqueness failed. The drift is now stated with the lower integral.

hypotheses.label: Lyapunov drift
hypotheses.note: $\int V\,dP(x,\cdot)\le\gamma V(x)+K$ for every state, with $0<\gamma<1$ and $K\ge0$, the integral taken in the lower sense.

hypotheses.label: minorization on a sublevel set
hypotheses.note: On $\{V\le R\}$ the kernel dominates $\alpha\nu$ for a fixed probability measure $\nu$ and some $\alpha\in(0,1]$.

hypotheses.label: high enough level set
hypotheses.note: $R>2K/(1-\gamma)$, so the sublevel set is large enough for the drift to be felt.

reference.formal: M. Hairer and J. C. Mattingly, "Yet another look at Harris' ergodic theorem for Markov chains," in *Seminar on Stochastic Analysis, Random Fields and Applications VI*, Progress in Probability **63**, Birkhäuser, Basel, 2011, pp. 109–117.
reference.biblio: The theorem is T. E. Harris, "The existence of stationary measures for certain Markov processes," in *Proceedings of the Third Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability* **2**, University of California Press, Berkeley, 1956, pp. 113–124; the drift-and-minorization formulation is S. P. Meyn and R. L. Tweedie, *Markov Chains and Stochastic Stability*, Springer-Verlag, London, 1993, Chapters 15–16. In time series it is what underlies the geometric-ergodicity criterion of J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series*, Springer, 2003, Theorem 2.4.

title: Geometric Ergodicity of a Nonlinear Autoregression
informal: Consider the nonlinear autoregression $X_t=f(X_{t-1},\dots,X_{t-p-1})+\varepsilon_t$, vectorized as a Markov chain on $\mathbb R^{p+1}$. Suppose $f$ is measurable and a sup-norm contraction up to a constant, $|f(\mathbf x)|\le\lambda\max_i|x_i|+c$ with $0\le\lambda<1$ and $c\ge0$, and that the innovations have an everywhere-positive density $g$ that is continuous, with a finite first moment and mean zero. Then the chain is geometrically ergodic: it has a unique invariant probability law, and the $n$-step transition laws approach it in total variation at a geometric rate from every starting state.
summary: A vectorized nonlinear autoregression whose drift is a sup-norm contraction and whose noise has a positive continuous density is geometrically ergodic.
leanSignature:
theorem nlARKernel_geometricallyErgodic
    {f : (Fin (p + 1) → ℝ) → ℝ}
    (hf : Measurable f)
    {g : ℝ → ℝ≥0∞} (hg : Measurable g)
    (hgc : Continuous g)
    (hgpos : ∀ x, 0 < g x)
    {ν : Measure ℝ} (hν : ν = MeasureTheory.volume.withDensity g)
    [IsProbabilityMeasure ν]
    (hint : Integrable (fun x : ℝ => x) ν) (hmean : ∫ x, x ∂ν = 0)
    {lam c : ℝ}
    (hlam0 : 0 ≤ lam) (hlam : lam < 1) (hc : 0 ≤ c)
    (hbound : ∀ x, |f x| ≤ lam * (⨆ i, |x i|) + c) :
    ∃ F : Measure (Fin (p + 1) → ℝ), IsProbabilityMeasure F ∧
      IsGeometricallyErgodic (nlARKernel f ν) F
formalizationNotes: We adjust the printed hypothesis by additionally requiring the innovation density to be continuous. Without continuity the density has no positive lower bound on a compact window, and the natural repair — restricting the noise rather than the value — makes the multi-step window law depend on the starting state, which destroys the minorization. Every consumer of this theorem in this development already supplies continuity. The mean-zero hypothesis is not used by the proof and is kept only because it is part of the frozen statement. The proof takes $V(\mathbf x)=\max_i\theta^{i}|x_i|$ with $\theta$ a root of a boosted contraction factor as Lyapunov function; after $p+1$ steps every coordinate has been refreshed and the law dominates a fixed multiple of a window measure not depending on the starting state, so Harris' theorem applies to the $(p+1)$-step kernel and invariance is transported back. Petite sets and irreducibility are avoided throughout, and no Jacobian or density of the triangular value map is ever formed: the chain is rewritten in value coordinates once and the induction peels one value at a time.

title: Two-Sided Stationary Realization of a Markov Chain
informal: Let $P$ be a Markov kernel on a standard Borel space and let $\pi$ be an invariant probability measure for $P$. Then there is a probability space carrying a process $\{Y_t\}_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ indexed by all of the integers such that every finite window has the stationary chain law: for every starting time $t$ and every window length, the joint law of $(Y_t,Y_{t+1},\dots,Y_{t+k})$ is the law of the chain started from $\pi$ and run for $k$ steps.
summary: An invariant law of a Markov kernel on a standard Borel space is realized by a strictly stationary process indexed by all of the integers.
leanSignature:
theorem exists_twoSided_stationary_chain
    (κ : ProbabilityTheory.Kernel S S) [ProbabilityTheory.IsMarkovKernel κ]
    (π : Measure S) [IsProbabilityMeasure π]
    (hinv : ProbabilityTheory.Kernel.Invariant κ π) :
    ∃ (Ω' : Type) (_ : MeasurableSpace Ω') (μ' : Measure Ω') (Y : ℤ → Ω' → S),
      IsProbabilityMeasure μ' ∧ (∀ t, Measurable (Y t)) ∧
      ∀ (t : ℤ) (k : ℕ),
        μ'.map (fun ω (i : Fin (k + 1)) => Y (t + (i : ℕ)) ω) = chainWindowLaw κ π k
formalizationNotes: The Mathlib pin supplies the Ionescu–Tulcea construction over the natural numbers but no Kolmogorov extension over the integers, so the two-sided chain cannot be obtained as a projective limit. The construction here takes the natural-extension route instead, which needs no extension theorem: on a standard Borel space the time-reversed transition kernel exists by disintegration, and the two-sided chain is realized concretely as a time-zero value together with a forward and a backward trajectory, conditionally independent given the time-zero value. The single exported conclusion is the family of window-law equalities, uniform in the starting time; strict stationarity, the Markov property and the marginals are all finite-dimensional consequences of it, so consumers never touch the construction.

hypotheses.label: invariant law
hypotheses.note: $\pi$ is a probability measure with $\pi P=\pi$.

title: Existence of a Stationary Causal ARMA Solution
informal: Consider the ARMA$(p,q)$ equation $b(B)X_t=a(B)\varepsilon_t$ with $b(z)=1-b_1z-\dots-b_pz^p$ and $a(z)=1+a_1z+\dots+a_qz^q$. If $b(z)\neq0$ for every complex $z$ with $|z|\le1$ and the innovations are white noise with variance $\sigma^2$, then the transfer coefficients $\psi_j=[z^j]\,a(z)/b(z)$ decay geometrically and are absolutely summable, and the linear process $X_t=\sum_{j\ge0}\psi_j\varepsilon_{t-j}$ is a solution of the ARMA equation that is weakly stationary and causal — a moving average of present and past innovations only.
summary: When the autoregressive polynomial has no roots in the closed unit disc, the ARMA equation has a stationary causal moving-average solution.
leanSignature:
theorem exists_stationary_arma [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {p q : ℕ} {b : Fin p → ℝ}
    {a : Fin q → ℝ} {σ2 : ℝ} {ε : ℤ → Ω → ℝ}
    (hb : NoRootClosedDisc b)
    (hε : IsWhiteNoise ε σ2 μ) :
    ∃ X : ℤ → Ω → ℝ, (∀ t, Measurable (X t)) ∧
      IsLinearProcessOf (armaPsi b a) X ε μ ∧ IsARMA b a σ2 X ε μ ∧
      IsStationary X μ ∧ IsCausalFor X ε μ
formalizationNotes: The transfer coefficients are defined through the formal power-series inverse of the autoregressive polynomial, which is legitimate because that polynomial has constant coefficient $1$; the analytic content enters only through the geometric bound on the coefficients. The source derives that bound from the geometric expansion of the reciprocal polynomial; here it is obtained from Cauchy estimates on a disc of radius larger than one, after identifying the formal and analytic expansions as the two power-series solutions of the same convolution equation. Existence of the $L^2$ limit defining the linear process comes from the fact that absolutely summable coefficients are square-summable, together with orthogonality of white noise.

hypotheses.label: no roots in the closed disc
hypotheses.note: $b(z)\neq0$ for every complex $z$ with $|z|\le1$.

hypotheses.label: white-noise innovations
hypotheses.note: The $\varepsilon_t$ have mean $0$, common variance $\sigma^2$, and are pairwise uncorrelated.

reference.formal: J. Fan and Q. Yao, *Nonlinear Time Series: Nonparametric and Parametric Methods*, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 2003.

title: Causality Forces the Autoregressive Polynomial to Have No Roots in the Closed Disc
informal: Let $\{X_t\}$ satisfy the ARMA$(p,q)$ equation with white-noise innovations of variance $\sigma^2$, and suppose it is weakly stationary and causal, i.e. a moving average of present and past innovations with absolutely summable coefficients, with $\sigma^2>0$. If in addition the autoregressive and moving-average polynomials have no common zero, then $b(z)\neq0$ for every complex $z$ with $|z|\le1$.
summary: For an ARMA equation with coprime polynomials, a stationary causal solution exists only if the autoregressive polynomial has no roots in the closed unit disc.
leanSignature:
theorem arma_causal_of_stationary_debt [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {p q : ℕ}
    {b : Fin p → ℝ} {a : Fin q → ℝ} {σ2 : ℝ} {X ε : ℤ → Ω → ℝ}
    (h : IsARMA b a σ2 X ε μ) (hstat : IsStationary X μ)
    (hσ : 0 < σ2)
    (hcop : IsCoprime (arPoly b) (maPoly a))
    (hcausal : IsCausalFor X ε μ) :
    NoRootClosedDisc b
formalizationNotes: We adjust the statement by adding the hypothesis that the two polynomials have no common zero. Without it the statement is refutable, and the witness is recorded in the source: taking $b(z)=1-z=a(z)$, the recursion $X_t=X_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t-\varepsilon_{t-1}$ is solved exactly by $X=\varepsilon$, which is stationary and causal for any white noise, yet $b$ vanishes at $z=1$. The added hypothesis is exactly the standing assumption under which Brockwell and Davis state the equivalence. The proof pairs the recursion with a past innovation and uses orthogonality of the innovations — this is where the positive noise variance is used, to cancel a common factor — turning the stochastic identity into a deterministic convolution; absolute summability then makes the transfer series converge on the closed disc, and the Cauchy product upgrades the convolution to the identity $a(z)=b(z)\Psi(z)$ there, so a root of $b$ in the disc would be a common root. The stationarity hypothesis is not used by the proof and is kept because it is the form in which the source states the equivalence.

title: Uniqueness of the Stationary ARMA Solution
informal: Suppose the autoregressive polynomial has no roots on the unit circle, $b(z)\neq0$ whenever $|z|=1$. If $\{X_t\}$ and $\{X'_t\}$ both satisfy the same ARMA equation driven by the same innovations and both are weakly stationary, then they agree: $X_t=X'_t$ almost everywhere at every time.
summary: Two stationary solutions of the same ARMA equation driven by the same noise coincide when the autoregressive polynomial has no roots on the unit circle.
formalizationNotes: The hypothesis is only that there are no roots on the unit circle, which is weaker than the closed-disc condition of the existence theorem: uniqueness holds in the non-causal case as well, where the solution involves future innovations. The difference of the two solutions satisfies the homogeneous equation $b(B)D_t=0$ with a stationary $D$, and the circle condition forces the difference to vanish. The declaration's name still carries the suffix under which it was first commissioned as a literature citation; the statement is proved.

title: Yule–Walker Recurrences for the ARMA Autocovariances
informal: Let $\{X_t\}$ satisfy the ARMA$(p,q)$ equation with white-noise innovations, be weakly stationary and causal, with $b(z)\neq0$ for $|z|\le1$. Then for every lag $k>q$ beyond the moving-average order the autocovariances satisfy the homogeneous recurrence $$\gamma(k)\ =\ \sum_{i=1}^{p} b_i\,\gamma(k-i).$$
summary: Beyond the moving-average order, the autocovariances of a causal stationary ARMA process satisfy the autoregressive recurrence.
formalizationNotes: The source's derivation uses independence of the innovations from the past; the formalization replaces it by uncorrelatedness, which is all the white-noise assumption gives and all the argument needs — causality kills the covariances of future innovations against the past through continuity of the covariance along $L^2$ limits. The companion exponential-decay statement avoids the source's partial-fraction argument, which implicitly assumes distinct roots: the geometric bound on the transfer coefficients gives the decay of the autocovariances directly, with no caveat about repeated roots.

title: Consistency of the ARMA Gaussian Maximum Likelihood Estimator
informal: Let the data come from a stationary causal ARMA$(p,q)$ process with independent and identically distributed innovations of positive variance, with true parameter $\theta_0=(b_0,a_0)$ in the invertibility region and with coprime polynomials. Let $K$ be a compact search region contained in that region, all of whose members are coprime pairs, containing $\theta_0$. If $\hat\theta_T$ is a measurable sequence of approximate minimisers of the profiled Gaussian criterion over $K$, the tolerance tending to $0$, then $\hat\theta_T\to\theta_0$ in probability.
summary: Approximate minimisers of the profiled Gaussian ARMA criterion over a compact identifiable region converge in probability to the true parameter.

formalizationNotes: We adjust the statement by requiring that the whole search region consist of minimal, i.e. coprime, models rather than only the truth. The requirement was added after a Lean witness showed it cannot be dropped: over a two-point region on which the profiled criterion is constant, a constant estimator sequence satisfies the approximate-minimisation condition while staying a fixed distance from the truth. The estimator is treated as a hypothesis — a measurable sequence of approximate minimisers with a vanishing tolerance — rather than constructed, which is the usual convention for M-estimators and matches the source's own reading of its display; the source prints an argument-minimum where an argument-maximum of the likelihood is meant, and the criterion here is the negative twice-log-likelihood, so the direction agrees. The proof shows that the profiled criterion converges, uniformly on compact subsets of the invertibility region, to a deterministic contrast uniquely minimised at the truth, the log-determinant term vanishing in the limit by a Szegő-type argument. The pointwise law of large numbers behind that convergence is proved without invoking the ergodic theorem, and the uniform half is a deterministic modulus-of-continuity estimate.

title: Consistency of the ARMA Innovation Variance Estimator
informal: In the setting of the Gaussian ARMA likelihood — data from a stationary causal ARMA$(p,q)$ process with independent and identically distributed innovations of positive variance $\sigma^2$, a coprime invertible true parameter of exact orders $p$ and $q$, and a measurable sequence of approximate minimisers of the profiled criterion over a compact region of minimal invertible models with the true parameter in its interior — if the minimisation tolerance is $o(1/T)$, then the profiled variance estimator is consistent: $$\hat\sigma^2_T\ =\ \frac{S(\hat\theta_T)}{T}\ \longrightarrow_p\ \sigma^2 .$$

title: Asymptotic Distribution of the Residual Autocorrelations
informal: Let the data come from a correctly specified stationary causal invertible ARMA$(p,q)$ model with independent and identically distributed innovations of positive variance and coprime polynomials. Let $\hat\theta_T$ be a measurable estimator sequence that is super-consistent at the parametric rate, $\sqrt T(\hat\theta_T-\theta_0)\to_p 0$. Then for every fixed lag $k\ge1$ the sample autocorrelation of the fitted residuals satisfies $$\sqrt T\,\hat\rho_e(k)\ \longrightarrow_d\ N(0,1).$$
summary: Residual autocorrelations at a fixed lag are asymptotically standard normal after root-T scaling, justifying the usual correlogram bands.

    (hB0 : ARMAInvertibleParams b0 a0)
    (hcop : IsCoprime (arPoly b0) (maPoly a0))

    (θ : (T : ℕ) → Ω → (Fin p → ℝ) × (Fin q → ℝ)) (hθmeas : ∀ T, Measurable (θ T))

      (μ {ω | δ ≤ Real.sqrt T * dist (θ T ω) (b0, a0)}).toReal) atTop (𝓝 0))
    {k : ℕ} (hk : 1 ≤ k) (u : ℝ) :
    Tendsto (fun T : ℕ => charFun (μ.map fun ω =>
        Real.sqrt T * sampleACF
          (fun t : Fin T => sampleResiduals (θ T ω).1 (θ T ω).2

That is what makes the conclusion true: under mere boundedness in probability at the parametric rate the limit law is not determined by the rate at all, since it depends on the limit law of $\sqrt T(\hat\theta_T-\theta_0)$, and the discrepancy is not covered by the finer Box–Pierce variance correction alone. Residuals are the finite-sample ones obtained from the autoregressive inversion of the fitted model truncated to the sample. The argument proceeds through a martingale-difference central limit theorem for the sample autocorrelation of the true innovations and a transfer step from the true to the fitted residuals; the martingale route needs no fourth moment, which the i.i.d. assumption does not supply. The exact Box–Pierce deflation of the variance at small lags is a strictly finer statement and is not formalized.

title: ARCH Model
informal: A process $\{X_t\}$ follows an autoregressive conditionally heteroscedastic model of order $p$ when $$X_t=\sigma_t\varepsilon_t,\qquad \sigma_t^2=c_0+b_1X_{t-1}^2+\dots+b_pX_{t-p}^2,$$ with nonnegative coefficients $c_0\ge0$ and $b_i\ge0$, innovations $\{\varepsilon_t\}$ that are independent and identically distributed with mean $0$ and variance $1$, each $\varepsilon_t$ independent of the strict past $\{X_{t-k}:k\ge1\}$, the observation equation holding almost everywhere at every time, and measurable coordinates.
summary: An ARCH process is a product of i.i.d. unit-variance noise with a volatility that is an affine function of the recent squared observations.

The volatility is not carried as a separate process but is the explicit measurable function of the last $p$ squared observations, defined as the square root of the manifestly nonnegative affine form. The model equation holds almost everywhere at each time point, which is the distributional reading of the book's displayed equation.

title: GARCH Model
informal: A process $\{X_t\}$ follows a generalized autoregressive conditionally heteroscedastic model of orders $(p,q)$ when $$X_t=\sigma_t\varepsilon_t,\qquad \sigma_t^2=c_0+\sum_{i=1}^{p}b_iX_{t-i}^2+\sum_{j=1}^{q}a_j\sigma_{t-j}^2,$$ with nonnegative coefficients, a nonnegative volatility process carried explicitly that is adapted to the strict past of the observations, innovations that are independent and identically distributed with mean $0$ and variance $1$, each independent of the strict past, and both model equations holding almost everywhere at every time.
summary: A GARCH process is a product of i.i.d. unit-variance noise with a past-adapted volatility obeying an affine recursion in past squared observations and past volatilities.

  b_nonneg : ∀ i, 0 ≤ b i
  a_nonneg : ∀ j, 0 ≤ a j
  measurableX : ∀ t, Measurable (X t)
  measurableVol : ∀ t, Measurable (σvol t)
  vol_nonneg : ∀ t, ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 ≤ σvol t ω

  indep_past : ∀ t : ℤ,

title: Existence of a Stationary ARCH Process
informal: Let $c_0\ge0$ and $b_1,\dots,b_p\ge0$ with $\sum_j b_j<1$, and let $\{\varepsilon_t\}$ be independent and identically distributed with mean $0$ and variance $1$. Then there is a strictly stationary ARCH$(p)$ process driven by these innovations with finite second moments, and every such solution satisfies $E X_t=0$ and $$E X_t^2\ =\ \frac{c_0}{1-\sum_j b_j}.$$

None of the Markov-chain apparatus of the source's Chapter 2 is used.

title: Existence of a Stationary GARCH Process
informal: Let $c_0\ge0$ and all $b_i,a_j\ge0$ with $\sum_i b_i+\sum_j a_j<1$, and let $\{\varepsilon_t\}$ be independent and identically distributed with mean $0$ and variance $1$. Then there exist a strictly stationary GARCH$(p,q)$ process with finite second moments together with its volatility process.

title: Necessity of the GARCH Stationarity Condition
informal: Conversely, if $\{X_t\}$ is a GARCH$(p,q)$ process that is strictly stationary with finite second moments and $c_0>0$, then $$\sum_i b_i+\sum_j a_j\ <\ 1 .$$
summary: A strictly stationary square-integrable GARCH process with positive intercept must have coefficients summing to less than one.
formalizationNotes: The positivity of the intercept is stated explicitly; it is what rules out the identically zero solution, for which the conclusion fails. The proof is Bollerslev's fixed-point argument: taking expectations in the two model equations and using that the innovation is independent of the past-measurable volatility with unit second moment, the common second moment $m=E X_t^2$ satisfies $m=c_0+(\sum_ib_i+\sum_ja_j)m$, where the volatility terms are folded in through the identity $E\sigma_t^2=E X_t^2$, itself a consequence of the volatility being the conditional variance. Positivity of $c_0$ then forces $m>0$ and the strict inequality.

        * (b1 + a1) ^ (k - 1)
formalizationNotes: The printed formula was checked against the recursion before formalization — the analogous formula for stochastic volatility models in the same chapter turned out to be misprinted — and is correct as printed. Worth stressing is that it carries no dependence on the innovation kurtosis, even though each individual moment it is assembled from does: the squared process is exactly an autoregressive moving-average process of orders $(1,1)$ in the martingale-difference errors, and the kurtosis factor common to the lag-zero and lag-one autocovariances cancels in the ratio. Accordingly the proof never introduces the kurtosis; the constancy in time of the second moment of the squared volatility is obtained from a contracting affine recursion together with an a priori bound, not from a fourth moment of the innovations. The nonvanishing of the denominator is stated explicitly since Lean's division convention would otherwise return a junk value.

title: Autocorrelation of the Squared Lognormal Stochastic Volatility Process
informal: Consider the stochastic volatility model $X_t=\varepsilon_t e^{h_t/2}$ with latent first-order autoregressive log-volatility $h_t=a_0+a_1h_{t-1}+e_t$. Assume the model equations, standard normal observation noise, a stationary Gaussian latent marginal with mean $\mu_h$ and positive variance $\sigma_h^2$, $|a_1|<1$ with the latent chain the causal solution of its recursion, joint normality of every pairwise sum of latent coordinates, latent autocovariances $\sigma_h^2a_1^{|k|}$, and a strictly stationary observation process with finite fourth moments. Then at every nonzero lag $k$ $$\operatorname{Corr}(X_t^2,X_{t-k}^2)\ =\ \frac{\exp\bigl(\sigma_h^2a_1^{|k|}\bigr)-1}{3\exp(\sigma_h^2)-1}.$$
summary: The squared lognormal stochastic volatility process has an explicit autocorrelation whose denominator carries the innovation kurtosis.
leanSignature:
theorem IsSV.acf_sq_lognormal [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {a0 a1 σe2 μh σh2 : ℝ}
    {X h ε e : ℤ → Ω → ℝ}
    (hSV : IsSV (fun x => Real.exp (x / 2)) a0 a1 σe2 X h ε e μ)
    (hgauss : μ.map (ε 0) = gaussianReal 0 1)
    (hlatent : μ.map (h 0) = gaussianReal μh (Real.toNNReal σh2)) (hσh : 0 < σh2)
    (ha1 : |a1| < 1)
    (hcausal : IsLinearProcessOf (fun j => a1 ^ j) (fun t ω => h t ω - a0 / (1 - a1))
      e μ)
    (hjoint : ∀ k : ℤ, ∃ (m : ℝ) (v : NNReal),
      μ.map (fun ω => h k ω + h 0 ω) = gaussianReal m v)
    (hacvf : ∀ k : ℤ, acvf h μ k = σh2 * a1 ^ k.natAbs)
    (hstat : IsStrictlyStationary X μ) (hL4 : ∀ t, MemLp (X t) 4 μ)
    {k : ℤ} (hk : k ≠ 0) :
    acf (fun t ω => X t ω ^ 2) μ k
      = (Real.exp (σh2 * a1 ^ k.natAbs) - 1) / (3 * Real.exp σh2 - 1)
formalizationNotes: We adjust the printed denominator. The source prints $e^{\sigma_h^2}-1$, which is the autocorrelation of the volatility $e^{h_t}$ itself, where the multiplier $\varepsilon_t^2$ is absent; for the squared observations the variance carries the fourth moment of the observation noise, $\operatorname{Var}(X_0^2)=e^{2\mu_h+\sigma_h^2}(3e^{\sigma_h^2}-1)$, while $\operatorname{Cov}(X_k^2,X_0^2)=e^{2\mu_h+\sigma_h^2}(e^{\sigma_h^2a_1^{|k|}}-1)$. The two expressions agree only when $a_1=0$. The statement is restricted to nonzero lags, since at lag zero the autocorrelation is $1$ by definition — the one place where the printed denominator is the right one. Two further hypotheses are stated that the printed model has but the bare model equations do not force: that the latent chain is the causal solution of its recursion, without which the identity is false and a witness satisfying everything else is recorded in the source; and that the latent chain is Gaussian jointly, not merely marginally, without which the moment generating function of a pairwise sum of latent coordinates is not determined. Both hold in the source's model, whose latent innovations are Gaussian.

title: Stationarity of a Threshold Autoregression
informal: Consider the $k$-regime threshold autoregression $$X_t=\sum_{i}\Bigl\{b_{i0}+\sum_{j}b_{ij}X_{t-j}+\sigma_i\varepsilon_t\Bigr\}\,\mathbf 1\{X_{t-d}\in A_i\},$$ with a measurable partition $\{A_i\}$ of the real line, delay $1\le d\le P$ within the state window, a common regime scale $\sigma_0>0$, and the uniform contraction $\max_i\sum_j|b_{ij}|<1$. If the innovation law has a continuous positive density with mean zero and a finite second moment, then a strictly stationary solution exists on some probability space.
summary: Equal regime scales and a uniform contraction of the regime coefficients give a strictly stationary threshold autoregression.

theorem exists_stationary_tar [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {k P : ℕ}

    (hA : ∀ i, MeasurableSet (A i))
    (hdisj : Pairwise fun i j => Disjoint (A i) (A j))
    (hcov : (⋃ i, A i) = Set.univ)
    (hσ : 0 < σ0)
    (hcontract : ∀ i, (∑ j, |b i j|) < 1)
    (hd : 1 ≤ d) (hdP : d ≤ P)
    {ν : Measure ℝ} [IsProbabilityMeasure ν]
    (hν : ∃ g : ℝ → ℝ, Continuous g ∧ (∀ x, 0 < g x) ∧
      ν = MeasureTheory.volume.withDensity fun x => ENNReal.ofReal (g x))
    (hν2 : Integrable (fun x : ℝ => x ^ 2) ν) (hνmean : ∫ x, x ∂ν = 0) :
    ∃ (Ω' : Type) (_ : MeasurableSpace Ω') (μ' : Measure Ω') (X' ε' : ℤ → Ω' → ℝ),
      IsProbabilityMeasure μ' ∧
        IsTAR b0 b (fun _ => σ0) A d X' ε' μ' ∧ IsStrictlyStationary X' μ'

Two adjustments are recorded. The innovation density is required to be continuous, which is the documented strengthening carried by the geometric-ergodicity theorem it delegates to; and the source's condition on equal regime scales is printed with an index typo, which does not affect the condition. The stationary solution is produced together with its own probability space and innovation process, and the innovation law fed to the ergodicity theorem is taken to be centred normal with the stated scale rather than the hypothesised law, because the conclusion asks for a threshold autoregression in the sense of the model definition, whose innovations have unit variance and enter through the scale; the substituted law satisfies the same hypotheses. The model definition uses a common maximal order with zero padding in place of per-regime orders, which is a reparametrization rather than a restriction. The threshold-estimation theory of the same section is outside the scope of this development.

title: The Empirical Measure and the Monte Carlo Average
informal: A sample $x_1,\dots,x_n$ carries a discrete uniform population of its own: the empirical measure $$\mathbb P_n \;=\; \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \delta_{x_i},$$ which places mass $1/n$ at each observation. Gentle's bootstrap principle is that this measure is a usable surrogate for the population the data came from. The corresponding Monte Carlo average of a function $g$ is $$\widehat I_n(g) \;=\; \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g(x_i),$$ the sample mean of the transformed observations.
summary: The empirical measure (1/n)Σδ_{x_i} of a sample and the Monte Carlo average (1/n)Σg(x_i), the two objects every Monte Carlo and resampling statement in this topic is built from.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def empiricalMeasure {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → 𝓧) : Measure 𝓧 :=
  (n : ℝ≥0∞)⁻¹ • ∑ i : Fin n, Measure.dirac (x i)

noncomputable def mcEstimate {n : ℕ} (g : 𝓧 → ℝ) (x : Fin n → 𝓧) : ℝ :=
  (n : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ i, g (x i)
formalizationNotes: Both objects are defined for an arbitrary measurable space and an arbitrary finite sample, with no probability structure assumed. Edge behaviour is fixed rather than excluded: at n = 0 the empirical measure is the zero measure (the empty sum, scaled by the junk value (0 : ℝ≥0∞)⁻¹ = ∞, collapses to 0) and the Monte Carlo average is the junk value 0, since (0 : ℝ)⁻¹ = 0 in Lean. Statements that need a genuine probability measure carry a positive-sample-size instance.

hypotheses.leanToken: (n : ℝ≥0∞)⁻¹ • ∑ i : Fin n, Measure.dirac (x i)
hypotheses.label: discrete uniform population
hypotheses.note: Mass $1/n$ at each of the $n$ observations; a probability measure as soon as $n \ge 1$.

hypotheses.label: Monte Carlo average
hypotheses.note: The sample mean $\frac1n\sum_i g(x_i)$, which is exactly the integral of $g$ against the empirical measure.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: The use of the empirical distribution as a surrogate population is B. Efron, "Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife," *Annals of Statistics* **7** (1979), 1–26.

title: Integration Against the Empirical Measure Is Averaging
informal: Integrating a function against the empirical measure of a sample returns the sample average of its values: $$\int f \, d\mathbb P_n \;=\; \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i).$$ This is the plug-in principle in its most basic form — a population functional $\Theta(P)=\int f\,dP$ evaluated at $\mathbb P_n$ is a finite sum — and it is what lets every later Monte Carlo and resampling statement move between measure-theoretic and finite-sum language without redoing the conversion.
summary: The integral of f against the empirical measure equals the sample average of f, the identity that converts every plug-in functional into a finite sum.

Strong measurability is what Mathlib's Dirac-integral lemma requires; it is a regularity hypothesis, not a restriction on the statistical content.

title: Weighted Particle Populations Are Probability Measures

The empirical measure is the special case $w_i \equiv 1/n$.

title: Bootstrap Draws Have the Empirical Distribution
informal: Resampling a datum in the bootstrap is the same as drawing an index uniformly and reading off the observation at that index: $$\text{Law}\big(x_{A}\big) \;=\; \mathbb P_n, \qquad A \sim \text{Uniform}\{1,\dots,n\}.$$ Formally, the empirical measure is the pushforward of the uniform categorical law on indices through the data map. This is the bridge between the two ways of describing a bootstrap sample — as values drawn from $\mathbb P_n$, or as indices drawn with replacement — and it is what makes the multinomial count representation available.
summary: The empirical measure is the pushforward of a uniform index draw through the data, identifying value resampling with index resampling with replacement.

The positive-sample-size instance excludes the degenerate n = 0 case, where the left side is the zero measure. title: Unbiasedness of an i.i.d. Coordinate Average
informal: Under the i.i.d. law of a sample of size $n$ from $P$, the average of an integrable function over the coordinates has expectation the population integral: $$\mathbb E\Big[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g(X_i)\Big] \;=\; \int g \, dP.$$ This is the exact, non-asymptotic statement behind "the sample mean estimates the population mean", stated on the canonical product space so that every estimator built from an i.i.d. sample can appeal to it directly.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.

title: Variance of an i.i.d. Coordinate Average
informal: For a square-integrable function of an i.i.d. sample, averaging divides the variance by the sample size: $$\operatorname{Var}\Big(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g(X_i)\Big) \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{Var}_P(g)}{n}.$$ Everything quantitative about Monte Carlo error rests on this identity — it is why the root-mean-square error of a simulation estimate decays like $n^{-1/2}$, independently of the dimension of the space being integrated over.
