title: Deleting One Observation Leaves an Independent i.i.d. Sample
informal: Split an i.i.d. sample of size $n+1$ into the $i$-th observation and the remaining $n$: the pair is distributed as $$ (X_i, X_{(-i)}) \;\sim\; P \otimes P^{\otimes n}. $$ The deleted observation is independent of the sample that remains, and that remaining sample is again i.i.d. from $P$. This elementary fact is used silently in every jackknife and cross-validation computation — it is what makes a delete-one statistic behave like a statistic computed from a genuine sample of size $n$, and what makes a held-out observation a fresh test point.

title: The Monte Carlo Estimator Is Unbiased
informal: Write the quantity of interest as an expectation, $\theta=\int g\,dP$, simulate $X_1,\dots,X_n$ independently from $P$, and average. The resulting estimator $$\widehat\theta \;=\; \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g(X_i)$$ has expectation exactly $\theta$, provided $g$ is integrable: simulation introduces no systematic error, only sampling error. This is the first of Gentle's three steps — decompose the integrand so that a probability density appears as a factor, identify an expectation, and estimate it by a sample average.

hypotheses.label: integrable
hypotheses.note: $g$ has a finite first moment under the sampling distribution $P$.

title: Monte Carlo Variance Is σ²/n
informal: The Monte Carlo estimator of $\int g\,dP$ from $n$ independent draws has variance $$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta) \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{Var}_P(g)}{n}$$ whenever $g$ is square-integrable. Two consequences shape all of simulation practice: the error decays like $n^{-1/2}$, so accuracy is bought by quadrupling the sample for each extra digit; and the rate does not depend on the dimension of the space, which is why Monte Carlo displaces quadrature for high-dimensional integrals.
summary: Var of the Monte Carlo estimator equals Var_P(g)/n — the dimension-free n^{-1/2} error rate of simulation.

hypotheses.label: square-integrable
hypotheses.note: $g$ has a finite second moment under $P$; without it the variance need not exist.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: Monte Carlo estimation of integrals dates to N. Metropolis and S. Handscomb, *Monte Carlo Methods*, Methuen, London, 1964.

title: Mean-Squared Error of the Monte Carlo Estimator
informal: Because the estimator is unbiased, its mean-squared error about the true value is exactly its variance: $$\mathbb E\big[(\widehat\theta-\theta)^2\big] \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{Var}_P(g)}{n}, \qquad \theta=\int g\,dP,$$ for square-integrable $g$. Stating the error in this form is what makes a simulation reportable: the root-mean-square error $\sigma/\sqrt n$ can be estimated from the same sample, which is the standard error attached to a Monte Carlo answer.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.

title: Strong Consistency of the Monte Carlo Estimator
informal: Along an infinite i.i.d. simulation stream, the Monte Carlo estimates converge to the true value with probability one: $$\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g(X_i) \;\longrightarrow\; \int g\,dP \qquad \text{almost surely},$$ for every integrable and measurable $g$. Gentle states exactly this as the guarantee that ordinary Monte Carlo estimation relies on; it is the reason a simulation can be run until its answer stabilises.
summary: Along an infinite i.i.d. stream the Monte Carlo estimates converge almost surely to ∫ g dP, by the strong law of large numbers.

title: The Importance-Sampling Identity
informal: If the target $P$ is dominated by a proposal $Q$, then integrating against $P$ is the same as integrating the reweighted function against $Q$: $$\int g \, dP \;=\; \int g \, w \; dQ, \qquad w = \frac{dP}{dQ}.$$ This change of measure is the whole of importance sampling: one may simulate from a convenient distribution $Q$ and correct by the weight $w$, and the answer is unchanged. Domination is not a technicality — where $P$ puts mass and $Q$ does not, no reweighting of $Q$-draws can recover it.
summary: ∫ g dP = ∫ g·(dP/dQ) dQ under P ≪ Q: the change-of-measure identity that licenses simulating from a proposal instead of the target.
formalizationNotes: The importance weight is defined as the real-valued Radon–Nikodym derivative `(P.rnDeriv Q z).toReal`. The theorem is a textbook-named wrapper of Mathlib's `integral_toReal_rnDeriv_mul`, kept so that downstream statements read in the language of importance sampling rather than of Radon–Nikodym derivatives.

hypotheses.label: dominated
hypotheses.note: $P \ll Q$: every $Q$-null set is $P$-null, so the density $dP/dQ$ exists. This is Gentle's support condition on the importance function.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: Importance sampling is H. Kahn and A. W. Marshall, "Methods of reducing sample size in Monte Carlo computations," *Journal of the Operations Research Society of America* **1** (1953), 263–278; the optimal-density calculation appears as Theorem 4.3.1 of R. Y. Rubinstein, *Simulation and the Monte Carlo Method*, Wiley, New York, 1981.

title: The Importance-Sampling Estimator Is Unbiased
informal: Draw $X_1,\dots,X_n$ independently from the proposal $Q$ and average the weighted values: $$\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{IS}} \;=\; \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g(X_i)\,w(X_i), \qquad w=\frac{dP}{dQ}.$$ Under domination and integrability of the weighted integrand, this estimator has expectation $\int g\,dP$ — it is unbiased for the target integral even though not a single draw came from the target.
summary: The importance-sampling estimator (1/n)Σ g(X_i)w(X_i), built from proposal draws, is unbiased for ∫ g dP.
leanSignature:
theorem importanceSampling_unbiased [IsProbabilityMeasure Q] [SigmaFinite P]
    {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] {g : 𝓧 → ℝ}
    (hPQ : P ≪ Q)
    (hgw : Integrable (fun z => g z * importanceWeight P Q z) Q) :
    ∫ x, mcEstimate (fun z => g z * importanceWeight P Q z) x
        ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => Q)
      = ∫ z, g z ∂P
formalizationNotes: Composed from the general coordinate-average lemma applied at the weighted integrand g·w under the proposal law, followed by the change-of-measure identity. The estimator is the ordinary Monte Carlo estimator of a different integrand, which is exactly why no new probabilistic content is needed.

hypotheses.label: domination
hypotheses.note: The target is absolutely continuous with respect to the proposal.

hypotheses.leanToken: hgw : Integrable (fun z => g z * importanceWeight P Q z) Q
hypotheses.label: integrability of the weighted integrand
hypotheses.note: $g\,w$ has a finite first moment under $Q$; equivalently $g$ is $P$-integrable.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.

title: Variance of the Importance-Sampling Estimator
informal: The importance-sampling estimator has variance $$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{IS}}) \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{Var}_Q(g\,w)}{n},$$ the variance now being that of the weighted integrand under the proposal. This is what makes the choice of proposal a design problem rather than a convenience: unbiasedness holds for any dominating $Q$, but the efficiency of the scheme is decided entirely by how nearly constant the product $g\,w$ is.
summary: Var(θ̂_IS) = Var_Q(g·w)/n: the proposal affects not the bias but the variance, through the spread of the weighted integrand.
leanSignature:
theorem importanceSampling_variance [IsProbabilityMeasure Q] {n : ℕ} [NeZero n]
    {g : 𝓧 → ℝ}
    (hgw : MemLp (fun z => g z * importanceWeight P Q z) 2 Q) :
    variance (mcEstimate fun z => g z * importanceWeight P Q z)
        (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => Q)
      = variance (fun z => g z * importanceWeight P Q z) Q / n
formalizationNotes: The general i.i.d. variance identity applied at the weighted integrand. No domination hypothesis appears: the statement is about the estimator actually computed from proposal draws, whose variance is well defined whether or not the weight represents a genuine density.

hypotheses.leanToken: hgw : MemLp (fun z => g z * importanceWeight P Q z) 2 Q
hypotheses.label: weighted integrand
hypotheses.note: $g\,w$ is square-integrable under the proposal; this can fail even when $g$ is bounded, if the weights are heavy-tailed.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.

title: Lower Bound on the Second Moment of Any Importance Density
informal: For any importance density $p$ and any nonnegative integrand $f$, $$\Big(\int f \, d\nu\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \int \frac{f^{2}}{p} \, d\nu.$$ The right-hand side is the second moment of the importance-sampling integrand $f/p$, so no choice of importance density can push it below the squared value of the integral itself. This is the Jensen — equivalently Cauchy–Schwarz — inequality that identifies how much variance reduction is available at best, and its companion result exhibits the density that attains it.
summary: (∫f)² ≤ ∫ f²/p for every importance density p: a floor on the second moment of the importance-sampling integrand, hence on its variance.
leanSignature:
theorem lintegral_sq_le_lintegral_sq_div {f p : 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞}
    (hf : Measurable f)
    (hp : Measurable p)
    (hp1 : ∫⁻ z, p z ∂ν = 1) :
    (∫⁻ z, f z ∂ν) ^ 2 ≤ ∫⁻ z, f z ^ 2 / p z ∂ν
formalizationNotes: Stated in ℝ≥0∞ so that no support condition is needed: where p vanishes but f does not, the right-hand side is ∞ by the division convention and the bound is trivially true. The substantive case splits off that null set and applies Hölder's inequality with conjugate exponents 2 and 2 to the factorization f = (f²/p)^{1/2} · p^{1/2}, the second factor integrating to 1.

hypotheses.label: nonnegative integrand
hypotheses.note: An ℝ≥0∞-valued measurable function; nonnegativity is built into the value type.

hypotheses.label: importance density
hypotheses.note: $p$ is a probability density with respect to the base measure $\nu$.

hypotheses.label: measurable density
hypotheses.note: Measurability of the importance density.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: Importance sampling is H. Kahn and A. W. Y. Rubinstein, *Simulation and the Monte Carlo Method*, Wiley, New York, 1981.

title: The Optimal Importance Density Attains the Bound
informal: The lower bound of the previous result is attained exactly at the density proportional to the integrand: for any measurable $f \ge 0$, taking $$p^{*} \;=\; rac{f}{\int f \, d u} \qquad ext{gives}\qquad \int rac{f^{2}}{p^{*}} \, d u \;=\; \Big(\int f \, d u\Big)^{2}.$$ At this choice the importance-sampling integrand $f/p^{*}$ is constant, so the estimator has zero variance. The catch, as Gentle observes, is that $p^{*}$ requires knowing $\int f\,d u$ — the very quantity being estimated — so in practice one seeks a density merely close to proportional to $|f|$.
summary: At p* = f/∫f the second moment equals (∫f)², so the importance-sampling integrand is constant and the estimator has zero variance — the unattainable ideal that guides proposal design.
formalizationNotes: Holds for every measurable f with no side conditions at all, including the degenerate cases ∫f = 0 (both sides vanish) and ∫f = ∞ (both sides are ∞), which the ℝ≥0∞ division conventions 0/0 = 0 and x/0 = ∞ resolve. The substantive case 0 < ∫f < ∞ reduces to the pointwise identity f²/(f/c) = f·c off the null set where f vanishes.

hypotheses.label: any measurable
hypotheses.note: Measurability is the only hypothesis; the degenerate cases are handled by the ℝ≥0∞ conventions rather than excluded.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.

title: Accepted Draws Carry a Rescaled Target Measure
informal: Run one step of the acceptance/rejection method: draw $Y$ from the proposal density $q$ and $U$ uniform on $[0,1]$, and accept when $U \le p(Y)/(c\,q(Y))$, where $c\,q$ majorizes the target $p$ with envelope constant $c$. Restricting the joint law of $(Y,U)$ to the acceptance event and reading off the first coordinate gives the target measure scaled by $1/c$: $$\text{(mass on accepted } Y) \;=\; \frac1c\,P.$$ Both the acceptance probability and the law of an accepted draw follow from this one computation.
summary: Restricting the proposal–uniform pair to the acceptance region and projecting to the proposed value yields c⁻¹ times the target measure.
leanSignature:
theorem rejectionSampling_restrict_map
    (hp : Measurable p)
    (hq : Measurable q)
    (hq1 : ∫⁻ z, q z ∂ν = 1)
    (henv : ∀ y, p y ≤ c * q y)
    (hc0 : c ≠ 0) (hcT : c ≠ ∞) :
    (((ν.withDensity q).prod uniform01).restrict (rejectionAccept p q c)).map
        Prod.fst
      = c⁻¹ • ν.withDensity p
formalizationNotes: The acceptance region is stated multiplicatively as ofReal u · (c · q y) ≤ p y, which is junk-free where q vanishes and agrees with the book's ratio form off a null set. The proof computes the y-section of the acceptance region under the uniform law, which has measure p(y)/(c q(y)) in the substantive case, and integrates against the proposal density; the cases q(y) = 0 and q(y) = ∞ are handled pointwise, the latter being ν-null thanks to the normalization hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: proposal density
hypotheses.note: The majorizing function is a genuine probability density. Without it the statement is false: an infinite-valued proposal makes the acceptance region null, and a machine-checked counterexample to that effect is kept in the source file.

hypotheses.label: majorizes
hypotheses.note: $p(y) \le c\,q(y)$ for every $y$ — Gentle's majorizing-function condition; the target's support must lie in the proposal's.

hypotheses.label: envelope constant
hypotheses.note: A nonzero, finite envelope constant $c$. Necessarily $c \ge 1$ when both densities integrate to one.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: The acceptance/rejection method is J. von Neumann, "Various techniques used in connection with random digits," *National Bureau of Standards Applied Mathematics Series* **12** (1951), 36–38; the majorizing-density formulation is standard since L. title: Acceptance Probability of Rejection Sampling Is 1/c
informal: With a target density $p$, a proposal density $q$ and an envelope constant $c$ for which $c\,q$ majorizes $p$, each round of the acceptance/rejection method succeeds with probability $$\Pr(\text{accept}) \;=\; \frac1c.$$ The envelope constant is therefore the exact cost of the method: on average $c$ proposals are consumed per delivered variate, so the number of trials until the first acceptance is geometric with mean $c$, and a proposal that fits the target tightly is what makes the sampler cheap.
summary: Each round of the acceptance/rejection method accepts with probability exactly 1/c, so the envelope constant is precisely the expected number of proposals per accepted draw.
leanSignature:
theorem rejectionSampling_acceptProb
    (hp : Measurable p)
    (hq : Measurable q)
    (hq1 : ∫⁻ z, q z ∂ν = 1)
    (hp1 : ∫⁻ z, p z ∂ν = 1)

    (hc0 : c ≠ 0) (hcT : c ≠ ∞) :

title: Rejection Sampling Returns Exactly the Target Distribution
informal: Conditionally on acceptance, the value delivered by the acceptance/rejection method has exactly the target distribution: $$\text{Law}\big(Y \mid \text{accepted}\big) \;=\; P.$$ No approximation and no asymptotics are involved — one accepted draw is already a perfect sample from $P$, which is what distinguishes rejection sampling from Markov chain methods, where the target is reached only in the limit. The result holds for a proposal density $q$ and envelope constant $c$ whenever $c\,q$ majorizes $p$.
summary: The accepted draw of the acceptance/rejection method is an exact sample from the target: its conditional law given acceptance is P itself.
leanSignature:

    (hp : Measurable p)

title: Category Counts of an i.i.d. Sample Are Multinomial
informal: Draw $n$ indices independently from a probability vector $q$ on $\{1,\dots,m\}$ and count how often each category appears. The count vector $$V_j \;=\; \#\{i : A_i = j\}$$ has the multinomial distribution $\mathcal M_m(n;q)$. This is the bridge between the sampling description of resampling — draw indices with replacement — and its combinatorial description as a multinomial count vector, and it is what turns Gentle's resampling vector into a distributional object one can compute with.
summary: The vector of category counts of n i.i.d. categorical draws has exactly the multinomial law M_m(n; q), linking index resampling to the multinomial distribution.
leanSignature:
theorem map_categoricalCounts_pi {q : Fin m → ℝ}
    (hq0 : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q i)
    (hq1 : ∑ i, q i = 1) :
    (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => categorical q).map categoricalCounts
      = StatLean.Bayesian.multinomialKernel m n q
formalizationNotes: The multinomial law is not rebuilt here: the statement lands on `StatLean.Bayesian.multinomialKernel`, the construction already used for Dirichlet–multinomial conjugacy. The proof compares the two measures on singletons of the countable count space; the combinatorial input — that the fiber over a count vector v with Σv = n has cardinality equal to the multinomial coefficient — has no counterpart in Mathlib and was proved from scratch by induction on n, peeling the first coordinate and using a Pascal-style recurrence for the coefficient.

hypotheses.label: probability vector
hypotheses.note: Nonnegative category probabilities.

hypotheses.label: normalized
hypotheses.note: The probabilities sum to one; off the simplex the multinomial weight is defined to vanish, while the pushforward would not.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: The multinomial law of category counts is classical (de Moivre); its role as the bootstrap resampling vector is Efron (1979), §2. Standard reference for multinomial moments: N. L. Johnson, S. Kotz and N. Balakrishnan, *Discrete Multivariate Distributions*, Wiley, New York, 1997, ch. 35.

title: Mean of a Multinomial Count
informal: Each category count of an i.i.d. categorical sample has mean proportional to its probability: $$\mathbb E[V_j] \;=\; n\,q_j.$$ For the bootstrap, where every index is equally likely, this says each observation appears once on average in a resample of the same size as the data.
summary: E[V_j] = n q_j for the category counts of an i.i.d. categorical sample.
leanSignature:
theorem integral_categoricalCount
    (hq0 : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q i)
    (hq1 : ∑ i, q i = 1) (j : Fin m) :
    ∫ a, (categoricalCounts a j : ℝ) ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => categorical q)
      = n * q j
formalizationNotes: Proved by writing the count as a sum of coordinate indicators and integrating termwise; each coordinate marginal is the categorical law, so each indicator contributes q_j. No multinomial pmf manipulation is needed, and integrability is automatic because the index space is finite.

hypotheses.label: probability
hypotheses.note: Nonnegative category probabilities.

hypotheses.label: normalized
hypotheses.note: The probabilities sum to one.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.

title: Variance of a Multinomial Count
informal: A multinomial count is a sum of Bernoulli indicators, one per draw, so its variance is $$\operatorname{Var}(V_j) \;=\; n\,q_j(1-q_j),$$ for a probability vector $q$. Note that the bound $q_j \le 1$ needed here is not assumed: it follows from nonnegativity and normalization of the whole vector.
summary: Var(V_j) = n q_j (1 − q_j): each multinomial count is a binomial count in disguise.
leanSignature:
theorem variance_categoricalCount
    (hq0 : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q i)
    (hq1 : ∑ i, q i = 1) (j : Fin m) :
    variance (fun a => (categoricalCounts a j : ℝ))
        (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => categorical q)
      = n * q j * (1 - q j)
formalizationNotes: The count is expanded into coordinate indicators, which are independent under the product law (`iIndepFun_pi`), so the variance of the sum is the sum of the variances; each summand is a Bernoulli(q_j) variance q_j − q_j². The inequality q_j ≤ 1 is derived inside the proof from the simplex hypotheses rather than added as an assumption.

hypotheses.label: probability vector
hypotheses.note: Nonnegative category probabilities.

hypotheses.label: normalization
hypotheses.note: The probabilities sum to one, which forces each $q_j \le 1$.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.

title: Multinomial Counts Are Negatively Correlated
informal: Counts in distinct categories have covariance $$\operatorname{Cov}(V_j, V_k) \;=\; -\,n\,q_j q_k \;<\; 0 .$$ The negative sign is forced by the total: the counts must add up to $n$, so a draw landing in one category is a draw denied to every other. This is the dependence that makes the bootstrap resampling vector something other than a collection of independent counts.
summary: Cov(V_j, V_k) = −n q_j q_k for distinct categories: multinomial counts are negatively correlated because they share a fixed total.
leanSignature:
theorem covariance_categoricalCount
    (hq0 : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q i)
    (hq1 : ∑ i, q i = 1) {j k : Fin m}
    (hjk : j ≠ k) :
    covariance (fun a => (categoricalCounts a j : ℝ))
        (fun a => (categoricalCounts a k : ℝ))
        (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => categorical q)
      = -(n * q j * q k)
formalizationNotes: Bilinearity of the covariance over the two indicator sums leaves only the diagonal terms, since indicators of different coordinates are independent; within one coordinate the product of the two indicators vanishes because a single draw cannot land in two categories at once, leaving −q_j q_k per draw.

hypotheses.label: probability vector
hypotheses.note: Nonnegative category probabilities.

hypotheses.label: normalized
hypotheses.note: The probabilities sum to one.

hypotheses.label: distinct
hypotheses.note: Distinct categories; at $j = k$ the covariance is the variance instead.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.

title: Multinomial Resampling Is Unbiased
informal: Given a weighted particle population $(x_i,w_i)$ with nonnegative, normalized weights, resample $N$ particle indices independently with probabilities $w$ and give every survivor equal weight. Conditionally on the population, the resampled average reproduces the weighted average exactly: $$\mathbb E\Big[\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N g\big(x_{A_j}\big)\Big] \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^n w_i\, g(x_i).$$ Resampling therefore discards weight information without introducing bias — the property that licenses the resampling step of a particle filter.
summary: Multinomial resampling of a weighted particle population preserves the weighted average in conditional expectation.
leanSignature:
theorem particleResampling_unbiased [NeZero N]
    (hw0 : ∀ i, 0 ≤ w i)
    (hw1 : ∑ i, w i = 1) :
    ∫ a, mcEstimate g (x ∘ a) ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin N => categorical w)
      = ∑ i, w i * g (x i)
formalizationNotes: Conditioning on the particle population is formalized by treating the particles and weights as parameters: the only randomness is the index draw, whose law is exactly the conditional law given the population. Integrability is automatic on the finite index space. Sequential Monte Carlo itself — the propagate–reweight–resample recursion and its Feynman–Kac limit theory — is deliberately out of scope; this is the reusable single-step correctness brick.

hypotheses.label: nonnegative
hypotheses.note: Nonnegative particle weights.

hypotheses.label: normalized
hypotheses.note: Weights sum to one, so the population is a probability distribution over particles.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: Multinomial resampling enters the particle-filter literature with N. J. Gordon, D. J. Salmond and A. F. M. title: Resampling Preserves the Particle Measure Setwise
informal: The unbiasedness of multinomial resampling holds set by set, not merely for averages: for every measurable set $S$, $$\mathbb E\big[\widehat{\mathbb P}_N(S)\big] \;=\; \widehat\pi(S), \qquad \widehat\pi=\sum_i w_i \delta_{x_i},$$ where $\widehat{\mathbb P}_N$ is the equally-weighted empirical measure of the resampled particles and the weights are nonnegative and normalized. In other words the resampled cloud is an unbiased estimate of the weighted cloud as a measure.
summary: The empirical measure of the resampled particles is, in expectation, the weighted particle measure — unbiasedness as measures rather than merely for a fixed test function.
leanSignature:
theorem particleResampling_measure_unbiased [NeZero N]
    (hw0 : ∀ i, 0 ≤ w i)
    (hw1 : ∑ i, w i = 1) {s : Set 𝓧}

    ∫ a, (empiricalMeasure (x ∘ a) s).toReal
        ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin N => categorical w)
      = (weightedMeasure w x s).toReal
formalizationNotes: Obtained from the function-level statement applied to the indicator of the set, after identifying the mass the resampled empirical measure gives to S with the Monte Carlo average of that indicator. Masses are compared as real numbers via `ENNReal.toReal`, which is faithful here because both measures are finite.

hypotheses.note: Nonnegative particle weights.

hypotheses.label: normalized
hypotheses.note: The weights sum to one.

hypotheses.note: Measurability of the event whose mass is compared.

reference.biblio: Multinomial resampling enters the particle-filter literature with N. J. Gordon, D. J. Salmond and A. F. M. Smith, "Novel approach to nonlinear/non-Gaussian Bayesian state estimation," *IEE Proceedings F* **140** (1993), 107–113; comparisons of resampling schemes are due to R. Douc and O. Cappé, "Comparison of resampling schemes for particle filtering," *Proceedings ISPA 2005*, 64–69.

title: The Bootstrap Sample Mean Is Centred at the Sample Mean
informal: Draw a bootstrap sample $Y_1^{*},\dots,Y_n^{*}$ with replacement from the observed data and average it. Conditionally on the data, $$\mathbb E^{*}\big[\bar Y^{*}\big] \;=\; \bar y .$$ The bootstrap world is centred where the real world's estimate sits: the resampling distribution of the mean is centred at the observed mean, not at the unknown population mean, which is precisely why the bootstrap estimates the spread and bias of a statistic rather than its value.
summary: Conditionally on the data, the bootstrap sample mean has expectation the observed sample mean.
leanSignature:
theorem bootstrapMean_expectation [NeZero n] :
    ∫ z, mcEstimate id z ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => empiricalMeasure y)
      = mcEstimate id y
formalizationNotes: The bootstrap resampling law is the product of n copies of the empirical measure, so the statement is the general i.i.d. unbiasedness identity instantiated at P = empiricalMeasure y — the empirical measure is a probability measure, and nothing else about it is used. This is the finite-sample, exact-conditional side of the bootstrap; its asymptotic theory lives in the Hypothesis Tests topic.

hypotheses.label: observed data
hypotheses.note: Resampling is i.i.d. drawing from the empirical measure of the observed sample $y$.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: The nonparametric bootstrap is B. Efron, "Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife," *Annals of Statistics* **7** (1979), 1–26; the standard monograph is B. Efron and R. J. Tibshirani, *An Introduction to the Bootstrap*, Chapman & Hall, New York, 1993.

title: Bootstrap Variance of the Sample Mean
informal: The ideal bootstrap variance of the sample mean is available in closed form: $$\operatorname{Var}^{*}\big(\bar Y^{*}\big) \;=\; \frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_i-\bar y\big)^{2},$$ conditionally on the observed data. This is the plug-in variance $\widehat\sigma^2/n$ with the divide-by-$n$ sample variance — Monte Carlo resampling is not needed to evaluate it, and comparing it with the usual $s^2/n$ shows exactly the $n/(n-1)$ factor the bootstrap omits.
summary: Var*(Ȳ*) = n⁻²Σ(y_i − ȳ)², the ideal (simulation-free) bootstrap variance of the sample mean.
leanSignature:
theorem bootstrapMean_variance [NeZero n] :
    variance (mcEstimate id) (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => empiricalMeasure y)
      = ((n : ℝ) ^ 2)⁻¹ * ∑ i, (y i - mcEstimate id y) ^ 2
formalizationNotes: Instantiates the general i.i.d. variance identity at the empirical measure and then evaluates the plug-in variance of the identity function, which is the divide-by-n sample variance. "Ideal bootstrap" means the exact conditional variance, not its Monte Carlo approximation from m resamples (Gentle eq. (4.7)); the latter needs no new theorem, being the ordinary Monte Carlo estimator applied to the resampling law.

hypotheses.label: observed data
hypotheses.note: The conditioning is on the observed sample; the only randomness is the resampling.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: The nonparametric bootstrap is B. Efron, "Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife," *Annals of Statistics* **7** (1979), 1–26; the standard monograph is B. Efron and R. J. Tibshirani, *An Introduction to the Bootstrap*, Chapman & Hall, New York, 1993.

title: Ideal Bootstrap Bias Correction for the Squared Mean
informal: The squared sample mean overestimates the squared population mean, and the bootstrap corrects it without simulation. Gentle's bias-corrected estimator $T_1 = 2T(\mathbb P_n) - \mathbb E^{*}\big[T(\mathbb P_n^{(1)})\big]$ evaluates, for $T$ the squared mean of the observed data, to $$T_1 \;=\; \bar y^{2} \;-\; \frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_i-\bar y\big)^{2}.$$ The correction subtracts exactly the bootstrap variance of the mean — the upward bias of $\bar y^2$ — which is the computation Gentle sets as Exercise 4.1.
summary: Gentle's bootstrap bias correction T₁ = 2T − E*[T*], evaluated in closed form for the squared mean: it subtracts precisely the bootstrap variance of the mean.
leanSignature:
theorem bootstrapBiasCorrection_sqMean [NeZero n] :
    2 * (mcEstimate id y) ^ 2
        - ∫ z, (mcEstimate id z) ^ 2
            ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => empiricalMeasure y)
      = (mcEstimate id y) ^ 2
          - ((n : ℝ) ^ 2)⁻¹ * ∑ i, (y i - mcEstimate id y) ^ 2
formalizationNotes: Follows from the companion identity for the bootstrap expectation of the squared mean, E*[(Ȳ*)²] = ȳ² + Var*(Ȳ*), which is the variance-plus-squared-mean decomposition applied under the resampling law. Everything is exact and conditional: no Monte Carlo approximation of the bootstrap expectation is involved.

hypotheses.label: observed data
hypotheses.note: The bootstrap expectation is taken under resampling from the observed sample.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: The nonparametric bootstrap is B. Efron, "Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife," *Annals of Statistics* **7** (1979), 1–26; the standard monograph is B. Efron and R. J. Tibshirani, *An Introduction to the Bootstrap*, Chapman & Hall, New York, 1993.

title: Efron's Resampling Vector Is Multinomial
informal: Record how many times each original observation appears in a bootstrap sample. That count vector is multinomial with equal cell probabilities: $$\big(N_1^{*},\dots,N_n^{*}\big) \;\sim\; \mathcal M_n\Big(n; \tfrac1n,\dots,\tfrac1n\Big).$$ Gentle's resampling vector $p^{*}$ is $N^{*}/n$, and this identification is what lets bootstrap replications be written as functions of a multinomial vector — the starting point for the variance-reduction and balanced-resampling schemes of §4.5.
summary: The bootstrap resampling counts (how often each datum is redrawn) follow the multinomial law with n equal cell probabilities 1/n.
leanSignature:
theorem bootstrapCounts_multinomial [NeZero n] :
    ((Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => categorical fun _ : Fin n => (n : ℝ)⁻¹).map
        categoricalCounts)
      = StatLean.Bayesian.multinomialKernel n n (fun _ => (n : ℝ)⁻¹)
formalizationNotes: The uniform-weight case of the general counts-are-multinomial bridge; the simplex side conditions are discharged from the positive-sample-size instance. The target law is the multinomial kernel already used for Dirichlet–multinomial conjugacy in the Bayesian area, so the two topics share one multinomial object.

hypotheses.label: nonempty sample
hypotheses.note: At least one observation, so that the uniform resampling probability $1/n$ is well defined.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: The nonparametric bootstrap is B. Efron, "Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife," *Annals of Statistics* **7** (1979), 1–26; the standard monograph is B. Efron and R. J. Tibshirani, *An Introduction to the Bootstrap*, Chapman & Hall, New York, 1993.

title: Pseudovalues of a Plug-In Average Are the Observations
informal: The jackknife pseudovalues of a statistic $T$ are $$T^{*}_i \;=\; n\,T \;-\; (n-1)\,T_{(-i)},$$ where $T_{(-i)}$ omits observation $i$. When $T$ is a plug-in average — a linear functional of the empirical distribution — the pseudovalues collapse to the observations themselves, $T^{*}_i = g(x_i)$. Gentle records exactly this, and it explains why the jackknife tells one nothing new about a sample mean: the pseudovalues are the data, so the jackknifed statistic is the original statistic and the jackknife variance is the classical one.
summary: For a plug-in average, the i-th jackknife pseudovalue is just g(x_i) — the jackknife reproduces the data for linear statistics.
leanSignature:
theorem jackknifePseudoValue_mcEstimate (g : 𝓧 → ℝ) (i : Fin (n + 1))
    (x : Fin (n + 1) → 𝓧) :
    jackknifePseudoValue (mcEstimate g) (mcEstimate g) i x = g (x i)
formalizationNotes: Pure finite-sum algebra: the deleted average is the full sum minus the deleted term (`Fin.sum_univ_succAbove`), and the weights n+1 and −n cancel everything but g(x_i). A statistic is passed as the pair of its full-sample and reduced-sample versions, since "a statistic defined at every sample size" is not a single Lean function; deletion is indexed by `Fin.succAbove`, so no n − 1 arithmetic appears.

hypotheses.label: plug-in average
hypotheses.note: The statistic is the sample average of $g$, i.e. a linear functional of the empirical distribution.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: The jackknife is M. H. Quenouille, "Approximate tests of correlation in time-series," *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B* **11** (1949), 68–84, and "Notes on bias in estimation," *Biometrika* **43** (1956), 353–360 (bias correction); pseudovalues and the variance estimator are J. W. Tukey, "Bias and confidence in not-quite large samples (abstract)," *Annals of Mathematical Statistics* **29** (1958), 614. Higher-order versions are W. R. Schucany, H. L. Gray and D. B. Owen, "On bias reduction in estimation," *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **66** (1971), 524–533.

title: Tukey's Jackknife Variance Estimate for the Sample Mean
informal: Tukey's jackknife variance estimator treats the pseudovalues as if they were independent and takes the variance of their mean. For a plug-in average over $n+1$ observations it evaluates to $$\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{J} \;=\; \frac{1}{(n+1)\,n}\sum_{i}\big(g(x_i)-\bar g\big)^{2} \;=\; \frac{s^{2}}{n+1},$$ the textbook standard error of a sample mean with the Bessel-corrected sample variance $s^2$. Gentle notes this coincidence as the sanity check on the definition: on the one statistic where the answer is already known, the jackknife reproduces it exactly.
summary: For the sample mean the jackknife variance estimator equals s²/(n+1), the classical standard error — the sanity check on Tukey's definition.
leanSignature:
theorem jackknifeVariance_mcEstimate (g : 𝓧 → ℝ) (x : Fin (n + 1) → 𝓧) :
    jackknifeVarianceEstimate (mcEstimate g) (mcEstimate g) x
      = (((n : ℝ) + 1) * n)⁻¹ * ∑ i, (g (x i) - mcEstimate g x) ^ 2
formalizationNotes: Immediate once the pseudovalues are identified with the observations and the jackknifed statistic with the original average: the estimator's defining sum becomes Σ(g(xᵢ) − ḡ)² divided by r(r−1) with r = n+1 groups. The file uses the delete-one grouping (group size k = 1), which Gentle notes is the common and optimal choice.

hypotheses.label: plug-in average
hypotheses.note: The statistic is the sample average of $g$.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.biblio: The jackknife is M. H. Quenouille, "Approximate tests of correlation in time-series," *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B* **11** (1949), 68–84, and "Notes on bias in estimation," *Biometrika* **43** (1956), 353–360 (bias correction); pseudovalues and the variance estimator are J. W. Tukey, "Bias and confidence in not-quite large samples (abstract)," *Annals of Mathematical Statistics* **29** (1958), 614. Higher-order versions are W. R. Schucany, H. L. Gray and D. B. Owen, "On bias reduction in estimation," *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **66** (1971), 524–533.

title: The Jackknife Annihilates First-Order Bias
informal: Suppose an estimator's bias admits the expansion $\mathbb E[T_m] = \theta + a_1/m + a_2/m^{2}$ at the two sample sizes involved — $n+1$ and $n$. Then the jackknifed statistic has $$\mathbb E\big[J(T)\big] \;=\; \theta \;-\; \frac{a_2}{(n+1)\,n}.$$ The $1/n$ term is gone: bias of order $n^{-1}$ has been reduced to order $n^{-2}$, with an explicit constant. This is the reason Quenouille introduced the device, and the reason it is worth computing $n+1$ extra estimates.
summary: Under a two-term bias expansion the jackknifed statistic has bias exactly −a₂/((n+1)n): the leading 1/n bias term is annihilated.
leanSignature:
theorem jackknife_bias_reduction [NeZero n] {θ a₁ a₂ : ℝ}
    (hT : Integrable T (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin (n + 1) => P))
    (hT' : Integrable T' (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => P))
    (hT'm : AEStronglyMeasurable T' (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => P))
    (hTn : ∫ x, T x ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin (n + 1) => P)
        = θ + a₁ / ((n : ℝ) + 1) + a₂ / ((n : ℝ) + 1) ^ 2)
    (hTn' : ∫ z, T' z ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => P)
        = θ + a₁ / (n : ℝ) + a₂ / (n : ℝ) ^ 2) :
    ∫ x, jackknifed T T' x ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin (n + 1) => P)
      = θ - a₂ / (((n : ℝ) + 1) * n)
formalizationNotes: Gentle assumes a full power series Σ a_q/n^q with constant coefficients and concludes that the bias is O(n⁻²); the formalization assumes only the two-term expansion at the two sample sizes actually used, which is weaker, and in exchange the conclusion is an exact identity rather than an order statement. The probabilistic input is that each delete-one sample is again i.i.d., so the delete-one average has the reduced-sample expectation.

hypotheses.leanToken:
hTn : ∫ x, T x ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin (n + 1) => P)
        = θ + a₁ / ((n : ℝ) + 1) + a₂ / ((n : ℝ) + 1) ^ 2
hypotheses.label: $n+1$
hypotheses.note: Two-term bias expansion of the statistic at sample size $n+1$.

hypotheses.leanToken:
hTn' : ∫ z, T' z ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => P)
        = θ + a₁ / (n : ℝ) + a₂ / (n : ℝ) ^ 2
hypotheses.label: $n$
hypotheses.note: The same expansion at sample size $n$, with the same coefficients — this is what makes the leading term cancel.

title: Holdout Loss Is Unbiased for the Trained Rule's Risk
informal: Fix a prediction rule $h$ — in practice, the rule fitted on the training set, so that the statement is conditional on the training data — and score it on an independent test sample of size $k$. Then the average test loss is unbiased for that rule's prediction risk: $$\mathbb E\Big[\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^k \ell\big(h, Z_j\big)\Big] \;=\; R(h) \;=\; \int \ell(h,z)\,dD(z),$$ provided the loss is integrable. Gentle's warning is the counterpoint: the apparent error computed on the data used for fitting is not unbiased and is systematically optimistic.
summary: The average loss on an independent test sample is unbiased for the prediction risk of the (fixed, or training-conditional) rule being scored.
leanSignature:
theorem holdout_unbiased {k : ℕ} [NeZero k] (h : H)
    (hint : Integrable (ℓ h) D) :
    ∫ t, mcEstimate (ℓ h) t ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin k => D)
      = predictionRisk D ℓ h
formalizationNotes: Conditioning on the training data is formalized by quantifying over the hypothesis h: the identity holds for every h, hence in particular at h = A(s) for every training outcome s, which is the conditional statement. It is the i.i.d. unbiasedness identity applied to the loss of a fixed rule.

hypotheses.label: loss is integrable
hypotheses.note: The loss of the rule being scored has a finite mean under the data distribution.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.pointer: §3.2 (cross validation for smoothing and fitting), eq. (3.2), p. 72
reference.biblio: Cross-validation in this form is M. Stone, "Cross-validatory choice and assessment of statistical predictions," *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B* **36** (1974), 111–147, and S. Geisser, "The predictive sample reuse method with applications," *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **70** (1975), 320–328; the leave-one-out prediction sum of squares is D. M. Allen, "The relationship between variable selection and data augmentation and a method for prediction," *Technometrics* **16** (1974), 125–127.

title: What Holdout Validation Estimates, Averaged Over Training Sets
informal: Averaging over the training sample as well as the test sample, holdout validation estimates the expected risk of the fitted rule: $$\mathbb E_{S,T}\Big[\frac1k\sum_{j}\ell\big(A(S),Z_j\big)\Big] \;=\; \mathbb E_{S}\big[R(A(S))\big],$$ for a learning rule $A$ with integrable loss. The target is a property of the training procedure at that sample size — not the risk of any one fitted rule, and not the risk of the rule fitted to all the data. Keeping this distinction explicit is what stops the standard overclaim about what cross-validation measures.
summary: Averaged over training and test samples, holdout validation is unbiased for the expected risk of the rule the procedure produces at that training-set size.
leanSignature:
theorem holdout_integrated {m k : ℕ} [NeZero k] (A : (Fin m → Z) → H)
    (hint : Integrable
      (fun p : (Fin m → Z) × (Fin k → Z) => mcEstimate (ℓ (A p.1)) p.2)
      ((Measure.pi fun _ : Fin m => D).prod (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin k => D)))
    (hloss : ∀ s, Integrable (ℓ (A s)) D) :
    ∫ p, mcEstimate (ℓ (A p.1)) p.2
        ∂((Measure.pi fun _ : Fin m => D).prod (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin k => D))
      = ∫ s, predictionRisk D ℓ (A s) ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin m => D)
formalizationNotes: Fubini over the independent training and test blocks, with the fixed-rule identity applied inside. The per-training-outcome integrability hypothesis is slightly stronger than the almost-everywhere version Fubini would supply; it is recorded as a regularity assumption a caller can discharge (bounded loss, say) rather than silently weakened.

hypotheses.label: learning rule
hypotheses.note: A map from training samples of size $m$ to hypotheses; no measurability or optimality is assumed of it.

hypotheses.label: integrable
hypotheses.note: For each training outcome the fitted rule has integrable loss.

reference.formal: J. E. Gentle, *Elements of Computational Statistics*, Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, New York, 2002.
reference.pointer: §3.2 (cross validation for smoothing and fitting), eq. (3.3), p. 73
reference.biblio: Cross-validation in this form is M. title: What K-Fold Cross Validation Estimates
informal: Split the data into $K+1$ folds; hold each fold out in turn, fit on the remaining $K$ folds with the learning rule $A$, score on the held-out fold, and average. The resulting estimate is unbiased for the expected risk of the rule trained on $K$ folds: $$\mathbb E\big[\mathrm{CV}_K\big] \;=\; \mathbb E_{S}\big[R(A(S))\big], \qquad |S| = K\,m .$$ The target is the risk at the reduced training-set size, which is the honest statement — cross-validation is not unbiased for the risk of the rule fitted to the full data, and that difference is the pessimistic bias of $K$-fold.
summary: K-fold cross validation is unbiased for the expected risk of a rule trained on K folds — the reduced-size risk, not the full-sample rule's risk.
leanSignature:
theorem kFold_unbiased {K m : ℕ} [NeZero m] (A : (Fin K → Fin m → Z) → H)
    (hint : Integrable
      (fun p : (Fin K → Fin m → Z) × (Fin m → Z) =>
        mcEstimate (ℓ (A p.1)) p.2)
      ((Measure.pi fun _ : Fin K => Measure.pi fun _ : Fin m => D).prod
        (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin m => D)))
    (hloss : ∀ s, Integrable (ℓ (A s)) D) :
    ∫ z, kFoldEstimate ℓ A z
        ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin (K + 1) => Measure.pi fun _ : Fin m => D)
      = ∫ s, predictionRisk D ℓ (A s)
          ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin K => Measure.pi fun _ : Fin m => D)
formalizationNotes: Folds are modelled as a matrix of observations, so fold deletion is the same `Fin.succAbove` operation used by the jackknife and no divisibility bookkeeping about n/K is needed. Each of the K+1 fold terms has the same expectation by exchangeability of the folds, and the held-out fold is independent of the training folds by the delete-and-split lemma.

hypotheses.label: learning rule
hypotheses.note: Fits a hypothesis from $K$ folds of $m$ observations each.

hypotheses.label: integrable loss
hypotheses.note: Each fitted rule has integrable loss under the data distribution.

title: Leave-One-Out Cross Validation and PRESS
informal: Hold out one observation at a time, fit on the other $n$, and average the $n+1$ prediction losses. This leave-one-out estimate is unbiased for the expected risk of the rule trained on $n$ observations: $$\mathbb E\big[\mathrm{LOO}\big] \;=\; \mathbb E_{S}\big[R(A(S))\big], \qquad |S| = n,$$ for any learning rule with integrable joint loss. With squared-error loss the sum is Allen's PRESS statistic, the prediction sum of squares used for variable selection in linear models.
summary: Leave-one-out cross validation is unbiased for the expected risk of the delete-one rule; with squared-error loss it is Allen's PRESS.
leanSignature:
theorem loo_unbiased {n : ℕ} (A : (Fin n → Z) → H)
    (hint : Integrable
      (fun p : (Fin n → Z) × Z => ℓ (A p.1) p.2)
      ((Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => D).prod D)) :
    ∫ x, looEstimate ℓ A x ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin (n + 1) => D)
      = ∫ s, predictionRisk D ℓ (A s) ∂(Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => D)
formalizationNotes: Each summand is transported through the delete-and-split map, whose law is the product of the reduced-sample law and the deleted observation's law; Fubini then produces the risk of the fitted rule, the same value for every deleted index, so the average collapses. Only the algebraic identity is claimed: model-selection consistency of cross-validation is out of scope.

hypotheses.note: Fits a hypothesis from $n$ observations; the held-out observation is the $(n+1)$-st.

title: Gross-Error Contamination
informal:
Let $P$ be a probability distribution (the ideal model) and $Q$ an arbitrary probability distribution (the contamination). For a contamination fraction $\varepsilon \in [0,1]$, the $\varepsilon$-contaminated distribution is the mixture $$P_{\varepsilon,Q} \;=\; (1-\varepsilon)\,P \;+\; \varepsilon\,Q,$$ under which a typical observation is drawn from $P$ with probability $1-\varepsilon$ and from $Q$ with probability $\varepsilon$. The gross-error neighbourhood of $P$ at level $\varepsilon$ is the set of all such mixtures as $Q$ ranges over the probability distributions: $$\mathcal F(P,\varepsilon) \;=\; \{(1-\varepsilon)P + \varepsilon Q : Q \text{ a probability distribution}\}.$$

Every robustness diagnostic on this site — the influence function, the breakdown point, the maximum bias — measures how an estimator behaves as its input ranges over this neighbourhood.
summary: The ε-contaminated mixture (1−ε)P + εQ and the gross-error neighbourhood F(P, ε) — the perturbation model underlying all robustness diagnostics.

hypotheses.leanToken: ENNReal.ofReal (1 - ε) • P + ENNReal.ofReal ε • Q
hypotheses.label: the mixture
hypotheses.note: The convex combination (1−ε)P + εQ of the ideal model and the contaminating distribution.

formalizationNotes: The mixture weights enter through nonnegative real coercions, so the definition is total in $\varepsilon$: outside $[0,1]$ the weights are clamped at $0$ and the result is a junk measure — every theorem carries $0 \le \varepsilon \le 1$ (or a strict version) explicitly. The mixture is definitionally the point-mass-path form used by the influence-function machinery, so the contamination derivative apparatus applies to it verbatim. The neighbourhood is a set of measures, with membership witnessed by the contaminating $Q$; monotonicity in $\varepsilon$ and closure under measurable push-forwards are proved alongside.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.

reference.biblio: The contaminated-distribution model enters with J. W. Tukey's survey of sampling from contaminated distributions (in *Contributions to Probability and Statistics*, Stanford, 1960, pp. 448–485); the $\varepsilon$-contamination neighbourhood as the domain of a minimax problem is P. J. Huber (*Ann. Math. Statist.* **35** (1964), 73–101). The systematic neighbourhood viewpoint is developed in P. J. Huber and E. M. Ronchetti, *Robust Statistics*, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2009, §1.2 and ch. 4.

title: The Finite-Sample Breakdown Point
informal:
Let $T$ be an estimator of location acting on samples $x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$. Say the sample resists $m$ replacements if there is a bound $M$ such that every corrupted sample $y$ obtained from $x$ by arbitrarily changing at most $m$ coordinates has $|T(y)| \le M$ — however wild the replacements, the estimate stays bounded. The breakdown count is the largest such $m$, $$m^\ast(T, x) \;=\; \max\{\,m \le n : T \text{ resists } m \text{ replacements of } x\,\},$$ and the finite-sample replacement breakdown point is the fraction $$\varepsilon_n^\ast(T,x) \;=\; \frac{m^\ast(T,x)}{n}.$$

The sample mean has $m^\ast = 0$: a single replacement already drives it beyond any bound. The sample median of $n = 2k+1$ points has $m^\ast = k$, the maximum any location-equivariant estimator can achieve.
summary: The replacement breakdown count m*(T, x) — the largest number of arbitrarily corrupted coordinates the estimate survives with a uniform bound — and the breakdown point m*/n.

hypotheses.leanToken: hammingDist x y ≤ m → |T y| ≤ M
hypotheses.label: resistance
hypotheses.note: Some bound M dominates |T(y)| over every sample y differing from x in at most m coordinates.

hypotheses.leanToken: sSup {m | m ≤ n ∧ Resists T x m}
hypotheses.label: the breakdown count
hypotheses.note: The largest replacement budget m ≤ n that the sample resists.

formalizationNotes: Corruption is measured by the Hamming distance on samples, which counts replaced coordinates — the population $\varepsilon$-mixture is a separate notion with its own asymptotic breakdown theory. The count is a supremum over a set of naturals containing $0$ (zero replacements are always resisted for a location estimator), so it is well-defined without side conditions; the lattice lemmas — antitonicity of resistance, the two-sided characterization by a resisted $m$ and a breaking $m+1$ — are proved alongside. Dispersion estimators need a boundary-aware variant that also guards against implosion to zero; that notion lives with the scale results.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.
reference.biblio: The finite-sample replacement formulation is D. L. Donoho and P. J. Huber (in *A Festschrift for Erich L. Lehmann*, Wadsworth, 1983, pp. 157–184); the asymptotic breakdown point descends from F. R. Hampel's qualitative-robustness framework (*Ann. Math. Statist.* **42** (1971), 1887–1896), with the first finite-sample tolerance computations in J. L. Hodges, Jr. (*Proc. Fifth Berkeley Symposium*, Vol. I, 1967).

title: The Maximal Breakdown of Equivariant Estimators
informal: Let $T$ be a location-equivariant estimator on samples of size $n$ — shifting every observation by $a$ shifts the estimate by $a$, $T(x_1+a,\dots,x_n+a) = T(x) + a$ — and let the sample be nonempty. Then its breakdown count at every sample obeys $$m^\ast(T, x) \;\le\; \Big\lfloor \frac{n-1}{2} \Big\rfloor.$$ No location-equivariant estimator can survive half the sample being corrupted: once the replacements can outvote the genuine observations, equivariance itself forces the estimate to follow them. The sample median attains this bound at odd sample sizes, which is the precise sense in which it is the most breakdown-robust location-equivariant estimator.
summary: No location-equivariant estimator has breakdown count above ⌊(n−1)/2⌋ — the ceiling that the sample median attains.
leanSignature:
theorem locEquivariant_breakdownCount_le (hT : PointEstimation.IsLocEquivariant T)
    (hn : 0 < n) : breakdownCount T x ≤ (n - 1) / 2

hypotheses.label: location equivariance
hypotheses.note: Shifting every coordinate of the sample by a shifts the estimate by a.

hypotheses.label: nonempty sample
hypotheses.note: At least one observation.

formalizationNotes: The proof is the classical pigeonhole: if $m$ replacements with $2m \ge n$ were resisted, a shift of the whole sample by a large constant $c$ could be realized in two ways as $m$-replacement corruptions of the same intermediate sample, and equivariance would force two values $c$ apart into one bounded window. Equivariance is the finite-sample predicate shared with the point-estimation library, so the theorem applies verbatim to the mean, the median, trimmed means, and every location M-estimate.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.
reference.biblio: The bound and the pigeonhole argument are D. L. Donoho and P. J. Huber (in *A Festschrift for Erich L. Lehmann*, Wadsworth, 1983, pp. 157–184).

title: The Influence Function
informal:
Let $T$ be a statistical functional, assigning a real value to each probability distribution, and let $P$ be a distribution. Contaminate $P$ in the direction of a point mass at $x_0$: for $\varepsilon \ge 0$ form the mixture $(1-\varepsilon)P + \varepsilon\,\delta_{x_0}$. The influence function of $T$ at $P$ is the one-sided derivative of the contamination path at $\varepsilon = 0$: $$\operatorname{IF}(x_0; T, P) \;=\; \lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{T\big((1-\varepsilon)P + \varepsilon\,\delta_{x_0}\big) - T(P)}{\varepsilon}.$$

It measures the first-order effect of an infinitesimal fraction of observations placed at $x_0$. A bounded influence function means no single contamination point can move the estimator disproportionately; the gross-error sensitivity $\sup_{x_0} |\operatorname{IF}(x_0)|$ summarizes it in one number.
summary: The influence function IF(x₀; T, P) — the one-sided derivative of ε ↦ T((1−ε)P + εδ_{x₀}) at ε = 0 — the infinitesimal robustness diagnostic.

hypotheses.label: one-sided limit
hypotheses.note: The derivative is taken along ε ↓ 0 from the right, where the mixture is a genuine probability distribution.

formalizationNotes: The derivative is one-sided by design: negative $\varepsilon$ does not define a probability measure, so the limit is taken along the right neighbourhood filter of $0$. This is cleaner than silently extending the contamination path to signed measures, and it is the same filter the von-Mises-derivative machinery of the semiparametric library uses, so the two apparatuses compose. Uniqueness of the influence value and the slope-comparison bridges are proved alongside the definition.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.
reference.biblio: The influence curve was introduced by F. R. Hampel (*J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* **69** (1974), 383–393), building on his 1968 Berkeley thesis; the derivative-of-a-functional viewpoint goes back to R. von Mises (*Ann. Math. Statist.* **18** (1947), 309–348). The book-length development is F. R. Hampel, E. M. Ronchetti, P. J. Rousseeuw, and W. A. Stahel, *Robust Statistics: The Approach Based on Influence Functions*, Wiley, 1986.

title: The Median Has Maximal Breakdown
informal:
Let the sample size be odd, $n = 2k+1$, and let $x$ be any sample. The breakdown count of the sample median is exactly $$m^\ast(\mathrm{med}, x) \;=\; k :$$ however adversarially at most $k$ observations are replaced, the corrupted median stays between the smallest and largest order statistics of the surviving data — while $k+1$ replacements, all placed beyond any bound $M$, drive the median past $M$.

Hence $\varepsilon_n^\ast(\mathrm{med}) = k/(2k+1) \to 1/2$: the median survives just under half the sample being corrupted, and by the general bound $m^\ast \le \lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor = k$ for location-equivariant estimators, no such estimator does better. The contrast with the sample mean, whose breakdown count is $0$, is the sharpest elementary expression of the median's robustness.
summary: For n = 2k+1 the sample median's breakdown count is exactly k — it resists k arbitrary replacements and breaks under k+1 — attaining the equivariant maximum ⌊(n−1)/2⌋.
leanSignature:
theorem sampleMedian_breakdownCount (hn : n = 2 * k + 1) (x : Fin n → ℝ) :
    breakdownCount sampleMedian x = k

theorem sampleMedian_breakdownCount_eq_max (hn : n = 2 * k + 1) (x : Fin n → ℝ) :
    breakdownCount sampleMedian x = (n - 1) / 2

hypotheses.label: odd sample size
hypotheses.note: The sample size is n = 2k+1, so the median is the unique middle order statistic.

formalizationNotes: The median is the low median — the order statistic of rank $k+1$ — which at odd sample sizes is the unique middle value. Resistance is quantitative: the corrupted median is bracketed by order statistics of the original sample at ranks shifted by the corruption budget, a perturbation bound proved in the order-statistics layer. The companion statement records that $k$ equals the equivariant maximum, so the two theorems together identify the median as an exact maximizer of finite-sample breakdown among location-equivariant estimators.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.
reference.biblio: The finite-sample computation and the maximality among equivariant estimators are D. L. Donoho and P. J. Huber (in *A Festschrift for Erich L. Lehmann*, Wadsworth, 1983, pp. 157–184); the asymptotic value $1/2$ is F. R. Hampel (*Ann. Math. Statist.* **42** (1971), 1887–1896), and the median's tolerance of extremes was first quantified by J. L. Hodges, Jr. (*Proc. Fifth Berkeley Symposium*, Vol. I, 1967).

title: The Mean Has Zero Breakdown
informal:
For every nonempty sample $x$, the breakdown count of the sample mean is $$m^\ast(\bar x, x) \;=\; 0 :$$ a single replacement suffices to move the mean beyond any prescribed bound, since sending one observation to $\pm\infty$ carries the average with it at rate $1/n$. The finite-sample breakdown point is $\varepsilon_n^\ast(\bar x) = 0$ — the mean tolerates no contamination at all in the breakdown sense.

This is one third of the mean's fragility trilogy: its influence function $x_0 - \mu(P)$ is unbounded in the contamination point, and its maximum contamination bias is infinite at every positive contamination level.
summary: The sample mean's breakdown count is 0: one arbitrary replacement drives it beyond any bound, so ε*ₙ = 0.
leanSignature:
theorem sampleMean_breakdownCount {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (x : Fin n → ℝ) :
    breakdownCount sampleMean x = 0

hypotheses.label: nonempty sample
hypotheses.note: At least one observation.

formalizationNotes: The breaking replacement is explicit: replacing one coordinate by $n(M+1) - \sum_{i} x_i$-sized values realizes any target mean, so the one-replacement neighbourhood of any sample already has unbounded image. Zero replacements are trivially resisted, which pins the count at exactly $0$ through the two-sided characterization of the breakdown count.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.
reference.biblio: The observation is folklore going back to the earliest robustness discussions; the formal replacement framework in which it is stated is D. L. Donoho and P. J. Huber (in *A Festschrift for Erich L. Lehmann*, Wadsworth, 1983, pp. 157–184), and the mean's zero tolerance of extremes was already noted by J. L. Hodges, Jr. (*Proc. Fifth Berkeley Symposium*, Vol. I, 1967).

title: The Influence Function of the Mean
informal:
Let $P$ be a distribution with a finite mean $\mu(P) = \int x \, dP$. At every contamination point $x_0$, the mean functional has influence value $$\operatorname{IF}(x_0; \mu, P) \;=\; x_0 - \mu(P).$$ Along the point-mass contamination path the computation is exact, not merely first-order: $\mu\big((1-\varepsilon)P + \varepsilon \delta_{x_0}\big) = \mu(P) + \varepsilon\,(x_0 - \mu(P))$ for all $\varepsilon$, so the difference quotient is constant.

The influence function is unbounded in $x_0$: the gross-error sensitivity of the mean is infinite, and no reweighting of a single contamination point has a diminishing effect. This infinitesimal fragility matches the mean's zero breakdown point and its infinite maximum bias.
summary: IF(x₀; mean, P) = x₀ − μ(P): the mean's influence function is exactly linear in the contamination point, hence unbounded.
leanSignature:
theorem meanFunctional_hasInfluenceAt {P : Measure ℝ}
    -- USER-INPUT: P has a well-defined mean; MMY §3.1
    (hP : Integrable id P) (x₀ : ℝ) :
    HasInfluenceAt meanFunctional P x₀ (x₀ - meanFunctional P)

hypotheses.label: finite mean
hypotheses.note: The identity is integrable under P, so μ(P) = ∫x dP is well-defined.

formalizationNotes: The mean functional is the Bochner integral of the identity, whose junk value at non-integrable inputs is $0$; integrability of $P$ is therefore carried as the one genuine hypothesis, and the point mass is always integrable. The unboundedness statement — for every candidate bound there is a contamination point whose influence value exceeds it — is proved as a companion theorem in the same file.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.
reference.biblio: The computation is Example 3.1-level classical material; the influence curve itself is F. R. Hampel (*J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* **69** (1974), 383–393), where the unboundedness of the mean's curve is the motivating example.

title: The Mean Has Infinite Maximum Bias
informal:
Let $P$ have a finite mean and let the contamination level $\varepsilon$ be positive (and at most one). Then no finite bound $b$ dominates the contamination bias of the mean over the gross-error neighbourhood: for every $b$ there is a contaminating distribution $Q$ with $$\big|\mu\big((1-\varepsilon)P + \varepsilon Q\big) - \mu(P)\big| \;>\; b.$$ In the language of maximum-bias curves, $\mathrm{MB}(\varepsilon; \mu, P) = \infty$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$.

The witness is a point mass pushed to infinity: contaminating with $\delta_M$ biases the mean by $\varepsilon(M - \mu(P))$, which is unbounded in $M$. Together with the unbounded influence function and the zero breakdown point, all three robustness diagnostics agree that the sample mean is maximally fragile.
summary: At every contamination level ε > 0 the mean's maximum bias over the gross-error neighbourhood is infinite: contaminate with δ_M and let M → ∞.
leanSignature:
theorem meanFunctional_bias_unbounded {P : Measure ℝ} {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε) (hε1 : ε ≤ 1)
    -- USER-INPUT: P has a well-defined mean; MMY §3.3
    (hP : Integrable id P) :
    ∀ b : ℝ, ¬ContaminationBiasLE meanFunctional P ε b

hypotheses.label: finite mean
hypotheses.note: μ(P) = ∫x dP is well-defined.

hypotheses.label: positive contamination
hypotheses.note: The contamination level is strictly positive (and at most 1).

formalizationNotes: The statement is phrased through a bounded-bias predicate — some $b$ dominates the bias over all probability contaminations — whose negation is proved; this avoids extended-real suprema while capturing exactly the divergence of the maximum-bias curve. The mixture mean is evaluated by the exact point-mass contamination formula, so the argument is three lines of algebra once the witness $\delta_M$ is chosen.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.
reference.biblio: Maximum-bias curves as a systematic diagnostic are developed from P. J. Huber's minimax analysis (*Ann. Math. Statist.* **35** (1964), 73–101); the modern min–max bias program is R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and R. H. Zamar (*Ann. Statist.* **17** (1989), 1608–1630).

title: The Huber Loss and Score
informal:
For a clipping constant $c \ge 0$, the Huber loss interpolates between squared loss near the origin and absolute loss in the tails: $$\rho_c(u) \;=\; \begin{cases} u^2/2, & |u| \le c,\\ c\,|u| - c^2/2, & |u| > c,\end{cases}$$ and its derivative, the Huber score, is the clipped identity $$\psi_c(u) \;=\; \max\big(-c,\; \min(c, u)\big) \;=\; \begin{cases} -c, & u < -c,\\ u, & |u| \le c,\\ c, & u > c.\end{cases}$$ The differentiation $\rho_c' = \psi_c$ holds everywhere, including at the knots $u = \pm c$.

The bounded score $|\psi_c| \le c$ is the analytic source of the Huber estimator's robustness: bounded score means bounded influence, in contrast with the unbounded score $\psi(u) = u$ of squared loss. Convexity, evenness, monotonicity, the $1$-Lipschitz property, and the tail limits $\psi_c(\pm\infty) = \pm c$ are proved alongside.
summary: Huber's loss ρ_c (quadratic core, linear tails) and its everywhere-derivative, the clipped score ψ_c(u) = max(−c, min(c, u)) with |ψ_c| ≤ c.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def huberRho (c u : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  if |u| ≤ c then u ^ 2 / 2 else c * |u| - c ^ 2 / 2

noncomputable def huberPsi (c u : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  max (-c) (min c u)

theorem hasDerivAt_huberRho {c : ℝ} (hc : 0 ≤ c) (u : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (huberRho c) (huberPsi c u) u

hypotheses.label: the clipped score
hypotheses.note: ψ_c clips the identity to the interval [−c, c].

formalizationNotes: We normalize the quadratic core as $u^2/2$ so that the score is exactly the clipped identity; the book's display carries $u^2$, a factor-two rescaling that changes no minimizer and is recorded where it matters. The derivative theorem at the knots carries the hypothesis $c \ge 0$; at $c = 0$ the loss and score degenerate to the zero function and the statement remains true. The tail-limit lemma at $+\infty$ requires $c \ge 0$ as well — for negative $c$ the score is constant — and the formalization keeps that hypothesis explicit.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.
reference.biblio: The loss, the clipped score, and their minimax justification are P. J. Huber (*Ann. Math. Statist.* **35** (1964), 73–101); the role of bounded scores in bounding influence is F. R. Hampel (*J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* **69** (1974), 383–393).

title: The Median Minimizes Absolute Loss
informal: For every sample $x_1, \dots, x_n$, the sample median minimizes the total absolute deviation: for every candidate $t$, $$\sum_{i=1}^n \big|x_i - \mathrm{med}(x)\big| \;\le\; \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i - t|.$$ The median is thus the location M-estimate for the absolute-value loss, exactly as the sample mean is the M-estimate for squared loss. These are the two poles of the M-estimation family that the Huber loss interpolates between — and the robustness gulf between them (breakdown $1/2$ versus $0$) is what M-estimation with a bounded score is designed to bridge.
summary: The sample median minimizes t ↦ Σ|xᵢ − t|: it is the location M-estimate for absolute loss, the robust pole of the M-estimation family.
leanSignature:
def IsMLocationEstimate (ρ : ℝ → ℝ) (x : Fin n → ℝ) (θ : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ t : ℝ, ∑ i, ρ (x i - θ) ≤ ∑ i, ρ (x i - t)

theorem isMLocationEstimate_abs_sampleMedian (x : Fin n → ℝ) :
    IsMLocationEstimate (fun u => |u|) x (sampleMedian x)

hypotheses.label: absolute-value loss
hypotheses.note: The objective is the L1 loss Σ|xᵢ − t|.

formalizationNotes: The median is the low median (the order statistic of rank $\lceil n/2 \rceil$), which at even sample sizes selects one endpoint of the interval of minimizers; the theorem asserts global minimality, which holds for every point of that interval. No sample-size hypothesis is needed: the empty-sample case is vacuous, both sides of the inequality being empty sums. The proof is the classical exchange argument on sorted data, carried out with the order-statistics API. The companion result that squared loss is minimized exactly by the sample mean is proved in the same file.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.
reference.biblio: The characterization of the median as the L1 minimizer is classical, running back through the early history of least absolute deviations; its role as the boundary member of the M-estimation family is set out in P. J. Huber (*Ann. Math. Statist.* **35** (1964), 73–101).

title: The Mean Minimizes Squared Loss
informal: For a nonempty sample $x_1,\dots,x_n$, a value $\theta$ minimizes the total squared deviation $\sum_i (x_i - \theta)^2$ if and only if $\theta$ is the sample mean $\bar x = \tfrac1n \sum_i x_i$. Squared loss thus has a unique location M-estimate, and it is the estimator whose fragility — zero breakdown, unbounded influence, infinite maximum bias — motivates the entire robust family: replacing $u^2$ by losses with bounded derivative trades a little efficiency at the normal model for bounded sensitivity everywhere.
summary: θ minimizes Σ(xᵢ − θ)² iff θ = x̄: squared loss characterizes the sample mean, the fragile pole of the M-estimation family.
leanSignature:
theorem isMLocationEstimate_sq_iff {x : Fin n → ℝ} {θ : ℝ} (hn : 0 < n) :
    IsMLocationEstimate (fun u => u ^ 2) x θ ↔ θ = sampleMean x

hypotheses.label: nonempty sample
hypotheses.note: At least one observation, so the mean is well-defined and the minimizer unique.

formalizationNotes: Stated as a two-sided characterization: the minimizing property is equivalent to equality with the sample mean, which packages both the first-order condition and strict convexity in one statement. The loss is normalized as $u^2$ (any positive multiple gives the same minimizer).

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.
reference.biblio: Classical least squares, here in its role as the non-robust boundary case of M-estimation as framed by P. J. Huber (*Ann. Math. Statist.* **35** (1964), 73–101).

title: Existence of Population M-Location Roots
informal:
Let $\psi$ be a nondecreasing, continuous score with limits $-k_1 \lt 0$ at $-\infty$ and $k_2 \gt 0$ at $+\infty$, and let $P$ be any probability distribution. Then the population M-estimating equation $$\int \psi(x - \theta)\, dP(x) \;=\; 0$$ has at least one root $\theta$. The population score $\lambda(\theta) = \int \psi(x-\theta)\,dP$ is continuous (by dominated convergence), nonincreasing, and tends to $k_2 \gt 0$ at $\theta \to -\infty$ and to $-k_1 \lt 0$ at $\theta \to +\infty$, so the intermediate value theorem produces a crossing.

Uniqueness holds when the population score is strictly decreasing — for instance under a strictly increasing $\psi$, or when $P$ charges every interval; without it, the root set is a closed interval.
summary: For a bounded monotone continuous score with limits of opposite signs, the population equation ∫ψ(x − θ)dP = 0 has a root — the asymptotic value of the location M-estimator.
leanSignature:
def IsMLocationRoot (ψ : ℝ → ℝ) (P : Measure ℝ) (θ : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∫ x, ψ (x - θ) ∂P = 0

title: The Influence Function of M-Estimators
informal:
Let $\psi$ be a differentiable score with derivative $\psi'$ that is bounded and measurable, let $\theta_0$ solve the population equation $\int \psi(x - \theta_0)\,dP = 0$ with $\psi(\cdot - \theta_0)$ integrable, and set $$A \;=\; \int \psi'(x - \theta_0)\, dP(x) \;\ne\; 0 \;\;\text{(nondegenerate)}.$$ Suppose a root path $\theta(\varepsilon)$ solves the $\delta_{x_0}$-contaminated equation for small $\varepsilon \ge 0$, starts at $\theta_0$, and is right-differentiable at $0$ with derivative $d$, where $A$ is the stated integral. Then $$d \;=\; \operatorname{IF}(x_0; T, P) \;=\; \frac{\psi(x_0 - \theta_0)}{A}.$$

The influence of an M-estimator is proportional to its own score. The immediate corollary: a score bounded by $c$ gives influence bounded by $c/|A|$ — bounded score means bounded influence, which is the design principle behind Huber's estimator.
summary: IF(x₀; T, P) = ψ(x₀ − θ₀)/A with A = ∫ψ′(x − θ₀)dP: an M-estimator's influence function is proportional to its score, so bounded score ⟹ bounded influence.

title: The Huber Estimator Has Bounded Influence
informal:
Let $\psi_c$ be the Huber score with clipping constant $c \gt 0$, let $\theta_0$ be the Huber location value at $P$, and suppose $P$ has no atoms at the two clipping knots $\theta_0 \pm c$ and that the central region has positive mass $A = P(|x - \theta_0| \lt c) \gt 0$. If a root path solves the $\delta_{x_0}$-contaminated Huber equation near $\varepsilon = 0$, starting from $\theta_0$, and is right-differentiable with derivative $d$, then $$d \;=\; \operatorname{IF}(x_0) \;=\; \frac{\psi_c(x_0 - \theta_0)}{P\big(|x - \theta_0| \lt c\big)},$$ and consequently $$\sup_{x_0} \big|\operatorname{IF}(x_0)\big| \;\le\; \frac{c}{P\big(|x - \theta_0| \lt c\big)} \;\lt \; \infty.$$

The mean's influence $x_0 - \mu$ grows without bound; the Huber estimator's influence is clipped at a constant. This is the precise sense in which M-estimation with a bounded score repairs the mean's infinitesimal fragility.
summary: IF(x₀) = ψ_c(x₀ − θ₀)/P(|x − θ₀| < c) for the Huber location functional — bounded by c/P(|x − θ₀| < c), in contrast with the mean's unbounded influence.

title: The Breakdown Point of Location M-Estimators
informal:
Let $\psi$ be a nondecreasing score with finite limits $-k_1 = \psi(-\infty)$ and $k_2 = \psi(+\infty)$, both nonzero with $k_1, k_2 \gt 0$. If the contamination level satisfies $$\varepsilon \;\lt \; \varepsilon^\ast \;=\; \frac{\min(k_1, k_2)}{k_1 + k_2},$$ then there is a single bound $B$ such that every solution $\theta$ of every $\varepsilon$-contaminated M-equation $\int \psi(x-\theta)\, d\big[(1-\varepsilon)P + \varepsilon Q\big] = 0$, over all contaminating distributions $Q$, satisfies $|\theta| \le B$. Beyond the threshold the conclusion fails: for $\varepsilon \gt k_1/(k_1+k_2)$, point-mass contamination pushed to $+\infty$ produces roots beyond every bound.

For an odd bounded score, $k_1 = k_2$ and $\varepsilon^\ast = 1/2$: a location M-estimator with a symmetric bounded score — the Huber estimator among them — attains the maximal asymptotic breakdown point.
summary: An M-estimator with monotone score bounded between −k₁ and k₂ resists contamination below ε* = min(k₁,k₂)/(k₁+k₂) — equal to 1/2 for odd scores, as for Huber's estimator — and breaks beyond it.

title: Consistency of Location M-Estimators
informal:
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be independent observations with common law $P$ and measurable coordinates, and let $\psi$ be a bounded, continuous, nondecreasing score whose population score $\lambda(\theta) = \int \psi(x - \theta)\,dP$ is strictly positive left of $\theta_0$ and strictly negative right of it — the root $\theta_0$ is well-separated. Let $\hat\theta_n$ be any sequence of estimates that asymptotically solves the empirical equation, $\tfrac1n \sum_{i\le n} \psi(X_i - \hat\theta_n) \to 0$ in probability. Then $\hat\theta_n$ is consistent: $$\hat\theta_n \;\xrightarrow{\;P\;}\; \theta_0.$$

The hypotheses are exactly those of the classical monotone Z-estimator consistency theorem, and the proof is an instantiation of that general result — the robust theory reuses the asymptotic machinery rather than rebuilding it.
summary: Any asymptotic root of the empirical ψ-equation converges in probability to the well-separated population root θ₀ — consistency of location M-estimators by reuse of monotone Z-estimator theory.

title: Asymptotic Normality of the Huber Estimator
informal:
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be independent observations with common law $P$ and measurable coordinates, let $c \gt 0$ be the Huber clipping constant, and let $\theta_0$ solve the population Huber equation. Assume $P$ has no atoms at the clipping knots $\theta_0 \pm c$ and that the central region has positive mass $B = P(|x-\theta_0| \lt c) \gt 0$. Let $\hat\theta_n = \hat\theta_n(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ be a measurable estimator sequence that is consistent for $\theta_0$ and solves the empirical Huber equation at rate $o_P(n^{-1/2})$. Then $$\sqrt n\,\big(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0\big) \;\rightsquigarrow\; N\!\left(0,\; \frac{\int \psi_c(x-\theta_0)^2\, dP}{P\big(|x-\theta_0| \lt c\big)^2}\right).$$

The asymptotic variance is the classical sandwich $E\psi^2/(E\psi')^2$: the derivative of the clipped score is the indicator of the central region, so its mean is the central mass $B$. No pointwise derivative of the score exists at the knots — the Lipschitz empirical-process route replaces it, with the no-atom conditions making the population score differentiable.
summary: √n(θ̂ₙ − θ₀) ⇝ N(0, Eψ_c²/P(|x−θ₀|<c)²) for the Huber location estimator: the sandwich variance with the central mass as denominator, via the Lipschitz Z-estimator route.
