title: The M-Regression Normal Equations
informal:
Consider the linear-regression M-estimation problem with design matrix $X \in \mathbb R^{n \times p}$ and responses $y \in \mathbb R^n$: a regression M-estimate $\hat\beta$ globally minimizes $b \mapsto \sum_{i=1}^n \rho(y_i - x_i^{\mathsf T} b)$. If the loss $\rho$ is differentiable with derivative $\psi$ and $\hat\beta$ is such a minimizer, then the score-weighted design columns vanish: for every coordinate $j$, $$\sum_{i=1}^n \psi\big(y_i - x_i^{\mathsf T}\hat\beta\big)\, x_{ij} \;=\; 0.$$

With $\rho(u) = u^2/2$ this is the least-squares normal equation $X^{\mathsf T}(y - X\hat\beta) = 0$; with the Huber loss it is the estimating equation of robust regression, whose residual score is clipped. The equations are necessary conditions; for convex losses they are also sufficient.
summary: At a regression M-estimate the ψ-weighted design columns sum to zero: Σᵢ ψ(yᵢ − xᵢᵀβ̂)xᵢⱼ = 0 — the M-analogue of the least-squares normal equations.

hypotheses.label: differentiable loss
hypotheses.note: ρ is differentiable everywhere with derivative ψ.

hypotheses.label: global minimizer
hypotheses.note: β̂ globally minimizes the M-objective b ↦ Σρ(yᵢ − xᵢᵀb).

formalizationNotes: The proof restricts the objective to the line through $\hat\beta$ in each coordinate direction and differentiates at the minimum; no convexity is needed for this necessary condition. The least-squares specialization and the convexity of the objective for convex losses (hence of Huber regression) are separate results in the same file.

title: Bounded Residual Score Does Not Bound Leverage
informal:
In the regression estimating equation, each observation contributes the term $x_i\,\psi_c(y_i - x_i\beta)$ — its design point times its clipped residual score. Even though the Huber score is bounded by the clipping constant $c \gt 0$, the contribution is not: for every bound $B$ there is a design–response pair $(x_0, y_0)$ whose single-observation term satisfies $$\big|x_0\, \psi_c(y_0 - x_0\beta)\big| \;\gt \; B.$$ Placing the residual at the clipping threshold and letting the design point grow realizes arbitrarily large contributions.

Clipping residuals protects against outlying responses but not against outlying design points — high-leverage observations retain unbounded influence on M-regression. This is the counterexample that motivates bounded-influence (generalized M-) estimators and the high-breakdown regression methods.
summary: One observation's estimating-equation term x₀ψ_c(y₀ − x₀β) is unbounded in the design point even for the bounded Huber score — leverage defeats residual clipping.

title: Regression Quantiles
informal:
For a quantile level $\alpha \in (0,1)$, the check loss (or pinball loss) is the tilted absolute value $$\rho_\alpha(u) \;=\; \max\big(\alpha u,\; (\alpha-1)u\big) \;=\; \begin{cases}\alpha\, u, & u \ge 0,\\ -(1-\alpha)\,u, & u \lt 0,\end{cases}$$ and the regression $\alpha$-quantile of Koenker–Bassett is any global minimizer of the check-loss objective $$\hat\beta_\alpha \;\in\; \arg\min_{b} \sum_{i=1}^n \rho_\alpha\big(y_i - x_i^{\mathsf T} b\big).$$

The case $\alpha = 1/2$ is median (least-absolute-deviations) regression, since $\rho_{1/2}(u) = |u|/2$. The objective is convex — the check loss is a maximum of two linear functions — and the fit is regression-equivariant and scale-equivariant; at the location level the same loss is minimized by the sample $\alpha$-quantile.
summary: The check loss ρ_α(u) = max(αu, (α−1)u) and the Koenker–Bassett regression α-quantile — quantile regression as check-loss M-estimation, with α = 1/2 giving L1 regression.

hypotheses.note: ρ_α is the maximum of the two linear functions αu and (α−1)u — the tilted absolute value.

hypotheses.note: β̂ globally minimizes the check-loss regression objective.

Convexity of the objective, both equivariances, the identity with L1 regression at $\alpha = 1/2$, and the location-level characterizations — the sample $\alpha$-quantile minimizes the empirical check loss, and the population root condition is exactly that $\theta$ has cumulative probability $\alpha$ — are all proved in the same file.

title: The Sample Quantile Minimizes the Check Loss
informal:
Fix a quantile level $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and a nonempty sample $x_1,\dots,x_n$. Let $r = \lceil \alpha n\rceil$ and let $x_{(r)}$ be the $r$-th order statistic of the sample. Then $x_{(r)}$ minimizes the empirical check-loss objective: for every $t$, $$\sum_{i=1}^n \rho_\alpha\big(x_i - x_{(r)}\big) \;\le\; \sum_{i=1}^n \rho_\alpha(x_i - t).$$ The sample $\alpha$-quantile is the location fit of quantile regression, exactly as the median ($\alpha = 1/2$) minimizes total absolute deviation.

The proof is the subgradient counting argument: at the order statistic of rank $\lceil \alpha n \rceil$, at least $\alpha n$ observations lie at or below and at least $(1-\alpha)n$ at or above, which makes a suitable choice of per-observation subgradients of the convex check loss sum to the correct sign in both directions.
summary: The order statistic of rank ⌈αn⌉ globally minimizes t ↦ Σρ_α(xᵢ − t): the sample α-quantile is the check-loss location fit.

    -- MMY §4.8 / Problem 2.13

title: Affine Equivariance of Location and Scatter
informal:
A multivariate location functional $T$ and a scatter functional $S$ are affine equivariant when, for every nonsingular matrix $A$ and vector $b$, transforming the underlying distribution by $x \mapsto Ax + b$ transforms the values by $$T \mapsto A\,T + b, \qquad S \mapsto A\,S\,A^{\mathsf T}.$$ The theorem verifies the scatter half for the covariance-matrix functional: if the distribution has square-integrable coordinates, then the covariance matrix of the image of $P$ under $x \mapsto Ax + b$ equals $A\,\Sigma(P)\,A^{\mathsf T}$, where $\Sigma(P)$ is the covariance matrix of $P$; the companion result gives the mean vector the location law $\mu \mapsto A\mu + b$.

Affine equivariance is the multivariate analogue of location–scale equivariance and the entrance requirement for robust location–scatter estimation: the classical mean and covariance satisfy it but break down under contamination, which is what the robust M-, S-, and MM-estimators of scatter are built to repair.
summary: Under x ↦ Ax + b the mean vector transforms as Aμ + b and the covariance matrix as AΣAᵀ — the affine-equivariance interface of multivariate robust estimation, verified for the classical functionals.

hypotheses.label: square-integrable coordinates
hypotheses.note: Each coordinate of the distribution has a finite second moment, so the covariance matrix exists.

formalizationNotes: The transformation acts entrywise through push-forward integrals; the proof expands the transformed centered coordinates as linear combinations of the original ones and integrates term by term, with integrability of the products supplied by the coordinatewise square-integrability. The robust replacements themselves — M-estimators of scatter and their high-breakdown refinements — are future-round material; this file fixes the interface they must satisfy.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.
reference.biblio: Affine-equivariant robust estimation of multivariate location and scatter begins with R. A. Maronna (*Ann. Statist.* **4** (1976), 51–67); see also ch. 8 of P. J. Huber, *Robust Statistics*, Wiley, 1981, and P. L. Davies (*Ann. Statist.* **15** (1987), 1269–1292).

title: Scale M-Estimation Is Location M-Estimation in the Log Scale
informal:
A scale M-functional at level $\delta$ assigns to a distribution $P$ the solutions $\sigma \gt 0$ of $$\int \rho\Big(\frac{x}{\sigma}\Big)\, dP(x) \;=\; \delta,$$ for an even loss $\rho$ that is measurable. Suppose $P$ has no atom at the origin, the loss is integrable at scale $\sigma$, and $\sigma \gt 0$. Then $\sigma$ solves the scale equation if and only if $\log \sigma$ solves the location M-equation for the transported score $\psi(t) = \rho(e^t) - \delta$ under the push-forward of $P$ by $x \mapsto \log|x|$.

Robustness of scale is a two-sided affair — contamination can explode $\sigma$ to infinity with outliers or implode it to zero with inliers — and the reduction turns both into the ordinary location breakdown analysis in the log scale, where the whole location toolkit applies.
summary: σ solves ∫ρ(x/σ)dP = δ iff log σ is a location M-root of ψ(t) = ρ(eᵗ) − δ under the law of log|x| — the reduction that turns scale robustness into location theory.

title: The Breakdown Point of Scale M-Estimators
informal:
Let $\rho$ be an even loss, nondecreasing on $[0,\infty)$ with $\rho(0) = 0$ and $\rho(\infty) = 1$, and continuous; fix a target level $\delta \in (0,1)$ and let $P$ have no atom at the origin. If the contamination level satisfies $$\varepsilon \;\lt \; \varepsilon^\ast \;=\; \min(\delta,\, 1-\delta),$$ then there are $0 \lt \sigma_{\mathrm{lo}} \le \sigma_{\mathrm{hi}}$ such that every scale M-root of every $\varepsilon$-contamination of $P$ (by atomless-at-zero contaminants) lies in $[\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{hi}}]$ — no explosion to infinity and no implosion to zero. The threshold is sharp: beyond $\delta$, far-out point masses explode the scale; beyond $1 - \delta$, point masses at small positive values implode it.

At $\delta = 1/2$ the breakdown point is $1/2$, the scale analogue of the median's optimality.
summary: Scale M-roots of all ε-contaminations stay in a fixed interval [σ_lo, σ_hi] ⊂ (0,∞) when ε < min(δ, 1−δ), and the threshold is sharp — δ is the explosion breakdown point, 1−δ the implosion one.

The two sharpness statements are separate theorems: explosion reuses the location sharpness result through the transport, while implosion — the mirror direction the location theory does not carry — runs its own intermediate-value argument, with the contaminating inliers at a small positive value rather than at zero, where the root set would simply be empty.

title: The Standard Deviation Has Zero Breakdown
informal:
For a dispersion estimator the parameter space is $(0,\infty)$, so breakdown must guard both ends: a corrupted sample breaks the estimator if it can drive the value beyond every bound (explosion) or below every positive bound (implosion). For a sample of size at least two whose standard deviation is positive, the dispersion breakdown count of the sample standard deviation is $$m^\ast(\mathrm{SD}, x) \;=\; 0 :$$ one arbitrarily large replacement explodes it, since a single outlier at distance $d$ from the data contributes on the order of $d/\sqrt n$ to the SD.

The median absolute deviation, by contrast, resists $k-1$ of $n = 2k+1$ replacements — the classical trio of dispersion breakdown values is $0$ for the SD, $1/2$ for the MAD, and $1/4$ for the interquartile range.
summary: The sample standard deviation's dispersion breakdown count is 0: one huge replacement explodes it — the fragile pole of scale estimation.
leanSignature:
def DispersionResists (S : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ) (x : Fin n → ℝ) (m : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ lo hi : ℝ, 0 < lo ∧
    ∀ y : Fin n → ℝ, hammingDist x y ≤ m → S y ∈ Set.Icc lo hi

noncomputable def sampleSD (x : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  Real.sqrt (sampleMean fun i => (x i - sampleMean x) ^ 2)

theorem sampleSD_dispersionBreakdownCount (hn : 2 ≤ n) {x : Fin n → ℝ}
    (hx : 0 < sampleSD x) : dispersionBreakdownCount sampleSD x = 0

hypotheses.note: With one observation the SD is identically zero and the question is vacuous.

hypotheses.label: positive dispersion
hypotheses.note: The uncorrupted SD is off the boundary, so zero replacements are resisted.

The SD is normalized with $1/n$ rather than the book's $1/(n-1)$; breakdown values are unaffected. The exploding replacement is exhibited by solving for the outlier that pins one residual at any target size.

title: The MAD Withstands Half the Sample
informal:
Let the sample size be odd, $n = 2k+1$ with $k \ge 1$, and let the sample have pairwise distinct values. The dispersion breakdown count of the median absolute deviation $$\mathrm{MAD}(x) \;=\; \operatorname{med}_i \big|x_i - \operatorname{med}(x)\big|$$ is exactly $$m^\ast(\mathrm{MAD}, x) \;=\; k - 1.$$ With at most $k-1$ replacements, at most $k$ of the $n$ values can crowd within half the minimal gap of the corrupted median, so the MAD stays above a fixed positive bound (and below a fixed one). With $k$ replacements the MAD implodes: duplicating $k$ coordinates at one remaining data point creates $k+1$ equal values, the corrupted median lands on them, and a majority of the absolute deviations vanish.

Hence $\varepsilon_n^\ast(\mathrm{MAD}) = (k-1)/(2k+1) \to 1/2$. The MAD pays one replacement more than the median's location count $k$ because implosion — impossible for a location estimator — binds first.
summary: For n = 2k+1 distinct points the MAD's dispersion breakdown count is exactly k−1: it resists k−1 replacements two-sidedly and implodes to zero under k duplicates — ε*ₙ → 1/2.

    dispersionBreakdownCount sampleMAD x = k - 1

hypotheses.note: n = 2k+1 with k ≥ 1, so both medians involved are unique middle order statistics.

hypotheses.label: distinct values

formalizationNotes: The distinctness hypothesis is genuine: a sample already carrying duplicates starts closer to implosion, and the exact count depends on its tie structure. The resisting bound is uniform — half the minimal gap of the original sample below, an order-statistic window above — and the imploding corruption is explicit. The asymptotic value $1/2$ matches the population statement that the MAD is the scale M-functional of the indicator loss at level one-half, a loss whose discontinuity keeps it outside the continuous-loss population theorems; the finite-sample route used here needs no continuity at all.

title: The Maximum-Bias Curve of M-Estimators
informal:
Between the influence function (infinitesimal contamination) and the breakdown point (catastrophic contamination) sits the maximum-bias curve: the worst value an estimator takes over the whole $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood. Let $\psi$ be nondecreasing, odd, and bounded by $k$ with $k \gt 0$; let $P$ be symmetric about zero with strictly increasing shift score $g(b) = \int \psi(x+b)\,dP$; fix a contamination level $0 \le \varepsilon \lt 1/2$ and let $b_\varepsilon$ solve $$g(b_\varepsilon) \;=\; \frac{k\,\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}.$$ Then every root $\theta$ of every $\varepsilon$-contaminated M-equation satisfies $$|\theta| \;\le\; b_\varepsilon,$$ and the bound is attained in the limit by point-mass contamination pushed to infinity.

For the median — $\psi = \operatorname{sign}$, $k = 1$ — the equation solves to the quantile formula $b_\varepsilon = F^{-1}\big(\tfrac{1}{2(1-\varepsilon)}\big)$, the reference curve of maximum-bias theory.
summary: Every root of every ε-contaminated M-equation lies in [−b_ε, b_ε], where g(b_ε) = kε/(1−ε) — the exact maximum-bias curve, attained by point mass at infinity.

title: The Minimax-Bias Property of the Median
informal:
Let the center distribution have a density $f_0$ that is a probability density, symmetric and unimodal — nonincreasing in $|x|$; fix a contamination level $0 \lt \varepsilon \lt 1/2$ and let $b_\varepsilon \ge 0$ solve the median's quantile equation $F_0(b_\varepsilon) = \tfrac{1}{2(1-\varepsilon)}$ — the median's own maximum bias. Then for every functional $T$ that is location equivariant on a domain containing the witness distribution: some member $F$ of the $\varepsilon$-gross-error neighbourhood of $F_0$ has $$|T(F)| \;\ge\; b_\varepsilon.$$ No location-equivariant functional has a smaller maximum bias than the median over symmetric unimodal centers.

The witness pair is explicit: $F_+$ keeps the density $(1-\varepsilon)f_0$ up to $b_\varepsilon$ and pastes the shifted density $(1-\varepsilon)f_0(\cdot - 2b_\varepsilon)$ beyond it; $F_-$ is $F_+$ shifted left by $2b_\varepsilon$. Both are $\varepsilon$-contaminations of $F_0$ — nonnegativity of the contaminating density is exactly unimodality, its total mass exactly the quantile equation — and equivariance forces $T(F_+) - T(F_-) = 2b_\varepsilon$, so the two values cannot both be smaller than $b_\varepsilon$.
summary: Huber's theorem: over a symmetric unimodal center, every location-equivariant functional suffers maximum bias at least b_ε — the median's own value F₀⁻¹(1/(2(1−ε))). The median is minimax-bias optimal.

title: The Chebyshev Baseline for the Empirical Mean
informal:
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent, identically distributed, measurable observations whose common law is square-integrable with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2 \gt 0$ (nondegenerate). For every confidence level $\delta \in (0,1)$ and nonempty sample, the empirical mean $\bar X_n$ satisfies $$\mathbb P\left(\big|\bar X_n - \mu\big| \;\ge\; \sigma\sqrt{\frac{1}{n\delta}}\right) \;\le\; \delta.$$

Under a bare second moment this $1/\sqrt{\delta}$ dependence on the confidence level is essentially the best the empirical mean can do — exponentially worse than the $\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}$ a Gaussian sample would give. The estimators of the heavy-tailed family — median-of-means, Catoni's estimator, the trimmed mean — exist precisely to replace $1/\sqrt\delta$ by $\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}$ without strengthening the moment assumption.
summary: P(|X̄ₙ − μ| ≥ σ√(1/(nδ))) ≤ δ under two moments — the baseline whose 1/√δ confidence dependence the sub-Gaussian estimators are built to beat.

title: The Median-of-Means Estimator
informal:
Partition a sample of $n = km$ observations into $k$ blocks of $m$ observations each, average within blocks, and take the median of the block means: $$\hat\mu_{\mathrm{MoM}} \;=\; \operatorname{med}\big(Z_1, \dots, Z_k\big), \qquad Z_j = \frac1m \sum_{i \in B_j} X_i.$$

Each block mean is an unbiased estimate of $\mu$ with standard deviation $\sigma\sqrt{k/n}$; the median of $k$ independent such estimates concentrates exponentially in $k$. Choosing the number of blocks by the target confidence level turns a bare-variance sample into a sub-Gaussian mean estimate — the simplest of the heavy-tailed estimators and the workhorse of the modern theory.
summary: Median-of-means: split the data into k blocks, average each block, take the median of the k block means — the block structure trades variance for exponential concentration.

title: Median-of-Means Is Sub-Gaussian
informal:
Let the $n = km$ observations be jointly independent, identically distributed with a square-integrable law of mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, nondegenerate, arranged into $k$ nonempty blocks of $m$ observations with measurable coordinates. The median-of-means estimator with $k$ blocks satisfies $$\mathbb P\left(\big|\hat\mu_{\mathrm{MoM}} - \mu\big| \;\gt \; \sigma\sqrt{\frac 4m}\right) \;\le\; e^{-k/8}.$$ Choosing $k = \lceil 8\log(1/\delta)\rceil$ blocks gives, with probability at least $1-\delta$, $$\big|\hat\mu_{\mathrm{MoM}} - \mu\big| \;\le\; \sigma\sqrt{\frac{32\log(1/\delta) + 4}{n}}.$$

A sub-Gaussian deviation bound from nothing but a finite variance: the block means land within $\sigma\sqrt{4/m}$ of $\mu$ with probability $3/4$ each (Chebyshev), and the median misses only if half the blocks do — a binomial tail event that Hoeffding's inequality makes exponentially small in $k$.
summary: P(|μ̂_MoM − μ| > σ√(4/m)) ≤ e^{−k/8} under bare finite variance; with k = ⌈8log(1/δ)⌉ blocks, |μ̂ − μ| ≤ σ√((32log(1/δ)+4)/n) with probability 1−δ.

title: Catoni's Estimator Achieves the Optimal Constant
informal:
Catoni's estimator replaces the empirical-mean equation $\sum_i (X_i - y) = 0$ by the softly truncated equation $\sum_i \psi\big(\alpha(X_i - y)\big) = 0$, with the influence function $\psi(x) = \log(1 + x + x^2/2)$ for $x \ge 0$, $\psi(x) = -\log(1 - x + x^2/2)$ for $x \lt 0$, and a tuning parameter $\alpha$. Let the observations be independent, identically distributed, measurable, with square-integrable law of mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2 \gt 0$ (nondegenerate); fix $\delta \in (0,1)$ with $n \gt 2\log(1/\delta)$ and the tuned parameter $$\alpha \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{2\log(1/\delta)}{n\sigma^2\big(1 + \tfrac{2\log(1/\delta)}{n - 2\log(1/\delta)}\big)}}.$$ Then every sequence $\hat y_n$ of roots of the estimating equation (measurably selected) satisfies, with probability at least $1 - 2\delta$, $$\big|\hat y_n - \mu\big| \;\lt \; \sqrt{\frac{2\sigma^2\log(1/\delta)}{n - 2\log(1/\delta)}}.$$

The leading constant $\sqrt 2$ matches the Gaussian-sample benchmark exactly — sub-Gaussian estimation from two moments with the best possible constant. The root exists and is unique: the estimating function is continuous and strictly decreasing from $+\infty$ to $-\infty$.
summary: Catoni's soft-truncation M-estimator satisfies |μ̂ − μ| < √(2σ²log(1/δ)/(n − 2log(1/δ))) with probability 1−2δ — the sub-Gaussian rate with the optimal constant √2, from two moments.

title: The Trimmed Mean Is Sub-Gaussian
informal:
Split $2n$ observations into two halves. The second half sets the truncation levels — its order statistics at ranks $\varepsilon n$ and $(1-\varepsilon)n$, for a trimming fraction $\varepsilon$ tied to the confidence level — and the estimator averages the first half after clamping each observation into $[\alpha, \beta]$: $$\hat\mu_{2n} \;=\; \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \phi_{\alpha,\beta}(X_i), \qquad \phi_{\alpha,\beta}(x) = \max\big(\alpha, \min(\beta, x)\big).$$ Let the $2n$ observations be jointly independent, identically distributed, measurable, with square-integrable, atomless law of mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2 \gt 0$ (nondegenerate); fix $\delta \in (0,1)$ with $n \gt \tfrac{16}{3}\log(8/\delta)$, take the trim count $r = \tfrac{16}{3}\log(8/\delta)$ (an integer, with $1 \le r$ and $4r \lt n$) and the corresponding order-statistic ranks. Then with probability at least $1 - \delta$, $$\big|\hat\mu_{2n} - \mu\big| \;\le\; 9\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log(8/\delta)}{n}}.$$

Trimming at data-driven quantiles is what makes this work — fixed truncation levels cannot adapt to the confidence level. Among the sub-Gaussian estimators the trimmed mean is the classical one, and the one that extends to adversarially contaminated data.
summary: The two-sample trimmed mean, clipping at order statistics of a held-out half with trim depth ∝ log(1/δ), satisfies |μ̂ − μ| ≤ 9σ√(log(8/δ)/n) with probability 1−δ under two moments.

title: No Estimator Beats the Sub-Gaussian Rate
informal:
For sample size $n \gt 5$, confidence level $\delta \in (2e^{-n/4}, 1/2)$, target variance $\sigma^2 \gt 0$, and any measurable mean estimator $\hat\mu : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R$, there is a probability distribution $P$ with variance $\sigma^2$ whose mean $\mu_P$ the estimator misses badly: $$\mathbb P^{\otimes n}\!\left(\big|\hat\mu(X_1,\dots,X_n) - \mu_P\big| \;\gt \; \sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log\frac{1}{2\delta}}{n}}\right) \;\ge\; \delta.$$

The sub-Gaussian deviation rate $\sigma\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n}$ is thus optimal up to constants: median-of-means, Catoni's estimator, and the trimmed mean achieve what no estimator can improve. The witness family is a pair of two-point distributions placing mass $p$ at $\pm c$ and $1-p$ at $0$, coupled so that the two samples coincide with probability $(1-p)^n = 2\delta$ — and on that event no estimator can be simultaneously close to both means.
summary: For any mean estimator there is a two-moment law on which |μ̂ − μ| > σ√(log(1/(2δ))/n) with probability ≥ δ — the minimax lower bound matching the sub-Gaussian estimators.

title: Dimension-Free Multivariate Median-of-Means
informal:
Extend median-of-means to random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$: block the sample, average within blocks to get $Z_1,\dots,Z_k$, and define the estimate $\hat\mu$ as a point whose majority ball — the smallest ball around it containing more than half of the block means — has minimal radius among all candidate centers. Let the $n = km$ observations be jointly independent, identically distributed, measurable random vectors with square-integrable law of mean $\mu$ and covariance trace $\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma) = \mathbb E\|X - \mu\|^2 \gt 0$ (nondegenerate), arranged in $k$ blocks of $m$ observations with $k = \lceil 8 \log(1/\delta)\rceil$ for a confidence level $\delta \in (0,1)$. Then any measurable selection of ball-MoM centers satisfies, with probability at least $1-\delta$, $$\big\|\hat\mu - \mu\big\| \;\le\; 4\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma)\big(8\log(1/\delta) + 1\big)}{n}}.$$

The bound involves the dimension only through $\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma)$ — no $\log d$ factor, unlike the coordinate-wise median. Chebyshev in norm puts each block mean within $r = 2\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma)/m}$ of $\mu$ with probability $3/4$; on the majority event both $\mu$ and $\hat\mu$ own majority balls of radius at most $r$, two majorities must share a block mean, and the triangle inequality gives $\|\hat\mu - \mu\| \le 2r$.
summary: The minimal-radius majority-ball median-of-means satisfies ‖μ̂ − μ‖ ≤ 4√(Tr(Σ)(8log(1/δ)+1)/n) with probability 1−δ — dimension-free multivariate mean estimation from second moments.

def IsBallMoMCenter {k : ℕ} (Z : Fin k → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d))

title: The Breakdown Point of the Trimmed Mean
informal:
The $m$-fold trimmed mean discards the $m$ smallest and $m$ largest order statistics and averages the rest: $$\bar x_{(m)} \;=\; \frac{1}{n - 2m} \sum_{i = m+1}^{n-m} x_{(i)}.$$ For a trim depth with $2m \lt n$, its breakdown count is exactly $$m^\ast\big(\bar x_{(m)}, x\big) \;=\; m :$$ up to $m$ arbitrary replacements land among the discarded order statistics (or displace retained ones only within the range of the surviving data), while $m+1$ replacements can plant a value that survives the trimming and drags the average beyond any bound.

The trim depth is thus exactly the contamination budget: $\varepsilon_n^\ast = m/n$, interpolating between the mean ($m = 0$, breakdown $0$) and the median (maximal trimming, breakdown $\to 1/2$).
summary: The m-fold trimmed mean's breakdown count is exactly m: the trim depth is the contamination budget, interpolating between mean (m = 0) and median.

  (∑ i ∈ univ.filter (fun i : Fin n => m ≤ (i : ℕ) ∧ (i : ℕ) < n - m), orderStat x i) /
    (n - 2 * m : ℝ)

theorem trimmedMean_breakdownCount {m : ℕ} (hm : 2 * m < n) (x : Fin n → ℝ) :
    breakdownCount (trimmedMean m) x = m

hypotheses.label: proper trimming
hypotheses.note: The trim depth leaves at least one retained observation: 2m < n.

formalizationNotes: Resistance is proved through the order-statistic perturbation bounds: after at most $m$ replacements, every retained order statistic of the corrupted sample is bracketed by order statistics of the original sample, so the trimmed average stays in the original range. The breaking corruption places $m+1$ copies of a huge common value, of which at least one survives the upper trimming. The classical asymptotic statement $\varepsilon^\ast \approx \alpha$ for $\alpha$-fraction trimming is the $m = \lceil \alpha n \rceil$ reading of this count.

reference.formal: R. A. Maronna, R. D. Martin, V. J. Yohai, and M. Salibián-Barrera, *Robust Statistics: Theory and Methods (with R)*, 2nd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, 2019.

title: The Median Absolute Deviation
informal:
The median absolute deviation of a sample centers at the median and takes the median of the absolute residuals: $$\mathrm{MAD}(x) \;=\; \operatorname{med}_i \big|x_i - \operatorname{med}(x)\big|.$$ For an odd sample size $n = 2k+1$ it satisfies the two defining conditions of a dispersion estimator: shift invariance and absolute-scale equivariance, $$\mathrm{MAD}(x + a\mathbf 1) = \mathrm{MAD}(x), \qquad \mathrm{MAD}(c\,x) = |c|\,\mathrm{MAD}(x).$$

The MAD is the robust counterpart of the standard deviation — the same double-median structure that gives the location median its maximal breakdown gives the MAD a breakdown point tending to one half, against zero for the standard deviation. In practice it is normalized by $1/\Phi^{-1}(3/4) \approx 1.483$ to be consistent for the standard deviation at the normal model.
summary: MAD(x) = medᵢ|xᵢ − med(x)| is shift invariant and |c|-scale equivariant — the dispersion axioms, making the double median the robust counterpart of the SD.
